entry.title: Delray Beach Veterans Day ceremony honors service with message of unity and appreciation
entry.summary: The message at the Veterans Day ceremony held in Delray Beach was that unity and appreciation are the best way to honor the brave men and women who have fought for freedom. Dozens gathered Wednesday inside the vintage gym at Old School Square in the heart of Delray Beach to commemorate those who have served the country. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Delray Beach honors veterans with message of unity The ceremony featured several speakers who talked about the sacrifices men and women in uniform go through, along with a performance from the Plumosa School of the Arts choir. The choir took the stage with two special songs honoring veterans' bravery. WPTV's Delray Beach reporter Victor Jorges connected with James Bassa, a former Marine, whose message focused on how we can all come together, put differences aside and show appreciation to those who served. 'Anyone who wakes up in the morning and says, 'I'm gonna join a force that fights for freedom, for people I don't even know, people I may never meet.' I think they realize there has to be something different about those people. That motivates me to do more and help people understand more what veterans really are,' Bassa said. We also asked him what we can do every day to honor those who fought for the country. 'Show understanding, feel mutual admiration; no matter what our conflicts are, disagreements, we have the ability to always show love,' Bassa said. entry.title: Atlantic Community High School students in Delray Beach train to become certified 911 dispatchers
entry.summary: A special program at Atlantic Community High School in Delray Beach gives students a look at what it's like to be a 911 dispatcher and a chance to graduate ready to step straight into the career. Students are learning to stay calm, ask the right questions and gather critical details for first responders. On one recent simulation, the voices sounded like a real emergency, but it was all practice. Victoria Simpson, a senior, is one of the students training to field those calls. 'It can be any extra thing, so clothing, weapons, any extra info that you can get that can help the officers or anyone that's arriving on scene,' Simpson said. Her classmate Liliana Munoz, also a senior, works the other side of the line, coming up with emergencies to put those skills to the test. 'We definitely do really hard calls with each other,' Munoz said. Simpson and Munoz are two of 28 students currently training to become certified 911 dispatchers. Michael Byrd, the school's criminal justice teacher, said the course mirrors professional training. 'It gives some real-world experience with us using the simulators. It also teaches them teamwork, communication, and gets them ready for the career field,' Byrd said. 'This is the same course an adult would take to become a 911 dispatcher.' Students will test for their certification at the end of the school year. If they pass, they become career-ready and could begin working as a dispatcher immediately.

entry.title: Martin County to begin phased restoration of MARTY transit service
entry.summary: Martin County will begin restoring public transportation services this week after securing a one-year emergency contract with MTM Transit, LLC. The announcement comes after the county's contracted transit provider walked away from its agreement last month, halting all MARTY bus service and laying off 29 employees with no warning to riders or county leaders. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Martin County begins restoring MARTY transit service The county said Tuesday that it will take a phased approach to restoring MARTY service after what officials described as an abrupt disruption caused by a contract breach involving the previous vendor. ADA paratransit service will be the first to return, with operations expected to resume Thursday. The service is available to eligible riders with disabilities who are unable to use regular fixed-route buses. MARTY customer service representatives are contacting active registered paratransit riders directly about the resumption of service. Riders can call 772-463-2822 for information about scheduling and reservations. As buses are prepared and drivers become available, the county said it will begin restoring fixed-route service, starting with the heavily traveled U.S. 1 corridor. The Indiantown route will also be among the priorities as service returns. 'Our priority is to restore public transportation as quickly and responsibly as possible, with particular attention to residents who depend on these services to access essential needs, as well as fiscal responsibility to the taxpayer,' Martin County Transit Administrator Ash Beecher said. Beecher acknowledged the disruption has affected riders and the broader community and said the county is working to reestablish service in a coordinated manner. During the interruption, United Way of Martin County helped coordinate transportation for people with critical travel needs. The county said additional routes will return as buses and drivers become available. Start dates, schedules and rider instructions will be announced as each phase is finalized. Residents can find updates through Martin County's transit website or call transit customer service at 772-463-2860 from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Monday through Friday.

entry.title: More workers say extra work is a must to cover holiday costs this year
entry.summary: As the holidays approach, many workers say it's adding pressure to budgets that are already stretched thin. Between gifts, travel and hosting, a new survey reveals how some are planning to cover the cost. New research from resume.io found 56% of workers have considered changing jobs or seeking a higher salary because of the cost of living or holiday expenses, while more than 53.6% have taken on or plan to take on extra work to cover holiday costs. WATCH: Workers look to additional employment hours to cover holiday expenses More workers say extra work is a must to cover holiday costs this year The study reveals at least one in four workers plan to borrow money to get through the holidays by either using credit cards or Buy Now Pay Later methods. Some also plan to lean on family and friends for financial support. While gifts are often seen as the biggest holiday expense, everyday costs are the top reason workers are taking on extra work. Nearly 23% say covering food and household expenses is their main reason, ahead of paying for Christmas gifts or existing debts or bills.

entry.title: Lighthouse for the Blind teaches skills that help people navigate independently in West Palm Beach
entry.summary: Learning to navigate without relying on sight requires skills many people may never have considered, from using a white cane to technology that reads or magnifies what's on a computer screen. At Lighthouse for the Blind of the Palm Beaches, Treasure Coast Okeechobee in West Palm Beach, those tools are helping people who are blind or visually impaired build greater independence. The organization serves people ranging from babies to seniors across five counties, executive director Lisa Stella told WPTV. For children, that can include activities designed to be sensory-oriented and inclusive in the community. Learning to navigate with a white cane One of the skills taught at the Lighthouse is how to use a white cane to navigate an environment. During WPTV's visit, Shining A Light reporter T.A. Walker put on a blindfold and attempted a mobility exercise with Elizabeth Prus, Lighthouse for the Blind's youth services director. Prus instructed Walker to sweep the cane back and forth roughly the width of his shoulders as he walked. The cane provided information about objects in his path, including a chair and a kitchen island. 'This is a tool that people who are visually impaired use to navigate environments,' Prus said. The training can begin at a young age. 'We start with little kids, teaching them how to use a cane so that way they can travel independently,' Prus said. For Walker, temporarily navigating without sight offered a firsthand look at how a white cane can provide information about the environment around him. Technology provides another tool for independence The Lighthouse also helps clients use technology designed to make computers more accessible to people who are blind or have low vision. entry.title: School bus crashes into Okeechobee County home after collision; no injuries reported
entry.summary: A school bus veered into a home Wednesday morning after crashing with another vehicle, the Okeechobee County School District said. District officials said preliminary information indicates the driver of the other vehicle failed to stop at a stop sign, causing the collision. The impact sent the school bus into a nearby residence. No students were on the bus at the time of the crash. Officials said no one was injured, including the bus driver, the occupants of the other vehicle and the people inside the home. Officials did not immediately provide additional details about the crash, including its location and whether any citations were issued.

entry.title: 77 homes hit by Martin County flooding. Where to get help now - WPEC
entry.summary: 77 homes hit by Martin County flooding. Where to get help now    WPEC
entry.article_text: A day after Jensen Beach residents told Martin County commissioners that flooding forced them from their homes, families can go to Hoke Library for recovery help while they wait for word on federal aid. The flood recovery center is open Wednesday even though regular library services are closed for Veterans Day. State agencies and local nonprofits are there to connect residents with recovery resources, and the county says more agencies and services will be added throughout the week. At Tuesday’s commission meeting, residents pressed county leaders about drainage and how they were warned. Martin County Emergency Management Director Sally Waite told commissioners the flooding affected 77 homes and that assessment teams planned to visit each one to document the damage. Where to get help The Multi-Agency Resource Center is at Hoke Library, 1150 NW Jack Williams Way in Jensen Beach . The county lists those hours for Wednesday through Saturday until further notice. The center is closed Sundays. Martin County is also accepting applications for state disaster housing assistance. Households must meet income requirements. Residents can call 772-320-3169 for details. They can also report flood damage and fill out a needs survey on the county’s flood recovery page. Read more: 'We're not getting any answers': Hamilton Bay residents frustrated as flooding continues Where FEMA aid stands Florida announced Monday that it had requested a presidential major disaster declaration for the flooding. As of Wednesday morning, federal approval had yet to be announced. The state’s announcement did not specify whether the request included FEMA Individual Assistance for Martin County. If that aid is authorized for Martin County, eligible households could apply for help with expenses such as temporary housing and essential home repairs.

entry.title: St. Lucie County rejects plan that could bring nearly 500 homes to low-lying site - WPEC
entry.summary: St. Lucie County rejects plan that could bring nearly 500 homes to low-lying site    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie County commissioners voted 3-2 to reject a land-use change for a roughly 34-acre property near South 25th Street and West Midway Road that could allow nearly 500 homes. The vote came as residents sought answers about recent flooding and commissioners questioned how the property handles drainage. An engineer said the property receives drainage from about 134 acres and uses a 24-inch pipe to direct water to nearby canals. Another pipe might be needed. The property sits lower than surrounding roads and would need to be raised for development, prompting concerns that construction could push water onto nearby properties. If designated for residential use, the site could allow up to 15 homes per acre, according to the discussion. County staff recommended approving the land-use change with adjustments to avoid or reduce impacts to wetlands and required buffers. Commissioners denied the request. See also: 77 homes hit by Martin County flooding. Where to get help now At the same meeting, residents from Creekside and White City asked commissioners to investigate last week’s flooding, identify who is responsible for local drainage systems, and explain how to prevent future flooding. I love my community, but it’s not fair that we’re suffering because nobody has taken the initiative to do what’s right for us, one resident said. Creekside residents called for an engineering review of the neighborhood and surrounding watershed, a reassessment of flood risk and a mitigation plan with deadlines. They also asked for a public meeting with county engineers and stormwater officials. White City residents described recurring flooding and called for drainage improvements and more stormwater storage. One resident said her home and yard had flooded four times since 2012. The county also made its emergency declaration official after days of heavy rain and flooding. It covers hazards including flooded roads and strained drainage systems.

entry.title: MARTY bus service begins phased return in Martin County after monthlong shutdown
entry.summary: MARTY public transportation is beginning a phased return in Martin County after more than a month without regular bus service, starting with ADA paratransit before service expands to the U.S. Highway 1 and Indiantown routes, according to the county. WATCH: MARTY bus service begins returning in Martin County MARTY Bus Service in Martin County: Phased Return Begins The restoration will not happen all at once. Martin County said additional service will be added as buses are prepared and drivers become available. The county has not announced a date for full MARTY service to return. For riders who rely on public transportation to get to work, buy groceries or reach medical appointments, the phased restart offers some relief after weeks of limited transportation options. MARTY shutdown left riders without regular transportation MARTY riders were left scrambling Oct. 8 when the county's transit provider abruptly stopped service. One rider, Joe, told WPTV at the time that he received no warning. 'No warning at all. Nothing. Zero,' Joe said. For him, losing bus service was more than an inconvenience. He told WPTV that injuries limited his mobility and made finding another way to get around difficult. 'I've had two broken necks, three broken backs. I can't feel my feet, so I'm not getting anywhere,' he said. United Way steps in with more than 750 rides As the shutdown continued, United Way of Martin County stepped in to help residents who had lost their usual transportation. Carol Houwaart-Diez with United Way of Martin County said the organization contacted the county and offered assistance through Ride United, a program that helps provide transportation for critical needs. Sager was complimentary of the customer service he received. 'It's a person who answers the phone, and they answer it within five minutes, and they want to help you. They want you to get the money. He advises homeowners to go carefully over all the steps, hire a licensed contractor, take notes when talking with the program representatives and be patient. It's expected to relaunch on Dec. 4. In an email to homeowners, all current applications in the system are secure while the website improvements are taking place.

entry.article_text: Lucie County commissioners voted 3-2 to reject a land-use change for a roughly 34-acre property near South 25th Street and West Midway Road that could allow nearly 500 homes. The vote came as residents sought answers about recent flooding and commissioners questioned how the property handles drainage. An engineer said the property receives drainage from about 134 acres and uses a 24-inch pipe to direct water to nearby canals. Another pipe might be needed. The property sits lower than surrounding roads and would need to be raised for development, prompting concerns that construction could push water onto nearby properties. If designated for residential use, the site could allow up to 15 homes per acre, according to the discussion. County staff recommended approving the land-use change with adjustments to avoid or reduce impacts to wetlands and required buffers. Commissioners denied the request. See also: 77 homes hit by Martin County flooding. Where to get help now At the same meeting, residents from Creekside and White City asked commissioners to investigate last week’s flooding, identify who is responsible for local drainage systems, and explain how to prevent future flooding. I love my community, but it’s not fair that we’re suffering because nobody has taken the initiative to do what’s right for us, one resident said. Creekside residents called for an engineering review of the neighborhood and surrounding watershed, a reassessment of flood risk and a mitigation plan with deadlines. They also asked for a public meeting with county engineers and stormwater officials. White City residents described recurring flooding and called for drainage improvements and more stormwater storage. One resident said her home and yard had flooded four times since 2012. The county also made its emergency declaration official after days of heavy rain and flooding. It covers hazards including flooded roads and strained drainage systems.

"So we actually tackle the parents as well."He describes that work as an effort to rebuild a support network around those families."Our kids definitely need it. Families need it as a whole. We're trying to recreate, no, not recreate, reestablish the village," Bates said. "They all, everybody says it takes a village. We want to reestablish and put a stronghold on that village."That village now includes volunteers like Christopher Hepburn, CEO and co-founder of a West Palm Beach branding and marketing agency.Hepburn said he has only been volunteering with the nonprofit for a few months, but its focus on bringing families together connected with his own childhood."Wow, it's really the families," Hepburn said. So yeah, it means everything."Hepburn has volunteered at events including a father-son grill challenge. Seeing fathers and sons spending time together was especially meaningful to him."Oh man, it was amazing," Hepburn said. So it's just been amazing, with just the love they've given our organization and seeing what we're doing in the community and willing to help," said Bates.The nonprofit is currently seeking volunteers and accepts donations to support its work in the community."We're looking for donations. entry.title: Democrat Scott Colom projected to flip Mississippi Senate seat in major upset
entry.summary: Democrat Scott Colom is projected to defeat Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi's U.S. Senate race, according to the Associated Press, pulling off a major upset in a state that has long favored Republicans. Colom's victory makes him the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from Mississippi since 1982. The state has not had a Democratic senator since John Stennis left office in 1989. WATCH: A new generation on Capitol Hill could challenge Chuck Schumer's Senate leadership New generation on Capitol Hill could challenge Schumer's leadership The race was not initially considered competitive, but polling tightened in the closing weeks of the campaign as voters expressed growing frustration with the economy. Hyde-Smith faced criticism after suggesting during an interview that consumers could choose other sources of protein when asked about rising beef prices. Colom seized on the remark, launching a campaign ad featuring voters who said they would rather choose another senator than another protein. The race also drew attention from national political figures. President Donald Trump visited Mississippi a week before Election Day to rally support for Hyde-Smith, while former Vice President Kamala Harris campaigned for Colom in the closing weeks of the race. Colom's victory delivers Democrats an unexpected pickup in the U.S. Senate.

entry.title: Delray Beach mayor looks to private sponsors to save 2027 St. Patrick’s Day Parade
entry.summary: Delray Beach Mayor Tom Carney says he's exploring a private-sector solution to keep the city's 2027 St. Patrick's Day Parade alive after a new Florida law prompted the city to announce it would cancel the event. WATCH WPTV'S COVERAGE BELOW: Delray Beach mayor looks to private sponsors to save St. Patrick's Day Parade The city's annual Pride Festival is also affected by the decision, which Carney says stems from Senate Bill 1134. The legislation restricts local governments from funding, promoting or taking official actions related to certain diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) activities. Carney said the potential impact on the two events has been top of mind since the bill passed. 'We learned very quickly that, within the scope of the definition of DEI, it could (impact both) the St. Patrick's Day parade and the Pride festival,' Carney said. After the city announced the cancellation, Carney said residents quickly voiced their concerns. 'I would say by Saturday I had a good 50 emails in my box saying, 'What are you doing?'' he said. Now, the mayor is looking at another option: allowing private organizers and sponsors to take the lead. Carney said the St. Patrick's Day parade used to be a private event and his family also participated in underwriting it in the past. He said he's already reached out to potential supporters, and others have contacted him offering to help fund the parade. 'I decided, well, let's just make it a private event again, so I reached out to a half dozen people. More than that reached out to me saying, 'We'll help underwrite the parade,' and we've already got people submitting applications to try and do the parade for us,' Carney said. The mayor said a similar arrangement could be considered for the Pride Festival. 'If the private sector wants to support that, I would as well,' Carney said. 'You don't want to cancel things people have grown accustomed to.' Residents said losing either event would have an impact beyond the festivities themselves, including on the local business community and residents who look forward to celebrating their traditions. Carney says discussions are still in the early stages, but he's confident the St. Patrick's Day Parade will go on as scheduled in 2027. The city has not yet announced a finalized plan for either event. Senate Bill 1143 takes effect Jan. 1, 2027.

Trump is constitutionally barred from running again, which means, as the lame duck portion of his presidency comes into view, its not too early to start thinking about who might replace him. Potential candidates certainly are. While they might bat away speculation, many are starting to think seriously about their potential path or wrestling with the ultimate question is it worth the investment of time and energy and the guarantee of being vilified by your political rivals in the off chance that you could be the most powerful person in the world? entry.summary: Veterans of all eras and residents of all ages packed Veterans Memorial Park in Port St. Lucie on Wednesday for the annual Veterans Day ceremony. WPTV anchor and Navy veteran Mike Trim connected with fellow veterans about the significance of the day. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Veterans honored at Port St. Lucie event Vietnam veteran Michael Greene wore a newly decorated vest commemorating his Army service 'It's all like my whole history. I started in transportation. I think it's very important. I enlisted and was not supposed to go but ended up over there,' Greene told Trim. Wayne Thomas, another Vietnam War veteran in attendance, told Trim he felt this day now properly honors their service, which was not previously recognized. 'It's good to get the recognition that we didn't get,' Thomas said. The Port St. Lucie High School Junior ROTC attended the ceremony in full force while crowds of all ages looked on. That included a member of the greatest generation: 98-year-old World War II veteran Robert Vogel. 'I'm one of the few left. I just thank God. I would really encourage anyone to come to these events because they're really important to support the veterans,' Vogel told Trim. Those veterans heard keynote speaker, Retired Air Force Master Sgt. Vincent Lavelle Jr. A special touch from the Port St. Lucie community band featured songs from each branch of service. That prompted service members in attendance to stand for their respective branch song. There was also a special flyover by the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office helicopter.

entry.title: St. Lucie County rejects plan that could bring nearly 500 homes to low-lying site - WPEC
entry.summary: St. Lucie County rejects plan that could bring nearly 500 homes to low-lying site    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie County commissioners voted 3-2 to reject a land-use change for a roughly 34-acre property near South 25th Street and West Midway Road that could allow nearly 500 homes. The vote came as residents sought answers about recent flooding and commissioners questioned how the property handles drainage. An engineer said the property receives drainage from about 134 acres and uses a 24-inch pipe to direct water to nearby canals. Another pipe might be needed. The property sits lower than surrounding roads and would need to be raised for development, prompting concerns that construction could push water onto nearby properties. If designated for residential use, the site could allow up to 15 homes per acre, according to the discussion. County staff recommended approving the land-use change with adjustments to avoid or reduce impacts to wetlands and required buffers. Commissioners denied the request. See also: 77 homes hit by Martin County flooding. Where to get help now At the same meeting, residents from Creekside and White City asked commissioners to investigate last week’s flooding, identify who is responsible for local drainage systems, and explain how to prevent future flooding. I love my community, but it’s not fair that we’re suffering because nobody has taken the initiative to do what’s right for us, one resident said. Creekside residents called for an engineering review of the neighborhood and surrounding watershed, a reassessment of flood risk and a mitigation plan with deadlines. They also asked for a public meeting with county engineers and stormwater officials. White City residents described recurring flooding and called for drainage improvements and more stormwater storage. One resident said her home and yard had flooded four times since 2012. The county also made its emergency declaration official after days of heavy rain and flooding. It covers hazards including flooded roads and strained drainage systems.

entry.title: Dolphins turn to Kyle McCord against Colts after injuries sideline Malik Willis, Zach Sieler
entry.summary: The Miami Dolphins will attempt to get their second win of the season in Indianapolis on Sunday, but they will have to do it without two of their best players. On Tuesday, it was reported that defensive tackle Zach Sieler will miss the rest of the season with a ruptured bicep. WATCH REPORT BELOW: QB Kyle McCord takes the reins with Malik Willis on IR 'I give him a ton of credit not only for pushing through that game and playing at a high level but just for everything he's done,' said Dolphins head coach Jeff Hafley said Wednesday. The second injury is quarterback Malik Willis, who's been battling a groin injury that has landed him on the injured reserve, meaning he will miss at least the next four games. 'The injury had progressed enough that the medical team believed that he needed the rest,' Hafley said. Quarterback Kyle McCord, in his second NFL season, will get the start against Indianapolis. Hafley said he has a live arm and has faith in his new signal caller. 'I'm excited, but at the same time the production on the field matters most so I'm doing everything I can to do everything I can to play,' said McCord. Arguably the best news of the day was linebacker Josh Uche being named team captain. Players cheered for the South Florida native, but for Uche, he says it's business as usual. 'I've been dreaming about this since I was a kid, and for the guys to trust me and to be a part of the leadership is everything,' said Uche. Kickoff against the Colts is scheduled for 1 p.m. at Lucas Oil Stadium.

entry.title: Community gathers to begin cleanup as Jensen Beach flooding slowly recedes - WPBF
entry.summary: Community gathers to begin cleanup as Jensen Beach flooding slowly recedes    WPBF
entry.article_text: After more than a week of standing floodwater, some residents near Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach are finally beginning to clean up their homes as water slowly recedes. Martin County began pumping water out of the neighborhood Monday, allowing some homeowners to begin assessing the damage. For Lisa French, the receding water means she can finally begin the difficult work of cleaning out her home. “I mean, we’ve been underwater for a week,” French said. When WPBF 25 News visited French’s home several days ago, water was still standing inside, reaching more than a foot deep in some rooms. CLICK HERE FOR INFORMATION ON HOW TO DONATE TO THE FRENCH FAMILY Now, the water is gone, but much of what she owns has been destroyed. Since early Wednesday morning, French, her husband and several neighbors have been removing damaged drywall, tearing out the kitchen and carrying ruined furniture and belongings into the front yard. “You know, you’re sitting there with your house full of water, sitting in the fact that you lost your entire home. But now we can actually move and work instead of think,” French said. While French has begun cleaning up, other residents are still waiting for floodwaters to recede. Susan Destafney, who has lived in the neighborhood for four decades, said she has never experienced anything like it. “We’ve lived in our home for 40 years. We’ve never seen the likes of this,” Destafney said. Community volunteers have also stepped in to help, including Alaura Macpherson, who runs the local group Quit Messen With Jensen. Macpherson said volunteers have been collecting cleaning supplies and other necessities for affected families. She is also organizing a community fundraiser and meal on November 25 to raise money for flood victims. Local restaurants are expected to donate food, while the event will also serve as a resource center connecting residents with contractors, cleanup services and other recovery assistance. “The community is what helps each other. We are a family,” Macpherson said. Martin County officials have opened a Multi-Agency Resource Center at the Hoke Library in Jensen Beach to connect flood victims with recovery assistance. entry.title: 77 homes hit by Martin County flooding. Where to get help now - WPEC
entry.summary: 77 homes hit by Martin County flooding. Where to get help now    WPEC
entry.article_text: A day after Jensen Beach residents told Martin County commissioners that flooding forced them from their homes, families can go to Hoke Library for recovery help while they wait for word on federal aid. The flood recovery center is open Wednesday even though regular library services are closed for Veterans Day. State agencies and local nonprofits are there to connect residents with recovery resources, and the county says more agencies and services will be added throughout the week. At Tuesday’s commission meeting, residents pressed county leaders about drainage and how they were warned. Martin County Emergency Management Director Sally Waite told commissioners the flooding affected 77 homes and that assessment teams planned to visit each one to document the damage. Cleanup begins in Skyline Heights On Wednesday, CBS12 News returned to Jensen Beach’s Skyline Heights neighborhood, where part of Hyline Drive remained underwater. At Lisa French’s home, the cleanup had finally started. French said hers was the first home in the neighborhood being cleared out and gutted. Cabinets, furniture and pieces of drywall covered the front yard as workers carried out nearly everything floodwater touched. After a week, this is like celebration, French said. But that progress came with tears as she watched her family’s belongings get thrown away. The crib was a rough one to watch go, French said. It’s just my kids, you know. One week earlier, streets throughout the neighborhood were underwater and residents used kayaks to check on their homes and neighbors. Waite told CBS12 News that some homes took on three to five feet of water. She estimated about 24 of the 77 affected homes were destroyed. French and her family are staying with her parents and waiting to hear about longer-term housing. She said they do not have flood insurance. Alaura Macpherson, co-founder of Quit Messing With Jensen, went to the Hoke Library resource center Wednesday to collect cleanup supplies for affected families. CBS12 News later met up with her at French’s home, where she was helping the family clear out the damage. Absolutely not, Macpherson said. I will do this any day for my community. For French, getting everything out is only the beginning. This is bittersweet because we’re moving forward, French said. But, you know, how do we rebuild? Where to get help The Multi-Agency Resource Center is at Hoke Library, 1150 NW Jack Williams Way in Jensen Beach . The county lists those hours for Wednesday through Saturday until further notice. The center is closed Sundays. Martin County is also accepting applications for state disaster housing assistance. Households must meet income requirements. Residents can call 772-320-3169 for details. They can also report flood damage and fill out a needs survey on the county’s flood recovery page. Read more: 'We're not getting any answers': Hamilton Bay residents frustrated as flooding continues Where FEMA aid stands Florida announced Monday that it had requested a presidential major disaster declaration for the flooding. As of Wednesday morning, federal approval had yet to be announced. The state’s announcement did not specify whether the request included FEMA Individual Assistance for Martin County. If that aid is authorized for Martin County, eligible households could apply for help with expenses such as temporary housing and essential home repairs.

entry.title: 'It's heartwarming': Fort Pierce community gathers to honor veterans and military families - WPBF
entry.summary: 'It's heartwarming': Fort Pierce community gathers to honor veterans and military families    WPBF
entry.article_text: Community members in Fort Pierce gathered Wednesday to honor veterans, military families, and those who continue to serve the country in a heartfelt ceremony. The event recognized the brave men and women who have worn the uniform and represented the United States Armed Forces. Dennis Mallon, who served in the U.S. Army from 1966 to 1968, shared his personal loss. "I lost my best friend," Mallon said. "He ended up going into the Marines, I ended up going in the Army, and he did the ultimate sacrifice. To this day, I miss him." The ceremony also expressed gratitude to military families for their support. I come from a military family," one attendee said. "Everything was pretty nice. I'm out here to support the veterans, and everything turned out pretty nice. I'm glad to be a part of it," Retired U.S. Army veteran Zachary Pressley said. Cynthia Shelton, representing the American Legion Post 171. Army veteran, who served from 1987 to 2021, highlighted the importance of supporting service members. "One of our members is deployed at this time, so we are also keeping her in our prayers because the wars are always going to be there, so we have to always show up and do our part," Shelton said. Vietnam veteran Dave Kauffman, who served in 1968, reflected on the progress made in honoring veterans. "When we came home from Vietnam, none of this existed. We were not welcomed home, and I think we learned from that, and we won't make that mistake again. It's heartwarming to see people coming out," Kauffman said. Members of Fort Pierce Central High School's JROTC attended the event, along with recent graduate Private First-Class Jason Salinas, now a U.S. "It's great that they're still doing things like this because it not only shows appreciation and love that we show due to the loss of veterans that we have, I'm so thankful that I'm here and able to follow in their footsteps so that I can still continue in their legacy and hold on to that no matter what," Salinas said. "I'm so thankful for the opportunity I was given and blessed with by not only my friends and family and the people that support me but also to God that gave me the opportunity to raise my right hand and take it further on," Salinas said. This year’s guest speaker, Sergeant Major Brian Huston, U.S. Army (Retired), shared a message of gratitude for veterans and those still serving, thanking them for answering the call. entry.title: St. Lucie County shelter waives adoption fees after taking in 114 cats from alleged hoarding case
entry.summary: A St. Lucie County animal shelter is making an urgent push to find homes for cats and kittens after taking in more than 100 animals from a home last month. The Humane Society of St. Lucie County is teaming up with BISSELL Pet Foundation for an emergency 'Empty the Shelters' adoption event on Nov. 13 and 14. Adoption fees will be waived for all cats and kittens during the two-day event. The shelter says it's facing a capacity crunch after taking in 114 cats from a Port St. Lucie home in October. The cats were rescued from a home at the center of an alleged animal hoarding case that led to a woman's arrest on 29 felony animal cruelty charges. Now, the Humane Society is hoping the adoption event will free up much-needed space so it can continue caring for the animals. All pets available for adoption are spayed or neutered, vaccinated and microchipped. The event runs from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. on Friday, Nov. 13, and Saturday, Nov. 14, at the Humane Society of St. Lucie County, located at 8890 Glades Cut-Off Road in Port St. Lucie. Anyone interested in adopting can view available pets at hsslc.org .

entry.title: Port St. Lucie Veterans Day ceremony honors generations of veterans and their service - WFLX
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie Veterans Day ceremony honors generations of veterans and their service    WFLX
entry.article_text: Veterans of all eras and residents of all ages packed Veterans Memorial Park in Port St. Lucie on Wednesday for the annual Veterans Day ceremony. WFLX anchor and Navy veteran Mike Trim connected with fellow veterans about the significance of the day. Vietnam veteran Michael Greene wore a newly decorated vest commemorating his Army service “It’s all like my whole history. I started in transportation. I think it’s very important. I enlisted and was not supposed to go but ended up over there,” Greene told Trim. Wayne Thomas, another Vietnam War veteran in attendance, told Trim he felt this day now properly honors their service, which was not previously recognized. “It’s good to get the recognition that we didn’t get,” Thomas said. Lucie High School Junior ROTC attended the ceremony in full force while crowds of all ages looked on. That included a member of the greatest generation: 98-year-old World War II veteran Robert Vogel. I would really encourage anyone to come to these events because they’re really important to support the veterans,” Vogel told Trim. Those veterans heard keynote speaker, Retired Air Force Master Sgt. A special touch from the Port St. Lucie community band featured songs from each branch of service. That prompted service members in attendance to stand for their respective branch song. There was also a special flyover by the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office helicopter.

entry.title: Community gathers to begin cleanup as Jensen Beach flooding slowly recedes - WPBF
entry.summary: Community gathers to begin cleanup as Jensen Beach flooding slowly recedes    WPBF
entry.article_text: After more than a week of standing floodwater, some residents near Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach are finally beginning to clean up their homes as water slowly recedes. Martin County began pumping water out of the neighborhood Monday, allowing some homeowners to begin assessing the damage. For Lisa French, the receding water means she can finally begin the difficult work of cleaning out her home. “I mean, we’ve been underwater for a week,” French said. When WPBF 25 News visited French’s home several days ago, water was still standing inside, reaching more than a foot deep in some rooms. CLICK HERE FOR INFORMATION ON HOW TO DONATE TO THE FRENCH FAMILY Now, the water is gone, but much of what she owns has been destroyed. Since early Wednesday morning, French, her husband and several neighbors have been removing damaged drywall, tearing out the kitchen and carrying ruined furniture and belongings into the front yard. “You know, you’re sitting there with your house full of water, sitting in the fact that you lost your entire home. But now we can actually move and work instead of think,” French said. While French has begun cleaning up, other residents are still waiting for floodwaters to recede. Susan Destafney, who has lived in the neighborhood for four decades, said she has never experienced anything like it. “We’ve lived in our home for 40 years. We’ve never seen the likes of this,” Destafney said. Community volunteers have also stepped in to help, including Alaura Macpherson, who runs the local group Quit Messen With Jensen. Macpherson said volunteers have been collecting cleaning supplies and other necessities for affected families. She is also organizing a community fundraiser and meal on Nov. 25 to raise money for flood victims. Local restaurants are expected to donate food, while the event will also serve as a resource center connecting residents with contractors, cleanup services and other recovery assistance. “The community is what helps each other. We are a family,” Macpherson said. Martin County officials have opened a Multi-Agency Resource Center at the Hoke Library in Jensen Beach to connect flood victims with recovery assistance. entry.title: 77 homes hit by Martin County flooding. Where to get help now - WPEC
entry.summary: 77 homes hit by Martin County flooding. Where to get help now    WPEC
entry.article_text: A day after Jensen Beach residents told Martin County commissioners that flooding forced them from their homes, families can go to Hoke Library for recovery help while they wait for word on federal aid. The flood recovery center is open Wednesday even though regular library services are closed for Veterans Day. State agencies and local nonprofits are there to connect residents with recovery resources, and the county says more agencies and services will be added throughout the week. At Tuesday’s commission meeting, residents pressed county leaders about drainage and how they were warned. Martin County Emergency Management Director Sally Waite told commissioners the flooding affected 77 homes and that assessment teams planned to visit each one to document the damage. Cleanup begins in Skyline Heights On Wednesday, CBS12 News returned to Jensen Beach’s Skyline Heights neighborhood, where part of Hyline Drive remained underwater. At Lisa French’s home, the cleanup had finally started. French said hers was the first home in the neighborhood being cleared out and gutted. Cabinets, furniture and pieces of drywall covered the front yard as workers carried out nearly everything floodwater touched. After a week, this is like celebration, French said. But that progress came with tears as she watched her family’s belongings get thrown away. The crib was a rough one to watch go, French said. It’s just my kids, you know. One week earlier, streets throughout the neighborhood were underwater and residents used kayaks to check on their homes and neighbors. Waite told CBS12 News that some homes took on three to five feet of water. She estimated about 24 of the 77 affected homes were destroyed. French and her family are staying with her parents and waiting to hear about longer-term housing. She said they do not have flood insurance. Alaura Macpherson, co-founder of Quit Messing With Jensen, went to the Hoke Library resource center Wednesday to collect cleanup supplies for affected families. CBS12 News later met up with her at French’s home, where she was helping the family clear out the damage. Absolutely not, Macpherson said. I will do this any day for my community. For French, getting everything out is only the beginning. This is bittersweet because we’re moving forward, French said. But, you know, how do we rebuild? Where to get help The Multi-Agency Resource Center is at Hoke Library, 1150 NW Jack Williams Way in Jensen Beach . The county lists those hours for Wednesday through Saturday until further notice. The center is closed Sundays. Martin County is also accepting applications for state disaster housing assistance. Households must meet income requirements. Residents can call 772-320-3169 for details. They can also report flood damage and fill out a needs survey on the county’s flood recovery page. Read more: 'We're not getting any answers': Hamilton Bay residents frustrated as flooding continues Where FEMA aid stands Florida announced Monday that it had requested a presidential major disaster declaration for the flooding. As of Wednesday morning, federal approval had yet to be announced. The state’s announcement did not specify whether the request included FEMA Individual Assistance for Martin County. If that aid is authorized for Martin County, eligible households could apply for help with expenses such as temporary housing and essential home repairs.

entry.title: St. Lucie County shelter waives adoption fees after taking in 114 cats from alleged hoarding case - WFLX
entry.summary: St. Lucie County shelter waives adoption fees after taking in 114 cats from alleged hoarding case    WFLX
entry.article_text: Lucie County animal shelter is making an urgent push to find homes for cats and kittens after taking in more than 100 animals from a home last month. Lucie County is teaming up with BISSELL Pet Foundation for an emergency "Empty the Shelters" adoption event on Nov. Adoption fees will be waived for all cats and kittens during the two-day event. The shelter says it's facing a capacity crunch after taking in 114 cats from a Port St. The cats were rescued from a home at the center of an alleged animal hoarding case that led to a woman's arrest on 29 felony animal cruelty charges. Now, the Humane Society is hoping the adoption event will free up much-needed space so it can continue caring for the animals. All pets available for adoption are spayed or neutered, vaccinated and microchipped. The event runs from 11 a.m. 14, at the Humane Society of St. Lucie County, located at 8890 Glades Cut-Off Road in Port St. Anyone interested in adopting can view available pets at hsslc.org .

entry.title: Martin County looks for flood fixes after Port St. Lucie pumping into Savannas Preserve
entry.summary: More than a week after historic rainfall hit the Treasure Coast, Martin County leaders are looking at how to prevent another flooding disaster after officials said Port St. Lucie pumped floodwater into the Savannas Preserve before water flowed south toward neighborhoods in Jensen Beach. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Martin County looks for flood fixes after Port St. Lucie pumping into Savannas Preserve The flooding and damage came days after the historic rainfall stopped, leaving residents questioning what happened, who was pumping water into the preserve and what can be changed before another major storm. WPTV's Michael Hoffman has been following those questions as families continue recovering from homes that were damaged or destroyed. Residents question what happened after the rain Residents have told WPTV they believe pumping floodwater from areas to the north contributed to the natural flow of water moving south and overflowing into their Jensen Beach neighborhoods. Tiffany Kincaid was among the residents whose homes were devastated. I've never seen anything like this, not this level of devastation that has been sort of sitting in water for now eight days, Kincaid said. Kincaid said her family believed protections were in place until rising water forced them out. 'We trusted that a plan was in place to protect us, until midnight when water became entering our home, and then we quickly realized that we needed to get out,' Kincaid said. Martin County official: 'The severity of that rainfall caught us unprepared' At a Martin County Commission meeting, Public Works Director James Gorton acknowledged the challenge presented by the historic rainfall. 'The severity of that rainfall caught us unprepared,' Gorton said. 'It caught St. Lucie County unprepared. It caught Indian River unprepared.' Gorton also addressed pumping from Port St. Lucie into the Savannas Preserve. 'They pumped Monday and they pumped Tuesday morning. They stopped Tuesday morning,' Gorton said. Gorton said one concern is that individual jurisdictions may be looking primarily at conditions within their own watersheds rather than what happens farther downstream. 'They're just looking at the water levels that are in their watershed,' Gorton said. 'They're not looking at their impacts to the downstream.' entry.article_text: More than a week after historic rainfall hit the Treasure Coast, Martin County leaders are looking at how to prevent another flooding disaster after officials said Port St. Lucie pumped floodwater into the Savannas Preserve before water flowed south toward neighborhoods in Jensen Beach.WATCH REPORT BELOW:The flooding and damage came days after the historic rainfall stopped, leaving residents questioning what happened, who was pumping water into the preserve and what can be changed before another major storm.WPTV's Michael Hoffman has been following those questions as families continue recovering from homes that were damaged or destroyed.Residents have told WPTV they believe pumping floodwater from areas to the north contributed to the natural flow of water moving south and overflowing into their Jensen Beach neighborhoods.Tiffany Kincaid was among the residents whose homes were devastated.“I've never seen anything like this, not this level of devastation that has been sort of sitting in water for now eight days,” Kincaid said.Kincaid said her family believed protections were in place until rising water forced them out."We trusted that a plan was in place to protect us, until midnight when water became entering our home, and then we quickly realized that we needed to get out," Kincaid said.At a Martin County Commission meeting, Public Works Director James Gorton acknowledged the challenge presented by the historic rainfall."The severity of that rainfall caught us unprepared," Gorton said. It caught Indian River unprepared."Gorton also addressed pumping from Port St. Lucie into the Savannas Preserve."They pumped Monday and they pumped Tuesday morning. They stopped Tuesday morning," Gorton said.Gorton said one concern is that individual jurisdictions may be looking primarily at conditions within their own watersheds rather than what happens farther downstream."They're just looking at the water levels that are in their watershed," Gorton said. "They're not looking at their impacts to the downstream."The pumping itself is not an illegal practice. Lucie has a permit allowing it to pump into the preserve, and Martin County leaders said there are not concrete regulation schedules governing the Savannas as a whole.That has raised a bigger question for local leaders: Who should be responsible for considering the consequences across the entire watershed?“I don't know that we can modify their permit, but I would hope that we'd be able to look at that and say, you know, do no harm, which is really what kind of — or shared adversity, I think, is a better way to say it,” Gorton said.One potential solution discussed by Martin County officials would put management of the Savannas watershed under one overarching organization rather than relying on decisions made by individual jurisdictions.“Once we get that water out, there's a larger discussion that we need to have, which is: What are we going to do to mitigate this in the future?” Gorton said.He suggested the water management district could potentially play a role."One such idea might be looking at treating the Savannas as a watershed that needs to be managed by one party," Gorton said. "Maybe it would be the water management district."Martin County Commissioner Edward Ciampi agreed that the current situation warrants another look."I agree with what your suggestion was, is that it just can't be whoever pumps fastest and first wins," Ciampi said.For people still dealing with the consequences in Jensen Beach, those discussions come as they search for answers, assistance and, in some cases, a dry place to call home.WPTV will continue following whether Martin County and other agencies develop a new plan for managing water in the Savannas and what changes could be made before another major rainfall event.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.summary: A St. Lucie County family is searching for answers after 18-year-old Omari Linzell Williams was struck and killed by a vehicle while walking to get groceries. His family told WPTV they are now calling for changes to make the roadway safer for pedestrians as the traffic homicide investigation continues. Williams' mother, Witney Williams, and aunt, Sharon Garcia, spoke with WPTV reporter Zitlali Solache about the loss and the questions they still have about what happened. 'He was pure, he was a beautiful, beautiful young man. He was a big brother,' Witney Williams said. WATCH REPORT BELOW: St. Lucie County family seeks answers after 18-year-old struck, killed Omari Linzell Williams was walking to get groceries Investigators said Williams was walking along the westbound lane of North Boulevard around 6 p.m. Tuesday when a 30-year-old driver struck him. According to investigators, the driver was unable to see Williams before the collision. Williams was taken to St. Mary's Medical Center, where he was pronounced dead. The driver was not injured and cooperated with investigators. Williams' family told WPTV he had left home to pick up groceries because the family did not have a vehicle. 'There was floodwaters on the opposite side of the road so he couldn't walk on that side,' Garcia said. 'At this moment they don't have a car and he was walking to the store to get the items and he didn't make it very far,' she said. 'I ran out of the house screaming my son's name because I knew that was him,' she said. Williams said she rushed toward the scene, hoping she would get there in time. 'I was just praying that I'd get there before he took his last breath and I didn't make it,' she said. The family is now seeking more information about the circumstances surrounding the crash. entry.title: 'Quit is not an option': Fort Pierce woman loses house for a second time to a storm - WPBF
entry.summary: 'Quit is not an option': Fort Pierce woman loses house for a second time to a storm    WPBF
entry.article_text: A Fort Pierce woman is recovering from devastating flooding that destroyed her childhood home, marking the second time in two years she has lost everything. Terri Polk, who previously lost her home in the Spanish Lakes community to a tornado during Hurricane Milton, moved back into her childhood home to care for her mother, who has Alzheimer’s. Now, that home has been severely damaged by floodwaters. “The heart throb of our whole family is here,” Polk said. Polk shared that the house, built by her parents, has always been a central place for her family. “My mother’s door has always been open to everyone in the family,” she said. “This breaks your heart because I grew up in this house, I actually grew up here.” Last Monday, floodwaters rushed into the home, leaving behind destruction. “In the morning, the water was up to the tops of the beds,” Polk said. By the time the water receded, the damage was done. Polk’s belongings, including her bed and bookcases, now lie in a pile on the front lawn. Polk said she hasn’t slept in days as she tries to process the loss. The home is now filled with dehumidifiers, and Polk’s flood insurance won’t cover all the damages. Despite the challenges, she remains determined to rebuild. “No is not the answer; quit is not an option,” she said. “I’m not going to give up." entry.title: Martin County looks for flood fixes after Port St. Lucie pumping into Savannas Preserve
entry.summary: More than a week after historic rainfall hit the Treasure Coast, Martin County leaders are looking at how to prevent another flooding disaster after officials said Port St. Lucie pumped floodwater into the Savannas Preserve before water flowed south toward neighborhoods in Jensen Beach. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Martin County looks for flood fixes after Port St. Lucie pumping into Savannas Preserve The flooding and damage came days after the historic rainfall stopped, leaving residents questioning what happened, who was pumping water into the preserve and what can be changed before another major storm. WPTV's Michael Hoffman has been following those questions as families continue recovering from homes that were damaged or destroyed. Residents question what happened after the rain Residents have told WPTV they believe pumping floodwater from areas to the north contributed to the natural flow of water moving south and overflowing into their Jensen Beach neighborhoods. Tiffany Kincaid was among the residents whose homes were devastated. I've never seen anything like this, not this level of devastation that has been sort of sitting in water for now eight days, Kincaid said. Kincaid said her family believed protections were in place until rising water forced them out. 'We trusted that a plan was in place to protect us, until midnight when water became entering our home, and then we quickly realized that we needed to get out,' Kincaid said. Martin County official: 'The severity of that rainfall caught us unprepared' At a Martin County Commission meeting, Public Works Director James Gorton acknowledged the challenge presented by the historic rainfall. 'The severity of that rainfall caught us unprepared,' Gorton said. 'It caught St. Lucie County unprepared. It caught Indian River unprepared.' Gorton also addressed pumping from Port St. Lucie into the Savannas Preserve. 'They pumped Monday and they pumped Tuesday morning. They stopped Tuesday morning,' Gorton said. Gorton said one concern is that individual jurisdictions may be looking primarily at conditions within their own watersheds rather than what happens farther downstream. 'They're just looking at the water levels that are in their watershed,' Gorton said. 'They're not looking at their impacts to the downstream.' They stopped Tuesday morning," Gorton said.Gorton said one concern is that individual jurisdictions may be looking primarily at conditions within their own watersheds rather than what happens farther downstream."They're just looking at the water levels that are in their watershed," Gorton said. "They're not looking at their impacts to the downstream."The pumping itself is not an illegal practice. Lucie has a permit allowing it to pump into the preserve, and Martin County leaders said there are not concrete regulation schedules governing the Savannas as a whole.That has raised a bigger question for local leaders: Who should be responsible for considering the consequences across the entire watershed?“I don't know that we can modify their permit, but I would hope that we'd be able to look at that and say, you know, do no harm, which is really what kind of — or shared adversity, I think, is a better way to say it,” Gorton said.One potential solution discussed by Martin County officials would put management of the Savannas watershed under one overarching organization rather than relying on decisions made by individual jurisdictions.“Once we get that water out, there's a larger discussion that we need to have, which is: What are we going to do to mitigate this in the future?” Gorton said.He suggested the water management district could potentially play a role."One such idea might be looking at treating the Savannas as a watershed that needs to be managed by one party," Gorton said. "Maybe it would be the water management district."Martin County Commissioner Edward Ciampi agreed that the current situation warrants another look."I agree with what your suggestion was, is that it just can't be whoever pumps fastest and first wins," Ciampi said.For people still dealing with the consequences in Jensen Beach, those discussions come as they search for answers, assistance and, in some cases, a dry place to call home.WPTV will continue following whether Martin County and other agencies develop a new plan for managing water in the Savannas and what changes could be made before another major rainfall event.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.summary: St. Lucie County shelter waives adoption fees after taking in 114 cats from alleged hoarding case    WFLX
entry.article_text: Lucie County animal shelter is making an urgent push to find homes for cats and kittens after taking in more than 100 animals from a home last month. Lucie County is teaming up with BISSELL Pet Foundation for an emergency "Empty the Shelters" adoption event on Nov. Adoption fees will be waived for all cats and kittens during the two-day event. The shelter says it's facing a capacity crunch after taking in 114 cats from a Port St. The cats were rescued from a home at the center of an alleged animal hoarding case that led to a woman's arrest on 29 felony animal cruelty charges. Now, the Humane Society is hoping the adoption event will free up much-needed space so it can continue caring for the animals. All pets available for adoption are spayed or neutered, vaccinated and microchipped. The event runs from 11 a.m. 14, at the Humane Society of St. Lucie County, located at 8890 Glades Cut-Off Road in Port St. Anyone interested in adopting can view available pets at hsslc.org .

entry.title: Port St. Lucie Veterans Day ceremony honors generations of veterans and their service - WFLX
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie Veterans Day ceremony honors generations of veterans and their service    WFLX
entry.article_text: Veterans of all eras and residents of all ages packed Veterans Memorial Park in Port St. Lucie on Wednesday for the annual Veterans Day ceremony. WFLX anchor and Navy veteran Mike Trim connected with fellow veterans about the significance of the day. Vietnam veteran Michael Greene wore a newly decorated vest commemorating his Army service “It’s all like my whole history. I started in transportation. I think it’s very important. I enlisted and was not supposed to go but ended up over there,” Greene told Trim. Wayne Thomas, another Vietnam War veteran in attendance, told Trim he felt this day now properly honors their service, which was not previously recognized. “It’s good to get the recognition that we didn’t get,” Thomas said. Lucie High School Junior ROTC attended the ceremony in full force while crowds of all ages looked on. That included a member of the greatest generation: 98-year-old World War II veteran Robert Vogel. I would really encourage anyone to come to these events because they’re really important to support the veterans,” Vogel told Trim. Those veterans heard keynote speaker, Retired Air Force Master Sgt. A special touch from the Port St. Lucie community band featured songs from each branch of service. That prompted service members in attendance to stand for their respective branch song. There was also a special flyover by the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office helicopter.

entry.title: St. Lucie County rejects plan that could bring nearly 500 homes to low-lying site - cw34.com
entry.summary: St. Lucie County rejects plan that could bring nearly 500 homes to low-lying site    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Lucie County commissioners voted 3-2 to reject a land-use change for a roughly 34-acre property near South 25th Street and West Midway Road that could allow nearly 500 homes. The vote came as residents sought answers about recent flooding and commissioners questioned how the property handles drainage. An engineer said the property receives drainage from about 134 acres and uses a 24-inch pipe to direct water to nearby canals. Another pipe might be needed. The property sits lower than surrounding roads and would need to be raised for development, prompting concerns that construction could push water onto nearby properties. If designated for residential use, the site could allow up to 15 homes per acre, according to the discussion. County staff recommended approving the land-use change with adjustments to avoid or reduce impacts to wetlands and required buffers. Commissioners denied the request. See also: 77 homes hit by Martin County flooding. Where to get help now At the same meeting, residents from Creekside and White City asked commissioners to investigate last week’s flooding, identify who is responsible for local drainage systems, and explain how to prevent future flooding. I love my community, but it’s not fair that we’re suffering because nobody has taken the initiative to do what’s right for us, one resident said. Creekside residents called for an engineering review of the neighborhood and surrounding watershed, a reassessment of flood risk and a mitigation plan with deadlines. They also asked for a public meeting with county engineers and stormwater officials. White City residents described recurring flooding and called for drainage improvements and more stormwater storage. One resident said her home and yard had flooded four times since 2012. The county also made its emergency declaration official after days of heavy rain and flooding. It covers hazards including flooded roads and strained drainage systems.

entry.title: Community gathers to begin cleanup as Jensen Beach flooding slowly recedes - WPBF
entry.summary: Community gathers to begin cleanup as Jensen Beach flooding slowly recedes    WPBF
entry.article_text: After more than a week of standing floodwater, some residents near Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach are finally beginning to clean up their homes as water slowly recedes. Martin County began pumping water out of the neighborhood Monday, allowing some homeowners to begin assessing the damage. For Lisa French, the receding water means she can finally begin the difficult work of cleaning out her home. “I mean, we’ve been underwater for a week,” French said. When WPBF 25 News visited French’s home several days ago, water was still standing inside, reaching more than a foot deep in some rooms. CLICK HERE FOR INFORMATION ON HOW TO DONATE TO THE FRENCH FAMILY Now, the water is gone, but much of what she owns has been destroyed. Since early Wednesday morning, French, her husband and several neighbors have been removing damaged drywall, tearing out the kitchen and carrying ruined furniture and belongings into the front yard. “You know, you’re sitting there with your house full of water, sitting in the fact that you lost your entire home. But now we can actually move and work instead of think,” French said. While French has begun cleaning up, other residents are still waiting for floodwaters to recede. Susan Destafney, who has lived in the neighborhood for four decades, said she has never experienced anything like it. “We’ve lived in our home for 40 years. We’ve never seen the likes of this,” Destafney said. Community volunteers have also stepped in to help, including Alaura Macpherson, who runs the local group Quit Messen With Jensen. Macpherson said volunteers have been collecting cleaning supplies and other necessities for affected families. She is also organizing a community fundraiser and meal on Nov. 25 to raise money for flood victims. Local restaurants are expected to donate food, while the event will also serve as a resource center connecting residents with contractors, cleanup services and other recovery assistance. “The community is what helps each other. We are a family,” Macpherson said. Martin County officials have opened a Multi-Agency Resource Center at the Hoke Library in Jensen Beach to connect flood victims with recovery assistance. entry.title: Martin County to begin phased restoration of MARTY transit service
entry.summary: Martin County will begin restoring public transportation services this week after securing a one-year emergency contract with MTM Transit, LLC. The announcement comes after the county's contracted transit provider walked away from its agreement last month, halting all MARTY bus service and laying off 29 employees with no warning to riders or county leaders. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Martin County begins restoring MARTY transit service The county said Tuesday that it will take a phased approach to restoring MARTY service after what officials described as an abrupt disruption caused by a contract breach involving the previous vendor. ADA paratransit service will be the first to return, with operations expected to resume Thursday. The service is available to eligible riders with disabilities who are unable to use regular fixed-route buses. MARTY customer service representatives are contacting active registered paratransit riders directly about the resumption of service. Riders can call 772-463-2822 for information about scheduling and reservations. As buses are prepared and drivers become available, the county said it will begin restoring fixed-route service, starting with the heavily traveled U.S. 1 corridor. The Indiantown route will also be among the priorities as service returns. 'Our priority is to restore public transportation as quickly and responsibly as possible, with particular attention to residents who depend on these services to access essential needs, as well as fiscal responsibility to the taxpayer,' Martin County Transit Administrator Ash Beecher said. Beecher acknowledged the disruption has affected riders and the broader community and said the county is working to reestablish service in a coordinated manner. During the interruption, United Way of Martin County helped coordinate transportation for people with critical travel needs. The county said additional routes will return as buses and drivers become available. Start dates, schedules and rider instructions will be announced as each phase is finalized. Residents can find updates through Martin County's transit website or call transit customer service at 772-463-2860 from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Monday through Friday.

entry.title: Martin County signs emergency contract to restore MARTY bus services - WPBF
entry.summary: Martin County signs emergency contract to restore MARTY bus services    WPBF
entry.article_text: Martin County has signed a one-year emergency contract to restore the MARTY bus services, which will resume in phases. The service ended abruptly on Oct. 8 after the last vendor, Martin County Transit LLC, canceled services, citing rising costs of fuel and maintenance. The county signed the emergency contract with MTM Transit, which has operated these buses in the past. The first phase begins Thursday and will prioritize eligible riders with disabilities who cannot use the regular fixed-route bus service. For details on scheduling and reservations, residents should call 772-463-2822. As for regular services, there is still no official start date. The county is working to restore buses and rehire bus drivers who were let go by the previous vendor.

entry.title: Tampa father jailed in Florida voter sweep as attorney questions state's evidence against him
entry.summary: A Tampa father accused of voting illegally is now behind bars one of 20 defendants charged with voter fraud as part of the state's latest sweep. But his attorney is questioning the state's evidence, telling investigative reporter Katie LaGrone she hasn't seen proof of her client's wrongdoing beyond a voter card the state sent him even though he was ineligible to vote. This court appearance was about scheduling his trial, but for the people waiting for the 44-year-old to return home, the consequences of his latest arrest have already settled in. 'I thought it was a prank. Like, what do you mean? There's officers here to arrest you for voting? He's like, 'I didn't do it,'' said Taquilla Allen, White's girlfriend. She's helping to care for his two young children while he remains in jail. 'It's been rough, but you know, we're just gonna take it a day at a time,' Allen said. entry.article_text: A Tampa father accused of voting illegally is now behind bars — one of 20 defendants charged with voter fraud as part of the state's latest sweep. But his attorney is questioning the state's evidence, telling investigative reporter Katie LaGrone she hasn't seen proof of her client's wrongdoing beyond a voter card the state sent him even though he was ineligible to vote.WATCH KATIE LAGRONE'S REPORT BELOW: In a Hillsborough County courtroom recently, Donta White sat in the inmate section, dressed in an orange jumpsuit, his expression stoic. This court appearance was about scheduling his trial, but for the people waiting for the 44-year-old to return home, the consequences of his latest arrest have already settled in."I thought it was a prank. There's officers here to arrest you for voting? He's like, 'I didn't do it,'" said Taquilla Allen, White's girlfriend. She's helping to care for his two young children while he remains in jail."It's been rough, but you know, we're just gonna take it a day at a time," Allen said.The state is accusing White of illegally voting. At the time, the convicted felon was still serving a 10-year probation for grand theft when, according to a press release issued by Florida's Attorney General's Office, White signed a state form warning him not to register or vote until after he completed his sentence.But according to prosecutors, White submitted two voter registration applications falsely claiming his voting rights had been restored, and then voted early in the 2024 general election. White is now charged with illegal voting and two counts of false swearing.A spokesperson for the AG's office said White admitted to authorities that he registered and voted, but his attorney, Lynley Flagler, is questioning the state's case."There is no clear-cut evidence that would support the fact that he actually went to the polls and voted himself," Flagler said.In addition, despite White not being eligible to vote because of his felony conviction, Flagler says the state sent him a voter ID card as if he was eligible."I feel that there's an entrapment issue. They want to prosecute voting, but they have not put any checks and balances in place to let people know when they're able to vote and when they can't vote," Flagler said.While a voter ID card does not, by itself, grant someone the right to vote, under Florida law certain convicted felons can get their voting rights restored once they complete their sentence, including probation. In White's case, his illegal voting charges triggered a violation of probation, which is how he landed back in jail."He runs a body shop. He's just, overall, really changed his life. So to see him in this position saddens me on a personal level as well as a professional level," Flagler said.Questions around voter eligibility for convicted felons aren't new in Florida. Ron DeSantis announced the arrests of 20 former felons who cast a ballot despite having disqualifying convictions. Several said they thought they could vote."What we discovered from a review of all those cases was there was more confusion than fraud," said Ramon De La Cabada, a Florida criminal defense attorney who co-chairs a committee formed after those arrests.De La Cabada believes White's case may be another example of that confusion — as is the recent arrest of Astrid Navarette Quintana. She's sitting in a Lee County jail after the state charged her for voting as a non-citizen. LaGrone recently investigated her case and found she's a permanent resident, married to a U.S. veteran and was also sent a voter ID card. When asked why voters shouldn't be responsible for knowing if they're eligible to vote, De La Cabada responded, "Absolutely, but I think the better question is why isn't the government creating better communication about eligibility? What you're finding in all these cases is massive confusion as to eligibility."Donta White's jury trial is set for early next year. He faces up to 15 years in prison for illegally voting and 30 years for his probation violation, which stemmed from his recent voting charges.In the meantime, he and his family remain apart, waiting for what's next."Who would throw their life away to vote? That's what it all boils down to," his girlfriend said. "It's petty, but we're dealing with it."

entry.title: Drowsy driving risks in focus as data shows hundreds of truck crashes on Florida's Turnpike
entry.summary: Drowsy driving can be dangerous for anyone behind the wheel, but fatigue involving a large commercial truck can have deadly consequences. During Drowsy Driving Prevention Week , crash data from the Florida Department of Transportation and Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration is putting renewed attention on the risks of driver fatigue, including here in Palm Beach County. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Drowsy driving puts truckers and motorists at risk on South Florida roads In 2025, West Palm Beach recorded 51 reported truck crashes, resulting in one fatality and 23 injuries, according to the data provided to WPTV. The numbers are even larger along Florida's Turnpike. There were 451 reported truck crashes, resulting in 21 fatalities and 245 injuries. Statewide data also points to the morning commute as a key period for truck crashes. Nearly 20% of reported truck crashes occurred between 6 a.m. and 9 a.m. Fatigue can affect a driver's reaction time, concentration and ability to make quick decisions. Those risks are especially concerning when the driver is operating a large commercial vehicle. Federal hours-of-service regulations limit how long commercial drivers can remain behind the wheel and require rest periods. But regardless of how much driving time remains under those limits, drivers are responsible for stopping when fatigue makes continuing unsafe. The message during Drowsy Driving Prevention Week is straightforward: recognize the warning signs of fatigue and don't try to push through them. For truck drivers and other motorists alike, getting off the road and resting could prevent a serious or deadly crash.
