entry.title: President Donald J. Trump International Airport named cheapest major U.S. airport for parking
entry.summary: Paying to park at the airport can eat up a good chunk of your travel budget. But one airport in South Florida was just named the cheapest major U.S. airport for parking. In an analysis by Florida Rentals, President Donald J. Trump International Airport in West Palm Beach ranked as the No. 1 least expensive major airport in the country for parking in a study of 'America's Most Expensive Airport Parking'. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Florida airport named one of the cheapest for parking in the U.S. Drivers will pay about $56 a week for general airport parking. The next least expensive major airport in Florida for parking is Miami International Airport . Parking at MIA will set drivers back at about $129 per week. Tampa International Airport came in as the most expensive parking airport in Florida. The weekly cost to leave your vehicle at TPA is roughly $168. Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood was second on the list at about $140. Orlando International and Southwest Florida International in Fort Myers came in around $133 for weekly parking The study, which examined parking rates at 50 of the busiest airports, found parking at all of Florida's largest airports is cheaper than the average airport cost, which is roughly $215 for parking a week or about $30 a day. LaGuardia was named the most expensive major airport in the U.S. to park for a week, costing drivers close to $525.

entry.title: Businesses impacted by Military Trail closure after Learjet crash can apply for grants of up to $5,000
entry.summary: Starting Thursday, Palm Beach County is making $250,000 available to help businesses and nonprofits that lost revenue after the Nov. 1 Learjet crash forced the partial closure of Military Trail near Greenacres. The Palm Beach County Board of County Commissioners approved funding for the Military Trail Business Interruption Grant Program on Tuesday. County Administrator Joseph Abruzzo initially launched the program Nov. 2 under local emergency authority. PREVIOUS COVERAGE BELOW: $250K in grants for Palm Beach County businesses impacted by Learjet crash Eligible businesses and nonprofits can receive a one-time grant of up to $5,000, while funding remains available. County officials said the closure of Military Trail near the crash site disrupted businesses by limiting access for customers and deliveries. The county's Department of Housing and Economic Development will administer the grants. Businesses can use the money for operating expenses including rent, payroll, utilities and essential inventory. The county will use an applicant's latest filed business tax return to estimate revenue losses based on a 30-day interruption. Grants will be awarded on a first-come, first-served basis until the $250,000 is exhausted or all eligible applicants have been served. Who is eligible? The eligible area stretches along Military Trail from Broadway Street on the south to Kelly Drive and Sussex Avenue on the north. Businesses and nonprofits must have been operating at a physical location within the designated area before Nov. 1. Applicants must also certify that the road closure disrupted their operations or access and that they intend to continue or resume operations. The county will verify addresses using the official program map. How to apply Applications and full program criteria will be available Thursday, Nov. 12, on the Palm Beach County Department of Housing and Economic Development website. Applicants will need to submit: A signed application A W-9 Their latest filed business tax return Proof of the business address Photo identification for the authorized signer Applicable Sunbiz documentation A business tax receipt or documentation showing an exemption Awards are capped at $5,000 for each eligible business or nonprofit.

entry.title: More people, limited freshwater: Treasure Coast plans for water needs through 2050 - WPEC
entry.summary: More people, limited freshwater: Treasure Coast plans for water needs through 2050    WPEC
entry.article_text: As the Treasure Coast prepares for decades of growth, water managers face a critical question: How will the region supply enough freshwater for more people while protecting the farms, waterways and wildlife that also depend on it? Water is a necessity that is being planned for at all times, years in advance. With the explosive growth in population unfolding now, the plan is even more critical. The South Florida Water Management District’s 2026 Upper East Coast Water Supply Plan looks ahead to 2050, outlining future needs in Martin and St. Lucie counties and northeastern Okeechobee County. The district says the region’s limited freshwater resources make conservation and alternative water supplies essential to planning for that growth. What we’re seeing is about a 36-percent increase in the population in the planning area by 2050, said Carolina Maran, Chief of District Resiliency with SFWMD, describing a population approaching three-quarters of a million people. The demand for water, however, is not necessarily increasing at the same rate, Maran says. Demand for water supplied to homes and businesses, along with commercial, landscaping, and recreational uses, is expected to rise. Agricultural water use, which is the region’s largest category, is projected to decline. See also: WPB police ask public for information on sidewalk assault outside Hook Fish and Chicken Meeting the shifting needs will depend on more than population forecasts. It will also require infrastructure, efficient water use, and planning for uncertain conditions, including drought and storms. Inside a University of Florida laboratory in Fort Pierce, Dr. Sandra Guzman and her team study how water moves through soil and across different land uses. Guzman is an Associate Professor of Smart Irrigation and Hydrology with the UF/IFAS Agricultural and Biological Engineering department. A demonstration table with sand and simulated farm fields shows how water’s movement changes depending on the ground beneath it. In another area, there are charts demonstrating how immediate communication can connect area farmers with real-time agriculture and weather data. I always tell my team: water is a blessing and a curse, Guzman said. The challenge is not simply whether water is available. Its quality also determines how it can be used. We suffer from a lot of issues regarding deficit of water because it’s not only the volume of water; it’s also the quality of water, Guzman said. That creates a balancing act: supplying people and farms while protecting the lagoons, estuaries, and wildlife that depend on the region’s water resources. The district’s approach includes alternative water sources, expanded treatment and storage, and conservation. What that means is that investing in reuse, investing in efficient water uses, and also alternative water sources like the Floridan Aquifer, Maran said. Projects described in the plan include reverse-osmosis treatment, reclaimed-water expansions, and stormwater storage. In coming years, some of the infrastructure needed to support future demand must still be built. SFWMD describes the plan as a framework for local governments, utilities, agricultural operations, and other water users to guide water supply decisions. Its recommendations are intended to inform local comprehensive plans, facility work plans and ordinances. Having a plan, however, does not guarantee that every project will be completed on time. Carrying it out will require follow-through by the communities and water providers preparing for growth. On farms, part of the solution is knowing more precisely when crops need water, and how much of it. Guzman’s team works on tools that help farmers measure soil moisture and irrigate more efficiently, directing water where crops need it. The research connects decisions made in the field to the broader challenge of stretching the region’s water supply. So, in this lab, we work for that: every single drop of water that is coming out of whatever aquifer or freshwater system becomes food to your table, Guzman said. As the Treasure Coast grows, its water future will depend both on the infrastructure communities build and on how efficiently people use the supplies already available. entry.title: St. Lucie County shelter waives adoption fees after taking in 114 cats from alleged hoarding case
entry.summary: A St. Lucie County animal shelter is urgently seeking homes for cats and kittens after taking in more than 100 animals from a home last month. The Humane Society of St. Lucie County is teaming up with BISSELL Pet Foundation for an emergency 'Empty the Shelters' adoption event on Nov. 13 and 14. Adoption fees will be waived for all cats and kittens during the two-day event. WATCH REPORT BELOW: St. Lucie County shelter waives adoption fees after taking in 114 cats The shelter says it's facing a capacity crunch after taking in 114 cats from a Port St. Lucie home in October. The cats were rescued from a home at the center of an alleged animal hoarding case that led to a woman's arrest on 29 felony animal cruelty charges. Now, the Humane Society is hoping the adoption event will free up much-needed space so it can continue caring for the animals. All pets available for adoption are spayed or neutered, vaccinated and microchipped. The event runs from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. on Friday, Nov. 13, and Saturday, Nov. 14, at the Humane Society of St. Lucie County, located at 8890 Glades Cut-Off Road in Port St. Lucie. Anyone interested in adopting can view available pets at hsslc.org .

entry.title: MARTY bus service begins phased return in Martin County after monthlong shutdown - WFLX
entry.summary: MARTY bus service begins phased return in Martin County after monthlong shutdown    WFLX
entry.article_text: MARTY public transportation is beginning a phased return in Martin County after more than a month without regular bus service, starting with ADA paratransit before service expands to the U.S. Highway 1 and Indiantown routes, according to the county. The restoration will not happen all at once. Martin County said additional service will be added as buses are prepared and drivers become available. The county has not announced a date for full MARTY service to return. For riders who rely on public transportation to get to work, buy groceries or reach medical appointments, the phased restart offers some relief after weeks of limited transportation options. MARTY riders were left scrambling Oct. 8 when the county’s transit provider abruptly stopped service. One rider, Joe, told WFLX at the time that he received no warning. For him, losing bus service was more than an inconvenience. He told WFLX that injuries limited his mobility and made finding another way to get around difficult. “I’ve had two broken necks, three broken backs. I can’t feel my feet, so I’m not getting anywhere,” he said. As the shutdown continued, United Way of Martin County stepped in to help residents who had lost their usual transportation. Carol Houwaart-Diez with United Way of Martin County said the organization contacted the county and offered assistance through Ride United, a program that helps provide transportation for critical needs. “We made the call to the county administrator and said, ‘Hey, how can we help?’” Houwaart-Diez said. “And we have a ride program that helps provide critical services in our community, and they said, ‘Please help us.’” Through Ride United, the nonprofit began scheduling Lyft rides for people who needed to make essential trips. Houwaart-Diez said United Way has helped 108 individual clients with 754 rides during the MARTY disruption. Those trips included transportation to work, grocery stores, medical appointments and physical therapy, according to United Way. The temporary transportation solution could not help everyone. Houwaart-Diez said the Lyft vehicles being used through the program were generally unable to accommodate people who are fully wheelchair-bound. “For those that were fully wheelchair bound, we couldn’t help them, which made me sad,” she said. “We did look into to see if we could do that.” The limitation makes the return of ADA paratransit an important first step for riders with disabilities who could not use the temporary Lyft option. Martin County said ADA paratransit is expected to return first, followed by the U.S. Highway 1 and Indiantown MARTY routes. United Way plans to continue providing other transportation assistance as MARTY service is restored. “Once that starts, we still will be able to provide the other services until everything gets back up in full gear,” Houwaart-Diez said. “I’m not sure how long that’s going to be, though.” Martin County said it will add service as buses are prepared and drivers become available. entry.title: Palm Beach County Thanksgiving pies help feed local seniors for a week
entry.summary: Palm Beach County residents can take one Thanksgiving task off their list while helping feed a neighbor in need through Pie It Forward , a fundraiser benefiting Meals on Wheels of the Palm Beaches. Meals on Wheels Special Events Director Maura Sartory said local chefs from restaurants and country clubs donate pies that are sold through the campaign. Proceeds from each pie sold help feed a senior for one week. 'You get a pie and the proceeds feed a senior for a week.' The campaign includes traditional Thanksgiving favorites such as pumpkin, pecan and apple pies, along with key lime pies. Orders are available through Nov. 18, although organizers say pies can sell out before the deadline. A pie without the pie People who will be traveling for Thanksgiving or simply don't need another dessert can still participate. Sartory said Pie It Forward offers a virtual pie, which allows people to make a donation without receiving a physical pie. entry.title: Lighthouse for the Blind teaches skills that help people navigate independently in West Palm Beach
entry.summary: Learning to navigate without relying on sight requires skills many people may never have considered, from using a white cane to technology that reads or magnifies what's on a computer screen. At Lighthouse for the Blind of the Palm Beaches, Treasure Coast Okeechobee in West Palm Beach, those tools are helping people who are blind or visually impaired build greater independence. The organization serves people ranging from babies to seniors across five counties, executive director Lisa Stella told WPTV. For children, that can include activities designed to be sensory-oriented and inclusive in the community. Learning to navigate with a white cane One of the skills taught at the Lighthouse is how to use a white cane to navigate an environment. During WPTV's visit, Shining A Light reporter T.A. Walker put on a blindfold and attempted a mobility exercise with Elizabeth Prus, Lighthouse for the Blind's youth services director. Prus instructed Walker to sweep the cane back and forth roughly the width of his shoulders as he walked. The cane provided information about objects in his path, including a chair and a kitchen island. 'This is a tool that people who are visually impaired use to navigate environments,' Prus said. The training can begin at a young age. 'We start with little kids, teaching them how to use a cane so that way they can travel independently,' Prus said. For Walker, temporarily navigating without sight offered a firsthand look at how a white cane can provide information about the environment around him. Technology provides another tool for independence The Lighthouse also helps clients use technology designed to make computers more accessible to people who are blind or have low vision. entry.title: 2 northbound lanes of Military Trail reopened near Learjet crash site in Greenacres
entry.summary: Two northbound lanes of Military Trail in Palm Beach County were reopened to traffic Thursday, 11 days after a fatal Learjet crashed at the site. The Florida Department of Transportation said they worked Wednesday to repair utilities and to fill the crater left by the plane crash. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Northbound Military Trail reopened near Learjet crash site Crews worked overnight and into Thursday morning to open the northbound lanes, which were previously closed from 10th Avenue to Forest Hill Boulevard. FDOT said in a Facebook post that crews plan to pave southbound lanes Thursday. Starting Thursday, Palm Beach County is making $250,000 available to help businesses and nonprofits that lost revenue after the crash forced road closures this month. Nine people were killed when the Learjet, which departed Austin, Texas, en route to the Bahamas, crashed near Greenacres earlier this month. No one on the ground was seriously injured.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie to break ground on new 6,000-seat soccer stadium in December
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie is getting closer to welcoming its first professional soccer team , with a groundbreaking ceremony for a new 6,000-seat stadium scheduled for Saturday, Dec. 12. Port St. Lucie Sports Club announced Thursday that construction will begin at Walton One, where the stadium will sit on approximately six acres. Port St. Lucie council approves 6,000-seat professional soccer stadium The club is preparing to compete in USL League One in 2027, and the new stadium is expected to serve as more than just a place to watch soccer. Plans call for a year-round destination where families and community members can gather for entertainment and other events. The development group will fully fund construction of the stadium and has entered into an agreement with the City of Port St. Lucie to use the land. 'From day one, we knew this had to be about much more than building a soccer club,' said Gustavo Surez, founder and CEO of Port St. Lucie Sports Club. 'We set out to create something that feels like a true part of this community, a place where families can gather, young players can dream, and new traditions can take shape.' The groundbreaking ceremony will begin at noon on Dec. 12, bringing together club leaders, USL representatives, partners and founding members. A public celebration will follow at 1:30 p.m., featuring food trucks, entertainment and activities for all ages. The club says more details about the event will be announced in the coming weeks.

entry.title: Nikki Haley rules out 2028 run, warns Republicans to ‘hear the signs’
entry.summary: Former South Carolina Gov. Nikki Haley announced this week that she does not intend to run for president in 2028, four years after an unsuccessful bid for the Republican nomination. Nikki Haley reiterated that decision in an interview with CNBC this week. Haley told CNBC that Republicans need to hear the signs after the party suffered major losses in last weeks midterm elections. I am not running in 2028, but I will continue to talk about the things that I care about, Haley said in an interview with CNBC . I will continue to push good policy. I will continue to support good candidates, and we want a strong America. She added she does not have a favored candidate for 2028, saying the Democrats have a 'talented' slate of candidates. RELATED STORY | Democrats are most excited to support three candidates for 2028 Haleys 2024 campaign struggled to gain traction as Donald Trump secured the GOP nomination for a third consecutive presidential election. Although Haley served in the Donald Trump administration as U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, she became a prominent critic of him during the campaign. Although Haley struggled to win over the partys conservative base, she attracted support from some moderate Republicans, including Sens. Lisa Murkowski and Susan Collins. While many initially expected Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis to emerge as Donald Trumps strongest challenger in 2024, Haley ultimately mounted the most sustained opposition to him. She finished second in the New Hampshire primary and went on to win Vermonts primary. Still, her 97 delegates were a fraction of the more than 2,000 Donald Trump accumulated during the primary campaign. With Haley ruling out a 2028 bid, several other prominent Republicans have yet to fully address their plans. Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are among the names being discussed as potential candidates, though neither has formally entered the race. entry.title: Delray Beach veteran says he's nearly been hit 9 times, wants red-light camera installed
entry.summary: A Delray Beach resident says reckless drivers have made him scared to cross the road connecting his neighborhood, and he's asking for a red-light camera to make people think twice about speeding. Marine Corps veteran Rolando Fernandez says he has almost been hit nine times in a single month simply trying to cross the road. He lives at the Bridge View community on Lake Ida and Petal roads. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Delray Beach veteran seeks red-light camera after near-misses crossing road 'I don't want to get in my car and just cross the street, so I don't get plowed by somebody who doesn't want to stop for a red light,' Fernandez said. He says drivers have been hostile toward him along the way. 'I've been given the finger. The guy has even gone through the light, stopped, rolled down his window, and told me, 'Don't have a heart attack',' Fernandez said. Fernandez said the near-misses have taken a toll. 'To the point that I asked the Lord to help me safely (cross the road) because these people, everybody's in a hurry,' Fernandez said. He believes a red-light camera installed by the Florida Department of Transportation would be a fix. 'People unfortunately understand only pain, whether it is physical or financial. You run that light, and it costs you $200 and two points on your license, you'll think about not only this light you're running, but in all the places,' Fernandez said. Fernandez said he reached out to the Florida Department of Transportation and U.S. Rep. Lois Frankel, but he couldn't find answers, so he turned to WPTV. The fear of getting hit has even cut into his daily walks with his service dog, Scout. He says other residents share his concern. 'We have a lot of people on this side, elderly people. They cross because we have the lake over there and stuff to walk around there. ... I see them when they walk in the street because they know what's coming,' Fernandez said. I've reached out to the Florida Department of Transportation to see if this is something it can help with and what the steps are to get something done. 'I'm glad that you came, that's for sure,' he said. 'Maybe something will get done. You'll be able to do something. If not, it'll just be what it is. I have to be more careful,' Fernandez said. They want to prosecute voting, but they have not put any checks and balances in place to let people know when they're able to vote and when they can't vote," Flagler said.While a voter ID card does not, by itself, grant someone the right to vote, under Florida law certain convicted felons can get their voting rights restored once they complete their sentence, including probation. In White's case, his illegal voting charges triggered a violation of probation, which is how he landed back in jail."He runs a body shop. He's just, overall, really changed his life. So to see him in this position saddens me on a personal level as well as a professional level," Flagler said.Questions around voter eligibility for convicted felons aren't new in Florida. Ron DeSantis announced the arrests of 20 former felons who cast a ballot despite having disqualifying convictions. She's sitting in a Lee County jail after the state charged her for voting as a non-citizen. LaGrone recently investigated her case and found she's a permanent resident, married to a U.S. veteran and was also sent a voter ID card. entry.title: St. Lucie County rejects plan that could bring nearly 500 homes to low-lying site - WPEC
entry.summary: St. Lucie County rejects plan that could bring nearly 500 homes to low-lying site    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie County commissioners voted 3-2 to reject a land-use change for a roughly 34-acre property near South 25th Street and West Midway Road that could allow nearly 500 homes. The vote came as residents sought answers about recent flooding and commissioners questioned how the property handles drainage. An engineer said the property receives drainage from about 134 acres and uses a 24-inch pipe to direct water to nearby canals. Another pipe might be needed. The property sits lower than surrounding roads and would need to be raised for development, prompting concerns that construction could push water onto nearby properties. If designated for residential use, the site could allow up to 15 homes per acre, according to the discussion. County staff recommended approving the land-use change with adjustments to avoid or reduce impacts to wetlands and required buffers. Commissioners denied the request. See also: 77 homes hit by Martin County flooding. Where to get help now At the same meeting, residents from Creekside and White City asked commissioners to investigate last week’s flooding, identify who is responsible for local drainage systems, and explain how to prevent future flooding. I love my community, but it’s not fair that we’re suffering because nobody has taken the initiative to do what’s right for us, one resident said. Creekside residents called for an engineering review of the neighborhood and surrounding watershed, a reassessment of flood risk and a mitigation plan with deadlines. They also asked for a public meeting with county engineers and stormwater officials. White City residents described recurring flooding and called for drainage improvements and more stormwater storage. One resident said her home and yard had flooded four times since 2012. The county also made its emergency declaration official after days of heavy rain and flooding. It covers hazards including flooded roads and strained drainage systems.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie Veterans Day ceremony honors generations of veterans and their service
entry.summary: Veterans of all eras and residents of all ages packed Veterans Memorial Park in Port St. Lucie on Wednesday for the annual Veterans Day ceremony. WPTV anchor and Navy veteran Mike Trim connected with fellow veterans about the significance of the day. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Veterans honored at Port St. Lucie event Vietnam veteran Michael Greene wore a newly decorated vest commemorating his Army service 'It's all like my whole history. I started in transportation. I think it's very important. I enlisted and was not supposed to go but ended up over there,' Greene told Trim. Wayne Thomas, another Vietnam War veteran in attendance, told Trim he felt this day now properly honors their service, which was not previously recognized. 'It's good to get the recognition that we didn't get,' Thomas said. The Port St. Lucie High School Junior ROTC attended the ceremony in full force while crowds of all ages looked on. That included a member of the greatest generation: 98-year-old World War II veteran Robert Vogel. 'I'm one of the few left. I just thank God. I would really encourage anyone to come to these events because they're really important to support the veterans,' Vogel told Trim. Those veterans heard keynote speaker, Retired Air Force Master Sgt. Vincent Lavelle Jr. A special touch from the Port St. Lucie community band featured songs from each branch of service. That prompted service members in attendance to stand for their respective branch song. There was also a special flyover by the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office helicopter.

entry.title: New women's high-tech golf league makes its Palm Beach Gardens debut at the SoFi Center
entry.summary: A new type of golf kicked off in Palm Beach Gardens, as the high-tech Women's Tomorrow's Golf League made its debut and brought a different kind of experience to the sport. Golfers compete in Womens Tomorrows Golf League Some of the world's best female golfers competed inside the SoFi Center. The new women's golf league combines technology with traditional golf, bringing a whole new energy to the game. The league features 25 of the world's top female golfers competing on five teams: the Atlanta Drive GC, Boston Common Golf, Los Angeles Golf Club, Motor City Golf Club and New York Golf Club. Golfers compete in the WTGL in Palm Beach Gardens When you think of professional golf, you're probably thinking beautiful fairways, sand traps and lots of sun. Throw in a giant simulator screen and mix it all up, and that's where you get the WTGL. Instead of playing on a traditional golf course, players hit shots into a massive simulator screen before moving to a real green to finish each hole. When it's time to chip or putt, they move to a short game area. The matches are fast-paced, featuring 15 holes of team competition inside the SoFi Center. Every player has 40 seconds to hit a shot. Every player is mic'd up, so you can hear them talking strategy or trash. There's also a referee, and the greens rotate and can be contoured to make holes harder.

entry.title: More people, limited freshwater: Treasure Coast plans for water needs through 2050 - WPEC
entry.summary: More people, limited freshwater: Treasure Coast plans for water needs through 2050    WPEC
entry.article_text: As the Treasure Coast prepares for decades of growth, water managers face a critical question: How will the region supply enough freshwater for more people while protecting the farms, waterways and wildlife that also depend on it? Water is a necessity that is being planned for at all times, years in advance. With the explosive growth in population unfolding now, the plan is even more critical. The South Florida Water Management District’s 2026 Upper East Coast Water Supply Plan looks ahead to 2050, outlining future needs in Martin and St. Lucie counties and northeastern Okeechobee County. The district says the region’s limited freshwater resources make conservation and alternative water supplies essential to planning for that growth. What we’re seeing is about a 36-percent increase in the population in the planning area by 2050, said Carolina Maran, Chief of District Resiliency with SFWMD, describing a population approaching three-quarters of a million people. The demand for water, however, is not necessarily increasing at the same rate, Maran says. Demand for water supplied to homes and businesses, along with commercial, landscaping, and recreational uses, is expected to rise. Agricultural water use, which is the region’s largest category, is projected to decline. See also: WPB police ask public for information on sidewalk assault outside Hook Fish and Chicken Meeting the shifting needs will depend on more than population forecasts. It will also require infrastructure, efficient water use, and planning for uncertain conditions, including drought and storms. Inside a University of Florida laboratory in Fort Pierce, Dr. Sandra Guzman and her team study how water moves through soil and across different land uses. Guzman is an Associate Professor of Smart Irrigation and Hydrology with the UF/IFAS Agricultural and Biological Engineering department. A demonstration table with sand and simulated farm fields shows how water’s movement changes depending on the ground beneath it. Demand for water supplied to homes and businesses, along with commercial, landscaping, and recreational uses, is expected to rise. Agricultural water use, which is the region’s largest category, is projected to decline. entry.title: 'Did its job': Indian River County beaches recovering after erosion from nor’easter and King Tides - WPBF
entry.summary: 'Did its job': Indian River County beaches recovering after erosion from nor’easter and King Tides    WPBF
entry.article_text: Indian River County beaches are recovering after a nor’easter and king tides caused erosion along the coastline, with officials noting improvements in shoreline conditions. Erosion officials said water levels had risen almost as high as a sign at Tracking Station Beach, but the sand has already begun shifting back into place. Waves and high water significantly impacted the county’s coastline. “This is a great example of coastal resistance at work,” officials said. Johnnie Sabin, a coastal specialist with Indian River County’s Department of Natural Resources, said the shoreline at Tracking Station Beach is already showing signs of recovery. “Much of the sand we placed on the beach, while it shifted briefly, has already been returning. I mean, these beaches, these berms, there's a lot more space. They're a little higher, a little wider so folks aren't in jeopardy to visit the beaches anymore,” Sabin said. Sabin explained that Tracking Station Beach experienced five to ten feet of erosion. He credited dune plants for helping hold the sand together and said the county’s Sector Five Beach Restoration Project performed as expected. “Luckily because of the sand being there, it buffered all private properties, the roads, all the infrastructure we care about and it did its job,” Sabin said. While major parks in the central beach area are open, some beach access points remain closed. Sabin advised visitors to check the county’s website before heading out. The county plans to repair beach parks where needed. Beachgoer Erin Dobrinski has noticed some of the damage but it's not stopping her from enjoying the beach. “You know down the Sebastian riverfront area down there there's a part of the sidewalk completely blocked off and if you peep around you can see it's all eroded,” Dobrinski said. Sabin said there are no current plans for another major sand project, but with more king tides expected, the county is closely monitoring the coast. There is good news for sea turtles, as Sabin reported that less than one percent of nests were affected by the erosion event. “They're resilient creatures. This is not their first rodeo. And they're going to continue doing what they do,” Sabin said. Erosion officials are asking the public to help protect the shoreline by picking up trash and debris. What residents described as 3 to 4 feet of floodwater currently covers parts of Hungryland Farms in the Trailside community, forcing cattle to wade and swim through submerged pastures in search of dry ground. "It's completely covered," Chirico said. they're all underwater."The flooding has left her animals without their primary food source and exposed them to potentially deadly hazards, including drowning, waterborne parasites and electrical dangers.Chirico pointed to an electrical transformer nearly submerged by floodwater, questioning whether her cattle could be electrocuted if they wandered too close.And despite the rain stopping, she said the water isn't draining — it's rising. "We always thought we were through because the rain had stopped, but the water kept rising," she said.For Trailside Homeowners Association President Kyla Shay, the flooding is the culmination of years of unresolved drainage concerns.In a 2018 letter obtained by WPTV, Shay warned homeowners that property south of Trailside had effectively become a reservoir, with water rising as much as 3.5 feet above community roads and breaching a berm — a raised barrier designed to control water flow.That same year, Shay contacted the South Florida Water Management District, warning that blocked drainage had left some pastures under 8 feet of water.She asked for help but says the underlying problems were never resolved."It's a combination of years of 'We'll get to it,' and we never got to it," Shay said.Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton acknowledges the community faces significant drainage challenges.Gorton said a berm breached Monday on the county-owned Elise J Property northeast of Trailside, sending water into a nearby canal, with some water backflowing into the community."We still can't get back to that breach," Gorton told investigative reporter Kate Hussey, explaining that high water levels have prevented crews from accessing the area.But the larger problem, he said, is Trailside's geography.The community is essentially a bathtub, surrounded by berms, hundreds of acres of wetlands and two independent water control districts.Water flows into the area, but there is only one drainage ditch for it to slowly escape."There's no easy way to get that water out except by pump or gravity," Gorton said.WPTV contacted engineer Bob Higgins, who works with both the Pal Mar Water Control District and the Hobe St. Lucie Conservancy District.Higgins said a potential solution had already been designed years ago: an outfall that would allow water to drain through the R G Mitigation Bank Preserve to the south and the neighboring Elise J property, which Martin County acquired in 2026. But that project was never built.When Hussey asked Gorton whether the county had been aware of the proposal, he confirmed officials had discussed it with the property's former owner."We did have some dialogue with the previous owner of Elise J about creating a formal water control structure that could discharge before the berms would breach," Gorton said.According to Gorton, the former owners submitted two permit applications to the South Florida Water Management District, but construction never began.WPTV contacted the former property owners, who said they did not know why the project was never completed.When Hussey reached out to the South Florida Water Management District, the agency said Trailside was outside its jurisdiction.However, Gorton said the district had permitted every property within Trailside and oversaw the proposed drainage project.Hussey followed up with the district, seeking clarification about its jurisdiction and asking why the drainage project was never constructed.The district has not responded to those follow-up questions.Despite the years of delays, Gorton said there may finally be a path forward."The good news is the county purchased that property, and it's our intent to bring that project forward," he said.Gorton said he has already requested the original permit applications in hopes of expediting approval — and construction— of the project.He also plans to return Friday to assess the flooding and determine what immediate relief may be possible."We're looking at ways to get the water out faster," he said.But for residents like Chirico, every additional day underwater carries a cost. "This could be a very costly natural disaster for us," she said.Her cattle still need to eat. Their pastures are submerged. And with no clear timeline for when the water will recede, the future of her farm remains uncertain."I don't have any food," Chirico said to her cows. "I'm sorry."For now, Hungryland Farms is living up to its name — and the families who depend on it are waiting for the water to go down.WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey continues to seek answers from the South Florida Water Management District about the proposed drainage project and why it was never completed.

She said family and friends usually enjoy bringing and preparing their own dishes. 'This is a great way to get everybody together and reduce the overall cost,' Woroch said.

entry.title: Businesses impacted by Military Trail closure after Learjet crash can apply for grants of up to $5,000
entry.summary: Starting Thursday, Palm Beach County is making $250,000 available to help businesses and nonprofits that lost revenue after the Nov. 1 Learjet crash forced the partial closure of Military Trail near Greenacres. The Palm Beach County Board of County Commissioners approved funding for the Military Trail Business Interruption Grant Program on Tuesday. County Administrator Joseph Abruzzo initially launched the program Nov. 2 under local emergency authority. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Businesses impacted by Learjet crash can apply for $5K grants Eligible businesses and nonprofits can receive a one-time grant of up to $5,000, while funding remains available. County officials said the closure of Military Trail near the crash site disrupted businesses by limiting access for customers and deliveries. The county's Department of Housing and Economic Development will administer the grants. Businesses can use the money for operating expenses including rent, payroll, utilities and essential inventory. PREVIOUS COVERAGE BELOW: $250K in grants for Palm Beach County businesses impacted by Learjet crash The county will use an applicant's latest filed business tax return to estimate revenue losses based on a 30-day interruption. Grants will be awarded on a first-come, first-served basis until the $250,000 is exhausted or all eligible applicants have been served. Who is eligible? The eligible area stretches along Military Trail from Broadway Street on the south to Kelly Drive and Sussex Avenue on the north. Businesses and nonprofits must have been operating at a physical location within the designated area before Nov. 1. Applicants must also certify that the road closure disrupted their operations or access and that they intend to continue or resume operations. The county will verify addresses using the official program map. How to apply Applications and full program criteria will be available Thursday, Nov. 12, on the Palm Beach County Department of Housing and Economic Development website. Applicants will need to submit: A signed application A W-9 Their latest filed business tax return Proof of the business address Photo identification for the authorized signer Applicable Sunbiz documentation A business tax receipt or documentation showing an exemption Awards are capped at $5,000 for each eligible business or nonprofit.

entry.article_text: Lucie has a permit allowing it to pump into the preserve, and Martin County leaders said there are not concrete regulation schedules governing the Savannas as a whole. That has raised a bigger question for local leaders: Who should be responsible for considering the consequences across the entire watershed? “I don’t know that we can modify their permit, but I would hope that we’d be able to look at that and say, you know, do no harm, which is really what kind of — or shared adversity, I think, is a better way to say it,” Gorton said. One potential solution discussed by Martin County officials would put management of the Savannas watershed under one overarching organization rather than relying on decisions made by individual jurisdictions. “Once we get that water out, there’s a larger discussion that we need to have, which is: What are we going to do to mitigate this in the future?” Gorton said.

entry.title: St. Lucie County rejects plan that could bring nearly 500 homes to low-lying site - WPEC
entry.summary: St. Lucie County rejects plan that could bring nearly 500 homes to low-lying site    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie County commissioners voted 3-2 to reject a land-use change for a roughly 34-acre property near South 25th Street and West Midway Road that could allow nearly 500 homes. The vote came as residents sought answers about recent flooding and commissioners questioned how the property handles drainage. An engineer said the property receives drainage from about 134 acres and uses a 24-inch pipe to direct water to nearby canals. Another pipe might be needed. The property sits lower than surrounding roads and would need to be raised for development, prompting concerns that construction could push water onto nearby properties. If designated for residential use, the site could allow up to 15 homes per acre, according to the discussion. County staff recommended approving the land-use change with adjustments to avoid or reduce impacts to wetlands and required buffers. Commissioners denied the request. See also: 77 homes hit by Martin County flooding. Where to get help now At the same meeting, residents from Creekside and White City asked commissioners to investigate last week’s flooding, identify who is responsible for local drainage systems, and explain how to prevent future flooding. I love my community, but it’s not fair that we’re suffering because nobody has taken the initiative to do what’s right for us, one resident said. Creekside residents called for an engineering review of the neighborhood and surrounding watershed, a reassessment of flood risk and a mitigation plan with deadlines. They also asked for a public meeting with county engineers and stormwater officials. White City residents described recurring flooding and called for drainage improvements and more stormwater storage. One resident said her home and yard had flooded four times since 2012. The county also made its emergency declaration official after days of heavy rain and flooding. It covers hazards including flooded roads and strained drainage systems.

entry.title: 'Quit is not an option': Fort Pierce woman loses house for a second time to a storm - WPBF
entry.summary: 'Quit is not an option': Fort Pierce woman loses house for a second time to a storm    WPBF
entry.article_text: A Fort Pierce woman is recovering from devastating flooding that destroyed her childhood home, marking the second time in two years she has lost everything. Terri Polk, who previously lost her home in the Spanish Lakes community to a tornado during Hurricane Milton, moved back into her childhood home to care for her mother, who has Alzheimer’s. Now, that home has been severely damaged by floodwaters. “The heart throb of our whole family is here,” Polk said. Polk shared that the house, built by her parents, has always been a central place for her family. “My mother’s door has always been open to everyone in the family,” she said. “This breaks your heart because I grew up in this house, I actually grew up here.” Last Monday, floodwaters rushed into the home, leaving behind destruction. “In the morning, the water was up to the tops of the beds,” Polk said. By the time the water receded, the damage was done. Polk’s belongings, including her bed and bookcases, now lie in a pile on the front lawn. Polk said she hasn’t slept in days as she tries to process the loss. The home is now filled with dehumidifiers, and Polk’s flood insurance won’t cover all the damages. Despite the challenges, she remains determined to rebuild. “No is not the answer; quit is not an option,” she said. “I’m not going to give up." entry.article_text: Yvette Drucker is beginning a new chapter in public service as Palm Beach County's new Clerk of the Circuit Court and Comptroller, taking over one of the county's most significant constitutional offices.Sworn in Tuesday, Drucker steps into the role following a turbulent period for the clerk's office under former Clerk Mike Caruso. She now oversees approximately 670 employees and an $87.4 million budget while serving as the county's chief financial officer, treasurer and auditor.WATCH REPORT BELOW: In an exclusive interview with WPTV's Joel Lopez, Drucker discussed her leadership priorities, her transition from Boca Raton City Council, questions about her experience and the future of the county's controversial investments in Israel bonds."It's a new day for the clerk's office. It's been a little bit of a challenging time for the individuals that work here. I have a phenomenal staff. They've kept it afloat, so my goal is to really listen, evaluate, and then execute what we can do to make it better," Drucker said.Drucker is the first Hispanic woman to hold the position of Palm Beach County clerk and comptroller.For her, the milestone carries personal significance. Her parents immigrated from Cuba in 1957, and she says her journey represents the American dream."It's really important to me because my parents are immigrants. I still have a living grandmother who's 91, and she's still here, and I am the American dream," she said.Drucker is also the first college graduate in her family. She credits her parents with instilling the values that helped shape her career."My parents didn't really have a lot of schooling. They had good work ethic and integrity. And they respected people, so really important for me to continue to inspire and lead in a way that others can look up to me and that they can also make their impact in the world."Her swearing-in ceremony was an especially meaningful moment, with her parents by her side."My mom held the Bible while I got sworn in. My dad anchored her to the left, and they're just so proud," Drucker said.She described the ceremony as a defining moment in both her professional and personal life."A surreal moment, but I took it all in. I've learned that you have to really be in the moment and be present," she said. "A really defining moment in my career and in my life."Drucker is no stranger to public service. She spent six years on the Boca Raton City Council, serving as deputy mayor and vice chair of the city's Community Redevelopment Agency before reaching her term limit."Six years you were with the City of Boca Raton, so why clerk of courts?" Lopez asked Drucker."I was term limited, so we do have term limits in the city, and after a couple of years, like about one year, a little over one year ago, I was just approached by a former clerk to look at this position," Drucker said. "I was not done with public service. I was born to serve, and I've been doing that since my student government days, back in high school and middle school."She said the clerk's position offered an opportunity to bring together her experience in business, government and community service."I have a background in human resources and out of corporate America, I worked for ADP TotalSource. I did 14 years there, so I also had an advocacy background and then my government. So it's a good way of marrying in my private sector with my public sector and my community service sector all in one," Drucker said.Although her time on the Boca Raton council ended, Drucker made clear that her commitment to public service had not.She said she wanted to finish her responsibilities in Boca Raton before beginning her new role, making sure the work she had started was completed.In the same week, she ended her time with Boca Raton and started with Palm Beach County, a process she said usually takes two months to transition."I pride myself with not missing meetings in six years and attending and participating, and I finished everything that I started," Drucker said.Drucker inherits an office with hundreds of employees and says she wants to build on the experience already in place while identifying opportunities to improve operations.Her message to employees is straightforward: public service must come before politics."This is a new day for this office. This office has been working, but we can make it work better for the people that we serve," she said. "I will stand by what I've been saying all along, people over politics, people over party, and definitely people over power, and that's just kind of the way that I've always led with a lot of heart. And a lot of integrity for the work that I do."Drucker says her first 100 days will focus on understanding how each department operates, reviewing the budget and identifying ways to make the office more efficient."I want to understand every department, their inner workings, the budget. We also have to understand Amendment 3, which obviously passed, and we have to respect the will of the voters and also just like I said earlier, listen, really evaluate and then execute how we're gonna serve the public," she said.She also emphasized the importance of putting the right people in the right positions."This is a public-facing operation. It's really important for me to have the right people in the right places so that we can continue serving the public," Drucker said.While some have questioned whether her background adequately prepares her for the office's court administration, accounting and auditing responsibilities, Drucker acknowledged she does not expect to know everything immediately."We have a chief of legal, runs the operations and we have subject matter experts and I'm not gonna tell you that I know everything on day one," she said. "But the way that I operate and the way that I've conducted myself throughout the city and throughout my career, I will learn as needed and will make changes as needed."She says she plans to rely on the office's existing leadership and experienced employees as she continues the transition. She recently hired her chief of staff and also the executive administrator to the clerk, but those names have not been made public."Also, this office has a deputy clerk who is interim clerk, Ms. Shannon Ramsey-Chessman, who's been incredible, and she has institutional data, and I believe that we're going to be a great team as we, you know, continue to take one day at a time."One of the biggest questions facing Drucker, who identified herself as Jewish, is the county's investment in Israel bonds.Palm Beach County has approximately $1 billion invested in the bonds, making it the largest investor in the world. The investment became a point of controversy during the campaign, and Drucker had previously expressed support for it.Now in office, she says she plans to take another look at the county's investment strategy, particularly following the passage of Amendment 3.Asked whether she still supports the county investing in Israeli bonds, Drucker said investment decisions must ultimately serve taxpayers."So I say to the public, like any investment portfolio, whether you have your own or you're overseeing an investment portfolio of this size, you always have to evaluate and make sure that your investments are aligned with what is best for the taxpayer base," she said.Drucker said the bonds have served the county well up to this point, but that does not mean the investment should go without review."And now with Amendment 3 passing, we really need to evaluate, and that's something that I'm gonna sit with our director of finance and with our county administrator," she said.She stopped short of committing to either maintaining or eliminating the investment."It's not a yes or a no; it's just, does it continue to make sense? Is this something that we have to evaluate and we always have to evaluate how we invest and how we are using the taxpayer dollar is important."When asked whether she would consider reducing or eliminating the investment if it no longer made financial sense, Drucker said the county would have to evaluate that possibility."Is it safe to say if it didn't make sense, you'd be willing to reduce, if not potentially eliminate this investment?" asked Lopez."If it didn't make sense, we would have to evaluate, correct," said Drucker.She also pointed out that Israel bonds make up only part of the county's broader investment portfolio."Even though we have a large amount in Israel bonds, we have a large portfolio. Seventy-five percent of our portfolio is not invested in Israel bonds," she said.For Drucker, the next step is making sure residents understand how the county's investments work and what they mean for the community."I think education is gonna go a long way," she said.She also pushed back on making the issue political, saying the focus should remain on the county's financial interests and the taxpayers who depend on those investments."I think we're going to leave politics out of it. It's not a political discussion. I think it's really, what are the returns to help the county?" Drucker said.She plans to meet with county officials and review the investment portfolio before making any decisions.Drucker says the transition has been busy, but she is encouraged by the employees already in place and the team she is building around her.She has brought on a chief of staff and an executive administrator to help guide her through the responsibilities of the office.She also thanked the voters and supporters who helped bring her into the position, including those who crossed party lines."I'm just really excited to be here. I think that we're gonna have this office is going to continue to produce amazing things for this community. I'm just so honored," she said. "And I'm just so proud to represent this office, and I really look forward to everything that we have to do."As she begins her tenure, Drucker says her commitment is to serve everyone in Palm Beach County, regardless of political affiliation."This office is here to serve everybody regardless of who and what you are; that's my promise to them," she said.And as for what comes next, Drucker has a simple message:"The best is yet to come, and I believe that," Drucker said.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: Milagro Center and United Way are making holidays brighter in Delray Beach

entry.summary: What was once a sprawling cattle pasture in western Martin County now looks more like a lake. What residents described as 3 to 4 feet of floodwater currently covers parts of Hungryland Farms in the Trailside community, forcing cattle to wade and swim through submerged pastures in search of dry ground. Documents obtained by WPTV show residents raised concerns about drainage problems long before last week's historic rainfall inundated the Treasure Coast. Now, with the rain gone but the water lingering, residents are questioning whether the devastation could have been prevented. 'All of our pastures ... they're all underwater' Melissa, who raises grass-fed cattle at Hungryland Farms in the rural Trailside community, says the flooding has transformed her property almost overnight. above community roads and breaching a berm — a raised barrier designed to control water flow.That same year, Shay contacted the South Florida Water Management District, warning that blocked drainage had left some pastures under 8 feet of water.She asked for help but says the underlying problems were never resolved."It's a combination of years of 'We'll get to it,' and we never got to it," Shay said.Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton acknowledges the community faces significant drainage challenges.Gorton said a berm breached Monday on the county-owned Elise J Property northeast of Trailside, sending water into a nearby canal, with some water backflowing into the community."We still can't get back to that breach," Gorton told investigative reporter Kate Hussey, explaining that high water levels have prevented crews from accessing the area.But the larger problem, he said, is Trailside's geography.The community is essentially a bathtub, surrounded by berms, hundreds of acres of wetlands and two independent water control districts.Water flows into the area, but there is only one drainage ditch for it to slowly escape."There's no easy way to get that water out except by pump or gravity," Gorton said.WPTV contacted engineer Bob Higgins, who works with both the Pal Mar Water Control District and the Hobe St. Lucie Conservancy District.Higgins said a potential solution had already been designed years ago: an outfall that would allow water to drain through the R G Mitigation Bank Preserve to the south and the neighboring Elise J property, which Martin County acquired in 2026. But that project was never built.When Hussey asked Gorton whether the county had been aware of the proposal, he confirmed officials had discussed it with the property's former owner."We did have some dialogue with the previous owner of Elise J about creating a formal water control structure that could discharge before the berms would breach," Gorton said.According to Gorton, the former owners submitted two permit applications to the South Florida Water Management District, but construction never began.WPTV contacted the former property owners, who said they did not know why the project was never completed.When Hussey reached out to the South Florida Water Management District, the agency said Trailside was outside its jurisdiction.However, Gorton said the district had permitted every property within Trailside and oversaw the proposed drainage project.Hussey followed up with the district, seeking clarification about its jurisdiction and asking why the drainage project was never constructed.The district has not responded to those follow-up questions.Despite the years of delays, Gorton said there may finally be a path forward."The good news is the county purchased that property, and it's our intent to bring that project forward," he said.Gorton said he has already requested the original permit applications in hopes of expediting approval — and construction— of the project.He also plans to return Friday to assess the flooding and determine what immediate relief may be possible."We're looking at ways to get the water out faster," he said.But for residents like Melissa, every additional day underwater carries a cost. "This could be a very costly natural disaster for us," she said.Her cattle still need to eat. Their pastures are submerged. entry.title: Martin County firefighters raise staffing concerns after it says hiring class canceled - WPEC
entry.summary: Martin County firefighters raise staffing concerns after it says hiring class canceled    WPEC
entry.article_text: The Martin County Firefighters Union is asking county leaders to reconsider canceling a firefighter hiring class planned for January, saying the department is already short-staffed and the loss of new hires could increase pressure on crews. In a Facebook post, the union said the county canceled the class, which was expected to bring about 25 firefighters into Martin County Fire Rescue . The county cited budget concerns tied to Amendment 3 , according to the union. The union said the department is 17 firefighters short now and could be about 25 short by January as employees retire or leave for other departments. Fewer firefighters mean fewer available personnel to respond to emergencies, increased reliance on mandatory and voluntary overtime, and greater demands placed on the firefighters who remain, the union wrote. The union said its members recently agreed to forgo negotiating a new contract that would have taken effect in October, giving up a cost-of-living pay adjustment to help the county address financial challenges. It said members did so after being assured that Fire Rescue would not be affected by hiring freezes tied to Amendment 3. See also: Bobcat rescued after getting caught in barbed-wire fence near Stuart The union also questioned county administrative pay increases, saying administrative employees received 6% raises in October while firefighters face staffing shortages. The post calls on the Board of County Commissioners and county administrator to move forward with the hiring class. The county was not quoted in the union’s post. Martin County is taking a measured approach to hiring as it evaluates its long-term financial outlook and operational needs. With rising operating costs, inflation, and potential revenue impacts following the passage of Amendment 3 and anticipated SAFER Grant repayment obligations in the upcoming budget cycle, the County is being mindful of additional staffing commitments. While the firefighter recruitment class was planned months before Amendment 3 passed, current fiscal considerations have prompted a review of future hiring. The County is currently taking a soft hiring freeze approach, carefully evaluating vacancies and staffing needs. Maintaining public safety remains a priority for Martin County," the County said in a statement.

entry.title: St. Lucie County shelter waives adoption fees after taking in 114 cats from alleged hoarding case
entry.summary: A St. Lucie County animal shelter is urgently seeking homes for cats and kittens after taking in more than 100 animals from a home last month. The Humane Society of St. Lucie County is teaming up with BISSELL Pet Foundation for an emergency 'Empty the Shelters' adoption event on Nov. 13 and 14. Adoption fees will be waived for all cats and kittens during the two-day event. WATCH REPORT BELOW: St. Lucie County shelter waives adoption fees after taking in 114 cats The shelter says it's facing a capacity crunch after taking in 114 cats from a Port St. Lucie home in October. The cats were rescued from a home at the center of an alleged animal hoarding case that led to a woman's arrest on 29 felony animal cruelty charges. Now, the Humane Society is hoping the adoption event will free up much-needed space so it can continue caring for the animals. All pets available for adoption are spayed or neutered, vaccinated and microchipped. The event runs from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. on Friday, Nov. 13, and Saturday, Nov. 14, at the Humane Society of St. Lucie County, located at 8890 Glades Cut-Off Road in Port St. Lucie. Anyone interested in adopting can view available pets at hsslc.org .

entry.title: After magical season, Park Vista High School bowling finishes in the top 5 in Florida
entry.summary: In life, we all start somewhere, and for a group of kids, AMF Bowling Alley in Boynton Beach is where it all began. 'I started at a Saturday league here at AMF probably when I was 12,' Jett Kramer, a sophomore bowler at Park Vista High School, said. 'My aunt showed me a youth league here, so I started doing it and have been doing it for five years now,' Mateo Ruiz, a junior bowler at Park Vista High School, said. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Park Vista HS bowling team finishes top five in the state Both young men met at the bowling lanes at AMF as kids and have now forged a deep bond at Park Vista High School. In fact, they're not the only two bowlers from the school who love AMF Bowling; the entire team does. It's their practice court, and it's also the place they knew this year would be special. 'Last year we also had a great team, so I knew our team this year would be just as good if not better,' said Kramer. So, how good were they this year? The team won both the county championship and district championship and qualified for state. 'That was pretty good considering we didn't make it last year; that was pretty much an upset,' co-captain Nate Banks said. 'It was awesome. We all bowled great. We had a phenomenal season; everyone bonded together. It was a phenomenal season,' co-captain Jordan Fein said. The team was on fire all season and finished fifth at state. While it wasn't the finish they'd hoped for, it was a building block for next season. Ruiz finished as a state runner-up. 'It was definitely an amazing moment. I wish I could've gotten first, but I appreciate getting there,' Ruiz said.

entry.title: Riviera Beach's Lone Pine community faces devastation after historic flooding
entry.summary: Residents of Riviera Beach's Lone Pine community are confronting the aftermath of devastating flooding, with gutted homes, piles of belongings lining neighborhood streets and families struggling to figure out what comes next. A week after floodwaters forced residents from their homes, the damage is becoming clearer, leaving some without flood insurance and questioning whether they can afford to rebuild. The flooding has turned once-familiar homes into cleanup projects and left residents facing the loss of belongings, memories and, in some cases, their sense of security. Thomas walked Hoffman through her damaged home, where much of her belongings had been removed and left in piles along the curb. 'I'm all alone. And all my life saving is on the sidewalk,' Thomas said. She described being trapped inside her home as floodwaters rose around her. entry.title: 'Bigger than ourselves': Florida Panthers host military appreciation night
entry.summary: Throughout the season, the Florida Panthers host themed nights at some home games. On Thursday, the Cats hosted the Detroit Red Wings for military appreciation night. Despite trailing most of the game, the Florida Panthers pulled off an epic third-period comeback. The Cats tied it up at 4 apiece, then scored in the final minutes to take the lead and send Detroit home with a loss. Watch report from Eleanor Sheahan: 'Bigger than ourselves': Florida Panthers host military appreciation night The Panthers beat the Red Wings 5-4 for their military appreciation game. Outside Amerant Bank Arena, members of the United States Coast Guard and Army welcomed fans before puck drop. Inside, military members and their families got early access to Pantherland for a first look at military appreciation merch. Then on the rink, the Panthers recognized retired Army veteran Joe St. John as their Heroes Among Us honoree of the night. Another army veteran at the game was Scott Sloane. As you get older and you recognize what you did and people serving today and what it takes to service and the sacrifice it takes and then people appreciating that, that's a warm feeling, that really makes you look back at your life a little bit and your service., Sloane said. Sloane is a part of the Panthers Warriors, a hockey club for disabled us military veterans who have served our country and want to play hockey. When you leave the military, some of us lose that camaraderie, and so we have to bring it back, and we do it through this organization, Sloane said. Panthers Warriors started in 2019. Sloane said they play in tournaments and, over the years, have built a strong community that combines veterans and Panther fans. On Thursday Sloane was among the many veterans cheering on the cats. Thank you for your service as well, like hockey it brings us together. It's a collaborative thing. All the military branches work together so that's what we learned from a young age, a collaborative environment and being a part of something bigger than ourselves, Sloane said. The Panthers Warriors are always looking for more players. To learn more, visit their Instagram @ pantherswarriorshockey . The Florida Panthers begin another road trip; they head to St. Louis to play the Blues.

entry.title: Fort Pierce mom demands answers after video shows moments before daughter’s death - WPEC
entry.summary: Fort Pierce mom demands answers after video shows moments before daughter’s death    WPEC
entry.article_text: A Fort Pierce mother is speaking out after watching body camera footage of the night her 19-year-old daughter was fatally shot in Fort Lauderdale near an Airbnb. She believes her daughter was asking police for help and wants to know whether the officers who first responded could have done more. I already knew half of what happened, and to see it and to hear it was heartbreaking, said Alacia Ford-Barron, the mother of Myrah Zeigler. She shared the video with CBS12 News. The body camera video shows officers arriving after an altercation involving two groups of women inside the Airbnb. Officers tell everyone to leave. Ford-Barron says her daughter had been attacked and that belongings, including car keys, were taken. The group needed to retrieve those items from a nearby park. In the footage, Zeigler asks officers to walk with the group to get their belongings. One officer asks whether they have a way to get to the park. Zeigler responds that they can. Ford-Barron says she believed officers were going to help. Minutes later, gunfire erupts nearby. An officer reports that shots were fired two blocks away. Friends can be heard screaming as officers try to revive Zeigler. She later died at a nearby hospital. See also: FDOT reopens all lanes on SR 809 and Military Trail after deadly Learjet 60 crash I wanted to know why they didn't call backup. I wanted to know why she did not listen to my daughter when she was trying to explain to her and asking her to walk down to the park, Ford-Barron said. Larry Lamar Smith was later arrested in connection with Zeigler’s death. Ford-Barron says she appreciates the detectives’ work but still has questions about the initial police response. I have to be my daughter's voice. I know that if I shut down, who's going to speak for my daughter? CBS12 News is waiting to hear back from Fort Lauderdale police.

entry.title: More people, limited freshwater: Treasure Coast plans for water needs through 2050 - WPEC
entry.summary: More people, limited freshwater: Treasure Coast plans for water needs through 2050    WPEC
entry.article_text: As the Treasure Coast prepares for decades of growth, water managers face a critical question: How will the region supply enough freshwater for more people while protecting the farms, waterways and wildlife that also depend on it? Water is a necessity that is being planned for at all times, years in advance. With the explosive growth in population unfolding now, the plan is even more critical. The South Florida Water Management District’s 2026 Upper East Coast Water Supply Plan looks ahead to 2050, outlining future needs in Martin and St. Lucie counties and northeastern Okeechobee County. The district says the region’s limited freshwater resources make conservation and alternative water supplies essential to planning for that growth. What we’re seeing is about a 36-percent increase in the population in the planning area by 2050, said Carolina Maran, Chief of District Resiliency with SFWMD, describing a population approaching three-quarters of a million people. The demand for water, however, is not necessarily increasing at the same rate, Maran says. Demand for water supplied to homes and businesses, along with commercial, landscaping, and recreational uses, is expected to rise. Agricultural water use, which is the region’s largest category, is projected to decline. See also: WPB police ask public for information on sidewalk assault outside Hook Fish and Chicken Meeting the shifting needs will depend on more than population forecasts. It will also require infrastructure, efficient water use, and planning for uncertain conditions, including drought and storms. Inside a University of Florida laboratory in Fort Pierce, Dr. Sandra Guzman and her team study how water moves through soil and across different land uses. Guzman is an Associate Professor of Smart Irrigation and Hydrology with the UF/IFAS Agricultural and Biological Engineering department. A demonstration table with sand and simulated farm fields shows how water’s movement changes depending on the ground beneath it. In another area, there are charts demonstrating how immediate communication can connect area farmers with real-time agriculture and weather data. I always tell my team: water is a blessing and a curse, Guzman said. The challenge is not simply whether water is available. Its quality also determines how it can be used. We suffer from a lot of issues regarding deficit of water because it’s not only the volume of water; it’s also the quality of water, Guzman said. That creates a balancing act: supplying people and farms while protecting the lagoons, estuaries, and wildlife that depend on the region’s water resources. The district’s approach includes alternative water sources, expanded treatment and storage, and conservation. What that means is that investing in reuse, investing in efficient water uses, and also alternative water sources like the Floridan Aquifer, Maran said. Projects described in the plan include reverse-osmosis treatment, reclaimed-water expansions, and stormwater storage. In coming years, some of the infrastructure needed to support future demand must still be built. SFWMD describes the plan as a framework for local governments, utilities, agricultural operations, and other water users to guide water supply decisions. Its recommendations are intended to inform local comprehensive plans, facility work plans and ordinances. Having a plan, however, does not guarantee that every project will be completed on time. Carrying it out will require follow-through by the communities and water providers preparing for growth. On farms, part of the solution is knowing more precisely when crops need water, and how much of it. Guzman’s team works on tools that help farmers measure soil moisture and irrigate more efficiently, directing water where crops need it. The research connects decisions made in the field to the broader challenge of stretching the region’s water supply. So, in this lab, we work for that: every single drop of water that is coming out of whatever aquifer or freshwater system becomes food to your table, Guzman said. As the Treasure Coast grows, its water future will depend both on the infrastructure communities build and on how efficiently people use the supplies already available. entry.title: 'It feels like Lake Okeechobee': Martin County community underwater after years of drainage concerns
entry.summary: What was once a sprawling cattle pasture in western Martin County now looks more like a lake. What residents described as 3 to 4 feet of floodwater currently covers parts of Hungryland Farms in the Trailside community, forcing cattle to wade and swim through submerged pastures in search of dry ground. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Martin County community underwater after years of drainage concerns But for the families who live and work there, the flooding is more than a natural disaster. They say it's a crisis years in the making one they warned officials about as far back as 2018. Documents obtained by WPTV show residents raised concerns about drainage problems long before last week's historic rainfall inundated the Treasure Coast. Now, with the rain gone but the water lingering, residents are questioning whether the devastation could have been prevented. 'All of our pastures ... they're all underwater' Melissa, who raises grass-fed cattle at Hungryland Farms in the rural Trailside community, says the flooding has transformed her property almost overnight. 'It feels like Lake Okeechobee,' she said. Her cattle, accustomed to grazing freely across the farm, are now navigating deep floodwater. 'It's completely covered,' Melissa said. 'All of our pastures ... they're all underwater.' The flooding has left her animals without their primary food source and exposed them to potentially deadly hazards, including drowning, waterborne parasites and electrical dangers. Melissa pointed to an electrical transformer nearly submerged by floodwater, questioning whether her cattle could be electrocuted if they wandered too close. And despite the rain stopping, she said the water isn't draining it's rising. 'We always thought we were through because the rain had stopped, but the water kept rising,' she said. Warnings dating back to 2018 For Trailside Homeowners Association President Kyla Shay, the flooding is the culmination of years of unresolved drainage concerns.
