They say it's a crisis years in the making — one they warned officials about as far back as 2018.Documents obtained by WPTV show residents raised concerns about drainage problems long before last week's historic rainfall inundated the Treasure Coast.Now, with the rain gone but the water lingering, residents are questioning whether the devastation could have been prevented.Melissa, who raises grass-fed cattle at Hungryland Farms in the rural Trailside community, says the flooding has transformed her property almost overnight."It feels like Lake Okeechobee," she said.Her cattle, accustomed to grazing freely across the farm, are now navigating deep floodwater. "It's completely covered," Melissa said. they're all underwater."The flooding has left her animals without their primary food source and exposed them to potentially deadly hazards, including drowning, waterborne parasites and electrical dangers.Melissa pointed to an electrical transformer nearly submerged by floodwater, questioning whether her cattle could be electrocuted if they wandered too close.And despite the rain stopping, she said the water isn't draining — it's rising. "We always thought we were through because the rain had stopped, but the water kept rising," she said.For Trailside Homeowners Association President Kyla Shay, the flooding is the culmination of years of unresolved drainage concerns.In a 2018 letter obtained by WPTV, Shay warned homeowners that property south of Trailside had effectively become a reservoir, with water rising as much as 3.5 feet above community roads and breaching a berm — a raised barrier designed to control water flow.That same year, Shay contacted the South Florida Water Management District, warning that blocked drainage had left some pastures under 8 feet of water.She asked for help but says the underlying problems were never resolved."It's a combination of years of 'We'll get to it,' and we never got to it," Shay said.Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton acknowledges the community faces significant drainage challenges.Gorton said a berm breached Monday on the county-owned Elise J Property northeast of Trailside, sending water into a nearby canal, with some water backflowing into the community."We still can't get back to that breach," Gorton told investigative reporter Kate Hussey, explaining that high water levels have prevented crews from accessing the area.But the larger problem, he said, is Trailside's geography.The community is essentially a bathtub, surrounded by berms, hundreds of acres of wetlands and two independent water control districts.Water flows into the area, but there is only one drainage ditch for it to slowly escape."There's no easy way to get that water out except by pump or gravity," Gorton said.WPTV contacted engineer Bob Higgins, who works with both the Pal Mar Water Control District and the Hobe St. Lucie Conservancy District.Higgins said a potential solution had already been designed years ago: an outfall that would allow water to drain through the R G Mitigation Bank Preserve to the south and the neighboring Elise J property, which Martin County acquired in 2026. But that project was never built.When Hussey asked Gorton whether the county had been aware of the proposal, he confirmed officials had discussed it with the property's former owner."We did have some dialogue with the previous owner of Elise J about creating a formal water control structure that could discharge before the berms would breach," Gorton said.According to Gorton, the former owners submitted two permit applications to the South Florida Water Management District, but construction never began.WPTV contacted the former property owners, who said they did not know why the project was never completed.When Hussey reached out to the South Florida Water Management District, the agency said Trailside was outside its jurisdiction.However, Gorton said the district had permitted every property within Trailside and oversaw the proposed drainage project.Hussey followed up with the district, seeking clarification about its jurisdiction and asking why the drainage project was never constructed.The district has not responded to those follow-up questions.Despite the years of delays, Gorton said there may finally be a path forward."The good news is the county purchased that property, and it's our intent to bring that project forward," he said.Gorton said he has already requested the original permit applications in hopes of expediting approval — and construction— of the project.He also plans to return Friday to assess the flooding and determine what immediate relief may be possible."We're looking at ways to get the water out faster," he said.But for residents like Melissa, every additional day underwater carries a cost. "This could be a very costly natural disaster for us," she said.Her cattle still need to eat. Their pastures are submerged. And with no clear timeline for when the water will recede, the future of her farm remains uncertain."I don't have any food," Melissa said to her cows. "I'm sorry."For now, Hungryland Farms is living up to its name — and the families who depend on it are waiting for the water to go down.WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey continues to seek answers from the South Florida Water Management District about the proposed drainage project and why it was never completed.

entry.title: 'Did its job': Indian River County beaches recovering after erosion from nor’easter and King Tides - WPBF
entry.summary: 'Did its job': Indian River County beaches recovering after erosion from nor’easter and King Tides    WPBF
entry.article_text: Indian River County beaches are recovering after a nor’easter and king tides caused erosion along the coastline, with officials noting improvements in shoreline conditions. Erosion officials said water levels had risen almost as high as a sign at Tracking Station Beach, but the sand has already begun shifting back into place. Waves and high water significantly impacted the county’s coastline. “This is a great example of coastal resistance at work,” officials said. Johnnie Sabin, a coastal specialist with Indian River County’s Department of Natural Resources, said the shoreline at Tracking Station Beach is already showing signs of recovery. “Much of the sand we placed on the beach, while it shifted briefly, has already been returning. I mean, these beaches, these berms, there's a lot more space. They're a little higher, a little wider so folks aren't in jeopardy to visit the beaches anymore,” Sabin said. Sabin explained that Tracking Station Beach experienced five to ten feet of erosion. He credited dune plants for helping hold the sand together and said the county’s Sector Five Beach Restoration Project performed as expected. “Luckily because of the sand being there, it buffered all private properties, the roads, all the infrastructure we care about and it did its job,” Sabin said. While major parks in the central beach area are open, some beach access points remain closed. Sabin advised visitors to check the county’s website before heading out. The county plans to repair beach parks where needed. Beachgoer Erin Dobrinski has noticed some of the damage but it's not stopping her from enjoying the beach. “You know down the Sebastian riverfront area down there there's a part of the sidewalk completely blocked off and if you peep around you can see it's all eroded,” Dobrinski said. Sabin said there are no current plans for another major sand project, but with more king tides expected, the county is closely monitoring the coast. There is good news for sea turtles, as Sabin reported that less than one percent of nests were affected by the erosion event. “They're resilient creatures. This is not their first rodeo. And they're going to continue doing what they do,” Sabin said. Erosion officials are asking the public to help protect the shoreline by picking up trash and debris. entry.title: Community gathers to begin cleanup as Jensen Beach flooding slowly recedes - WPBF
entry.summary: Community gathers to begin cleanup as Jensen Beach flooding slowly recedes    WPBF
entry.article_text: After more than a week of standing floodwater, some residents near Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach are finally beginning to clean up their homes as water slowly recedes. Martin County began pumping water out of the neighborhood Monday, allowing some homeowners to begin assessing the damage. For Lisa French, the receding water means she can finally begin the difficult work of cleaning out her home. “I mean, we’ve been underwater for a week,” French said. When WPBF 25 News visited French’s home several days ago, water was still standing inside, reaching more than a foot deep in some rooms. CLICK HERE FOR INFORMATION ON HOW TO DONATE TO THE FRENCH FAMILY Now, the water is gone, but much of what she owns has been destroyed. Since early Wednesday morning, French, her husband and several neighbors have been removing damaged drywall, tearing out the kitchen and carrying ruined furniture and belongings into the front yard. “You know, you’re sitting there with your house full of water, sitting in the fact that you lost your entire home. But now we can actually move and work instead of think,” French said. While French has begun cleaning up, other residents are still waiting for floodwaters to recede. Susan Destafney, who has lived in the neighborhood for four decades, said she has never experienced anything like it. “We’ve lived in our home for 40 years. We’ve never seen the likes of this,” Destafney said. Community volunteers have also stepped in to help, including Alaura Macpherson, who runs the local group Quit Messen With Jensen. Macpherson said volunteers have been collecting cleaning supplies and other necessities for affected families. She is also organizing a community fundraiser and meal on Nov. 25 to raise money for flood victims. Local restaurants are expected to donate food, while the event will also serve as a resource center connecting residents with contractors, cleanup services and other recovery assistance. “The community is what helps each other. We are a family,” Macpherson said. Martin County officials have opened a Multi-Agency Resource Center at the Hoke Library in Jensen Beach to connect flood victims with recovery assistance. The northbound entrance ramp from Indrio Road was closed, according to Florida 511. Lucie County, the northbound I-95 entrance ramp from Exit 138 at Indrio Road was also closed. An alert reported emergency vehicles at the ramp as of 5:42 a.m. The Indian River County crash was first reported at 10:42 p.m. The alerts did not provide information about injuries or what caused the crash.

entry.summary: A law enforcement investigation has shut down both directions of Interstate 95 in Indian River County early Friday morning, creating a major traffic disruption for drivers near the Indian River-St. Lucie county line. The closure begins near mile marker 141, according to Florida 511 traffic cams. The Indian River County Sheriff's Office said the highway is closed due to a law enforcement investigation. All northbound and southbound lanes of I-95 are closed at this time. The southbound entrance ramp at Oslo Road is also shut down. Northbound drivers were being directed off I-95 at Indrio Road, while southbound drivers were being directed to exit at Oslo Road. The northbound entrance ramp from Indrio Road is also closed. The crash was initially reported at around 10:45 p.m. Thursday. Authorities have not released information about possible injuries or what led to the crash. WPTV is working to learn more about the investigation and when the interstate could reopen.

entry.title: Community gathers to begin cleanup as Jensen Beach flooding slowly recedes - WPBF
entry.summary: Community gathers to begin cleanup as Jensen Beach flooding slowly recedes    WPBF
entry.article_text: After more than a week of standing floodwater, some residents near Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach are finally beginning to clean up their homes as water slowly recedes. Martin County began pumping water out of the neighborhood Monday, allowing some homeowners to begin assessing the damage. For Lisa French, the receding water means she can finally begin the difficult work of cleaning out her home. “I mean, we’ve been underwater for a week,” French said. When WPBF 25 News visited French’s home several days ago, water was still standing inside, reaching more than a foot deep in some rooms. CLICK HERE FOR INFORMATION ON HOW TO DONATE TO THE FRENCH FAMILY Now, the water is gone, but much of what she owns has been destroyed. Since early Wednesday morning, French, her husband and several neighbors have been removing damaged drywall, tearing out the kitchen and carrying ruined furniture and belongings into the front yard. “You know, you’re sitting there with your house full of water, sitting in the fact that you lost your entire home. But now we can actually move and work instead of think,” French said. While French has begun cleaning up, other residents are still waiting for floodwaters to recede. Susan Destafney, who has lived in the neighborhood for four decades, said she has never experienced anything like it. “We’ve lived in our home for 40 years. We’ve never seen the likes of this,” Destafney said. Community volunteers have also stepped in to help, including Alaura Macpherson, who runs the local group Quit Messen With Jensen. Macpherson said volunteers have been collecting cleaning supplies and other necessities for affected families. She is also organizing a community fundraiser and meal on Nov. 25 to raise money for flood victims. Local restaurants are expected to donate food, while the event will also serve as a resource center connecting residents with contractors, cleanup services and other recovery assistance. “The community is what helps each other. We are a family,” Macpherson said. Martin County officials have opened a Multi-Agency Resource Center at the Hoke Library in Jensen Beach to connect flood victims with recovery assistance. entry.title: Fort Pierce mom demands answers after video shows moments before daughter’s death - WPEC
entry.summary: Fort Pierce mom demands answers after video shows moments before daughter’s death    WPEC
entry.article_text: A Fort Pierce mother is speaking out after watching body camera footage of the night her 19-year-old daughter was fatally shot in Fort Lauderdale near an Airbnb. She believes her daughter was asking police for help and wants to know whether the officers who first responded could have done more. I already knew half of what happened, and to see it and to hear it was heartbreaking, said Alacia Ford-Barron, the mother of Myrah Zeigler. She shared the video with CBS12 News. The body camera video shows officers arriving after an altercation involving two groups of women inside the Airbnb. Officers tell everyone to leave. Ford-Barron says her daughter had been attacked and that belongings, including car keys, were taken. The group needed to retrieve those items from a nearby park. In the footage, Zeigler asks officers to walk with the group to get their belongings. One officer asks whether they have a way to get to the park. Zeigler responds that they can. Ford-Barron says she believed officers were going to help. Minutes later, gunfire erupts nearby. An officer reports that shots were fired two blocks away. Friends can be heard screaming as officers try to revive Zeigler. She later died at a nearby hospital. See also: FDOT reopens all lanes on SR 809 and Military Trail after deadly Learjet 60 crash I wanted to know why they didn't call backup. I wanted to know why she did not listen to my daughter when she was trying to explain to her and asking her to walk down to the park, Ford-Barron said. Larry Lamar Smith was later arrested in connection with Zeigler’s death. Ford-Barron says she appreciates the detectives’ work but still has questions about the initial police response. I have to be my daughter's voice. I know that if I shut down, who's going to speak for my daughter? CBS12 News did not receive a response from Fort Lauderdale Police before publication. Update : In a statement provided Friday, the department said it remains saddened by the loss of Myrah Zeigler and extends its condolences to her family and loved ones. Police said the lead detective has maintained regular communication with the family and encouraged any concerns about the handling of the case to be addressed directly with the department through its established complaint process. The department declined an interview, citing the active and ongoing investigation.

entry.title: Florida flooding survivors praise heroes who came to their aid
entry.summary: From high-water rescues to the heroes who live next door, people are sharing their stories about the good Samaritans who came to their aid during the recent floods that ravaged our area. Tessie Watts from Riviera Beach says first responders and the mayor of her city pulled her to safety after she fled her home and more than 20 inches of water. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Heroes emerge after historic flooding swamps Palm Beach County, Treasure Coast Nicole Vazquez from Fort Pierce shared with WPTV anchor Hollani Davis that her brother is her hero. She said he helped the family sandbag their home before leaving, then came back by boat to get them out. 'He left, and he came back Tuesday to evacuate us, and then we took shelter with him that night,' says Vazquez. The selfless acts stretched to West Palm Beach, where Miles Bradford and his friend jumped in to help stranded drivers. 'If it was me, I would want someone to get out there and help me,' says Bradford. Long after the water is gone, even though there will undoubtedly be more tough days ahead, it's these acts of kindness that people say they'll remember.

entry.title: FHP trooper-involved shooting incident shuts down I-95 in Indian River County
entry.summary: Interstate 95 in Indian River County is shut down in both directions early Friday morning, creating a major traffic disruption for drivers near the Indian River-St. Lucie County line. On Nov. 12, around 11:20 p.m., FHP said a trooper was involved in a shooting incident on I-95 near mile marker 141. According to FHP, the incident began when the trooper initiated a traffic stop, and the suspect fled, resulting in a pursuit. The pursuit escalated and turned into a gunfire exchange between the trooper and the suspect. Authorities said no troopers were injured during the shooting. FHP said the suspect sustained injuries from what appeared to be a self-inflicted gunshot wound and was pronounced dead at the scene. The Indian River County Sheriff's Office said the highway is closed due to the ongoing investigation. All northbound and southbound lanes of I-95 are closed at this time. The southbound entrance ramp at Oslo Road is also shut down. Northbound drivers were being directed off I-95 at Indrio Road, while southbound drivers were being directed to exit at Oslo Road. The northbound entrance ramp from Indrio Road is also closed. Officials said all body cam and dash cam video will be reviewed during the investigation. The FDLE will take over as the lead on the investigation. WPTV is working to learn more about when the interstate could reopen.

entry.title: Boca Helping Hands aims to provide Thanksgiving meals for more than 4,000 Palm Beach County families
entry.summary: Boca Helping Hands is asking the community to help provide Thanksgiving meals for more than 4,000 Palm Beach County families through its annual Thanksgiving Box Brigade . The nonprofit is asking donors to contribute $29.72, the cost of a Thanksgiving box that helps provide families facing food insecurity with the ingredients for a holiday meal. WATCH REPORT BELOW: What can a $30 Thanksgiving box become? For families already stretching household budgets, Boca Helping Hands CEO Dr. Andrew Hagen said the added cost of Thanksgiving can make the holiday particularly difficult. 'You know this has been a tough year for a lot of people economically, and we want to make sure they have a good Thanksgiving,' Hagen said. Boca Helping Hands plans to distribute turkeys and Thanksgiving meal boxes to current Pantry Bag Program clients Nov. 21 and 22 at five drive-thru locations in East Boca Raton, West Boca Raton, Delray Beach, Boynton Beach and Lake Worth Beach. Volunteers pack thousands of Thanksgiving boxes Preparing thousands of Thanksgiving meals requires plenty of hands. Volunteers gathered at the Boca Helping Hands food center in Boca Raton to pack the boxes, including a group from Vivmark Residential. Hagen credited the volunteers and community supporters with making the effort possible. 'We're going to be able to provide at least 4,000 families with Thanksgiving meals, and that's because of the people here today, thanks to you and thanks to all the people that support Boca Helping Hands,' Hagen said. To demonstrate the work that goes into the effort, volunteers from Vivmark Residential and The Boca Raton (who donated 100 turkeys) turned packing into a friendly competition. Each team packed 12 boxes, ending the challenge in a tie. Turning a Thanksgiving box into dinner The ingredients inside the boxes are intended to give families the foundation for preparing their own Thanksgiving meals at home. Chef Andrew 'Andy' Roenbeck, vice president of culinary operations and group executive chef at The Boca Raton, demonstrated how some additional ingredients families may already have can add new flavors to the meal. Roenbeck added apples to stuffing and Florida orange to cranberry sauce. He topped pumpkin pie with meringue and gave it a toasted finish. And when it came to the stuffing, he offered a simple Thanksgiving philosophy. 'Everything's better with butter,' Roenbeck said. See also: FDOT reopens all lanes on SR 809 and Military Trail after deadly Learjet 60 crash I wanted to know why they didn't call backup. I wanted to know why she did not listen to my daughter when she was trying to explain to her and asking her to walk down to the park, Ford-Barron said. Larry Lamar Smith was later arrested in connection with Zeigler’s death. Ford-Barron says she appreciates the detectives’ work but still has questions about the initial police response. I have to be my daughter's voice. I know that if I shut down, who's going to speak for my daughter? CBS12 News did not receive a response from Fort Lauderdale Police before publication. Update : In a statement provided Friday, the department said it remains saddened by the loss of Myrah Zeigler and extends its condolences to her family and loved ones. Police said the lead detective has maintained regular communication with the family and encouraged any concerns about the handling of the case to be addressed directly with the department through its established complaint process. The department declined an interview, citing the active and ongoing investigation.

entry.title: Wellington man sentenced to 7 years for $2.3 million fraud scheme involving sham cosmetic surgery clinics
entry.summary: A Wellington man has been sentenced to seven years in federal prison for a fraud scheme that prosecutors say used fake cosmetic surgery clinics and the stolen identities of more than 100 people to obtain millions of dollars from medical lenders. Jacquez Dion Tullis, 42, was sentenced Thursday to 84 months in prison after previously pleading guilty to conspiracy to commit bank fraud and aggravated identity theft, according to the U.S. Department of Justice. U.S. District Judge Rodolfo A. Ruiz II sentenced Tullis to 60 months for the bank fraud conspiracy charge and a consecutive 24 months for aggravated identity theft. Tullis was also ordered to serve five years of supervised release and pay more than $2.3 million in restitution. The court also ordered a forfeiture money judgment of more than $2.3 million. Prosecutors detail sham medical clinics According to court documents and Tullis' admissions in his plea, Tullis and his co-conspirators created six sham medical clinics between April 2018 and February 2024. The clinics purported to provide cosmetic surgery and other medical services but provided no actual care, prosecutors said. The conspirators registered the clinics with the Florida Department of State using stolen personal information belonging to practicing doctors and other people without their knowledge or consent, according to the Justice Department. Prosecutors said some doctors were falsely identified as clinic owners in applications seeking approval as merchants with medical lenders. Once the clinics were approved, the conspirators submitted fraudulent credit applications in the names of more than 100 people. The applications sought approximately $3.1 million and falsely claimed the money would pay for cosmetic surgery and other medical services. The people whose identities were used did not authorize the applications or receive treatment, prosecutors said. According to the Justice Department, death records showed some of the purported patients had died before the dates they supposedly received medical care. The scheme ultimately defrauded medical lenders of approximately $2.3 million, according to prosecutors. entry.title: Stuart Air Show: What to know about traffic, parking and getting to Witham Field
entry.summary: The Stuart Air Show is preparing to take flight at Witham Field, bringing aircraft, crowds and heavier traffic to the Stuart area. The air show is celebrating its 37th year at Witham Field. Lee Potter with the Stuart Air Show said this year's event will feature the F-16 demo team along with a variety of other aircraft arriving throughout the week. For drivers, planning the route before leaving home can help make the trip easier. Getting to the Stuart Air Show Drivers coming from Interstate 95 can take the Stuart exit and use Kanner Highway to Monterey Road. Drivers using Florida's Turnpike can take Southwest Martin Downs Boulevard. U.S. 1 and Dixie Highway are also options for reaching Monterey Road. As drivers approach Witham Field, they should follow posted signs and directions from law enforcement. The air show has two drive-in entrances off Monterey Road, with the Martin County Sheriff's Office directing traffic in the area. Where to park General parking is free in designated Stuart Air Show parking areas. Complimentary shuttle service will take visitors from the parking areas to the main gates. ADA parking is also available. Drivers should not create their own parking spots or park outside the designated areas. The best advice: stick with the official parking lots, watch for posted signs and follow law enforcement directions as you approach the air show. WPTV Traffic Reporter Johann Hoffend will be at Witham Field with traffic and transportation information for people heading to the Stuart Air Show.

entry.title: 911 caller said Palm City man was chasing her with guns, newly released video shows - WPEC
entry.summary: 911 caller said Palm City man was chasing her with guns, newly released video shows    WPEC
entry.article_text: A woman who called 911 during a Palm City standoff told dispatchers a man was chasing her with guns and had fired them, according to the call transcript released through a public records request. Please, quickly, the woman said at the start of the call. She told the dispatcher she was running down the street and that the man was so drunk and had tried to get into a car. The call adds detail to the September standoff involving Darrel Abbey, which lasted several hours and brought Martin County Sheriff’s Office deputies, SWAT team members and hostage negotiators to the home. In an earlier report, investigators said Abbey allegedly threatened his ex-girlfriend and pointed a gun at her. The woman told the dispatcher Abbey had put a gun to his head and pulled the trigger about an hour and a half earlier. She said the gun did not fire and that he was not in a good state of mind. As she ran, the caller said Abbey turned around and headed back toward the home. She stopped on the side of the road, where she said another woman had pulled over to help her. The caller also told dispatchers there were multiple guns at the property, though she was unsure whether they were inside the house, in a vehicle or in an RV. Newly released sheriff’s office video shows deputies and a tactical vehicle at the property during the response. The footage is partially obscured, and the provided clip does not clearly show Abbey or the events described in the 911 call. See also: 18-year-old dies after being struck by car in St. Lucie County; family raises concerns According to the arrest report, Abbey’s ex-girlfriend went to his home after their breakup. She told investigators he appeared intoxicated and had a rifle in his Tesla and a 10 mm handgun in his shorts. The report says he brought the guns inside, yelled at her and pointed a gun at her several times. It also says he later tried to get into his vehicle and reached for her phone when he realized she was recording. She ran down the road and called 911. Deputies later tried to contact Abbey at the home, but he refused to open the door or speak with them, according to the arrest report. He was booked into the Martin County Jail without bond on charges including battery and aggravated assault with a deadly weapon without intent to kill. The report also identifies him as a convicted felon with a prior vehicular assault conviction in Washington state.

entry.article_text: A Tampa father accused of voting illegally is now behind bars — one of 20 defendants charged with voter fraud as part of the state's latest sweep. But his attorney is questioning the state's evidence, telling investigative reporter Katie LaGrone she hasn't seen proof of her client's wrongdoing beyond a voter card the state sent him even though he was ineligible to vote.WATCH KATIE LAGRONE'S REPORT BELOW: In a Hillsborough County courtroom recently, Donta White sat in the inmate section, dressed in an orange jumpsuit, his expression stoic. This court appearance was about scheduling his trial, but for the people waiting for the 44-year-old to return home, the consequences of his latest arrest have already settled in."I thought it was a prank. There's officers here to arrest you for voting? He's like, 'I didn't do it,'" said Taquilla Allen, White's girlfriend. She's helping to care for his two young children while he remains in jail."It's been rough, but you know, we're just gonna take it a day at a time," Allen said.The state is accusing White of illegally voting. At the time, the convicted felon was still serving a 10-year probation for grand theft when, according to a press release issued by Florida's Attorney General's Office, White signed a state form warning him not to register or vote until after he completed his sentence.But according to prosecutors, White submitted two voter registration applications falsely claiming his voting rights had been restored, and then voted early in the 2024 general election. White is now charged with illegal voting and two counts of false swearing.A spokesperson for the AG's office said White admitted to authorities that he registered and voted, but his attorney, Lynley Flagler, is questioning the state's case."There is no clear-cut evidence that would support the fact that he actually went to the polls and voted himself," Flagler said.In addition, despite White not being eligible to vote because of his felony conviction, Flagler says the state sent him a voter ID card as if he was eligible."I feel that there's an entrapment issue. They want to prosecute voting, but they have not put any checks and balances in place to let people know when they're able to vote and when they can't vote," Flagler said.While a voter ID card does not, by itself, grant someone the right to vote, under Florida law certain convicted felons can get their voting rights restored once they complete their sentence, including probation. In White's case, his illegal voting charges triggered a violation of probation, which is how he landed back in jail."He runs a body shop. He's just, overall, really changed his life. So to see him in this position saddens me on a personal level as well as a professional level," Flagler said.Questions around voter eligibility for convicted felons aren't new in Florida. Ron DeSantis announced the arrests of 20 former felons who cast a ballot despite having disqualifying convictions. Several said they thought they could vote."What we discovered from a review of all those cases was there was more confusion than fraud," said Ramon De La Cabada, a Florida criminal defense attorney who co-chairs a committee formed after those arrests.De La Cabada believes White's case may be another example of that confusion — as is the recent arrest of Astrid Navarette Quintana. She's sitting in a Lee County jail after the state charged her for voting as a non-citizen. LaGrone recently investigated her case and found she's a permanent resident, married to a U.S. veteran and was also sent a voter ID card. When asked why voters shouldn't be responsible for knowing if they're eligible to vote, De La Cabada responded, "Absolutely, but I think the better question is why isn't the government creating better communication about eligibility? What you're finding in all these cases is massive confusion as to eligibility."Donta White's jury trial is set for early next year. He faces up to 15 years in prison for illegally voting and 30 years for his probation violation, which stemmed from his recent voting charges.In the meantime, he and his family remain apart, waiting for what's next."Who would throw their life away to vote? That's what it all boils down to," his girlfriend said. "It's petty, but we're dealing with it."

entry.title: Military Trail reopens in both directions after repairs following deadly Learjet crash
entry.summary: Military Trail reopened Thursday night in both directions near Greenacres after crews completed roadway repairs following the fatal Learjet crash on Nov. 1, according to the Florida Department of Transportation. FDOT said two northbound and two southbound lanes opened to drivers as of 7:05 p.m. Thursday. Crews spent the past 48 hours repairing the roadway, including paving and striping the road. Sidewalk repairs also began Thursday. Earlier Thursday, FDOT said crews had worked overnight and into Thursday morning to reopen the northbound lanes. This area of Military Trail had been closed between 10th Avenue and Forest Hill Boulevard after the Learjet crash created a large crater in the road. The reopening restores traffic in both directions along the affected stretch of Military Trail. Nine people were killed when the Learjet, which departed Austin, Texas, en route to the Bahamas, crashed near Greenacres earlier this month. No one on the ground was seriously injured.

When Attorney General James Uthmeier announced the sweep on illegal voting in September, just before the midterm elections, his office named 12 of the 20 people charged. After repeated requests, a spokesperson from his office sent investigative reporter Katie LaGrone the full list this week. The 20 defendants span across 13 counties. They include four convicted felons and 16 non-citizens all of whom, according to the attorney general's office, were ineligible to vote at the time they are accused of casting a ballot. WATCH KATIE LAGRONE'S REPORT BELOW: DEFENDANTS NAMED IN VOTER FRAUD CASES But over the past few weeks, LaGrone has discovered some of these cases are raising questions. Among them is Astrid Quintana, a lawful permanent resident who had been in the country since she was a toddler and is married to a U.S. veteran. Her attorney told us she received a voter ID card before she voted in 2024, believing she could. When asked how the state could charge her over a law that didn't exist at the time of her alleged crime, Martin responded, 'Well, they cannot.' In response to LaGrone's findings, a spokesperson for the attorney general said those investigations are still pending. entry.title: FHP trooper-involved shooting incident shuts down I-95 in Indian River County
entry.summary: Interstate 95 in Indian River County was shut down in both directions early Friday morning, creating a major traffic disruption for drivers near the Indian River-St. Lucie County line. On Thursday, at about 11:20 p.m., FHP said a trooper was involved in a shooting incident on I-95 near mile marker 141. According to FHP, the incident began when the trooper initiated a traffic stop, and the suspect fled, resulting in a pursuit. The pursuit escalated and turned into a gunfire exchange between the trooper and the suspect. Authorities said no troopers were injured during the shooting. FHP said the suspect sustained injuries from what appeared to be a self-inflicted gunshot wound and was pronounced dead at the scene. The Indian River County Sheriff's Office said the highway is closed due to the ongoing investigation. All northbound and southbound lanes of I-95 are closed at this time. The southbound entrance ramp at Oslo Road is also shut down. Northbound drivers were being directed off I-95 at Indrio Road, while southbound drivers were being directed to exit at Oslo Road. The northbound entrance ramp from Indrio Road is also closed. Officials said all body cam and dash cam video will be reviewed during the investigation. The FDLE will take over as the lead on the investigation. WPTV is working to learn more about when the interstate could reopen.

entry.title: Riviera Beach's Lone Pine community faces devastation after historic flooding
entry.summary: Residents of Riviera Beach's Lone Pine community are confronting the aftermath of devastating flooding, with gutted homes, piles of belongings lining neighborhood streets and families struggling to figure out what comes next. A week after floodwaters forced residents from their homes, the damage is becoming clearer, leaving some without flood insurance and questioning whether they can afford to rebuild. The flooding has turned once-familiar homes into cleanup projects and left residents facing the loss of belongings, memories and, in some cases, their sense of security. WPTV reporter Michael Hoffman returned to Lone Pine after witnessing the flooding begin to speak with residents now trying to recover. Watch report from Michael Hoffman: Riviera Beach's Lone Pine community faces devastation after historic flooding 81-year-old resident loses everything in flooding For 81-year-old Hazeline Thomas, the damage is deeply personal. Thomas walked Hoffman through her damaged home, where much of her belongings had been removed and left in piles along the curb. 'I'm all alone. And all my life saving is on the sidewalk,' Thomas said. She described being trapped inside her home as floodwaters rose around her. Thomas said the water eventually reached her neck before firefighters rescued her by boat. 'The water was up to my neck,' Thomas said. 'So the firefighters, the men, had to pick me up and put me in the boat.' She said rescuers also helped evacuate neighbors across the street. Now, Thomas is facing the financial burden of cleaning out her home. She said she has had to pay people to remove damaged belongings, using money she can hardly afford to spend. 'Everybody's just stuck, and we have to be doing things on our own,' Thomas said. With her home destroyed and few resources available, Thomas said she is considering leaving Florida and returning to New York. 'What I really need to do is pack up and go back to New York,' she said. What residents described as 3 to 4 feet of floodwater currently covers parts of Hungryland Farms in the Trailside community, forcing cattle to wade and swim through submerged pastures in search of dry ground. Documents obtained by WPTV show residents raised concerns about drainage problems long before last week's historic rainfall inundated the Treasure Coast. Now, with the rain gone but the water lingering, residents are questioning whether the devastation could have been prevented. 'All of our pastures ... they're all underwater' Melissa, who raises grass-fed cattle at Hungryland Farms in the rural Trailside community, says the flooding has transformed her property almost overnight. 'It feels like Lake Okeechobee,' she said. Her cattle, accustomed to grazing freely across the farm, are now navigating deep floodwater. 'It's completely covered,' Melissa said. 'All of our pastures ... they're all underwater.' Melissa pointed to an electrical transformer nearly submerged by floodwater, questioning whether her cattle could be electrocuted if they wandered too close. above community roads and breaching a berm — a raised barrier designed to control water flow.That same year, Shay contacted the South Florida Water Management District, warning that blocked drainage had left some pastures under 8 feet of water.She asked for help but says the underlying problems were never resolved."It's a combination of years of 'We'll get to it,' and we never got to it," Shay said.Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton acknowledges the community faces significant drainage challenges.Gorton said a berm breached Monday on the county-owned Elise J Property northeast of Trailside, sending water into a nearby canal, with some water backflowing into the community."We still can't get back to that breach," Gorton told investigative reporter Kate Hussey, explaining that high water levels have prevented crews from accessing the area.But the larger problem, he said, is Trailside's geography.The community is essentially a bathtub, surrounded by berms, hundreds of acres of wetlands and two independent water control districts.Water flows into the area, but there is only one drainage ditch for it to slowly escape."There's no easy way to get that water out except by pump or gravity," Gorton said.WPTV contacted engineer Bob Higgins, who works with both the Pal Mar Water Control District and the Hobe St. Lucie Conservancy District.Higgins said a potential solution had already been designed years ago: an outfall that would allow water to drain through the R G Mitigation Bank Preserve to the south and the neighboring Elise J property, which Martin County acquired in 2026. But that project was never built.When Hussey asked Gorton whether the county had been aware of the proposal, he confirmed officials had discussed it with the property's former owner."We did have some dialogue with the previous owner of Elise J about creating a formal water control structure that could discharge before the berms would breach," Gorton said.According to Gorton, the former owners submitted two permit applications to the South Florida Water Management District, but construction never began.WPTV contacted the former property owners, who said they did not know why the project was never completed.When Hussey reached out to the South Florida Water Management District, the agency said Trailside was outside its jurisdiction.However, Gorton said the district had permitted every property within Trailside and oversaw the proposed drainage project.Hussey followed up with the district, seeking clarification about its jurisdiction and asking why the drainage project was never constructed.The district has not responded to those follow-up questions.Despite the years of delays, Gorton said there may finally be a path forward."The good news is the county purchased that property, and it's our intent to bring that project forward," he said.Gorton said he has already requested the original permit applications in hopes of expediting approval — and construction— of the project.He also plans to return Friday to assess the flooding and determine what immediate relief may be possible."We're looking at ways to get the water out faster," he said.But for residents like Melissa, every additional day underwater carries a cost. "This could be a very costly natural disaster for us," she said.Her cattle still need to eat. Their pastures are submerged. And with no clear timeline for when the water will recede, the future of her farm remains uncertain."I don't have any food," Melissa said to her cows. "I'm sorry."For now, Hungryland Farms is living up to its name — and the families who depend on it are waiting for the water to go down.WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey continues to seek answers from the South Florida Water Management District about the proposed drainage project and why it was never completed.

entry.title: St. Lucie County rejects plan that could bring nearly 500 homes to low-lying site - cw34.com
entry.summary: St. Lucie County rejects plan that could bring nearly 500 homes to low-lying site    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Lucie County commissioners voted 3-2 to reject a land-use change for a roughly 34-acre property near South 25th Street and West Midway Road that could allow nearly 500 homes. The vote came as residents sought answers about recent flooding and commissioners questioned how the property handles drainage. An engineer said the property receives drainage from about 134 acres and uses a 24-inch pipe to direct water to nearby canals. Another pipe might be needed. The property sits lower than surrounding roads and would need to be raised for development, prompting concerns that construction could push water onto nearby properties. If designated for residential use, the site could allow up to 15 homes per acre, according to the discussion. County staff recommended approving the land-use change with adjustments to avoid or reduce impacts to wetlands and required buffers. Commissioners denied the request. See also: 77 homes hit by Martin County flooding. Where to get help now At the same meeting, residents from Creekside and White City asked commissioners to investigate last week’s flooding, identify who is responsible for local drainage systems, and explain how to prevent future flooding. I love my community, but it’s not fair that we’re suffering because nobody has taken the initiative to do what’s right for us, one resident said. Creekside residents called for an engineering review of the neighborhood and surrounding watershed, a reassessment of flood risk and a mitigation plan with deadlines. They also asked for a public meeting with county engineers and stormwater officials. White City residents described recurring flooding and called for drainage improvements and more stormwater storage. One resident said her home and yard had flooded four times since 2012. The county also made its emergency declaration official after days of heavy rain and flooding. It covers hazards including flooded roads and strained drainage systems.

entry.title: South Florida families turn to resale shopping to save money as holiday season approaches
entry.summary: Shoppers were out at the South Florida Fairgrounds on Friday looking for bargains at a large resale event featuring children's items. 'I love the fact that I can save a lot of money, and I like the shopping experience,' said Tatiana, a shopper who drove from Port St. Lucie. WATCH REPORT BELOW: South Florida families turn to resale shopping to save The resale event is run by Just Between Friends Palm Beach, a consignment shop. Among the items for sale were tables of toys, racks of clothing and various accessories from playpens to bicycles and strollers. 'Everything here is brought in by local families that have gently used items that their kids have outgrown, and instead of throwing it away, they're able to come bring it here and help other families save on items,' says store owner Kim Hazim. Resale shops are growing in popularity as inflation strains family budgets, and Hazim said this event has grown over the years. 'We used to be in 15,000 square feet; now we're in 30,000 square feet because that's how many families really need to come out,' Hazim said. Many were getting an early jump on holiday shopping with Black Friday coming later this month, but deals are already out there. 'Black Friday is almost a month-long event,' says money-saving expert Andrea Woroch. 'Retailers like Best Buy, Nordstrom, even Sephora, they started rolling out doorbuster-like deals on Nov. 1.' She added that good deals are already out there. 'If you're seeing a good deal, and again, I think that 30% off benchmark is a great place to make a purchase at,' Woroch said. 'And keep in mind, some retailers will offer price adjustments within a week or two weeks.'

entry.title: Russian national pleads guilty in $7 million Palm Beach County Medicare fraud, laundering scheme
entry.summary: A Russian national pleaded guilty Friday to his role in a Medicare fraud scheme rooted in Palm Beach County, marking the first conviction in a case I first brought to you last year. In federal court, 29-year-old Nika Machutadze, with the help of a translator, pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit money laundering. He is one of the defendants linked to a fraudulent medical equipment company in Delray Beach called Sunshine Senior Solutions , and he admitted under oath to his involvement in a money laundering scheme totaling more than $7 million. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Russian national pleads guilty in $7 million Palm Beach County Medicare fraud Machutadze could face up to 20 years in prison, plus fines, restitution and deportation. Seniors first contacted me last year, sharing Medicare statements for medical equipment they didn't need or receive from Sunshine Senior Solutions. While I tallied up hundreds of thousands of dollars in false claims from the statements I reviewed, that was a drop in the bucket, according to federal prosecutors. Federal prosecutors say Sunshine Senior Solutions billed insurers for more than $3 billion, though only a fraction of that was paid out. Machutadze admitted to opening bank accounts for Sunshine Senior Solutions and a second similar business in Texas, and transferring some of the money paid by insurers overseas. 'I'm glad to hear that,' said Mike Parrett, of Ohio. I spoke with Machutadze's attorney, Tony Mirvis, after Friday's hearing. 'The government's evidence was overwhelming,' Mirvis said. entry.title: Democrat Eileen Laubacher flips Colorado House seat, ousting Lauren Boebert
entry.summary: Democrat Eileen Laubacher has defeated Republican Rep. Lauren Boebert in Colorado's 4th Congressional District, according to a race call by The Associated Press more than a week after Election Day. The race remained too close to call for days as election officials continued counting ballots. Laubacher's victory unseats one of President Donald Trump's most outspoken allies in Congress. Boebert has represented Colorado's 4th Congressional District since 2025. She previously represented the state's 3rd Congressional District but switched districts in late 2023, citing the need for a 'fresh start following a difficult year' that included family turmoil and several controversies. Laubacher, a retired Navy admiral who served in the military for more than 30 years, said her decision to run for Congress was driven by concerns about the country's future. 'I have never felt as much of a threat to our country, our Constitution, our very democracy, as I do at this time,' Laubacher said.

entry.title: Man dies in FHP trooper-involved shooting incident shuts down I-95 in Indian River County
entry.summary: Interstate 95 in Indian River County was shut down in both directions early Friday morning, creating a major traffic disruption for drivers near the Indian River-St. Lucie County line. WATCH: Lt. Indiana Miranda gives update after man dies in trooper-involved shooting incident FHP gives update on trooper-involved shooting incident On Thursday, at about 11:20 p.m., FHP said a trooper was involved in a shooting incident on I-95 near mile marker 141. According to FHP, the incident began when the trooper initiated a traffic stop for a man driving over 90 mph near mile marker 138. Another trooper joined as back up and that's when, FHP said, the man got aggressive and was uncooperative. 'The primary trooper who completed the stop addressed the driver and advised him the reason for the stop was the speed, asked him for his driver's license and registration, he noticed that the driver was hostile,' Lt. Indiana Miranda said during a press conference on Friday. entry.title: Martin County firefighters raise staffing concerns after it says hiring class canceled - cw34.com
entry.summary: Martin County firefighters raise staffing concerns after it says hiring class canceled    cw34.com
entry.article_text: The Martin County Firefighters Union is asking county leaders to reconsider canceling a firefighter hiring class planned for January, saying the department is already short-staffed and the loss of new hires could increase pressure on crews. In a Facebook post, the union said the county canceled the class, which was expected to bring about 25 firefighters into Martin County Fire Rescue . The county cited budget concerns tied to Amendment 3 , according to the union. The union said the department is 17 firefighters short now and could be about 25 short by January as employees retire or leave for other departments. Fewer firefighters mean fewer available personnel to respond to emergencies, increased reliance on mandatory and voluntary overtime, and greater demands placed on the firefighters who remain, the union wrote. The union said its members recently agreed to forgo negotiating a new contract that would have taken effect in October, giving up a cost-of-living pay adjustment to help the county address financial challenges. It said members did so after being assured that Fire Rescue would not be affected by hiring freezes tied to Amendment 3. See also: Bobcat rescued after getting caught in barbed-wire fence near Stuart The union also questioned county administrative pay increases, saying administrative employees received 6% raises in October while firefighters face staffing shortages. The post calls on the Board of County Commissioners and county administrator to move forward with the hiring class. The county was not quoted in the union’s post. Martin County is taking a measured approach to hiring as it evaluates its long-term financial outlook and operational needs. With rising operating costs, inflation, and potential revenue impacts following the passage of Amendment 3 and anticipated SAFER Grant repayment obligations in the upcoming budget cycle, the County is being mindful of additional staffing commitments. While the firefighter recruitment class was planned months before Amendment 3 passed, current fiscal considerations have prompted a review of future hiring. The County is currently taking a soft hiring freeze approach, carefully evaluating vacancies and staffing needs. Maintaining public safety remains a priority for Martin County," the County said in a statement.

entry.article_text: Interstate 95 reopened in both directions around noon Friday after a shooting involving a Florida Highway Patrol trooper shut down the highway near mile marker 141. "It's crazy, something you'd never see. You see it in the movies, but you would never expect gunshots," said Jason Thompson, a Port St. Thompson was on I-95 southbound Thursday night near Vero Beach and his 16 year old daughter was in the backseat when he says gunfire broke out between vehicles in the northbound lanes about 50 feet away. "It was a very dark stretch of highway right there and suddenly, crack, crack, crack! I saw the muzzle discharge. I scooted over a few lanes and just kind of hurried up and got away from the area," Thompson said. FHP said the incident began around 11:20 p.m. Thursday, when a trooper tried to stop a motorist for speeding. FHP says the driver was doing over 90 miles per hour. "The primary trooper who completed the stop addressed the driver and advised him the reason for the stop was his speed and asked him for his driver license, registration. He noticed that the driver was hostile during the time," said Lt. Indiana Miranda, FHP spokesperson. See also: FAA orders nationwide ground stop at all U.S. airports amid 'extraordinary circumstances' At that point there were two troopers at the traffic stop. Miranda says the driver would not provide his drivers license and sped away. "Both troopers entered their vehicles and they engaged in a pursuit. The primary trooper called out the locations as they were traveling northbound, the speed that he was traveling and subsequently he said over the radio that there were shots being fired at them. Our trooper returned fire while driving his vehicle. The subject engaged open fire to the officers as they were in an active pursuit and that's when the officers called it on the radio they were being shot at," Lt. One of the troopers performed a maneuver to stop the car about three miles from where the driver was first pulled over. The driver was found dead near his car. FHP was asked if the troopers in this incident followed proper policy. "In our policy there is different scenarios. Not every scenario can be picture perfect or fit just in a box. Our policy has to become flexible in the point that you have less than a second to even think or take action," Lt. The person’s name has not been released. FHP and the Florida Department of Law Enforcement are investigating. The road was closed for several hours overnight and again Friday morning while the investigation continued. FHP said any available dash camera or body-worn camera footage will not be released until authorized by the investigating agency. The investigation remains active.

entry.summary: Fort Pierce mom demands answers after video shows moments before daughter’s death    cw34.com
entry.article_text: A Fort Pierce mother is speaking out after watching body camera footage of the night her 19-year-old daughter was fatally shot in Fort Lauderdale near an Airbnb. She believes her daughter was asking police for help and wants to know whether the officers who first responded could have done more. I already knew half of what happened, and to see it and to hear it was heartbreaking, said Alacia Ford-Barron, the mother of Myrah Zeigler. She shared the video with CBS12 News. The body camera video shows officers arriving after an altercation involving two groups of women inside the Airbnb. Officers tell everyone to leave. Ford-Barron says her daughter had been attacked and that belongings, including car keys, were taken. The group needed to retrieve those items from a nearby park. In the footage, Zeigler asks officers to walk with the group to get their belongings. One officer asks whether they have a way to get to the park. Zeigler responds that they can. Ford-Barron says she believed officers were going to help. Minutes later, gunfire erupts nearby. An officer reports that shots were fired two blocks away. Friends can be heard screaming as officers try to revive Zeigler. She later died at a nearby hospital. See also: FDOT reopens all lanes on SR 809 and Military Trail after deadly Learjet 60 crash I wanted to know why they didn't call backup. I wanted to know why she did not listen to my daughter when she was trying to explain to her and asking her to walk down to the park, Ford-Barron said. Larry Lamar Smith was later arrested in connection with Zeigler’s death. Ford-Barron says she appreciates the detectives’ work but still has questions about the initial police response. I have to be my daughter's voice. I know that if I shut down, who's going to speak for my daughter? CBS12 News did not receive a response from Fort Lauderdale Police before publication. Update : In a statement provided Friday, the department said it remains saddened by the loss of Myrah Zeigler and extends its condolences to her family and loved ones. Police said the lead detective has maintained regular communication with the family and encouraged any concerns about the handling of the case to be addressed directly with the department through its established complaint process. The department declined an interview, citing the active and ongoing investigation.

The Federal Aviation Administration issued the ground stop as officials investigated the communications problems affecting air traffic control. At President Donald J. Trump International Airport, departure boards showed numerous delays, with some flights being canceled as the disruption continued. One traveler told WPTV reporter Michael Hoffman that she and her husband had planned to fly to Atlanta for a weekend trip but were told they likely would not be leaving Friday night. 'They said it didn't look good,' she said, describing what her husband had been told by TSA. 'Probably not leaving tonight.' Although disappointed, she said their travel wasn't urgent. 'This (travel to Atlanta) was just for fun, so disappointing,' she said. 'You know, rather safe than sorry.' Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said officials had no indication at the time that a malicious act or hacking contributed to the communications issues. The FAA remained in the early stages of investigating the problem, and additional information about what caused the disruption and what was being done to resolve it was not immediately available.

"And he was a larger-than-life character. The whole place is him," DeStout said."He's the one that decorated all the stuff," he added.DeStout said many of the items inside the bar were collected during Harry's travels, with pieces from places including Australia and China.Inside, the bar's walls are a collage of Harry's travels and adventures with treasures at every inch.Harry was also behind another unmistakable piece of the bar's personality: its roadside sign."He was the original sign guy," DeStout said. "Yeah, way back when he started a tradition."DeStout eventually took over the tradition of putting messages on the sign and said he shared Harry's sense of humor."He always enjoyed it too," DeStout said. "But like I said, he was the original guy who did the sign."Harry's health began declining years ago. DeStout said Harry suffered a stroke roughly 17 years ago that paralyzed one side of his body. He recovered before suffering another stroke that took away his voice."He's had numerous other medical problems over the years, and then he started having heart problems and things like that," DeStout said. "So it's, it's been a difficult bunch of years for him."Still, DeStout said Harry continued living his life, traveling and attending events despite those challenges."He still lived life, and he got around more than I did," DeStout said. "He'd go to Las Vegas to the Sphere and the Kravis Center to plays, and, he got out and about a lot more than I did."Since Harry's death, DeStout said he's repeatedly heard one question from customers and employees: What happens to Harry's Banana Farm now?His answer is simple."Nothing. We're gonna continue on like we always do," DeStout said. "I've had to answer that question 100 times in the last two days. It's gonna keep on being Harry's Banana Farm."DeStout said that longevity is notable as Lake Worth Beach and the surrounding area continue to change. He recalled a time when Harry's was one of several similar neighborhood bars along Dixie Highway."When Harry and I tended bar here together 40 years ago, there was 10 places like Harry's up and down Dixie, and they're all gone," DeStout said. "Harry's is the only one that survives, and not only survives but thrives."For the people closest to Harry, his legacy extends beyond the walls of his neighborhood bar.DeStout said roughly 30 years ago, Harry began dressing as Santa Claus and visiting Barton Elementary School to give wrapped gifts to underprivileged children."He started going to Barton Elementary School and handing out wrapped gifts to all the little kids, underprivileged kids," DeStout said.What started at one school grew to include four elementary schools and eventually became a nonprofit, Harry's Helping Hands."And I just thought when we had the idea of making a legitimate nonprofit, it'd be a great legacy to leave behind," DeStout said. And now, after 30 years, it's gangbusters."The effort is marking its 30th year of giving back to the Lake Worth Beach community."He'd be here for the Christmas party; he'd be proud of everybody here for everything that they've done," DeStout said. "We've come so far, for a little neighborhood bar, we've done quite an impact."For DeStout, giving back is part of the responsibility that comes with operating a successful community business."And I believe, you know, very strongly that when, when you do business in the community, you profit from the community, you have a responsibility and obligation to contribute to that community, you know, so that's, and that was always Harry," DeStout said. "Harry was just so generous."DeStout is now encouraging people who want to honor Harry to donate to Harry's Helping Hands in lieu of flowers."He would much prefer a donation because that goes directly to the kids," DeStout said.Customers have also been stopping by Harry's Banana Farm to remember the man behind the business."He was very sarcastic, funny. He not only gave back, but he was a contributor, an active contributor," said Billy Miller, a patron at Harry's Banana Farm. entry.summary: A Russian national pleaded guilty Friday to his role in a Medicare fraud scheme rooted in Palm Beach County, marking the first conviction in a case I first brought to you last year. In federal court, 29-year-old Nika Machutadze, with the help of a translator, pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit money laundering. He is one of the defendants linked to a fraudulent medical equipment company in Delray Beach called Sunshine Senior Solutions , and he admitted under oath to his involvement in a money laundering scheme totaling more than $7 million. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Russian national pleads guilty in $7 million Palm Beach County Medicare fraud Machutadze could face up to 20 years in prison, plus fines, restitution and deportation. Seniors first contacted me last year, sharing Medicare statements for medical equipment they didn't need or receive from Sunshine Senior Solutions. While I tallied up hundreds of thousands of dollars in false claims from the statements I reviewed, that was a drop in the bucket, according to federal prosecutors. Federal prosecutors say Sunshine Senior Solutions billed insurers for more than $3 billion, though only a fraction of that was paid out. Machutadze admitted to opening bank accounts for Sunshine Senior Solutions and a second similar business in Texas, and transferring some of the money paid by insurers overseas. I reached out to some of the seniors to share the news of the guilty plea. 'Oh, that's terrific,' said Laura Carmine, of Illinois. 'Nice to know that justice can be done.' 'I'm glad to hear that,' said Mike Parrett, of Ohio. I spoke with Machutadze's attorney, Tony Mirvis, after Friday's hearing. 'The government's evidence was overwhelming,' Mirvis said. Mirvis said his client thought he was just taking a job. 'What I think is important is he's like the tip of the spear,' Mirvis said. entry.title: Florida releases full list of 20 charged in voter fraud sweep; some arrests spark questions
entry.summary: Nearly seven weeks after announcing a statewide voter fraud sweep, Florida's attorney general has released the full list of people charged and some of the arrests have already raised questions. When Attorney General James Uthmeier announced the sweep on illegal voting in September, just before the midterm elections, his office named 12 of the 20 people charged. After repeated requests, a spokesperson from his office sent investigative reporter Katie LaGrone the full list this week. The 20 defendants span across 13 counties. They include four convicted felons and 16 non-citizens all of whom, according to the attorney general's office, were ineligible to vote at the time they are accused of casting a ballot. WATCH KATIE LAGRONE'S REPORT BELOW: DEFENDANTS NAMED IN VOTER FRAUD CASES But over the past few weeks, LaGrone has discovered some of these cases are raising questions. Among them is Astrid Quintana, a lawful permanent resident who had been in the country since she was a toddler and is married to a U.S. veteran. Her attorney told us she received a voter ID card before she voted in 2024, believing she could. 'She had no intention to deceive anybody or to do anything that she believed was illegal,' attorney Connor Martin said. In her Quintana's case and in at least seven other cases involving non-citizens now facing these charges LaGrone discovered the state citing a law that didn't even exist at the time they were accused of voting . When asked how the state could charge her over a law that didn't exist at the time of her alleged crime, Martin responded, 'Well, they cannot.' In response to LaGrone's findings, a spokesperson for the attorney general said those investigations are still pending. In Tampa, LaGrone recently caught up with the attorney for Donta White , a convicted felon who is not eligible to vote because he's still on probation for grand theft. The state said the father of two admitted to registering to vote twice and voting early in 2024. According to his attorney, he was also sent a voter ID card. entry.title: Martin County firefighters express concerns over staffing levels at Fire Rescue - WPBF
entry.summary: Martin County firefighters express concerns over staffing levels at Fire Rescue    WPBF
entry.article_text: A day after the firefighters' union in Martin County expressed concerns about staffing, the County Administrator is responding by acknowledging the concerns while also saying there's not much that can be done right now. The union raised its concerns in a Thursday social media post, pointing out that the county had canceled an upcoming hiring class of 25 new firefighters even as Fire Rescue is understaffed. "It is about public safety, firefighter working conditions, and ensuring Martin County residents receive the level of emergency services they pay for and deserve," the post said. Don Donaldson, the county administrator for Martin County, acknowledged the union's concerns. "I think the concern of the public is real and legitimate," Donaldson said. Donaldson confirmed that fire rescue is already short-staffed by 17 firefighters and that the hiring class will not proceed as planned. However, he clarified that the class is postponed, not canceled. "I don't want to have to lay somebody off six months right after I hire them," Donaldson said. He explained that the delay is due to uncertainties in the county budget caused by Amendment 3, a measure recently approved by Florida voters that will lower property taxes statewide. Martin County estimates the amendment will result in a $75 million revenue loss over the next two years. Donaldson emphasized the need to assess the budget before committing to new hires. "What I didn't want to have happen is to fully fund all of our firefighters and then find we have to eliminate a position or two with somebody already in the position," Donaldson said. Donaldson said he hopes to have more clarification on the hiring of firefighters within the next few months. entry.title: 911 caller said Palm City man was chasing her with guns, newly released video shows - WPEC
entry.summary: 911 caller said Palm City man was chasing her with guns, newly released video shows    WPEC
entry.article_text: A woman who called 911 during a Palm City standoff told dispatchers a man was chasing her with guns and had fired them, according to the call transcript released through a public records request. Please, quickly, the woman said at the start of the call. She told the dispatcher she was running down the street and that the man was so drunk and had tried to get into a car. The call adds detail to the September standoff involving Darrel Abbey, which lasted several hours and brought Martin County Sheriff’s Office deputies, SWAT team members and hostage negotiators to the home. In an earlier report, investigators said Abbey allegedly threatened his ex-girlfriend and pointed a gun at her. The woman told the dispatcher Abbey had put a gun to his head and pulled the trigger about an hour and a half earlier. She said the gun did not fire and that he was not in a good state of mind. As she ran, the caller said Abbey turned around and headed back toward the home. She stopped on the side of the road, where she said another woman had pulled over to help her. The caller also told dispatchers there were multiple guns at the property, though she was unsure whether they were inside the house, in a vehicle or in an RV. Newly released sheriff’s office video shows deputies and a tactical vehicle at the property during the response. The footage is partially obscured, and the provided clip does not clearly show Abbey or the events described in the 911 call. See also: 18-year-old dies after being struck by car in St. Lucie County; family raises concerns According to the arrest report, Abbey’s ex-girlfriend went to his home after their breakup. She told investigators he appeared intoxicated and had a rifle in his Tesla and a 10 mm handgun in his shorts. The report says he brought the guns inside, yelled at her and pointed a gun at her several times. It also says he later tried to get into his vehicle and reached for her phone when he realized she was recording. She ran down the road and called 911. Deputies later tried to contact Abbey at the home, but he refused to open the door or speak with them, according to the arrest report. He was booked into the Martin County Jail without bond on charges including battery and aggravated assault with a deadly weapon without intent to kill. The report also identifies him as a convicted felon with a prior vehicular assault conviction in Washington state.

entry.title: Delays, cancellations mount at President Donald J. Trump International Airport amid nationwide ground stop
entry.summary: A nationwide ground stop prompted by air traffic control communications issues caused widespread flight disruptions Friday, with passengers across South Florida facing delays and cancellations. The Federal Aviation Administration said communications issues affecting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers prompted it to ground flights at airports nationwide while technicians investigated. The agency later lifted the ground stop Friday night, though flight disruptions continued. FAA nationwide ground stop disrupts flights, strands travelers at DJT International Airport WPTV's Michael Hoffman spent Friday at Donald J Trump International Airport speaking with travelers as departure boards showed numerous delays and cancellations and passengers scrambled to figure out what would happen to their trips. Departure boards showed numerous delays, with some flights being canceled as the disruption continued. One traveler told WPTV reporter Michael Hoffman that she and her husband had planned to fly to Atlanta for a weekend trip but were told they likely would not be leaving Friday night. 'They said it didn't look good,' she said, describing what her husband had been told by TSA. 'Probably not leaving tonight.' Although disappointed, she said their travel wasn't urgent. 'This (travel to Atlanta) was just for fun, so disappointing,' she said. 'You know, rather safe than sorry.' For some, the disruption came just as they were preparing to leave. 'I'm about to board the plane, and the pilot stopped everyone and said, 'Hold on, we might have to deplane. Give us a second,'' traveler Hailey Desser said. 'And then he's like, 'Yep, everyone needs to get off the plane.'' Sara Haseney appeared to arrive just before operations ground to a halt. 'I guess we probably were one of the last planes to board or to land, I guess,' Haseney said. 'But yeah, it was definitely crazy, and I think we're all pretty shocked.' For Lindsay Funes, the timing made the disruption particularly stressful. 'Just kind of annoying the whole situation, especially like it's my first time traveling on my own and like not with a family member,' Funes said. entry.summary: The northbound lanes of Florida's Turnpike are closed in Palm City following a crash involving a tractor-trailer and a pickup truck Friday morning. The crash happened just before 11 a.m. near mile marker 137, according to Martin County Fire Rescue. Officials said both drivers are safe and no injuries have been reported. Martin County Fire Rescue, the Martin County Sheriffs Office and Florida Highway Patrol are working to clear debris from the roadway. Drivers are being asked to avoid the area, seek alternate routes and expect delays. It was not immediately clear when the northbound lanes would reopen.

entry.title: Stuart Air Show: What to know about traffic, parking and getting to Witham Field
entry.summary: The Stuart Air Show is preparing to take flight at Witham Field, bringing aircraft, crowds and heavier traffic to the Stuart area. The air show is celebrating its 37th year at Witham Field. Lee Potter with the Stuart Air Show said this year's event will feature the F-16 demo team along with a variety of other aircraft arriving throughout the week. For drivers, planning the route before leaving home can help make the trip easier. Getting to the Stuart Air Show Drivers coming from Interstate 95 can take the Stuart exit and use Kanner Highway to Monterey Road. Drivers using Florida's Turnpike can take Southwest Martin Downs Boulevard. U.S. 1 and Dixie Highway are also options for reaching Monterey Road. As drivers approach Witham Field, they should follow posted signs and directions from law enforcement. The air show has two drive-in entrances off Monterey Road, with the Martin County Sheriff's Office directing traffic in the area. Where to park General parking is free in designated Stuart Air Show parking areas. Complimentary shuttle service will take visitors from the parking areas to the main gates. ADA parking is also available. Drivers should not create their own parking spots or park outside the designated areas. The best advice: stick with the official parking lots, watch for posted signs and follow law enforcement directions as you approach the air show. WPTV Traffic Reporter Johann Hoffend will be at Witham Field with traffic and transportation information for people heading to the Stuart Air Show.
