entry.title: What airlines owe you after a canceled flight as FAA ground stop disruptions linger
entry.summary: Flight cancellations are dropping as airlines recover from Friday's nationwide Federal Aviation Administration ground stop , but passengers are still dealing with delays, long layovers and an important question: What does an airline owe you when your flight is canceled? WATCH: Samantha Gutierrez's report for what passengers need to know Flight Canceled After FAA Ground Stop? Know Your Rights | WPTV Federal passenger protections provide a clear right in one key situation. If an airline cancels your flight and you decide not to travel, you are entitled to a refund, regardless of what caused the cancellation. That includes nonrefundable tickets. Hotels, meals and ground transportation are a different story. Because Friday's disruption originated with the FAA rather than an airline, carriers are not universally required to cover those additional expenses, though individual airlines may voluntarily provide assistance. Traveler: 'There's no consequence' At President Donald J. Trump International Airport, passenger Scott Danforth said the disruption left him frustrated by what he sees as an imbalance between the responsibilities of travelers and airlines. 'If we make cancellations, we get to pay a lot of money,' Danforth told WPTV. 'But they can make cancellations, and there's no consequence. That's what I don't like.' Paul Hudson of FlyersRights.org said passengers whose flights are canceled have an important decision to make. 'You can choose the offer of rebooking, or you can get a refund,' Hudson said. Under U.S. Department of Transportation rules, passengers do not have to accept airline credits or travel vouchers in place of a refund when the airline cancels their flight and they decide not to travel. What about hotels and meals? Another family WPTV met at the airport said their journey home now includes a 13-hour layover. 'Maybe they could give us, like, a hotel or something through all this chaos,' traveler Jessica Soros said. Hudson said passengers should ask their airline what assistance is available, but accommodations such as meals, hotel rooms and ground transportation aren't guaranteed when the disruption is outside the carrier's control. 'They may provide it to some passengers ... but they don't have to,' Hudson said. Travelers should still ask their carrier about meal vouchers, hotel assistance, discounted hotel rates and travel waivers. Travel insurance or benefits included with some credit cards may offer another option for qualifying expenses. '

Trump International Airport, passenger Scott Danforth said the disruption left him frustrated by what he sees as an imbalance between the responsibilities of travelers and airlines."If we make cancellations, we get to pay a lot of money," Danforth told WPTV. "But they can make cancellations, and there's no consequence. The continued disruption stems partly from aircraft and flight crews being left out of position following the nationwide stoppage. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said it takes time for airlines to move crews and planes back where they need to be.The FAA has said faulty equipment led to Friday's ground stop, while officials continue investigating the precise cause. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said officials had found no evidence of anything nefarious.A preliminary investigation found that an L3Harris contractor was working at a remote FAA site to replace copper wiring with fiber and replace a router when the router began flooding other routers with data, according to Duffy. The exact cause remains under investigation.U.S. Lois Frankel, D-Fla., said the disruption underscores the importance of ensuring the nation's aviation system remains reliable."We need to take whatever steps we can to make sure people are always safe and on time," Frankel said.While the cancellation numbers are improving, travel disruptions on this scale can take time to fully work through an airline network.For anyone still affected, the key is knowing the distinction: You may be entitled to your money back if the airline canceled your flight and you choose not to travel, but additional expenses such as meals and hotels depend on the circumstances and the airline's policies. entry.title: West Palm Beach neighbors brace for more rain after record flooding left streets underwater for 11 days
entry.summary: The chance of heavy rain this week is lingering over our five-county viewing area days after some communities in West Palm Beach dried out from a major flood event. The Hamilton Bay neighborhood in West Palm Beach was underwater last Monday, a full week after record-breaking rainfall came down. With more heavy rain in the forecast this week, neighbors tell me they're concerned. WATCH REPORT BELOW: West Palm Beach residents fear more flooding if heavy rain returns Late Monday morning, Ashley Debrowski was out strolling the sidewalks of Hamilton Bay with her children. 'A week ago today, I would still be trapped in my house,' Debrowski said. Around the corner, Tushar Bulsara was in his driveway wrapping a vehicle. 'That whole week was just unbelievable. It almost felt like a dream,' Bulsara said. Neighbors told me their community off of Jog Road was underwater for 11 days. 'Eleven days of essentially being afraid to leave the house,' Debrowski said. 'Vehicles have to be able to come in for me to do my work,' Bulsara said. 'And you know, that's business lost.' The severe, prolonged flooding impacted communities in the Hamal Community Development District, a roughly 250-acre area near Jog Road and Florida's Turnpike that includes Hamilton Bay, Briar Bay and other neighborhoods. 'It's a situation that we never thought was going to happen,' said Dwayne Barrett, the operations manager for the Hamal CDD. Barrett tells me that since then, the CDD has been working with other government entities to make sure that doesn't happen again. 'I think we're in a bigger and better place right now with additional larger pumps to what we already have already, and so that's going to help a lot to move water. It's currently in operation,' Barrett said. As those extra pumps moved water out of nearby lakes and into a canal by the turnpike, the streets in Hamilton Bay are dry. But the neighbors' minds are still flooded with worry. When I asked Bulsara if he was keeping his eye on the forecast this week, he said, 'Yes.' 'If that happens again, you know, it disrupts work, it disrupts kids going to school,' Bulsara said. 'I will say the lake behind my house definitely looks lower today, but it still makes me really nervous because you don't want to be trapped in your house. Definitely not the way you want to live,' Debrowski said. "And you know, that's business lost."The severe, prolonged flooding impacted communities in the Hamal Community Development District, a roughly 250-acre area near Jog Road and Florida's Turnpike that includes Hamilton Bay, Briar Bay and other neighborhoods."It's a situation that we never thought was going to happen," said Dwayne Barrett, the operations manager for the Hamal CDD.Barrett tells me that since then, the CDD has been working with other government entities to make sure that doesn't happen again."I think we're in a bigger and better place right now with additional larger pumps to what we already have already, and so that's going to help a lot to move water. It's currently in operation," Barrett said.As those extra pumps moved water out of nearby lakes and into a canal by the turnpike, the streets in Hamilton Bay are dry. But the neighbors' minds are still flooded with worry.When I asked Bulsara if he was keeping his eye on the forecast this week, he said, "Yes.""If that happens again, you know, it disrupts work, it disrupts kids going to school," Bulsara said."I will say the lake behind my house definitely looks lower today, but it still makes me really nervous because you don't want to be trapped in your house. Definitely not the way you want to live," Debrowski said.A spokeswoman for the City of West Palm Beach told me in an email that city officials are "meeting daily with regional partners to review pumping operations, monitor local water levels, and assess system capacity to ensure resources are in place to respond as conditions warrant."The city is also extending the local state of emergency through Sunday, Nov. 22.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.summary: West Palm Beach residents are being urged to prepare for another round of heavy rain and possible flooding this week while parts of the city are still recovering from historic rainfall earlier this month. The city said Monday that heavy rainfall and isolated flash flooding are possible from Tuesday through Thursday. According to information provided by the city from the National Weather Service, there is a 40% to 60% chance that 2 to 4 inches of rain could fall across much of South Florida's east coast, with significantly higher amounts possible in isolated locations. Additional rain could worsen flooding in areas where the ground remains saturated from the Nov. 1-2 flooding, particularly in low-lying neighborhoods. Mayor Keith James has extended West Palm Beach's local state of emergency through Sunday, Nov. 22. City officials said the extension allows West Palm Beach to continue emergency measures, coordinate resources and assist residents affected by the flooding. West Palm Beach prepares for additional flooding City crews and emergency personnel are continuing recovery work while preparing for the possibility of more flooding. According to the city, crews are monitoring affected neighborhoods and inspecting and clearing city-maintained storm drain grates. Officials are also evaluating whether garbage, recycling and yard waste collection can be accelerated in western communities hit hardest by the recent flooding to reduce the risk of additional service disruptions. The city is continuing to operate an auxiliary pumping station to lower water levels in the Apoxee Reserve. Water-control structures at Grassy Waters are also being managed to increase available storage capacity ahead of additional rainfall. entry.article_text: Military Trail has reopened, and the crater left behind by the deadly Learjet crash has been filled, but for families who lived just feet from where the plane came down, the road to recovery is far from over.Mariano Garcia, an attorney with Searcy Denney Scarola Barnhart & Shipley, is representing four families from the Greenacres mobile home community whose homes, vehicles and other property were damaged by crash debris.WATCH REPORT BELOW: "The immediate need right now is that people who were displaced still have to pay rent. They still have to pay bills. They have to replace food and items that they lost. They have repairs to their homes that need to be made, and so we're dealing with those immediate needs," Garcia said.Those financial concerns have been a part of the aftermath since the first days following the crash.For the four families Garcia represents, the focus is now turning to financial relief for their specific losses.One of those families is a household of eight living in a mobile home roughly 50 feet from the impact site. Garcia said seven members of the family were home when the crash happened, including three who were outside."Dad was on the porch holding his 1-year-old child. Mom was standing nearby when a chunk of sidewalk came busting through their porch, narrowly missing them," Garcia said.Other members of the family were inside."They all felt the explosion, the shock. They breathed all of the residue that was in the air," Garcia said. "It was a very traumatic event for them, as you can imagine."The damage to the family's home was significant."You had chunks of aircraft parts busting through the roofs, you know, allowing the water intrusion into these residences, and when you combine that with the power being out, food spoiling in refrigerators, folks being unable to return to their homes, it had a pretty significant impact on their lives," Garcia said.Power and water have since been restored to the mobile home community, according to Garcia, but the family of eight has not been able to return to its home because the residence remains unsafe. He said the family has been staying in Airbnbs provided through charity.Garcia said there is no lawsuit at this point.Instead, he is communicating with attorneys for Aurora Aviation Inc., which does business as Upper Jets and operated the Learjet, and the company's insurance carrier in an effort to secure immediate financial relief for the four families he represents.When WPTV asked whether the company has been cooperating, Garcia's response was direct."Very much so," he said. "I'm encouraged that at least the company for this charter operator, the insurance company, is responding and acknowledging that there were losses and are doing what they can to advance sums to these families and help them out."An inspector is expected to assess the affected properties as Garcia's team works to determine the extent of the losses.For now, Garcia said the immediate focus is on expenses families are already facing."The immediate need right now is that people who were displaced still have to pay rent. They still have to pay bills. They have to replace food and items that they lost. They have repairs to their homes that need to be made, and so we're dealing with those immediate needs," he said.WPTV previously spoke with Perez, a handyman whose mobile home is about 250 feet from where the Learjet crashed. At the time, he couldn't access his home, vehicle or the tools he depends on for work. Perez is not one of the residents represented by Garcia, but when WPTV recently returned to the neighborhood, our crew found an orange notice on his mobile home that read "UNSAFE.""Working materials are there. My screwdrivers, my drills, my saws, they're stuck there," Perez told WPTV at the time.He worried then about what the disruption would mean financially."We're not asking for nothing else but the necessary that's been lost or gonna get lost because of this, because my job wages, when rent comes down, who is gonna be, is my landlord or the people who I pay for that lot gonna say, ‘Oh, we feel sorry for you to have a discount?’ No, full payments are gonna have to be made," Perez said.Other organizations have also stepped in to address those immediate needs. The Emergency Assistance Foundation, a West Palm Beach-based nonprofit, launched a fund offering $1,000 cash grants to eligible residents impacted by the crash. Other groups have provided food, shelter, supplies and services for displaced residents.But some of what these families experienced is more difficult to measure."The photos and the aerials really don't do justice to just how close these families came to being seriously hurt or killed," Garcia said.He said some of the people he's spoken with are still dealing with the emotional and psychological effects of what they experienced."It's not something you see every day, and so it definitely had an emotional or psychological impact on them," Garcia said. "Many of them are having trouble sleeping, which is a very common report when someone undergoes a very sudden, tragic and unexpected event."Garcia, who has practiced law for 32 years, is also a longtime pilot. He described himself as a commercial multi-engine instrument-rated pilot and said he previously co-owned a flight school and charter service out of Palm Beach International Airport.He said determining the impact of emotional trauma will take time."There's no formula for that, Joel. It really depends upon the degree. We rely on medical experts to make that assessment and then use our judgment based on experience," Garcia said.While representing families impacted on the ground, Garcia stressed the magnitude of the loss suffered by the families of those aboard the Learjet."My heart goes out to the victims on board the plane. They suffered a massive loss, and I think what the public needs to understand is that this had a much broader impact," Garcia said.He said his focus now is helping the families he represents move toward some sense of normalcy."It's such a massive loss, particularly to the families of the occupants of the aircraft. It's hard to put words around what those families must be going through," Garcia said. "I can't imagine what they must be going through. And so if I can do something, even just a little bit to help others who were impacted by it, then, you know, I think that's the right thing to do."WPTV has reached out to Aurora Aviation for comment and is working to hear back.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.summary: Joe Namath's Lucky Shuck coming to Jensen Beach as waterfront village breaks ground    WPEC
entry.article_text: Football legend Joe Namath is bringing his popular Lucky Shuck restaurant to Jensen Beach as a massive waterfront development takes shape along the St. Rio Marine Village , a 30-acre mixed-use development in Martin County, broke ground Thursday, following more than five years of planning. The project will feature 342 apartments, a 131-slip marina, more than a half-mile of public riverwalk, and several waterfront dining and entertainment destinations. Among them is a new location of The Lucky Shuck Oyster Bar & Taphouse , owned by Namath and his business partner Charlie Modica, along with a second, yet-to-be-named outdoor dining concept. See also: New 24/7 animal cruelty hotline launching across Florida "The Lucky Shuck has always been about good food, good people and being on the water," Namath said. "Rio Marine Village gives us a home right on the river, and I can't wait to see boats pulling up and families sitting down together." The development will also feature the Osprey Club, a waterfront wedding and event venue, along with a public park, boardwalk, beach, and kayak and paddleboard rentals. Martin County commissioners unanimously approved the project's first two phases following years of community discussions. Construction is expected to begin this month, with the first phase scheduled for completion in late 2028.

entry.summary: Teen thrown 50 feet in Jensen Beach e-bike crash, sheriff warns parents of crackdown    WPEC
entry.article_text: Parents could face criminal charges in a crackdown on illegal e-bikes after a teen was thrown 50 feet in a crash, the Martin County sheriff warned Monday. During a news conference, the sheriff revealed that a 14-year-old Port St. Lucie boy suffered catastrophic injuries in Sunday's crash near U.S. 1 and Northwest Goldenrod Road. The teen was airlifted to St. Mary's Medical Center , where he is now in stable condition. According to the sheriff, the boy and a friend had traveled roughly five miles from home on separate e-bikes when they attempted to cross U.S. See also: Kids, 6,000 fentanyl pills and stolen gun uncovered in massive Florida drug bust The first teen made it across, but the 14-year-old was struck by a northbound vehicle that had a green light. The impact sent the boy flying approximately 50 feet, while his e-bike landed about 100 feet away. "Had he not been wearing a helmet, and had he been hit just a little different, we'd be talking about a 14-year-old die in a fatality crash," the sheriff said. Investigators determined the teen was riding a 3,300-watt electric bike, more than four times the 750-watt limit cited by the sheriff. The motorbike-style vehicle was not street-legal, he said. The crash comes amid growing concerns over e-bike safety in Martin County, where the sheriff reported 41 e-bike crashes this year, involving riders as young as 7 and as old as 80. The sheriff said educational workshops, warnings, and previous enforcement efforts have failed to curb dangerous riding. Now, deputies are considering tougher consequences, including seizing illegal e-bikes and potentially pursuing criminal charges against parents who knowingly allow their children to ride them. I'm not anti-e-bikes, but I'm anti-illegal e-bikes being ridden irresponsibly on our streets." The Florida Highway Patrol is leading the crash investigation, with assistance from the Martin County Sheriff's Office.

entry.title: Jensen Beach residents concerned that forecasted heavy rainfall will cause repeat flooding - WPBF
entry.summary: Jensen Beach residents concerned that forecasted heavy rainfall will cause repeat flooding    WPBF
entry.article_text: As residents in Jensen Beach continue cleaning up after this month’s historic flooding, another round of heavy rainfall is heading their way. Many of the homes on Hyline Drive were flooded for eight long days, and residents are finally starting to get inside to start cleaning up. Related: Community gathers to begin cleanup as Jensen Beach flooding slowly recedes They’re hoping the rain doesn’t ruin their progress. “Eight days of standing water. There was nothing that we could do but watch everything deteriorate and mold,” Susan Destafney said. Destafney’s home sits next to the Hyline Pond and was filled with dirty floodwater for eight days. She said they lost almost everything, and now volunteers are tearing the home down to the studs and treating it for mold. “I've cried more than I've ever cried before. It's just a lot to take in, and it should never have happened,” Destafney said. County officials have pumped water from the neighborhood and the pond, and they have set up a recovery assistance webpage for residents. But Destafney said for their day-to-day needs, they are relying on the volunteers and nonprofits to help them get by. She worries they could be knocked back to square one if the forecasted rainfall this week causes more flooding. I mean, things that I was able to save, I do have on my back porch. So, it's going to be raining. So, what's going to happen to the few things that I was able to save? It's a lot,” Destafney said. Others in the community we spoke to are also concerned about the forecast. We're trying to recover right now. My friends are trying to recover right now. All these efforts for cleanup to get us in a place to where it's dried up, the water is gone, and now they're expecting flash flooding again. So, yeah, we're nervous that this is going to be like what it was a couple of days ago all over again in a few days,” Crystal van Duyme said. WPBF 25 News reached out to the county to see what they’re doing to prep for the upcoming rainfall. The public works director was not available Monday, but we’re hoping to speak with him on Tuesday. However, residents did tell us that crews are currently draining the Hyline Pond again, likely in preparation for that rain. entry.title: Port St. Lucie to break ground on new 6,000-seat soccer stadium in December
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie is getting closer to welcoming its first professional soccer team , with a groundbreaking ceremony for a new 6,000-seat stadium scheduled for Saturday, Dec. 12. Port St. Lucie Sports Club announced Thursday that construction will begin at Walton One, where the stadium will sit on approximately six acres. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Port St. Lucie to break ground on new pro soccer stadium in December The club is preparing to compete in USL League One in 2027, and the new stadium is expected to serve as more than just a place to watch soccer. Plans call for a year-round destination where families and community members can gather for entertainment and other events. The development group will fully fund construction of the stadium and has entered into an agreement with the City of Port St. Lucie to use the land. 'From day one, we knew this had to be about much more than building a soccer club,' said Gustavo Surez, founder and CEO of Port St. Lucie Sports Club. 'We set out to create something that feels like a true part of this community, a place where families can gather, young players can dream, and new traditions can take shape.' The groundbreaking ceremony will begin at noon on Dec. 12, bringing together club leaders, USL representatives, partners and founding members. A public celebration will follow at 1:30 p.m., featuring food trucks, entertainment and activities for all ages. The club says more details about the event will be announced in the coming weeks.

entry.title: St. Lucie County shelter waives adoption fees after taking in 114 cats from alleged hoarding case
entry.summary: A St. Lucie County animal shelter is urgently seeking homes for cats and kittens after taking in more than 100 animals from a home last month. The Humane Society of St. Lucie County is teaming up with BISSELL Pet Foundation for an emergency 'Empty the Shelters' adoption event on Nov. 13 and 14. Adoption fees will be waived for all cats and kittens during the two-day event. WATCH REPORT BELOW: St. Lucie County shelter waives adoption fees after taking in 114 cats The shelter says it's facing a capacity crunch after taking in 114 cats from a Port St. Lucie home in October. The cats were rescued from a home at the center of an alleged animal hoarding case that led to a woman's arrest on 29 felony animal cruelty charges. Now, the Humane Society is hoping the adoption event will free up much-needed space so it can continue caring for the animals. All pets available for adoption are spayed or neutered, vaccinated and microchipped. The event runs from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. on Friday, Nov. 13, and Saturday, Nov. 14, at the Humane Society of St. Lucie County, located at 8890 Glades Cut-Off Road in Port St. Lucie. Anyone interested in adopting can view available pets at hsslc.org .

entry.article_text: Home Schools InnovatED Phase 2 town hall set for Monday at Sebastian River Middle by Tina Hodges Nov 15, 2026 / 12:23 PM A A A A Reset InnovatED (School District of IRC) Share on Twitter Share via Email SEBASTIAN — The School District of Indian River County will hold an InnovatED Phase 2 town hall Monday, November 16, from 5:30 to 6:30 p.m. at Sebastian River Middle School to gather public feedback on two facility proposals still under consideration. District officials have invited families, staff, and community members to hear details, ask questions, and share thoughts on the plans. The two proposals focus on a future home for Wabasso School that would add capacity and specialized learning spaces, and on creating a connected arts pathway in Sebastian. Both remain under review, with School Board consideration expected in December. Wabasso School currently serves students with specialized needs on U.S. District leaders have previously described the campus as at capacity and have discussed relocating the program to the former Glendale Elementary site in Vero Beach to allow room for growth and more tailored spaces for life skills and independent learning. The arts pathway proposal involves Sebastian Elementary School of the Arts, which officials have said could share the Sebastian River Middle School campus as a separate school while maintaining its own identity. This is the latest in a series of InnovatED community sessions. Phase 1 of the initiative, which included several school relocations, shared campuses, and boundary adjustments, took effect for the 2026-27 school year after School Board approval in December 2025. entry.summary: Joe Namath's Lucky Shuck coming to Jensen Beach as waterfront village breaks ground    WPEC
entry.article_text: Football legend Joe Namath is bringing his popular Lucky Shuck restaurant to Jensen Beach as a massive waterfront development takes shape along the St. Rio Marine Village , a 30-acre mixed-use development in Martin County, broke ground Thursday, following more than five years of planning. The project will feature 342 apartments, a 131-slip marina, more than a half-mile of public riverwalk, and several waterfront dining and entertainment destinations. Among them is a new location of The Lucky Shuck Oyster Bar & Taphouse , owned by Namath and his business partner Charlie Modica, along with a second, yet-to-be-named outdoor dining concept. See also: New 24/7 animal cruelty hotline launching across Florida "The Lucky Shuck has always been about good food, good people and being on the water," Namath said. "Rio Marine Village gives us a home right on the river, and I can't wait to see boats pulling up and families sitting down together." The development will also feature the Osprey Club, a waterfront wedding and event venue, along with a public park, boardwalk, beach, and kayak and paddleboard rentals. Martin County commissioners unanimously approved the project's first two phases following years of community discussions. Construction is expected to begin this month, with the first phase scheduled for completion in late 2028.

entry.title: Florida Panthers are one-fourth of the way through their regular season. Where do they stand?
entry.summary: At 22 games played, the Florida Panthers are a quarter of the way through their regular season. The Panthers have 27 points, tied with Boston for the first Eastern Conference wild card spot. WATCH: Florida Panthers are one-fourth done with their season. Where do they stand? Florida Panthers are one-fourth of the way through their regular season. Where do they stand? The Panthers are currently playing without Captain Alexander Barkov and Brad Marchand. After a 2-1 overtime loss to the Dallas Stars Sunday night, heres what Matthew Tkachuk said about the teams performance so far this season. Fine, you know, it's been OK, some good and some bad, but we're in the fight. That's all you can ask for, and I can promise you it's going to be a fight to the end of this with the division,' Tkachuk told reporters. Tkachuk is having one of the best starts of a season in his career with 5 goals and 25 assists. WPTV Panthers anchor and Panthers 360 host Mike Trim connected with Associated Press reporter Tim Reynolds, who's covered the Panthers for two decades. Trim asked Reynolds who his pick would be for first-quarter team MVP. Seth Jones has been absolutely elite for this team. For me, even with a lot of great statistical numbers, leadership performances, all those things Seth Jones, far and away the most important player for the Panthers to date, Reynolds told Trim. Jones is tied for second on the Panthers with 23 points, notching 20 assists and 3 goals. Tuesday night, the Edmonton Oilers visit Sunrise at Amerant Bank Arena. The Oilers are a team the Panthers are familiar with as they beat them two times in recent years in the Stanley Cup Final. This season, Edmonton is off to a hot start. They have 35 points, which is currently the most in the Western Conference. Through 22 games, Oilers center Connor McDavid has 12 goals and 41 assists. McDavid recently matched former Edmonton captain Wayne Gretzky as the fastest player to 40 assists in a season. The puck drops at 7 p.m. Tuesday evening. The game will air locally on The Spot South Florida.

entry.title: 'Today we are homeless': Jensen Beach family displaced by historic flooding pleads for help rebuilding home - WPTV
entry.summary: 'Today we are homeless': Jensen Beach family displaced by historic flooding pleads for help rebuilding home    WPTV
entry.article_text: A Jensen Beach family displaced by historic flooding is searching for more permanent housing and money to rebuild after water destroyed much of the inside of their home. Lisa and Jeremy French, who have two young boys, told WPTV's Michael Hoffman they ultimately have one goal: to get their family back home.WATCH REPORT BELOW:WPTV first met the French family shortly after historic rainfall hit South Florida and the Treasure Coast. Floodwater had surrounded their neighborhood, forcing residents to use kayaks to get around and check on neighbors.Days later, much of the water has receded. The damage has not."My floorboards are outside," Lisa French said.Hoffman returned to the French family's Jensen Beach home for an update, but the family said it was not safe to go inside.French said the flooding wiped out much of what her family had accumulated over the years."Our appliances are gone, our cabinets are gone, every piece of furniture," French said.The family is now trying to determine how to pay for repairs while securing a more permanent place to live.WPTV met French again at the Hoke Library in Jensen Beach, where a Multi-Agency Resource Center has been helping people looking for assistance following the flooding.French told Hoffman that her home flooded days after the rain had stopped.Martin County told WPTV that the family's home is near the Savannah Preserves, an area where excess water naturally flows from other flooded areas.French, however, questions whether other actions involving water entering the preserve contributed to what happened at her home."They're saying it's from natural rain, but they dumped Monday and Tuesday, nonstop into the savannas," French said.The impact of the flooding extends beyond the physical damage.Through tears, Lisa and Jeremy French pleaded for help before the Martin County Commission as they described what their family is facing."Today we are homeless," Lisa French told commissioners. "We have nowhere to host Thanksgiving. We have nowhere for our boys to have Christmas. We don't have beds to come home to."The couple has two young boys. French said she wants them to continue growing up in the Jensen Beach home the family worked hard to maintain.For now, however, the family says it needs more permanent housing while trying to determine where the money to repair the home will come from.French said the uncertainty surrounding assistance has left her worried there could still be a significant financial gap, even if additional aid becomes available."Who's going to fill in the gaps?" French said. "And, you know, maybe I feel like somebody should take accountability."Despite the uncertainty and extensive damage, the family says it has not given up hope of returning."We just want to go home," French said. "Like, that's at the end, that we just want to be home with our family."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.article_text: A 14-year-old boy was flown to St. Mary’s Medical Center in West Palm Beach after being injured in an illegal e-bike crash at U.S. 1 and NW Goldenrod Road in Jensen Beach over the weekend, according to the Martin County Sheriff’s Office. Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek expressed frustration over the incident and emphasized the risks associated with illegal e-bikes. “We’re not trying to pick on people, but there’s nothing worse than having a child laid up in a trauma center as we go into the holidays,” Budensiek said. The sheriff’s office released footage of the crash, showing two e-bikes attempting to cross U.S. While the first bike crossed safely, the second rider was struck by a vehicle that had a green light. Budensiek highlighted the importance of helmet use in preventing fatalities. “Had he not been wearing a helmet, we’d be talking about a 14-year-old dying in a fatality crash,” Budensiek said. Earlier this year, the sheriff’s office adopted a zero-tolerance policy on illegal e-bike use to address reckless riding and growing safety concerns. However, Budensiek said the message has not been effective. “So, this is serious for us. I know it’s fun for the kids, but our softer approach has not been working. We’ve had 41 e-bike crashes in Martin County this last year,” Budensiek said. Jason Moore, associate trauma medical director at HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital in Fort Pierce, said his hospital has treated numerous patients injured in e-bike crashes. “Yes, unfortunately we’ve seen a lot of e-bike accident patients. I’d say over the last 12 months we’ve seen hundreds of e-bike accidents,” Moore said. Moore described the severity of injuries resulting from e-bike crashes. “Unfortunately, we’ve seen pretty significant injuries, involving brain injuries, broken bones including those in the neck, the collarbone, the ribs. We see quite a few rib fractures,” Moore said. Budensiek said his office is committed to raising awareness about the dangers of illegal e-bikes and is exploring whether parents who knowingly purchase illegal e-bikes for their children could face criminal prosecution. “Parents are knowingly buying illegal e-bikes, giving them to their kids, and allowing their kids to ride them, so we are looking at criminal prosecution for parents if we can make that stick,” Budensiek said. Vincent Lavelle Jr. A special touch from the Port St. Lucie community band featured songs from each branch of service. That prompted service members in attendance to stand for their respective branch song. There was also a special flyover by the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office helicopter.

entry.title: Riviera Beach flood victims seek relief as city weighs $2 million aid plan
entry.summary: Riviera Beach residents demand help after historic flooding Hundreds of Riviera Beach residents packed an emergency City Council meeting seeking financial assistance after November flooding damaged homes, displaced families and left residents questioning how they will pay for repairs. The city discussed setting aside $2 million for a proposed forgivable loan or grant program for residents whose homes were damaged by the flooding. The proposed assistance would help pay for interior and exterior repairs needed to make homes safe and livable. But during the heated meeting, city Finance Director Randy Sherman said the city faces restrictions on using public money to pay for damage to private property, creating uncertainty about how the proposed relief could move forward. Riviera Beach weighs $2M flood relief plan as residents demand help Lone Pine Estates residents press city for financial relief Weeks after floodwaters inundated homes in Lone Pine Estates, residents filled the meeting room, with others standing outside, hoping city leaders would provide a path toward recovery. Keisha Hartys lives in the neighborhood and her home was impacted by the flooding. She summed up the growing frustration in the neighborhood. No help is coming. We are on our own, said Harty. Another resident challenged the city's position that public funding could not be used directly to help private homeowners, pointing to other causes the city has supported. When you say you cant use federal dollars or public funding for private citizens, I have to disagree, the resident said. Im looking for a Lone Pine relief fundraiser. Council member Shirley Lanier argued the flooding and its impact on residents should be treated as a broader public safety concern. That is a public safety issue, Lanier said. There is no way that we cannot use public money for a public concern. Residents describe the toll of the flooding Residents also used the meeting to show city leaders what recovery has looked like on the ground. One woman said firefighters rescued her from floodwaters. At the podium, she displayed basic items she said she received afterward, including a T-shirt, deodorant and socks. Why is this being given to a taxpayer on an emergency event? she asked. entry.article_text: At the podium, she displayed basic items she said she received afterward, including a T-shirt, deodorant and socks.“Why is this being given to a taxpayer on an emergency event?” she asked.The frustrations come as families continue trying to clean up and repair homes weeks after the flooding.Many residents are also concerned about additional rainfall and the possibility that already hard-hit neighborhoods could face more flooding.The Riviera Beach City Council unanimously voted to amend a motion to continue considering the $2 million emergency set-aside while seeking a legal opinion on how the money could be used.The proposal calls for establishing a forgivable loan or grant program specifically for residents whose homes were damaged by the November flooding.City leaders also considered partnerships that could provide emergency shelter, hotel or motel vouchers and temporary housing for displaced residents.Another proposal would allow the city to coordinate mutual aid with neighboring cities, counties and partner agencies for debris removal, collection and other flood recovery needs.The vote does not mean homeowners will immediately receive money. Instead, it keeps the proposed assistance moving forward as city officials examine the legal options available for providing relief.A representative from U.S. Lois Frankel’s office told residents that the office was working with federal and state officials to seek disaster assistance.

entry.title: 37th Stuart Air Show draws big crowds for picture-perfect weekend
entry.summary: The 37th Stuart Air Show brought aviation fans young and old together for a picture-perfect weekend filled with aircraft, family traditions, and appreciation for veterans. Organizers said the weekend got off to a strong start Friday night with a drone and fireworks show and continued with large crowds throughout the weekend. 'Stuart Air Show has had an amazing weekend Friday night with our drone and fireworks show. We had a great turnout,' Chrissy Valvano said. 'Sunday, we're looking at a record turnout for Veterans Appreciation Day, and this weather could not be better.' For some families, attending the Stuart Air Show has become a tradition passed down through the years. 'The Stuart Air Show has been a part of our community for many years,' Sarah Naylor said. 'We have many memories of coming in the past, as long as I can remember.' For younger aviation fans Wyatt and Ivy Rotan, some of the biggest attractions were the military aircraft. 'I like coming to the Stuart Air Show because I like to see the C-17 and the F-16 fly,' Wyatt said. 'I like seeing the C-17,' Ivy added. The event also gave young people a chance to learn more about aviation while honoring those who served. 'You get to have a lot of fun around here, just going around and seeing a bunch of planes,' John Gefell said. 'Also, because I'm working on my aviation merit badge as a Boy Scout and my grandpa was a veteran, so its just real fun to come out here and just have a lot of fun.' With beautiful weather and a strong turnout, the 37th Stuart Air Show once again brought the community together, giving longtime fans and a new generation of aviation enthusiasts a weekend to remember.

It’s pretty amazing."Residents seek answers about flooding and drainageAs cleanup continues, residents say they also want answers about what contributed to the severe flooding.Some are questioning how much pumping from Port St. Lucie and Fort Pierce into the Savannas Preserve may have contributed to flooding in their neighborhood.Stephen Leighton, chief of staff for U.S. Brian Mast, R-Fla., told WPTV that questions remain as officials work through the recovery process."There's a lot of answers that these residents need, and hopefully we can do that," Leighton said.Leighton also said the state had taken steps toward an emergency declaration and reached out to the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA).Families look for financial assistanceFor some homeowners, rebuilding also brings financial uncertainty.French said her home is not in a flood zone and she does not have flood insurance, leaving her family dependent on whatever assistance, donated materials and volunteer help becomes available."We're trying to get any type of help. We don't have flood insurance here," French said. "We're way above sea level; we are not a flood zone. So it's just whatever volunteers and help and materials we can get is what we get."Community calls for more volunteersResidents say more hands are still needed as families work to make their homes livable again.Leighton said a question-and-answer town meeting with residents and county, state and federal officials is planned this week as the community seeks clarity about the flooding and available assistance.For volunteers, Leighton said even small acts can make a difference for families trying to put their lives back together."To help somebody take that picture off the wall and put it in a box, so they can move on, is a big deal," he said.With Thanksgiving approaching, he said the need for community support remains urgent."We're two weeks out from Thanksgiving, and we really need the community to come together and help," Leighton said.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: Port St. Lucie family offers free heart screenings to honor late daughter - WPBF
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie family offers free heart screenings to honor late daughter    WPBF
entry.article_text: The parents of Jessica Clinton, a Port St. Lucie teen who died of cardiac arrest in 2003, are hosting a free heart screening event this Saturday at the St. Lucie County Health Department to raise awareness about children's heart health. Jessica Clinton's parents Ray and Cheryl Lalloo are preparing for the event, which is expected to draw about 600 children. He stressed the importance of identifying heart problems early. "You hear it all the time. Kids go to sleep, parents come in the morning, they're not awake, and it's now just infants, or SIDS, it's kids that are 10, 12, 13 years old," Ray Lalloo said. Jessica was 17 years old and at cheerleading practice at St. Lucie West Centennial High School when she went into cardiac arrest. At the time, there were no automated external defibrillators (AEDs) on campus, and Jessica died that day. Her parents said she had undergone two sports physicals in the months before her death, but no heart problem was detected. In response to their loss, Jessica's parents founded the Jessica Clinton MVP Foundation and began offering heart screenings 17 years ago. They said the screenings have helped identify previously undiagnosed heart conditions. Last year, they said about 19 children learned they had a condition that had not been detected before. "We've had a couple of kids with pretty significant diagnoses. You know, things like syndrome, the really bad ones, you know," Ray Lalloo said. Cheryl Lalloo is grateful they were able to offer free screenings. "Blessed is the word, Cheryl Lalloo said. "It makes us feel like we also have a lot more work to do. That there's still kids out there that are still diagnosed." The free screenings are available for children and young adults ages 5 to 20 and include an electrocardiogram (EKG) and a check of vital signs. A cardiologist reviews the results, and an Echocardiogram is available if needed. The Lalloos said close to 650 children have signed up for this year's event. Appointments are booked, but families can call to ask about the waiting list. Organizers said they'll try to fill openings if someone cancels or doesn't show up. Jessica's parents hope their efforts will prevent other families from experiencing a loss like theirs. "The one child could be the next president of our country. It could be the person who invents the cure for cancer. So, every life is important. Children should not die like this," Ray Lalloo said. The event will take place Saturday from 8 a.m. Lucie County Health Department, 5150 NW Milner Drive, Port St. The number to call for scheduling is 772-462-3800. entry.article_text: Weeks after historic flooding devastated homes in Jensen Beach, Martin County families are still cleaning up and rebuilding, with volunteers, churches, firefighters, contractors and local leaders joining the recovery effort. Water marks remain visible on some homes, showing how high floodwaters rose. Residents are now removing damaged drywall, clearing debris and collecting donated supplies while seeking financial assistance and answers about the area's drainage systems. Neighbors step in to help Jensen Beach families Before-and-after video from the Jensen Beach neighborhood shows the extent of the flooding, which left several homes under feet of water. Weeks later, homeowner Lisa Marie French said cleaning up has been a major undertaking. We first told you about French's circumstances last week. You first have to empty the houses," French said. "We have to clean the houses; they're filled with mold, we have to take the drywall out." French, whose home was impacted by the flooding, has also helped coordinate community cleanup efforts alongside Christ of Church, Family Church and other organizations. She said neighbors and other volunteers have repeatedly shown up asking what families need and then immediately gotten to work. "People have been just coming and just hands-on," French said. "People are like, 'Hey, are you taking donations? What do you need?' And they get out of their cars, and they start working, and that's our neighbors. It’s pretty amazing." Residents seek answers about flooding and drainage As cleanup continues, residents say they also want answers about what contributed to the severe flooding. Some are questioning how much pumping from Port St. Lucie and Fort Pierce into the Savannas Preserve may have contributed to flooding in their neighborhood. Stephen Leighton, chief of staff for U.S. Brian Mast, R-Fla., told WPTV that questions remain as officials work through the recovery process. "There's a lot of answers that these residents need, and hopefully we can do that," Leighton said. Leighton also said the state had taken steps toward an emergency declaration and reached out to the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA). Families look for financial assistance For some homeowners, rebuilding also brings financial uncertainty. French said her home is not in a flood zone and she does not have flood insurance, leaving her family dependent on whatever assistance, donated materials and volunteer help becomes available. "We're trying to get any type of help. We don't have flood insurance here," French said. "We're way above sea level; we are not a flood zone. So it's just whatever volunteers and help and materials we can get is what we get." Community calls for more volunteers Residents say more hands are still needed as families work to make their homes livable again. Leighton said a question-and-answer town meeting with residents and county, state and federal officials is planned this week as the community seeks clarity about the flooding and available assistance. For volunteers, Leighton said even small acts can make a difference for families trying to put their lives back together. "To help somebody take that picture off the wall and put it in a box, so they can move on, is a big deal," he said. With Thanksgiving approaching, he said the need for community support remains urgent. "We're two weeks out from Thanksgiving, and we really need the community to come together and help," Leighton said. entry.title: FAU researchers find the best treatment for Childhood Apraxia of Speech could come down to timing
entry.summary: For families with children who have an acute speech disorder known as Child Apraxia of Speech, it's always a race against the clock to find the most optimal therapy. Researchers at Florida Atlantic University may have recently discovered that helping to connect the dots between a child's brain and their speech could come down to the time of day of their therapy. WATCH: The best treatment for complex speech disorder could come down to timing Study: Time of day could make speech therapy more effective Sara Tutoni's daughter was too young to participate in the study, but the family does seek treatment at FAU for CAS. Tutoni says she realized something wasn't right around age 2. 'She could make every sound an animal makes, every sound a car makes, but no words,' Tutoni said. In the study, published in the journal Clinical Linguistics Phonetics , FAU researchers shared a striking difference in how speech-motor learning unfolded for participants with and without CAS. Their findings suggest that the time of day may influence speech-motor learning differently in young people with CAS and could eventually help clinicians identify ways to make therapy more effective without simply adding more hours of treatment. The study consisted of 82 adolescents and young adults ages 12 to 21 with and without CAS. Researchers found that participants with typical speech showed a slight benefit from evening training, while those with CAS performed better after morning training. Dr. Anne van Zelst, one of the lead researchers, says further study is needed, but believes this starting point could be critical to helping families and other stakeholders save time and money on expensive therapies. '(It could save) parents, school districts and insurance companies. It's very demanding on families,' van Zelst said. Tutoni said she wishes she would've had tools like this early on and sees it as a game changer for other families navigating CAS. Her focus is on her daughter and giving her the best chance at success.

entry.article_text: Crews are clearing drainage systems and checking waterways in St. Lucie County as another round of rain threatens areas still recovering from historic flooding. Lucie Public Schools is releasing students two hours early Tuesday. The district is asking families to monitor its official channels for updates as weather conditions change. Lucie officials say Public Works crews are inspecting drainage systems, clearing blockages and lowering water levels where possible. The ground remains saturated, increasing the risk of flooding even if rainfall is lighter than it was during the early November storms. See also: Heavy rain returns this week, bringing major threat of flooding across South Florida The National Weather Service has issued a flood watch for St. Lucie County from Tuesday afternoon through Friday evening. Forecasters expect 3 to 6 inches of rain across the area, with higher amounts possible in some locations. Two weeks ago, floodwaters stranded cars, trapped families and forced some residents to wade through deep water. Videos from that flooding showed high school freshman Noah Julian swimming from his school bus toward his home in a flooded Port St. Another video showed 7-year-old Ella Ghodooshim walking through chest-deep water with her mother near Oak Hammock K-8. Officials are urging residents to plan ahead, monitor forecasts and local alerts, and limit unnecessary travel. Drivers should never enter standing or moving water. Floodwater can stall a vehicle and cause costly engine damage. If you cannot tell how deep the water is, turn around and find another route. Residents can report flooding concerns to St. Lucie County at flooding@stlucieco.org .

"Had he not been wearing a helmet, and had he been hit just a little different, we'd be talking about a 14-year-old die in a fatality crash," the sheriff said. Investigators determined the teen was riding a 3,300-watt electric bike, more than four times the 750-watt limit cited by the sheriff. The motorbike-style vehicle was not street-legal, he said. The sheriff said educational workshops, warnings, and previous enforcement efforts have failed to curb dangerous riding. Now, deputies are considering tougher consequences, including seizing illegal e-bikes and potentially pursuing criminal charges against parents who knowingly allow their children to ride them. entry.title: Treasure Coast counties prepare for flooding as heavy rain and gusty winds move in - WPEC
entry.summary: Treasure Coast counties prepare for flooding as heavy rain and gusty winds move in    WPEC
entry.article_text: The Treasure Coast is bracing for a soggy stretch as counties prepare for possible flooding from heavy rain. Indian River County The Indian River County Emergency Operations Center remains at Level 2, or partial activation, because of ongoing flooding and the potential for more heavy rain. Emergency services, human services and infrastructure partners are coordinating response and recovery efforts. The county urges residents to avoid flooded roads and floodwaters, watch for rising water in low-lying areas and monitor weather conditions and official updates. Residents with flood-related questions or information can call the Emergency Information Center at 772-226-4000 during operating hours. Heavy rain and gusty winds are forecast in Indian River County from Tuesday, Nov. Solid waste services may be disrupted. Waste Management curbside collections may be delayed, and residents should not put carts in the street if it is flooded. Waste Management collects recycling in blue carts countywide. It collects garbage, yard waste and bulk waste in unincorporated Indian River County, Fellsmere, Sebastian and Indian River Shores. Residents in other cities and towns should check with their local governments for service updates. The county recommends putting carts out by 6 a.m. on collection day, closing lids, bagging garbage and avoiding overfilled carts. Cardboard should be flattened and placed inside recycling carts, and yard waste should stay inside yard waste carts. Residents should bring carts back in as soon as possible after collection. The landfill and all five Customer Convenience Centers may close early or remain closed if conditions become unsafe. The east-central Florida coast faces a Slight Risk, or Level 2 out of 4, for excessive rainfall. Localized flooding is possible, especially along the coast, and some areas could receive 4 inches or more of rain. Martin County Martin County officials expect 3 to 6 inches of rain, with localized amounts of 8 to 12 inches, beginning Tuesday afternoon and continuing through Nov. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office says it is working with the county’s emergency operations center to monitor rainfall and identify roads that could become difficult to pass. The sheriff’s office plans to deploy high-water rescue vehicles in flood-prone areas. Having the vehicles nearby could help deputies reach residents who need assistance and motorists who become stranded, the office said. The sheriff’s office advises residents: If water covers the road, turn around. Standing water may be deeper than it appears and can hide damage to the road. If your usual route home is flooded, take another route or wait somewhere safe. Never drive around a barricade. Stay out of flooded areas and avoid driving to see how high the water is. Keeping roads clear gives deputies and rescue crews room to reach people who need help. Martin County Fire Rescue advises residents to be prepared to evacuate if flooding threatens their homes or neighborhoods. Residents should also have an emergency kit ready for household members and pets. The Community Information Center will be open to provide flood-related information. Okeechobee County Okeechobee County is also preparing for severe flooding. The Okeechobee County Sheriff’s Office says its emergency operations center will remain active as staff coordinate response and recovery efforts from past flooding. Sandbags are available at Okeechobee County Public Works, 804 Northwest Second St. Lucie County Public Safety Department is monitoring the forecast and reminding residents to secure loose items that could be damaged by wind. Gusty northeast winds of 25 to 30 mph are forecast Tuesday and Wednesday, with gusts of 35 to 40 mph along the coast. Residents should secure tarps, patio furniture and unsecured recovery materials. A rip current advisory remains in effect for St. Strong onshore winds can create dangerous rip currents and rough surf. The county has extended the deadline to Nov. 30 for residents to report flood damage through an online survey. The information will help document flooding across the community and inform recovery efforts. The survey is open to property owners and tenants throughout St. Lucie County, including Fort Pierce, Port St. Lucie Village and unincorporated areas. It asks where flooding occurred, how buildings were affected and what impacts residents and businesses experienced. Lucie County asks that the survey be completed by November 30, https://arcg.is/05f4b13 .

entry.title: Trump's Presidential Library foundation amasses $57.6 million
entry.summary: The foundation overseeing President Donald Trumps future presidential library amassed $57.6 million by the end of last year, new tax filings show, as the president turned legal battles with major media and tech companies into an unusual source of funding for the project. The filings do not identify the donors or reveal how much of the money came from controversial settlements. But the documents, provided to CNN by the Donald J. Trump Presidential Library Foundation, confirm the organization has a sizable head start on his unconventional vision for a presidential library a towering Miami skyscraper that he has suggested could also serve as a hotel. RELATED STORY | Eric Trump shares renderings of a proposed Trump presidential library and museum The foundation reported spending just $349,000 during its first seven months. Much of that was paid to Bermello Ajamil Partners, the architecture firm that produced renderings of the proposed 47-story library. It previously told the Internal Revenue Service that it expected to raise about $50 million by the end of 2025. But it anticipated fundraising would accelerate considerably: The organization estimated it will bring in nearly $1 billion by the end of 2027. Its unclear whether the organization remains on track toward reaching that goal. Recently, two of Trumps top political operatives, James Blair and Chris LaCivita, donated to the foundation amid revelations they left the country ahead of the midterms to provide counsel for Republika Srpska, a pro-Russia Balkan government. In the months since Trump circulated renderings for his proposed library including a gilded entranceway and an Air Force One on display he has announced other expensive legacy construction projects, including a White House ballroom that has attracted seven- and eight-figure checks from large companies and political allies. A pro-Trump super PAC, MAGA Inc., closely connected to the president has also brought in hundreds of millions of dollars. Trumps planned library was designated to receive sizable sums from settlements with companies he sued during the presidential campaign and after his first term. entry.title: Teen arrested in hit-and-run crash that critically injured 24-year-old woman in Port St. Lucie
entry.summary: An 18-year-old driver has been arrested after a hit-and-run crash critically injured a 24-year-old woman on an electric scooter in Port St. Lucie, police said. The incident happened Monday morning near Southwest Gatlin Boulevard and Southwest Feather Terrace, Port St. Lucie police said. According to investigators, the victim was riding an electric scooter westbound on the sidewalk toward Southwest Rosser Boulevard. As the woman on the scooter entered the crosswalk, she was struck by the 18-year-old driver of a gray Chevrolet Tahoe making a left turn onto Southwest Feather Terrace. Police said the driver fled the scene and failed to stop to render aid to the woman. The Port St. Lucie Police Department's Traffic Homicide Investigations Unit identified the driver as Tristan Sanchez-Chasmer and located the vehicle through its investigation. Investigators learned Sanchez-Chasmer had been playing 'ding dong ditch' just before the crash. He was arrested on a charge of leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury, police said. The Port St. Lucie Police Department is expected to hold a press conference on Tuesday at 2 p.m. Chief Leo Niemczyk will address the incident, providing additional details about the investigation, the arrest and an update on the victim's condition.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie prepares for more rain after viral video shows student swimming home - WPEC
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie prepares for more rain after viral video shows student swimming home    WPEC
entry.article_text: Families across the Treasure Coast are watching the forecast closely after historic flooding overwhelmed parts of Port St. Just as many neighborhoods are drying out, forecasters are warning another 4 to 6 inches of rain could fall over the next few days, raising concerns about renewed flooding in areas still recovering from the record rainfall. The flooding two weeks ago left cars stranded, some families trapped in their homes and others wading through deep water. "It was horrible," said Port St. Lucie resident Crisostomo Santiago Perez. "Water was on top of the cars almost, covering hoods." Among those caught off guard was freshman Noah Julian. 2, Noah stepped off his school bus to find his neighborhood along Coleman Avenue flooded. A video recorded by neighbor Martina Elieson quickly spread on social media, showing the teenager swimming through floodwaters just to reach his driveway. "When I see the video, I'm like, what?" said Noah's father, Romeo Julian. We got alligators here, snakes, sharp objects could have cut him up. A thousand things could've happened to him." With another round of heavy rain in the forecast, residents say they aren't taking any chances." "Today I'm going to get stuff before flood comes," Perez said. See also: From banks to flights, outages leave south Floridians frustrated St. Lucie Public Schools is also preparing ahead of the storm. The district announced a two-hour early release Tuesday in an effort to avoid a repeat of the flooding issues that affected students taking the bus home earlier this month. "But why it always takes one thing to make them wake up." Meanwhile, county crews have been inspecting and clearing canals and drainage systems ahead of the expected rainfall. Officials warn that because the ground is still saturated from recent storms, it will take far less rain than usual to cause flooding in neighborhoods, streets and other low-lying areas. Residents are encouraged to monitor local forecasts and be prepared for changing conditions as the rain moves into the area.

entry.title: Treasure Coast counties prepare for flooding as heavy rain and gusty winds move in - WPEC
entry.summary: Treasure Coast counties prepare for flooding as heavy rain and gusty winds move in    WPEC
entry.article_text: The Treasure Coast is bracing for a soggy stretch as counties prepare for possible flooding from heavy rain. Indian River County The Indian River County Emergency Operations Center remains at Level 2, or partial activation, because of ongoing flooding and the potential for more heavy rain. Emergency services, human services and infrastructure partners are coordinating response and recovery efforts. The county urges residents to avoid flooded roads and floodwaters, watch for rising water in low-lying areas and monitor weather conditions and official updates. Residents with flood-related questions or information can call the Emergency Information Center at 772-226-4000 during operating hours. Due to the heavy rain and gusty winds, solid waste services may be disrupted. Waste Management curbside collections may be delayed, and residents should not put carts in the street if it is flooded. See also: Florida deputies rescue 2-year-old girl found in pond near apartment complex Waste Management collects recycling in blue carts countywide. It collects garbage, yard waste and bulk waste in unincorporated Indian River County, Fellsmere, Sebastian and Indian River Shores. Residents in other cities and towns should check with their local governments for service updates. The county recommends putting carts out by 6 a.m. on collection day, closing lids, bagging garbage, and avoiding overfilled carts. Cardboard should be flattened and placed inside recycling carts, and yard waste should stay inside yard waste carts. Residents should bring carts back in as soon as possible after collection. The landfill and all five Customer Convenience Centers may close early or remain closed if conditions become unsafe. The east-central Florida coast faces a Slight Risk, or Level 2 out of 4, for excessive rainfall. Localized flooding is possible, especially along the coast, and some areas could receive 4 inches or more of rain. Martin County Martin County officials expect 3 to 6 inches of rain, with localized amounts of 8 to 12 inches, beginning Tuesday afternoon and continuing through Nov. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office says it is working with the county’s emergency operations center to monitor rainfall and identify roads that could become difficult to pass. The sheriff’s office plans to deploy high-water rescue vehicles in flood-prone areas. Having the vehicles nearby could help deputies reach residents who need assistance and motorists who become stranded, the office said. The sheriff’s office advises residents to turn around if water covers the road. Standing water may be deeper than it appears and can hide damage. If a regular route is flooded, drivers should take another route or wait somewhere safe. Residents should never drive around barricades or enter flooded areas to see how high the water is. Martin County Fire Rescue also advises residents to be prepared to evacuate if flooding threatens their homes or neighborhoods and to have an emergency kit ready for household members and pets. The Community Information Center will be open to provide flood-related information. Okeechobee County Okeechobee County is also preparing for severe flooding. The Okeechobee County Sheriff’s Office says its emergency operations center will remain active as staff coordinate response and recovery efforts from past flooding. Sandbags are available at Okeechobee County Public Works, 804 Northwest Second St. Lucie County Public Safety Department is monitoring the forecast and reminding residents to secure loose items that could be damaged by wind. Gusty northeast winds of 25 to 30 mph are forecast Tuesday and Wednesday, with gusts of 35 to 40 mph along the coast. Residents should secure tarps, patio furniture and other unsecured items. A rip current advisory remains in effect for St. Strong onshore winds can create dangerous rip currents and rough surf. Lucie County Fire District says its firefighters, paramedics and telecommunicators are prepared to respond as the area faces more heavy rain and recovers from recent flooding. The district has high-water vehicles and a rescue boat available to assist during flood-related emergencies. Free sand is available while supplies last at two self-service locations: County Fairgrounds: 5601 W. Midway Road, Fort Pierce, in the west parking lot Lawnwood Stadium: 2000 Virginia Ave., Fort Pierce Residents should bring their own bags, shovel and other supplies. Residents can use Community Connect to share household information that could help firefighters prepare for an emergency. The county has extended the deadline to Nov. 30 for residents to report flood damage through an online survey. The information will help document flooding across the community and inform recovery efforts. The survey is open to property owners and tenants throughout St. Lucie County, including Fort Pierce, Port St. Lucie Village and unincorporated areas. It asks where flooding occurred, how buildings were affected and what impacts residents and businesses experienced. Residents can complete the flood damage survey by Nov. Officials urge residents across the region to avoid flooded roads and keep roadways clear for emergency responders. If you encounter flooding, turn around and find a safe alternate route.

entry.title: Joe Namath's Lucky Shuck coming to Jensen Beach as waterfront village breaks ground - WPEC
entry.summary: Joe Namath's Lucky Shuck coming to Jensen Beach as waterfront village breaks ground    WPEC
entry.article_text: Football legend Joe Namath is bringing his popular Lucky Shuck restaurant to Jensen Beach as a massive waterfront development takes shape along the St. Rio Marine Village , a 30-acre mixed-use development in Martin County, broke ground Thursday, following more than five years of planning. The project will feature 342 apartments, a 131-slip marina, more than a half-mile of public riverwalk, and several waterfront dining and entertainment destinations. Among them is a new location of The Lucky Shuck Oyster Bar & Taphouse , owned by Namath and his business partner Charlie Modica, along with a second, yet-to-be-named outdoor dining concept. See also: New 24/7 animal cruelty hotline launching across Florida "The Lucky Shuck has always been about good food, good people and being on the water," Namath said. "Rio Marine Village gives us a home right on the river, and I can't wait to see boats pulling up and families sitting down together." The development will also feature the Osprey Club, a waterfront wedding and event venue, along with a public park, boardwalk, beach, and kayak and paddleboard rentals. Martin County commissioners unanimously approved the project's first two phases following years of community discussions. Construction is expected to begin this month, with the first phase scheduled for completion in late 2028.

entry.title: Rough surf and rip currents create dangerous conditions along Treasure Coast - WPBF
entry.summary: Rough surf and rip currents create dangerous conditions along Treasure Coast    WPBF
entry.article_text: Strong winds and high surf are creating dangerous conditions along the Treasure Coast and Palm Beaches, with red flag warnings and a high risk of rip currents keeping most beachgoers out of the water. At Stuart Beach, the wind is whipping through the area, churning up rough water conditions. The beach is nearly empty, with no one in the water and only a few people on the sand. "Take advantage of this; it may not be great weather, but there's not a lot of people. So, you got quiet time to yourself. It's beautiful," said Jon Ciffolillo, a beachgoer. Despite the roaring wind, some are still venturing out to enjoy the morning before another round of heavy rain is expected to move through the area. "It's a beautiful day out here. The wind and the surf is just a different view of nature's beauty," said Frank Harvey, who was walking on the beach with his wife, Joan. Joan Harvey added, "A lot of time in your condo is not always ideal. So, you got to take it when it's not raining." Beachgoers are being urged to take caution, as conditions in the water remain dangerous. A high surf advisory is in effect along the Palm Beaches and Treasure Coast, along with a high risk for rip currents. Red flag warnings are also in place along Martin County's beaches, signaling that even experienced swimmers can be pulled away from shore. Martin County Ocean Rescue advises beachgoers to check with lifeguards about water conditions and to swim in guarded areas when conditions improve. The high surf advisory and high risk for rip currents are expected to last through Thursday. You can check the latest beach conditions across Martin County on their Safe Beach Day website. entry.title: Port St. Lucie police discuss hit-and-run crash that left scooter rider critically hurt - WPBF
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie police discuss hit-and-run crash that left scooter rider critically hurt    WPBF
entry.article_text: Lucie Police Department provides an update on a hit-and-run crash that left a 24-year-old woman critically injured. The crash happened Monday morning near SW Gatlin Boulevard and SW Feather Terrace, where police say the woman was riding an electric scooter when she was struck by a vehicle. Investigators say the driver fled the scene without stopping to render aid. According to police, detectives with the Traffic Homicide Investigations Unit identified the driver and located the vehicle involved. During the investigation, authorities learned the driver had allegedly been participating in a "ding dong ditch" prank shortly before the crash. Police arrested the 18-year-old driver and charged him with leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury. Lucie Police Chief Leo Niemczyk is expected to provide additional details about the investigation, discuss the arrest, and share an update on the victim's condition during today's briefing. The briefing began at 2 p.m., and this story will be updated with the latest information as it becomes available. entry.article_text: An apparent overturned trailer is causing major traffic delays on Florida's Turnpike in St. Lucie County on Sunday afternoon, with southbound traffic backed up behind the crash. According to Florida 511 , the crash was reported around 12:40 p.m. in the southbound lanes around Mile Marker 165 near Fort Pierce. Traffic camera footage near mile marker 164.9 shows what appears to be a large pink vehicle or trailer overturned across part of the highway, with several vehicles backed up behind it. The right lane is blocked, according to the latest traffic report. See also: Teen seriously injured in Jensen Beach e-bike crash, airlifted to hospital The crash is classified as major, and traffic cameras show congestion stretching four miles behind the crash scene. It is unclear whether anyone was injured or how many vehicles were involved. Drivers traveling southbound through St. Lucie County should expect delays as crews respond to the crash. This is a developing story.

Omari Linzell Williams was walking west in the westbound lane near Lee Boulevard when a Chevrolet sedan traveling west struck him with its front right corner, the report said. The crash was reported at 6:45 p.m. Mary’s Medical Center in West Palm Beach, where he was pronounced dead at 9:54 p.m., according to the report. The 30-year-old driver, who is from Vero Beach, was not injured and cooperated with law enforcement, the report said. Neighbors came outside after hearing the crash and provided aid. The Traffic Homicide Investigation is ongoing, FHP said. The report does not say whether any citations have been issued.
