entry.title: Treasure Coast counties prepare for flooding as heavy rain and gusty winds move in - WPEC
entry.summary: Treasure Coast counties prepare for flooding as heavy rain and gusty winds move in    WPEC
entry.article_text: The Treasure Coast is bracing for a soggy stretch as counties prepare for possible flooding from heavy rain. Indian River County The Indian River County Emergency Operations Center remains at Level 2, or partial activation, because of ongoing flooding and the potential for more heavy rain. Emergency services, human services and infrastructure partners are coordinating response and recovery efforts. The county urges residents to avoid flooded roads and floodwaters, watch for rising water in low-lying areas and monitor weather conditions and official updates. Residents with flood-related questions or information can call the Emergency Information Center at 772-226-4000 during operating hours. Due to the heavy rain and gusty winds, solid waste services may be disrupted. Waste Management curbside collections may be delayed, and residents should not put carts in the street if it is flooded. See also: Florida deputies rescue 2-year-old girl found in pond near apartment complex Waste Management collects recycling in blue carts countywide. It collects garbage, yard waste and bulk waste in unincorporated Indian River County, Fellsmere, Sebastian and Indian River Shores. Residents in other cities and towns should check with their local governments for service updates. The county recommends putting carts out by 6 a.m. on collection day, closing lids, bagging garbage, and avoiding overfilled carts. Cardboard should be flattened and placed inside recycling carts, and yard waste should stay inside yard waste carts. Residents should bring carts back in as soon as possible after collection. The landfill and all five Customer Convenience Centers may close early or remain closed if conditions become unsafe. The east-central Florida coast faces a Slight Risk, or Level 2 out of 4, for excessive rainfall. Localized flooding is possible, especially along the coast, and some areas could receive 4 inches or more of rain. Martin County Martin County officials expect 3 to 6 inches of rain, with localized amounts of 8 to 12 inches, beginning Tuesday afternoon and continuing through Nov. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office says it is working with the county’s emergency operations center to monitor rainfall and identify roads that could become difficult to pass. The sheriff’s office plans to deploy high-water rescue vehicles in flood-prone areas. Having the vehicles nearby could help deputies reach residents who need assistance and motorists who become stranded, the office said. The sheriff’s office advises residents to turn around if water covers the road. Standing water may be deeper than it appears and can hide damage. If a regular route is flooded, drivers should take another route or wait somewhere safe. Residents should never drive around barricades or enter flooded areas to see how high the water is. Martin County Fire Rescue also advises residents to be prepared to evacuate if flooding threatens their homes or neighborhoods and to have an emergency kit ready for household members and pets. The Community Information Center will be open to provide flood-related information. Okeechobee County Okeechobee County is also preparing for severe flooding. The Okeechobee County Sheriff’s Office says its emergency operations center will remain active as staff coordinate response and recovery efforts from past flooding. Sandbags are available at Okeechobee County Public Works, 804 Northwest Second St. Lucie County Public Safety Department is monitoring the forecast and reminding residents to secure loose items that could be damaged by wind. Gusty northeast winds of 25 to 30 mph are forecast Tuesday and Wednesday, with gusts of 35 to 40 mph along the coast. Residents should secure tarps, patio furniture and other unsecured items. A rip current advisory remains in effect for St. Strong onshore winds can create dangerous rip currents and rough surf. Lucie County Fire District says its firefighters, paramedics and telecommunicators are prepared to respond as the area faces more heavy rain and recovers from recent flooding. The district has high-water vehicles and a rescue boat available to assist during flood-related emergencies. Free sand is available while supplies last at two self-service locations: County Fairgrounds: 5601 W. Midway Road, Fort Pierce, in the west parking lot Lawnwood Stadium: 2000 Virginia Ave., Fort Pierce Residents should bring their own bags, shovel and other supplies. Residents can use Community Connect to share household information that could help firefighters prepare for an emergency. The county has extended the deadline to Nov. 30 for residents to report flood damage through an online survey. The information will help document flooding across the community and inform recovery efforts. The survey is open to property owners and tenants throughout St. Lucie County, including Fort Pierce, Port St. Lucie Village and unincorporated areas. It asks where flooding occurred, how buildings were affected and what impacts residents and businesses experienced. Residents can complete the flood damage survey by Nov. Officials urge residents across the region to avoid flooded roads and keep roadways clear for emergency responders. If you encounter flooding, turn around and find a safe alternate route.

entry.summary: 18-year-old charged in Port St. Lucie hit-and-run that critically injured woman riding e-scooter    WPTV
entry.article_text: An 18-year-old driver has been arrested after Port St. Lucie Police Department investigators say he struck a 24-year-old woman riding an electric scooter to work and left the scene, leaving her critically injured. Police say the driver had been playing a "ding-dong-ditch" prank with friends shortly before Monday morning's crash.WATCH: E-Scooter Hit-and-Run in Port St. LuciePolice identified the driver as Tristan Sanchez-Chasmer. He was arrested on a felony charge of leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury, according to the department.The crash happened near Southwest Gatlin Boulevard and Southwest Feather Terrace. Investigators said the woman was traveling west on the sidewalk toward Southwest Rosser Boulevard and had entered a crosswalk when she was hit by a gray Chevrolet Tahoe making a left turn onto Southwest Feather Terrace.Port St. Lucie Police Chief Leo Niemczyk said Tuesday the woman remained unconscious and in critical condition."We're deeply concerned for her recovery, and our thoughts are with her loved ones," Niemczyk said.Police said a witness stopped to help the woman, called 911 and was able to get the SUV's license plate information. Investigators used that information to identify the vehicle and the driver. Investigators said Sanchez-Chasmer had two friends with him and had been playing "ding-dong-ditch" shortly before the crash. "They were specifically playing, I'll call it ring and run, ding-dong-ditch, at a house that belonged to a friend of theirs, and apparently the mother came to the door and they fled the scene," Niemczyk told WPTV.Niemczyk said investigators believe the people inside the SUV realized a collision had occurred."They're aware that they hit something. I'll say that," he said.According to Niemczyk, Sanchez-Chasmer and the two passengers did not call 911.Niemczyk said the decision to leave the scene was key to the criminal investigation."Had they remained on scene, provided aid, it would have been a very different criminal outcome," Niemczyk said. "There probably wouldn't have been criminal charges at that point."Sanchez-Chasmer was charged with leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury. According to published reports citing law enforcement records, he was being held on a $5,000 bond. Police have not announced charges against the two passengers. WPTV returned to the intersection after the crash and spoke with 15-year-old John Rogalewski, who said he rides an e-scooter to school and is sometimes on the road early in the morning."I'm looking at my surroundings almost the whole time," Rogalewski said. "I'm making sure every time I have to cross the street that there's not a car coming up, and that it is my sign to go, no matter how long I have to wait to cross."Police said the 24-year-old woman was wearing a helmet when she was struck.The investigation remains active, according to police, and toxicology results are still pending.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: Historic Vero Beach neighborhood gets new life as vibrant village for artists
entry.summary: A historic Vero Beach neighborhood is getting a new life through art, as sculptor Ross Power leads an effort to transform Edgewood into a vibrant community of artists, galleries, studios and public gathering spaces. Known as the 'Father of the Vero Beach Art Village,' Power is helping turn a once-overlooked neighborhood into a destination for creativity, where artists can live, work and share their talents. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Historic Vero Beach neighborhood gets new life as vibrant village for artists The transformation is already underway, with murals, public art and community projects taking shape. Power says more galleries, studios, cafes and bed-and-breakfasts are in the works, bringing new opportunities for artists, residents and visitors. A historic Vero Beach neighborhood becomes a canvas Under the shade of a century-old lychee tree, Power reads from a poem dedicated to the tree as a dancer performs beneath its branches. 'A place where you and me can become we,' Power said. For the longtime sculptor, the tree represents something bigger: a gathering place where art can bring people together. That vision is unfolding in Edgewood, a neighborhood established in 1916 that was once home to Vero Beach's first public school and first motel, according to the Vero Beach Art Village organization. Over the years, parts of the neighborhood fell into disrepair. But where others saw aging properties and neglected alleyways, Power saw potential. 'It spoke to me, and I heard I was once great and now I have fallen into disrepair and not respected at all, and I said we're going to change that,' Power told WPTV anchor Meghan McRoberts during a tour of the neighborhood. Power has spent decades creating art and helping develop artistic communities, including an art center in Miami. Now, he's bringing that experience to Vero Beach, with an entire neighborhood as his canvas. Turning Edgewood's alleyways into works of art One of Power's biggest ambitions is transforming 11 alleyways throughout Edgewood into colorful destinations filled with murals and public art. entry.article_text: A historic Vero Beach neighborhood is getting a new life through art, as sculptor Ross Power leads an effort to transform Edgewood into a vibrant community of artists, galleries, studios and public gathering spaces.Known as the "Father of the Vero Beach Art Village," Power is helping turn a once-overlooked neighborhood into a destination for creativity, where artists can live, work and share their talents.WATCH REPORT BELOW: The transformation is already underway, with murals, public art and community projects taking shape. Power says more galleries, studios, cafes and bed-and-breakfasts are in the works, bringing new opportunities for artists, residents and visitors.A historic Vero Beach neighborhood becomes a canvasUnder the shade of a century-old lychee tree, Power reads from a poem dedicated to the tree as a dancer performs beneath its branches."A place where you and me can become we," Power said.For the longtime sculptor, the tree represents something bigger: a gathering place where art can bring people together.That vision is unfolding in Edgewood, a neighborhood established in 1916 that was once home to Vero Beach's first public school and first motel, according to the Vero Beach Art Village organization.Over the years, parts of the neighborhood fell into disrepair. But where others saw aging properties and neglected alleyways, Power saw potential."It spoke to me, and I heard I was once great and now I have fallen into disrepair and not respected at all, and I said we're going to change that," Power told WPTV anchor Meghan McRoberts during a tour of the neighborhood.Power has spent decades creating art and helping develop artistic communities, including an art center in Miami.Now, he's bringing that experience to Vero Beach, with an entire neighborhood as his canvas.Turning Edgewood's alleyways into works of artOne of Power's biggest ambitions is transforming 11 alleyways throughout Edgewood into colorful destinations filled with murals and public art."I'm taking the alleys which are the ugliest part of the neighborhood and turning them into mural opportunities where the alleys are going to be like unbelievable for people to come and visit," Power said."There's a lack of buildings but there's not a lack of fences."Power sees those fences, walls and underused spaces as opportunities to showcase local artists and create an outdoor art experience.But the effort goes beyond beautifying back streets.Special zoning allows artists to live and work in the villageThe city of Vero Beach has established Cultural Arts Village zoning districts designed to encourage artistic businesses while preserving Edgewood's historic residential character.According to the city and the Vero Beach Art Village organization, the zoning creates opportunities for art galleries, studios, live-work spaces and other businesses, depending on the property's classification and applicable approvals.The goal is to create a walkable neighborhood where historic homes can become studios and galleries, and artists can collaborate with their neighbors.“I’ve been working on a bunch of different paintings. And we have projects; there's a bunch of different projects we’ve been working on whether it’s for the city or for trying to save big blue, or our community garden, “ said Linwood Addison Fuller IV, an artist who moved to Edgewood for the focus on art. His wife is also an artist.“It’s so much better to be an artist in a community with other artists,” said sculptor Andrew Draminski. “I’m sitting here working and my neighbors are walking their dog down the alley and come on in and we have a cup of coffee or something like that.”The village's vision extends beyond traditional galleries. Organizers hope to create spaces for music, dance, poetry, photography, workshops and other community events.More galleries, studios and community spaces plannedAccording to the nonprofit Friends of the Vero Beach Art Village, the neighborhood's transformation is a grassroots effort involving artists, residents, businesses and volunteers.The organization highlights ongoing initiatives involving murals, public art, studios, galleries, streetscape improvements and community events.Power says additional galleries, studios, cafes and bed-and-breakfasts are also in the works.For him, the goal isn't simply to attract visitors. It's to create a community where artists can thrive together and residents can take pride in their neighborhood."If you want to eat great food, hear great music, see great things, meet great artists, this is the place," Power said.And beneath the sprawling branches of that century-old lychee tree, Power hopes the community he's helping cultivate will continue to grow.Where is the Vero Beach Art Village?The Vero Beach Art Village is located in the historic Edgewood neighborhood, just west of downtown Vero Beach.The neighborhood generally stretches between 14th and 20th avenues and 18th and 20th streets.The Friends of the Vero Beach Art Village nonprofit encourages residents and visitors to support the effort through volunteering, donations and participation in community art projects.Click here for more information about the village, its projects and opportunities to get involved.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: Dolphins defense takes major hit as 3 defensive tackles suffer season-ending injuries
entry.summary: The 1-8 Miami Dolphins are facing a major shakeup on defense after three top defensive tackles suffered season-ending injuries recently. Head coach Jeff Hafley announced this week that defensive tackles Zeek Biggers and Jordan Phillips are done for the year after injuries on Sunday against the Indianapolis Colts. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Dolphins face defensive shakeup after 3 season-ending injuries The bad news comes after veteran defensive tackle Zach Sieler suffered a season-ending injury in Week 9 against the Detroit Lions. 'Is it hard losing three guys to (injured reserve), all at the same position with the span of a couple days? Yeah, I mean for sure,' Hafley said. Despite the news, the coach was optimistic about their careers moving forward. 'I mean, those are two players who will be really missed. Obviously, top down with Zach not being here. But those guys, what they've shown us in this year, they got a very, very bright future. So I know this is hard for them right now and hard for our team. But those guys are good football players, and they're going to have really good careers in the NFL. So wishing them the best, and they'll be missed,' Hafley said. Hafley said other players will need to step up to fill the void. 'That's what we need to find this week in practice. Who are the next guys like (Jordan) Jefferson, right? Those are the guys that we're going to have to see, and we're going to have to get them ready to go,' Hafley said. The team will do that with extra meetings and walk-throughs. 'We'll continue to develop the new guys who come in,' Hafley said. It's another challenge for the Dolphins, who have already faced a season full of setbacks as they rebuild their roster. 'This year is full of adversity. I mean, we lose our quarterback. We lose one of the best running backs in the league. We got all these rookies. So what? Like, what are we going to do about it? We all have to be at our best. We can't sulk. We have to understand the situation and we got to work. When Sunday comes, the one thing I know about this team, they are going to go out there and they are going to compete,' Hafley said. Heading into another divisional matchup Sunday, the Dolphins will travel to Buffalo to play the Bills. 'We will give them everything we got,' Hafley said.

entry.title: 'Overwhelming': St. Lucie County residents prepare for heavy rainfall with sandbag stations - WPBF
entry.summary: 'Overwhelming': St. Lucie County residents prepare for heavy rainfall with sandbag stations    WPBF
entry.article_text: Lucie County residents are preparing for heavy rainfall this week, with officials offering free self-serve sandbag stations and working to clear drainage systems to address potential flooding. Dreamland Park in Fort Pierce, residents were seen filling sandbags to protect their homes. Resident Lisa Powell is concerned. "My ditches are full from the last storm, they haven't gone down, so this could be very bad. The water is just still standing there, up to the yard." Another resident shared their concerns, saying, "My crawlspace got a foot of water in there, so trying to get all these bags to try and cover up the opening, you know." Public works crews in St. Lucie County are actively checking and clearing swales and drainage systems as the area braces for more severe weather. Recent flooding left parts of the county submerged, with residents in the Creekside development trapped inside, some using kayaks to navigate flooded streets while others waded through the water. Fredrick Reeves, a resident whose home was previously flooded, is preparing for the upcoming rain by using sandbags and mulch to block water from entering his house. "It was pretty bad, and the house itself, once it started coming in, I thought maybe we would be alright. I threw down all my clothes trying to soak it up, but that didn't do anything. The next thing you knew, it was in the house," Reeves said. He described the situation as "overwhelming." The City of Fort Pierce is offering free self-serve sandbag stations at Martin Luther King Jr. Dreamland Park and Jaycee Park. Residents are advised to bring their own bags and shovels. Both parks are open daily from dawn to dusk. Lucie County has also set up self-service sandbag distribution points at the St. Lucie County Fairgrounds West Parking Lot and Lawnwood Stadium Parking Lot, thanks to donations of sand from Dickerson Infrastructure and Stewart Materials. Residents must bring their own supplies and fill their own bags. For updates about the precautions residents should take, please visit St. Lucie County’s emergency management portal at: www.readystlucie.org. For more information, residents can contact the Public Works Department or visit the county’s emergency management portal. My husband, me, and my son run it."Casselman's family has been operating the Auto Care Center at its current location for 15 years after spending another 10 years just a few blocks away."We pride ourselves on integrity," she added. "We don't do any advertising. We rely strictly on word of mouth, and we have a great following."Casselman says the problem is that while her business was affected by the road closures after the crash, its location falls outside the boundaries Palm Beach County established for its grant program.Now time is of the essence, and she hopes the county can reconsider her application."Because that grant was first come, first served, I didn't want to lose my place in line for that grant based on a possible clerical error," she said.Palm Beach County's Housing and Economic Development Department says the boundary was not a clerical error.In its latest response to WPTV, it confirmed the Auto Care Center application was deemed ineligible because the business is outside the approved program boundaries.The county said those boundaries were never intended to include the entire area affected by the crash investigation's road closures. Instead, officials focused on a smaller area immediately surrounding the crash site where, based on information from officials at the scene, closures were expected to last longer."We should be entitled to some grant money too because we did lose probably anywhere from $5 to $10,000 during those 11 days," she said.For an auto repair business, Casselman said losing vehicle access essentially meant losing the ability to do business."My business is auto repair. No vehicles could come in here," she said. "We had to ask customers to go to competition because we couldn't service them." The timing made the potential losses particularly difficult, she said, because flooding in the area meant more drivers could have needed repairs."We had a lot of flooding in Palm Beach County, a lot in this area, and people did have their cars stranded and needed them looked at and we couldn't do it," Casselman said.Casselman said the crash itself was only about three blocks from her business and argues officials could have opened up her portion of the roadway much quicker but didn't.When WPTV first reported on the grant program, we spoke with Eddie Rivera, owner of Señor Lechon along Military Trail. His restaurant had been open for only about three months when the Learjet crash forced the business to close for more than a week.Rivera estimates he lost $30,000 to $40,000 during the shutdown, which was especially difficult with 15 employees relying on the restaurant and expenses continuing even while customers couldn't get through. "Financially wise, it's been a pretty economical impact, considering we've got 15 employees and we've got a lot of businesses in the area," Rivera told WPTV at the time. WPTV caught up with Rivera again today. He told us he has applied for the county grant and is scheduled to meet with county officials this week.The county's Military Trail Business Interruption Grant Program was created with $250,000 to help eligible businesses affected by the crash and road closure, with grants capped at $5,000.Palm Beach County told WPTV it has received 79 applications from businesses interested in the grant program.Of those, 27 have been approved, with $111,098 awarded. Another 20 were determined to be ineligible, while 32 applications remain in various stages of review.The county says $138,901 remains available.For now, however, the county has not decided to expand its program boundaries. Officials said they are first working through applications submitted by businesses located within the approved area.Casselman believes the county should take a second look."I think they should reach out and rather than just shutting you off saying you're not on this piece of paper, the map," she said. "They should have taken a few minutes, a few days, say we're working on it and look and see, yes, they were impacted, and then accept our applications."Casselman said the impact extends beyond her own shop."I'm not doing this to promote my business or anything," she said. "There's a grocery store to the south of me that they were, in fact, impacted. They could not get any customers, and you think about the local community that uses that grocery store."Casselman confirmed to WPTV that the county put its decision on her application in writing.Casselman said she's now waiting to see whether county officials will reconsider the boundaries."I'm waiting right now to hear from the county administrator to see if I will be included in that first area due to the lack of, um, understanding what actually happened when the roads were closed," she said. "So I'm leaving that open. Hopefully they'll make it right. If not, I'll just have to accept it and I'll be out that money."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: GTA 6 finally arrives as Florida gamers prepare for one of the most anticipated video game launches ever
entry.summary: It's the most anticipated video game in the last 10 years. At midnight Thursday, video gamers in Florida will finally have an opportunity to play Grand Theft Auto 6. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Grand Theft Auto 6 Releases at Midnight 'Everything I'm seeing so far looks like the hype has been worth it,' said Adriano, who was outside Skinny Louie restaurant in West Palm Beach on Wednesday. The restaurant has been rebranded as Burger Shot, a fictional fast-food place featured in the game. GTA 6, as it is being called, is set in a place that looks very much like South Florida. The game reportedly had a $1 billion budget and has generated so much buzz among fans that the Wall Street Journal estimates 1.5 million may skip work on Thursday. Sportsinsider.com reports Florida ranks first in the nation for people expected to use a PTO or vacation day to play the game. 'No work tomorrow or for the next five days,' said Laury, who was grabbing lunch Thursday at the West Palm Burger Shot. 'It's a little bit of a religious experience. It's a little crazy.' GTA 6 sells for $79.99 for the standard edition and $99.99 for the ultimate edition for PlayStation 5 and Xbox. WATCH BELOW: Could GTA 6 become best-selling game of all time? Could Grand Theft Auto VI become the best-selling video game of all time? 'It's really reached this level of like mainstream awareness that's pretty unprecedented for a game like this,' Jordan Minor, principal writer at PCMag, said. Minor wrote a review of the game , calling it 'a masterpiece I never want to leave.' 'For a lot of other people, this is going to be the only game they play all year or all next year,' Minor said. 'It may be the only game they've played in like the past five years.'

entry.title: Boynton Beach nonprofit serving 5,000 people weekly urgently searches for new home
entry.summary: A Palm Beach County nonprofit that provides food to thousands of families every week is urgently searching for a new home as the Boynton Beach Mall prepares for a major transition. Restoration Bridge International (RBI) says it must secure a new location for its weekly Saturday food distribution before Jan. 15, 2027. That's when its agreement to use the mall's parking lot expires following the property's sale. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Boynton Beach nonprofit searching for new home for weekly food distribution serving 5,000 people The organization has operated at the Boynton Beach Mall since March 2024. Its Saturday distribution now regularly serves more than 5,000 people and provides approximately 100,000 pounds of supplemental food each week. According to executive director Jason Mandle, the organization has distributed more than 13 million pounds of food since moving its operation to Boynton Beach. Mandle says the nonprofit was aware the property could be sold, but the news that it would need to find another location came as a surprise. The mall's prospective buyer, homebuilding company Lennar, plans to transform the 91-acre property into a mixed-use community with housing, retail, commercial space and other amenities. The purchase is expected to be completed in early 2027. While the redevelopment could bring new life to the area, RBI says the transition could leave thousands of families without a food resource they have come to depend on. 'Every Saturday morning, more than 5,000 neighbors count on this distribution to put food on their tables,' Mandle said. Cars often begin lining up Friday evening ahead of the Saturday morning distribution, which runs from 9 a.m. to noon. Mandle said the nonprofit has benefited from a no-cost agreement to use the mall's parking lot, allowing it to operate with a limited budget. Finding a similar arrangement is now a priority. The organization is looking for a large parking lot, commercial property, house of worship or municipal site in Palm Beach County that can safely accommodate its operations. Mandle says the next location needs enough space to handle approximately 800 vehicles on a Saturday morning. Without a new host site, the organization warns the weekly distribution could come to an end, affecting thousands of residents who rely on the assistance. entry.title: Flood victims demand answers as FEMA delays disaster decision amid millions in damage
entry.summary: Dumpsters line driveways, bulldozers tear through debris and homes sit gutted along Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach, where families are still picking up the pieces after historic flooding devastated parts of Martin County. For some residents, the water is still receding. For others, the cleanup has only just begun. Now, as another round of rain threatens the Treasure Coast, families already facing thousands of dollars in repairs are asking a question they can't afford to leave unanswered: How will they pay to rebuild? WATCH REPORT BELOW: Flood victims demand answers as FEMA delays disaster decision 'It's like an apocalypse here' For Linda Weisbecker, the destruction is difficult to put into words. 'It's like an apocalypse here,' she said, standing amid the devastation in her neighborhood. For nine days, Weisbecker and her neighbors navigated waist-deep floodwaters, unable to begin assessing the full extent of the damage. 'Once we got through that and the water came out, we just all started pitching in, going in to see what we can salvage from each home,' said Weisbecker. Neighbors worked together, sorting through waterlogged belongings and salvaging whatever they could. Now, the home she once knew is little more than an empty shell. 'We are fully gutted. Our house is empty,' she said. 'We lost everything, from pictures of our children and their lives, our friends, our grandkids, now we have great-grandkids. Everything [my husband] had since he was 13 on is gone.' Demolition is supposed to be the first step toward rebuilding. But for Weisbecker, it's also a painful reminder of how much work and money lies ahead. 'You do think about that process and you sit there and you say to yourself, how am I gonna do this?' Weisbecker said. Weisbecker was approved for a $25,000 grant through Florida's State Housing Initiatives Partnership, or SHIP, program, which provides housing assistance to eligible residents. While the grant offers some relief, the cost of rebuilding a flood-damaged home can quickly exceed that amount. And not every family will qualify for the same assistance. 'This is very urgent for people to get back into their daily lives,' Weisbecker said. 'This is total devastation. For everyone.' Millions in damage but no federal disaster declaration New estimates released by Martin County reveal the staggering financial toll of the flooding. According to county officials, the storm caused: $14 million in beach damage Nearly $1 million in damaged roads that now
entry.article_text: For everyone."New estimates released by Martin County reveal the staggering financial toll of the flooding.According to county officials, the storm caused:$14 million in beach damageNearly $1 million in damaged roads that now need to be repaved$3 million in residential losses affecting families still struggling to recoverAdditional costs in county staff overtime associated with the emergency responseThose figures put the known damage at approximately $18 million, not including additional expenses.A federal major disaster declaration could open the door to FEMA assistance for the public infrastructure repairs and potentially provide additional relief to affected residents.But so far, no such declaration has been approved.Without federal reimbursement, County Spokesperson Martha Ann Kniess said Martin County could be left responsible for covering millions of dollars in public recovery costs itself, forcing officials to find funding elsewhere in the county budget or identify other sources of assistance.And that uncertainty comes as residents are already struggling to afford repairs to their own homes.During an emotional Martin County Commission meeting Tuesday, flood victims pleaded with local leaders to do more to secure financial assistance."Please. Fight for us!" one resident urged commissioners.Others questioned why help was taking so long, particularly as more rain threatened their already damaged properties."And the answer from this dais is wait 13 more days?!?" another resident asked.Commissioner Eileen Vargas of District 1 told residents she is doing everything she can to try to expedite the process, but 'doesn't have all the answers.'"I did, through contacts, reach out to FEMA to try and get this going," Vargas said.According to Vargas, a new FEMA director is expected to take office Nov. 30, which she hopes will turn the tide. "He is going to personally petition President Trump to declare our area a disaster," Vargas said.However, a federal declaration is not guaranteed, and even if approved, not all damages or recovery expenses would necessarily qualify for reimbursement.WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey contacted FEMA, questioning the length of the response and when residents could expect answers.In its response, FEMA confirmed it had received the major disaster declaration request and that the request remains under review.The agency referred additional questions about the response and recovery timeline to the Florida Division of Emergency Management.WPTV also contacted the state agency but had not received a response as of Wednesday.In the meantime, Martin County is working to distribute emergency housing assistance through Florida's SHIP program.The county currently has approximately $1 million in SHIP funding available, with eligible residents able to apply for grants of up to $25,000.Additional assistance may be available through loans of up to $75,000, though those loans are subject to repayment requirements and liens.County officials acknowledged that the existing funding could run out quickly, particularly given the scale of the destruction.Michelle Miller, Martin County's human services director, told commissioners the state has promised additional disaster relief funding, but doesn't know when that funding could come in. "They haven't confirmed the amount yet but has assured us we will be getting some disaster relief funds," Miller said.But there are limitations.Some programs require homeowners to pay for repairs upfront before seeking reimbursement.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie restores water service, but boil water notice remains
entry.summary: Water service has been fully restored to the Tradition and western Port St. Lucie areas following a major water main break Tuesday, but a precautionary boil water notice remains in effect. The break happened near Glades Cut Off Road when a contractor working on a construction project unrelated to the city damaged a 36-inch water main, according to city officials. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Tradition water service restored after water main break Crews completed repairs Tuesday evening and began flushing the water main shortly afterward. The city initially recommended a 48-hour precautionary boil water notice Tuesday at noon for the Tradition area, including Western Grove, Riverland, Wilson Grove and Southern Grove, west of Interstate 95 to Becker Road. The notice also covers communities along Glades Cut Off Road, including Copper Creek, Wylder and Verano. City officials said water quality testing began Wednesday. Because of the number of customers affected, a significant number of samples must be collected and tested before the notice can be lifted. Residents should continue boiling water until the city confirms it is safe to use without boiling. Restored water service does not mean the boil water notice has ended. The city is investigating the incident and expects to pursue appropriate action to recover costs from those responsible. Updates will be posted at CityofPSL.com .

entry.title: Boca Raton opens its first climate-controlled indoor pickleball and padel club with 25 courts
entry.summary: A massive indoor pickleball facility is opening its doors in Boca Raton. Boca Paddle by City Pickle is officially welcoming players to 25 brand-new courts. It's the city's first fully climate-controlled indoor pickleball and padel club. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Massive pickleball facility opens in Boca Raton Day passes cost $40, with Boca Raton residents getting $5 off. The center also features a restaurant and bar, a shop, and fitness and recovery spaces like a sauna and cold plunge. One of its co-founders says Boca Paddle is unlike anything else in the city. Boca Raton's mayor says the city is the right fit for this type of facility. The area that we're in right now, here in North Park, is in need of revitalization. And this facility, by itself, takes a huge step in that direction to help revitalize this part of the city,' Boca Raton Mayor Andy Thomson said. The facility will also be the home of a new professional team. 'I'm excited that we're a home for the Palm Beach Royals , which is major league pickleball's newest franchise. They paid $16 million last year. They're going to be based here,' Boca Paddle Co-Founder Brian Levine said. By the numbers, the facility spans 100,000 square feet and cost around $20 million to build. It has 14 indoor pickleball courts and nine outdoor courts, along with two padel courts. entry.title: St. Lucie County prepares for more rain after historic flooding; schools closed Wednesday - WPEC
entry.summary: St. Lucie County prepares for more rain after historic flooding; schools closed Wednesday    WPEC
entry.article_text: Crews are clearing drainage systems and checking waterways in St. Lucie County as another round of rain threatens areas still recovering from historic flooding. Lucie Public Schools is releasing students two hours early Tuesday. The district announced Tuesday afternoon that schools and offices will be closed Wednesday as a precaution. All after-school activities, aftercare programs, and athletic events scheduled for Wednesday are also canceled. District officials will continue monitoring rainfall, flooding, road closures, and the accessibility of schools, bus stops, and transportation routes throughout Wednesday. A decision regarding school operations for Thursday, November 19, will be announced Wednesday evening. Lucie officials say Public Works crews are inspecting drainage systems, clearing blockages and lowering water levels where possible. The ground remains saturated, increasing the risk of flooding even if rainfall is lighter than it was during the early November storms. See also: Heavy rain returns this week, bringing major threat of flooding across South Florida The National Weather Service has issued a flood watch for St. Lucie County from Tuesday afternoon through Friday evening. Forecasters expect 3 to 6 inches of rain across the area, with higher amounts possible in some locations. Two weeks ago, floodwaters stranded cars, trapped families and forced some residents to wade through deep water. Videos from that flooding showed high school freshman Noah Julian swimming from his school bus toward his home in a flooded Port St. Another video showed 7-year-old Ella Ghodooshim walking through chest-deep water with her mother near Oak Hammock K-8. That mother, Thassia Rodrigues, told CBS12 her only concern was getting her daughter safely across the flooded intersection. "As long as I can get her across and get her to safety, that was my main concern," Rodrigues said. She described how quickly the flooding overwhelmed the neighborhood, leaving parents struggling to reach their children. "It was pretty scary and in a matter of minutes we had everything just flood," she said. Lucie Public Schools told CBS12 News that decisions about closures and early dismissal are based on forecasts and information from the National Weather Service and Emergency Operations Center. The district said the information available before the previous flooding did not indicate schools needed to close or dismiss students earlier. This time, officials said the forecast supported releasing students two hours early to get them home before the heaviest rain. The district said it was awaiting additional updates from the National Weather Service at 2 p.m. and Emergency Operations Center at 4 p.m. Tuesday before making any further decisions about school schedules. Parents picking up their children near Oak Hammock K-8 Tuesday told CBS12 News they welcomed the earlier dismissal. "It's kind of nice that they're doing it early so we have time to get them and not have to rush," said Nathan Leach, whose child attends the school. Rhett Linton, another parent, recalled kayaking through the flooded intersection during the previous storm. "I'm super happy that they are stepping up and taking precautions," Linton said. Rodrigues, who was captured on video helping her daughter through the floodwaters, also praised the district's decision. Lucie County, we appreciate you guys," she said. Officials are urging residents to plan ahead, monitor forecasts and local alerts, and limit unnecessary travel. Drivers should never enter standing or moving water. Floodwater can stall a vehicle and cause costly engine damage. If you cannot tell how deep the water is, turn around and find another route. Residents can report flooding concerns to St. Lucie County at flooding@stlucieco.org .

entry.article_text: Lucie County schools and district offices are closed Wednesday as families prepare for more heavy rain, two weeks after flooding left roads underwater and damaged homes. All aftercare programs, after-school activities and athletic events scheduled for Wednesday are also canceled. See also: Flood risk continues for the Treasure Coast and Palm Beaches through Friday evening The school district said forecasts show the potential for significant rainfall and localized flooding. With the ground already saturated, the district said closing schools was the cautious choice for students, families and employees. Officials are monitoring rainfall, flooding, road closures and access to schools, bus stops and transportation routes. The district plans to announce Wednesday evening whether schools will reopen Thursday. Across the Treasure Coast, some residents are filling sandbags to protect their homes. Others are stocking up on groceries and preparing to stay home if roads flood again. Lucie says floodwater rose to his knees two weeks ago, damaging his garage and guitars. He filled sandbags at the St. Lucie County Fairgrounds and is adding more around his home. We had a lot of water go into the garage and we just got over the fact that it stopped smelling like mold in there, Vargas said. And then here we go again with this inclement weather. Lucie County set up self-service sand distribution sites at the county fairgrounds in Fort Pierce and the Lawnwood Stadium parking lot. Residents need to bring their own bags and shovels and fill the bags themselves. Sand is available while supplies last. Tuesday, the two truckloads at Lawnwood Stadium were nearly gone. Glen Ferlance was out for a morning walk Wednesday morning when he spoke with CBS12. He said the flooding two weeks ago kept him from reaching his children. I could not get to cross over to go and see my kids, Ferlance said. I had to park in the um the plaza here and just look on. Ferlance said he lives in Port St. Lucie and he’s preparing for more rain, but hopes the flooding won’t be as severe this time. I just hope that is not too bad like last time. Yes, I’m prepared, he said. I’m going to get something to eat, and I’m running back home in my bed to watch TV and relax until all this is over. He also said he’s glad St. Lucie County schools are closed. I just thank God they’re not school today, so the kids then should be more safe at home, he said. Some residents are also stocking up on food and supplies. Shoppers told CBS12 they’re preparing to stay home if roads flood again. The district said updates about school operations will be shared on its website and social media channels. Martin County canceled after-school activities. Schools in Indian River and Okeechobee counties remain open as of Wednesday morning. Palm Beach County schools and offices are open Wednesday, but the district canceled all after-school activities and athletics because of the afternoon forecast. Aftercare families must pick up their children by 4 p.m., the district said.

entry.title: Teen thrown 50 feet in Jensen Beach e-bike crash, sheriff warns parents of crackdown - cw34.com
entry.summary: Teen thrown 50 feet in Jensen Beach e-bike crash, sheriff warns parents of crackdown    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Parents could face criminal charges in a crackdown on illegal e-bikes after a teen was thrown 50 feet in a crash, the Martin County sheriff warned Monday. During a news conference, the sheriff revealed that a 14-year-old Port St. Lucie boy suffered catastrophic injuries in Sunday's crash near U.S. 1 and Northwest Goldenrod Road. The teen was airlifted to St. Mary's Medical Center , where he is now in stable condition. According to the sheriff, the boy and a friend had traveled roughly five miles from home on separate e-bikes when they attempted to cross U.S. See also: Kids, 6,000 fentanyl pills and stolen gun uncovered in massive Florida drug bust The first teen made it across, but the 14-year-old was struck by a northbound vehicle that had a green light. The impact sent the boy flying approximately 50 feet, while his e-bike landed about 100 feet away. "Had he not been wearing a helmet, and had he been hit just a little different, we'd be talking about a 14-year-old die in a fatality crash," the sheriff said. Investigators determined the teen was riding a 3,300-watt electric bike, more than four times the 750-watt limit cited by the sheriff. The motorbike-style vehicle was not street-legal, he said. The crash comes amid growing concerns over e-bike safety in Martin County, where the sheriff reported 41 e-bike crashes this year, involving riders as young as 7 and as old as 80. The sheriff said educational workshops, warnings, and previous enforcement efforts have failed to curb dangerous riding. Now, deputies are considering tougher consequences, including seizing illegal e-bikes and potentially pursuing criminal charges against parents who knowingly allow their children to ride them. I'm not anti-e-bikes, but I'm anti-illegal e-bikes being ridden irresponsibly on our streets." The Florida Highway Patrol is leading the crash investigation, with assistance from the Martin County Sheriff's Office.

entry.title: From unrecruited walk-on to NFL hopeful: FAU's Easton Messer eyes becoming NFL draft pick
entry.summary: After back-to-back 1,000-yard receiving seasons, FAU wide receiver Easton Messer is on several NFL Draft boards and looks to be the Owls' first draft pick in six years. I sat down with the FAU Owls standout for a one-on-one conversation about his journey one that spanned multiple countries before leading him to South Florida. WATCH REPORT BELOW: FAU's Easton Messer aims to become Owls' first NFL Draft pick since 2020 Messer moved around a lot over the years. 'My first place was Costa Rica, then I moved back to Louisville, then Panama, and lastly Malaysia,' Messer said. Growing up, he played both soccer and American football a combination he credits with shaping his footwork and technique. 'I really haven't thought about the fact that soccer helped out my feet and helped me play receiver, but soccer is big pretty much everywhere but the U.S. Just being over in those places and trying to get integrated into the culture,' Messer said. Football, though, was always his sport. 'Growing up, that was my sport. I played football, basketball and a little bit of baseball, but football was my favorite one. I went to high school at Christian Academy in Louisville,' Messer said. In high school, Messer was a standout receiver but felt he was under-recruited. 'It was pretty short; it wasn't a ton of recruiting with me being undersized and not passing the eye test. I had a couple offers, and I wasn't sure if they were commitable, and I ended up having to walk on at Western Kentucky,' Messer said. After standing out over three years at Western Kentucky, Messer entered the transfer portal and ultimately arrived at FAU. 'My transfer portal recruitment wasn't really popping either; not a lot of people reached out,' Messer said. Since 2020, no Owls player has heard their name called in the NFL Draft. Messer could change that in a few months. 'Personally, for me, going from a walk-on and not really getting recruited to possibly getting my name called on draft night, it doesn't even feel real at this point, but we got some other guys too,' Messer said. entry.title: Joe Namath's Lucky Shuck coming to Jensen Beach as waterfront village breaks ground - WPEC
entry.summary: Joe Namath's Lucky Shuck coming to Jensen Beach as waterfront village breaks ground    WPEC
entry.article_text: Football legend Joe Namath is bringing his popular Lucky Shuck restaurant to Jensen Beach as a massive waterfront development takes shape along the St. Rio Marine Village , a 30-acre mixed-use development in Martin County, broke ground Thursday, following more than five years of planning. The project will feature 342 apartments, a 131-slip marina, more than a half-mile of public riverwalk, and several waterfront dining and entertainment destinations. Among them is a new location of The Lucky Shuck Oyster Bar & Taphouse , owned by Namath and his business partner Charlie Modica, along with a second, yet-to-be-named outdoor dining concept. See also: New 24/7 animal cruelty hotline launching across Florida "The Lucky Shuck has always been about good food, good people and being on the water," Namath said. "Rio Marine Village gives us a home right on the river, and I can't wait to see boats pulling up and families sitting down together." The development will also feature the Osprey Club, a waterfront wedding and event venue, along with a public park, boardwalk, beach, and kayak and paddleboard rentals. Martin County commissioners unanimously approved the project's first two phases following years of community discussions. Construction is expected to begin this month, with the first phase scheduled for completion in late 2028.

entry.title: 'Today we are homeless': Jensen Beach family displaced by historic flooding pleads for help rebuilding home - WPTV
entry.summary: 'Today we are homeless': Jensen Beach family displaced by historic flooding pleads for help rebuilding home    WPTV
entry.article_text: A Jensen Beach family displaced by historic flooding is searching for more permanent housing and money to rebuild after water destroyed much of the inside of their home. Lisa and Jeremy French, who have two young boys, told WPTV's Michael Hoffman they ultimately have one goal: to get their family back home.WATCH REPORT BELOW:WPTV first met the French family shortly after historic rainfall hit South Florida and the Treasure Coast. Floodwater had surrounded their neighborhood, forcing residents to use kayaks to get around and check on neighbors.Days later, much of the water has receded. The damage has not."My floorboards are outside," Lisa French said.Hoffman returned to the French family's Jensen Beach home for an update, but the family said it was not safe to go inside.French said the flooding wiped out much of what her family had accumulated over the years."Our appliances are gone, our cabinets are gone, every piece of furniture," French said.The family is now trying to determine how to pay for repairs while securing a more permanent place to live.WPTV met French again at the Hoke Library in Jensen Beach, where a Multi-Agency Resource Center has been helping people looking for assistance following the flooding.French told Hoffman that her home flooded days after the rain had stopped.Martin County told WPTV that the family's home is near the Savannah Preserves, an area where excess water naturally flows from other flooded areas.French, however, questions whether other actions involving water entering the preserve contributed to what happened at her home."They're saying it's from natural rain, but they dumped Monday and Tuesday, nonstop into the savannas," French said.The impact of the flooding extends beyond the physical damage.Through tears, Lisa and Jeremy French pleaded for help before the Martin County Commission as they described what their family is facing."Today we are homeless," Lisa French told commissioners. "We have nowhere to host Thanksgiving. We have nowhere for our boys to have Christmas. We don't have beds to come home to."The couple has two young boys. French said she wants them to continue growing up in the Jensen Beach home the family worked hard to maintain.For now, however, the family says it needs more permanent housing while trying to determine where the money to repair the home will come from.French said the uncertainty surrounding assistance has left her worried there could still be a significant financial gap, even if additional aid becomes available."Who's going to fill in the gaps?" French said. "And, you know, maybe I feel like somebody should take accountability."Despite the uncertainty and extensive damage, the family says it has not given up hope of returning."We just want to go home," French said. "Like, that's at the end, that we just want to be home with our family."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: Martin County commissioners approve emergency funding for flood victims - WPBF
entry.summary: Martin County commissioners approve emergency funding for flood victims    WPBF
entry.article_text: Martin County officials announced their plans to support flood victims as they begin the long road to recovery. County commissioners fielded hours of public comment at their meeting Tuesday. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 The county has set up a sandbag distribution site at Halpatiokee Regional Park where folks can fill up to 25 sandbags per household. That is just one part of what they’re doing to prepare for more storms and help residents. “The county needs to help us. Somebody needs to come forward. There's got to be an emergency fund. I can't understand how Martin County, one of the richest counties in Florida, does not have one,” Mary Berner, who lost her home on Hyline Drive in the flood, said. One by one, residents stepped to the podium at the meeting airing their frustrations at the flood disaster response. “We sat there for eight days and didn't have any response until we had a, you know, a meeting and made several phone calls to our commissioner and got no response from her. So, it's hard to not be heard,” Berner said. Commissioners made sure those pleas were heard Tuesday. They approved an increase of an up to $25,000 in grant funding for each eligible household from the county’s SHIP Disaster Assistance fund. Eligibility is determined by household income based on HUD guidelines. “These funds come through the state through something called the Sadowski funds. These funds are captured for each county when there's a real estate transaction, and then the state delivers to each county a certain amount each year to allocate for not only disaster, but things like rehabilitation of your home,” Michelle Miller, Martin County Human Services director, said. The county currently has $900,000 in that fund. “There are certain eligibility uses for that disaster funding, which, again, are expenses to weatherproof your house, rental assistance ... also, emergency hotel vouchers,” Miller said. As far as preps go, Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton told commissioners that right now, crews are pumping several lakes and ponds to create more space for any excess water to go. He said they’re especially focusing on the Hyline Drive area where Berner’s home is and was destroyed. “There's no way to rebuild if you have nothing. And I mean, literally nothing is left. And then, of course, long-term goals, they need to figure out this problem; they need to stop developing in wetlands,” Berner said. To apply for the SHIP emergency funding, applicants should go to the county’s human services office or call 772-320-3169. As for the sandbags, residents can grab them Wednesday from 7 a.m. Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app.

entry.article_text: Two weeks after historic flooding damaged homes and left some Treasure Coast families stranded, locals are stocking up on supplies and filling sandbags as another round of heavy rain threatens the area. At the Lawnwood Stadium Parking Lot in Fort Pierce, the demand for free sandbags was so high Tuesday that a large pile of sand was nearly gone by dinner time. Many residents said they aren't willing to take any chances after what they experienced earlier this month. Lucie was filling sandbags at the St. He said floodwaters rose to his knees and damaged his garage during the last storm. Now, more sandbags line the outside of his home. "I did 20 bags the first time," Vargas said. "I lined it up on the garage. It wasn't enough, so I'm getting another 10." Vargas loaded the bags in his trunk saying he isn't taking any chances this time. "Will this storm bring another 15 inches of rain? "But we're prepared and we're ready." Other families were making similar preparations. Lucie County prepares for more rain after historic flooding; schools closed Wednesday Port St. Lucie father of two Eddie Dillon said flooding in his neighborhood rose so quickly during the last storm that roads and retention ponds appeared to blend together. "It was bad," Dillon said. "Our house was like an island because the pond was connecting with the road." Earlier this month, Dillon said he even used a surfboard to help pick up his wife and children after their car was trapped in floodwaters. On Tuesday, he filled several sandbags at Lawnwood Stadium. "Ultimately, God's in control," Dillon said. "Just hoping he spares us all that rain that's going to happen." By 6 p.m., both truckloads of sand available at staduim parking lot had nearly disappeared. While some people across the Treasure Coast were filling sandbags, others were filling shopping carts. At a Publix in Fort Pierce, shoppers stocked up on essentials in case flooding makes it difficult to get around. "Bread, ham, cans, water," said Fort Pierce resident Genoveva Duran. Lucie resident Benson Medor kept his list simple. "The water, and the bread. Many residents said they're preparing to stay home if streets flood again. "We never know," Duran said. "We never know." Vargas said his family has already gathered supplies, but they're also trying to keep a sense of normalcy. "We went to Sam's Club, got water, got a Christmas tree," he said. "Got to make sure we're in the spirits." Neighbors were helping other neighbors fill sandbags throughout the day, hoping their preparations won't be needed this time around. Lucie Public Schools has already canceled classes Wednesday ahead of the expected rain and flooding threat, hoping to avoid a repeat during the historic flooding two weeks ago when school buses struggled to make their way down streets.

entry.title: 'Please no flood tours': Indian River County prepares for potential flooding after recent storms - WPBF
entry.summary: 'Please no flood tours': Indian River County prepares for potential flooding after recent storms    WPBF
entry.article_text: Indian River County officials are preparing for the possibility of more flooding as heavy rain threatens areas already impacted by recent storms. Emergency management officials said the ground is saturated, and additional heavy rain could lead to flooding in areas that did not flood during the last storm. Earlier this month, the county dealt with flooded neighborhoods, impassable roads, and traffic disruptions. Officials are closely monitoring flood-prone communities, including Heritage Plantation, Whispering Palms, and areas near Highland Drive, as they remain concerned about incoming weather conditions. Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates Ryan Lloyd, who serves as the Deputy Director and Emergency Management Chief for the Indian River County Department of Emergency Services, is concerned about the weather that could be heading this way. "There could be areas that flood that we're not expecting per se or that necessarily flooded in the past," Lloyd said. So, we're asking that our residents be prepared countywide for any type of flood event that could occur over the next 72 hours." Lloyd has a message for the public. "We also ask our residents to please not do flood tours where they're going out just by standing and looking on at flooded neighborhoods, as they drive through those neighborhoods," Lloyd said. "It can create waves that actually go into the houses, and it can make the flooding even worse for residents." Visitors Ed and Jackie Brookes shared their thoughts on the situation. "That's unusual for Florida. I'm here to get more and more of the extreme weather here, but we're just glad to be with our family. It's still beautiful, visitor Ed Brookes said. Crews spent the day cleaning swales and inspecting drainage systems across the county. As of Tuesday, the county reported two properties destroyed and seven with major damage from the previous storm. Sixty-five had minor damage, and 97 others were affected. The county's local state of emergency has been extended through Monday, Nov. 23, as officials prepare for more rain. The county's emergency information center is open for questions about the flood threat. Residents can call 772-226-4000 for assistance. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25

entry.title: Woman dies after Port St. Lucie hit-and-run; police say driver was playing 'ding dong ditch' beforehand
entry.summary: A 24-year-old woman has died from injuries she suffered after she was struck while riding an electric scooter in a hit-and-run crash in Port St. Lucie , police said Wednesday. The woman died at approximately 9:23 p.m. Tuesday, according to the Port St. Lucie Police Department. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Teen Charged in Port St. Lucie E-Scooter Hit-and-Run | WPTV The crash happened around 5:10 a.m. Monday near the intersection of Southwest Gatlin Boulevard and Southwest Feather Terrace. Police said the woman was riding an electric scooter when a vehicle struck her. Investigators allege the driver left the scene without stopping to help her or notify law enforcement. The department's Traffic Homicide Investigations Unit later identified the vehicle as a gray Chevrolet Tahoe and located it at a Port St. Lucie home, according to police. Investigators identified the alleged driver as 18-year-old Tristan Sanchez-Chasmer. Police said investigators learned Sanchez-Chasmer had been playing 'ding dong ditch' with friends shortly before the crash. According to the department, the group was leaving a home where they had been participating in the prank when the vehicle struck the woman. Sanchez-Chasmer was arrested and charged with leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury, a second-degree felony, police said. Following the woman's death, police said they anticipate the State Attorney's Office will pursue enhanced or additional charges as appropriate based on the circumstances and the outcome of the investigation. Police did not identify the woman in Wednesday's news release.

entry.title: Martin County Teacher of the Year Richard Acosta celebrates educators who inspire students - WPTV
entry.summary: Martin County Teacher of the Year Richard Acosta celebrates educators who inspire students    WPTV
entry.article_text: Pinewood Elementary School science teacher Richard Acosta has been named the 2026-27 Martin County Teacher of the Year, earning the opportunity to represent the county in the Florida Department of Education’s statewide Teacher of the Year competition.The Education Foundation of Martin County announced Acosta as the overall winner during its Teacher of the Year Award Celebration on Nov. 6 at the MIDFLORIDA Event Center in Port St. Lucie.Acosta was also named Elementary Teacher of the Year.“This is phenomenal,” Acosta said after the honor was revealed. “I feel incredibly invigorated and inspired to go to the next level and represent Martin County at the state competition.”Acosta was among three educators recognized with top honors.Miriam Hernández, an intensive reading teacher at Indiantown Middle School, was named Middle School Teacher of the Year.Marc Turull, who teaches International Baccalaureate physics and chemistry at South Fork High School, was named High School Teacher of the Year.Turull said the award also represents the people he works alongside.“It’s such an honor,” Turull said. “I teach physics, and I work with amazing people, so to represent them and be Teacher of the Year makes me so grateful.”Hernández described the recognition as both a privilege and an honor.During the celebration, the three teachers emphasized the importance of educators at every stage of a student's education.“The fact is that it takes all three of us for excellence in Martin County schools,” Acosta said. “We start with the foundation in elementary school. We move on to middle school intensive reading, and then we finish at the high school at South Fork. So we, we feel very blessed to be working together.”The Education Foundation said Acosta’s 35-year career in education can be traced partly to his own experience as a teenager.According to the Education Foundation of Martin County, at 16, Acosta was struggling with confidence and direction when he entered teacher John Lynskey’s American history class. According to the foundation, Lynskey’s storytelling and encouragement helped Acosta develop a love of learning.Acosta still keeps two history books Lynskey gave him.His path toward teaching became clearer when Acosta later tutored a younger student after school and watched the child's confidence and enthusiasm for learning grow, according to the foundation.Today, Acosta teaches science to students from prekindergarten through fifth grade at Pinewood Elementary.“I love what I do, and I love energizing the classroom and engaging them to the greatest possibility,” Acosta said.His lessons include hands-on investigations tied to the natural environment around Martin County. The Education Foundation said students have examined sea turtle skull models, shells and other materials connected to the Indian River Lagoon while studying how adaptations help turtles survive.Acosta also helped develop a “Birds of the Everglades” curriculum with environmental partners and has been involved with schoolwide science initiatives and family STEAM events.For Acosta, the recognition provides another opportunity beyond representing Martin County at the state level.“I feel very blessed to be in this position because I get to mentor other teachers from other schools,” Acosta said.Acosta also receives a one-year vehicle lease provided through Audi Stuart and Infiniti Stuart.“That is amazing and spectacular,” Acosta said. “I cannot wait to pick out a car on Saturday.”The celebration recognized 24 school-level Teachers of the Year who were selected by their peers. According to the Education Foundation, nominees submitted application portfolios and participated in interviews before a panel of judges.Felix A. Williams Elementary School also won the Spirit Award for its enthusiasm, interpretation of the event's theme, and props.The recognition comes as Martin County educators continue the everyday work behind the awards: helping children learn, building their confidence and creating connections that can influence students long after they leave the classroom.For Acosta, that circle is especially meaningful. A teacher once helped him see greater possibilities for his own future. Decades later, he is working to create those possibilities for another generation.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.summary: Treasure Coast families stock up, fill sandbags as more rain threatens area Nov. 17, 2026    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Two weeks after historic flooding damaged homes and left some Treasure Coast families stranded, locals are stocking up on supplies and filling sandbags as another round of heavy rain threatens the area. At the Lawnwood Stadium Parking Lot in Fort Pierce, the demand for free sandbags was so high Tuesday that a large pile of sand was nearly gone by dinner time. Many residents said they aren't willing to take any chances after what they experienced earlier this month. Lucie was filling sandbags at the St. He said floodwaters rose to his knees and damaged his garage during the last storm. Now, more sandbags line the outside of his home. "I did 20 bags the first time," Vargas said. "I lined it up on the garage. It wasn't enough, so I'm getting another 10." Vargas loaded the bags in his trunk saying he isn't taking any chances this time. "Will this storm bring another 15 inches of rain? "But we're prepared and we're ready." Other families were making similar preparations. Lucie County prepares for more rain after historic flooding; schools closed Wednesday Port St. Lucie father of two Eddie Dillon said flooding in his neighborhood rose so quickly during the last storm that roads and retention ponds appeared to blend together. "It was bad," Dillon said. "Our house was like an island because the pond was connecting with the road." Earlier this month, Dillon said he even used a surfboard to help pick up his wife and children after their car was trapped in floodwaters. On Tuesday, he filled several sandbags at Lawnwood Stadium. "Ultimately, God's in control," Dillon said. "Just hoping he spares us all that rain that's going to happen." By 6 p.m., both truckloads of sand available at staduim parking lot had nearly disappeared. While some people across the Treasure Coast were filling sandbags, others were filling shopping carts. At a Publix in Fort Pierce, shoppers stocked up on essentials in case flooding makes it difficult to get around. "Bread, ham, cans, water," said Fort Pierce resident Genoveva Duran. Lucie resident Benson Medor kept his list simple. "The water, and the bread. Many residents said they're preparing to stay home if streets flood again. "We never know," Duran said. "We never know." Vargas said his family has already gathered supplies, but they're also trying to keep a sense of normalcy. "We went to Sam's Club, got water, got a Christmas tree," he said. "Got to make sure we're in the spirits." Neighbors were helping other neighbors fill sandbags throughout the day, hoping their preparations won't be needed this time around. Lucie Public Schools has already canceled classes Wednesday ahead of the expected rain and flooding threat, hoping to avoid a repeat during the historic flooding two weeks ago when school buses struggled to make their way down streets.

entry.title: Historic Vero Beach neighborhood gets new life as vibrant village for artists - WPTV
entry.summary: Historic Vero Beach neighborhood gets new life as vibrant village for artists    WPTV
entry.article_text: A historic Vero Beach neighborhood is getting a new life through art, as sculptor Ross Power leads an effort to transform Edgewood into a vibrant community of artists, galleries, studios and public gathering spaces.Known as the "Father of the Vero Beach Art Village," Power is helping turn a once-overlooked neighborhood into a destination for creativity, where artists can live, work and share their talents.WATCH REPORT BELOW: The transformation is already underway, with murals, public art and community projects taking shape. Power says more galleries, studios, cafes and bed-and-breakfasts are in the works, bringing new opportunities for artists, residents and visitors.A historic Vero Beach neighborhood becomes a canvasUnder the shade of a century-old lychee tree, Power reads from a poem dedicated to the tree as a dancer performs beneath its branches."A place where you and me can become we," Power said.For the longtime sculptor, the tree represents something bigger: a gathering place where art can bring people together.That vision is unfolding in Edgewood, a neighborhood established in 1916 that was once home to Vero Beach's first public school and first motel, according to the Vero Beach Art Village organization.Over the years, parts of the neighborhood fell into disrepair. But where others saw aging properties and neglected alleyways, Power saw potential."It spoke to me, and I heard I was once great and now I have fallen into disrepair and not respected at all, and I said we're going to change that," Power told WPTV anchor Meghan McRoberts during a tour of the neighborhood.Power has spent decades creating art and helping develop artistic communities, including an art center in Miami.Now, he's bringing that experience to Vero Beach, with an entire neighborhood as his canvas.Turning Edgewood's alleyways into works of artOne of Power's biggest ambitions is transforming 11 alleyways throughout Edgewood into colorful destinations filled with murals and public art."I'm taking the alleys which are the ugliest part of the neighborhood and turning them into mural opportunities where the alleys are going to be like unbelievable for people to come and visit," Power said."There's a lack of buildings but there's not a lack of fences."Power sees those fences, walls and underused spaces as opportunities to showcase local artists and create an outdoor art experience.But the effort goes beyond beautifying back streets.Special zoning allows artists to live and work in the villageThe city of Vero Beach has established Cultural Arts Village zoning districts designed to encourage artistic businesses while preserving Edgewood's historic residential character.According to the city and the Vero Beach Art Village organization, the zoning creates opportunities for art galleries, studios, live-work spaces and other businesses, depending on the property's classification and applicable approvals.The goal is to create a walkable neighborhood where historic homes can become studios and galleries, and artists can collaborate with their neighbors.“I’ve been working on a bunch of different paintings. And we have projects; there's a bunch of different projects we’ve been working on whether it’s for the city or for trying to save big blue, or our community garden, “ said Linwood Addison Fuller IV, an artist who moved to Edgewood for the focus on art. His wife is also an artist.“It’s so much better to be an artist in a community with other artists,” said sculptor Andrew Draminski. “I’m sitting here working and my neighbors are walking their dog down the alley and come on in and we have a cup of coffee or something like that.”The village's vision extends beyond traditional galleries. Organizers hope to create spaces for music, dance, poetry, photography, workshops and other community events.More galleries, studios and community spaces plannedAccording to the nonprofit Friends of the Vero Beach Art Village, the neighborhood's transformation is a grassroots effort involving artists, residents, businesses and volunteers.The organization highlights ongoing initiatives involving murals, public art, studios, galleries, streetscape improvements and community events.Power says additional galleries, studios, cafes and bed-and-breakfasts are also in the works.For him, the goal isn't simply to attract visitors. It's to create a community where artists can thrive together and residents can take pride in their neighborhood."If you want to eat great food, hear great music, see great things, meet great artists, this is the place," Power said.And beneath the sprawling branches of that century-old lychee tree, Power hopes the community he's helping cultivate will continue to grow.Where is the Vero Beach Art Village?The Vero Beach Art Village is located in the historic Edgewood neighborhood, just west of downtown Vero Beach.The neighborhood generally stretches between 14th and 20th avenues and 18th and 20th streets.The Friends of the Vero Beach Art Village nonprofit encourages residents and visitors to support the effort through volunteering, donations and participation in community art projects.Click here for more information about the village, its projects and opportunities to get involved.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI.
