entry.title: 'Today we are homeless': Jensen Beach family displaced by historic flooding pleads for help rebuilding home - WPTV
entry.summary: 'Today we are homeless': Jensen Beach family displaced by historic flooding pleads for help rebuilding home    WPTV
entry.article_text: A Jensen Beach family displaced by historic flooding is searching for more permanent housing and money to rebuild after water destroyed much of the inside of their home. Lisa and Jeremy French, who have two young boys, told WPTV's Michael Hoffman they ultimately have one goal: to get their family back home.WATCH REPORT BELOW:WPTV first met the French family shortly after historic rainfall hit South Florida and the Treasure Coast. Floodwater had surrounded their neighborhood, forcing residents to use kayaks to get around and check on neighbors.Days later, much of the water has receded. The damage has not."My floorboards are outside," Lisa French said.Hoffman returned to the French family's Jensen Beach home for an update, but the family said it was not safe to go inside.French said the flooding wiped out much of what her family had accumulated over the years."Our appliances are gone, our cabinets are gone, every piece of furniture," French said.The family is now trying to determine how to pay for repairs while securing a more permanent place to live.WPTV met French again at the Hoke Library in Jensen Beach, where a Multi-Agency Resource Center has been helping people looking for assistance following the flooding.French told Hoffman that her home flooded days after the rain had stopped.Martin County told WPTV that the family's home is near the Savannah Preserves, an area where excess water naturally flows from other flooded areas.French, however, questions whether other actions involving water entering the preserve contributed to what happened at her home."They're saying it's from natural rain, but they dumped Monday and Tuesday, nonstop into the savannas," French said.The impact of the flooding extends beyond the physical damage.Through tears, Lisa and Jeremy French pleaded for help before the Martin County Commission as they described what their family is facing."Today we are homeless," Lisa French told commissioners. "We have nowhere to host Thanksgiving. We have nowhere for our boys to have Christmas. We don't have beds to come home to."The couple has two young boys. French said she wants them to continue growing up in the Jensen Beach home the family worked hard to maintain.For now, however, the family says it needs more permanent housing while trying to determine where the money to repair the home will come from.French said the uncertainty surrounding assistance has left her worried there could still be a significant financial gap, even if additional aid becomes available."Who's going to fill in the gaps?" French said. "And, you know, maybe I feel like somebody should take accountability."Despite the uncertainty and extensive damage, the family says it has not given up hope of returning."We just want to go home," French said. "Like, that's at the end, that we just want to be home with our family."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: Martin County flood victims fear more devastation as county braces for another foot of rain - WPTV
entry.summary: Martin County flood victims fear more devastation as county braces for another foot of rain    WPTV
entry.article_text: Just weeks after historic flooding destroyed homes and displaced families in Jensen Beach, Martin County residents are bracing for another round of heavy rain — with up to 12 inches forecast over the next three days.For families still struggling to recover, the threat of more flooding comes as county commissioners work to determine what caused the initial disaster and how to help those who lost nearly everything.On Tuesday, flood victims packed a Martin County Commission meeting, pleading for financial assistance and answers.WATCH REPORT BELOW: Along Cheri Drive in Jensen Beach, the signs of destruction remain. Dumpsters line driveways, damaged belongings sit outside and families are still trying to salvage what's left of their homes.Lisa French, her husband, Jeremy, and their two young sons are among those displaced after floodwaters rose as high as 3 feet inside some homes two weeks ago."It's like we're kind of stuck," French told WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey. French said her home had about 3 to 6 inches of flooding that sat inside for more than a week, causing mold to grow 3 to 4 feet up the walls. "So they, yeah, they tore the walls down in the house," said French. "They just chipped up the last bit of the tile, and it's empty." Now, with more rain approaching, French fears her family could face another disaster before recovering from the first."Of course, we're afraid because we all flooded in our houses," she said.New figures released by Martin County show at least 36 homes sustained damage, with an estimated $3 million in residential losses. Commissioners estimated another $14 million in damage to beaches, and at least $1 million in damage to roadways that now need repairs. For some residents, the destruction represents a lifetime of memories washed away."We've lost everything," one elderly Jensen Beach resident told commissioners. "We have 60 years of our life — kids, grandkids, everything. It's all gone."As residents demand answers about what went wrong, commissioners approved shifting $200,000 from the county's stormwater budget to investigate whether development and changes to local drainage systems contributed to the flooding.Commissioner Blake Capps called the investigation "a good starting point.""It may be that we need to augment the study beyond the $200,000 that we approve today," said Capps. Meanwhile, county crews are working around the clock to prepare for the next storm, lowering retention pond levels, deploying additional pumps and draining flooded properties."We have people 24 hours a day pumping that material down," Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton said.Commissioners also approved financial assistance for eligible flood victims through the state's State Housing Initiatives Partnership (SHIP) program.The assistance includes grants of up to $25,000 for income-eligible homeowners and loans of up to $75,000 secured by liens on their properties.But there's a catch: The grants are reimbursement-based, meaning homeowners must first pay for eligible repairs before receiving the money.For families who lost everything, that presents another obstacle."We don't have $25,000," French said. "A lot of people don't have $25,000, so it's great, and we're appreciative, but I mean, our house is empty, and $25,000 is not going to do much for us." The other problem: the county currently has just $1 million in SHIP funding available, and commissioners warned the money could run out quickly, even with additional state funding promised."They haven't given us the amount yet, but they have assured us that we will be getting some disaster relief funds," said Human Services Director Michelle Miller Strict income limits could also disqualify some flood victims who cannot afford to rebuild on their own. The income cap for a family of one is $86,040. The cap for a family of two is $98,400. For a family of four, it's $122,880. When reporter Kate Hussey asked Capps what would happen to those families, he acknowledged the county needs to explore other options."There are going to be a lot of heart-wrenching cases where someone barely missed the limit, and we're going to need to take a look at what we can do for those folks," Capps said.For residents like French, the need is immediate."We just need somebody to step up," she said. "We need funding." With another round of heavy rain approaching, Martin County is distributing sandbags at Halpatiokee Regional Park to help residents protect their properties, with a limit of 25 per person. The County's Emergency Operations Center is scheduled to be staffed beginning Tuesday at 2 p.m., and the county is coordinating with the National Weather Service and Florida Division of Emergency Management (FDEM).Fire Rescue is also standing by with multiple high-water rescue trucks.Commissioners also said a Federal Emergency Management Agency representative is expected to visit Nov. 30 to assess the damage — a potential step toward securing federal disaster assistance.But for families still displaced and facing the possibility of more flooding, the uncertainty remains.

A repair assessment reviewed by WPTV documents unrepaired storm damage and work needed inside her home. During WPTV's visit, rainwater could be seen dripping inside the home. 'I'm scared my ceiling's gonna come down,' McGregor said. Buckets and towels have become a temporary solution while she waits for more permanent repairs. 'Water is coming in our house, and we're experiencing so much now,' McGregor said. 'I just can't believe the events that are happening.' Assessment documents unrepaired Hurricane Milton damage McGregor said her roof was damaged when Hurricane Milton struck Florida in October 2024. entry.title: Indian River County schools closed Thursday as heavy rain raises flooding concerns
entry.summary: All School District of Indian River County public schools and district offices will be closed Thursday, Nov. 19, because of expected heavy rain and potential flooding, district officials announced Wednesday. Officials cited already saturated ground and concerns about whether students and employees could safely travel to and from schools. The storm system is expected to affect Indian River, Brevard and Volusia counties between 3 a.m. and 3 p.m. Thursday, according to the district. Saturated ground raises travel concerns Indian River County remains under a flood watch as another round of rain moves through the Treasure Coast. The National Weather Service forecast calls for a 95% chance of precipitation Thursday, with about 1.74 inches of rain possible. The district said saturated conditions were a key factor in its decision to cancel classes and close offices. 'With ground conditions already saturated, we cannot be confident that students and staff will be able to travel safely to and from school,' the district said. 'Weather conditions may also affect staff members' ability to report to work.' The closure comes about two weeks after prolonged rainfall caused significant flooding in Indian River County. Flood watch remains in effect A flood watch for Indian River County remains in effect through Friday evening. The National Weather Service is also reporting a high surf advisory and rip current statement for the area. Indian River County officials have warned residents that roads not officially listed as closed could still have standing water or other hazards. Drivers should obey barricades and never attempt to drive through floodwater. The school district said student, family and employee safety remains its highest priority. Officials will continue monitoring conditions and said any additional information will be released through official district communication channels. entry.title: PSL police have a GTA VI release-day warning: Port St. Lucie is not Vice City - WPEC
entry.summary: PSL police have a GTA VI release-day warning: Port St. Lucie is not Vice City    WPEC
entry.article_text: The wanted level in Port St. Lucie should stay at zero, police say. As Grand Theft Auto VI arrives Thursday, the Port St. Lucie Police Department posted a playful safety briefing reminding fans that real life doesn’t come with a respawn button and that U.S. 1 and Crosstown are not racetracks. Five stars might be impressive in GTA , but trust us, you don’t want that kind of attention in Port St. Lucie, the department wrote. Its other reminders: patrol vehicles aren’t available for test drives, red lights aren’t suggestions, sidewalks aren’t shortcuts and the SWAT team isn’t a feature anyone wants to unlock. What happens in Vice City stays in Vice City, the post said. Lucie might come with a police report. The game officially launches Nov. 19 for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S. Rockstar’s fictional state of Leonida draws on Florida , with Vice City serving as its Miami-inspired centerpiece. The game follows Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos, whose criminal plans pull them into a conspiracy spanning the state. CBS12 has been following the Sunshine State’s transformation into a real-life part of the game’s promotion. In September, a giant pink Welcome to Vice City sign went up on Miami’s Kaseya Center as part of a deal between Miami-Dade County and Rockstar Games. County officials said the arrangement was expected to bring in nearly $1 million in revenue and create marketing opportunities. Miami has also leaned into the Vice City connection with release-week events. The Miami Heat held a Night in Vice City celebration Wednesday, the night before launch. A release-day party is planned Thursday at the Clevelander South Beach, and Rockstar’s GTA VI : The Festival is scheduled for Saturday, Nov. See also: Who’s responsible for improving drainage after St. Lucie County’s historic flooding? Police in other cities have also used the GTA VI release to remind players to keep the game’s crime on screen. The Atlanta Police Department posted that GTA is not a real place, but Atlanta is! and warned that reckless driving, drunk driving, auto theft and violence have real consequences. Keep it in the game, the department wrote . In South Florida, law enforcement leaders raised a different concern before release day. The Miami-Dade Association of Chiefs of Police opposed plans to promote the county as Vice City, saying the game depicts violence against women and law enforcement. Miami-Dade Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz also questioned whether public agencies should promote a game built around crimes her department works to prevent. For drivers tempted to bring a little of the game’s chaos onto local roads, PSLPD’s advice is simpler: drive safe, play smart and leave the wanted level in the game. Could 'sick days' coincide with release? The release could affect more than gamers’ free time. A GameSquare survey of 1,000 U.S. employees found that 10% of full-time employees surveyed who identify as gamers planned to skip work on launch day, while another 30% were considering taking time off. Of those considering time off, 36% said they would call in sick. The survey also found that 42% expected the game to make them less productive at work. Surveyed gamers expected to spend about $400 on the game and related purchases, and anticipated playing a median of 15 hours during the opening weekend. The survey found 70% might skip watching sports to spend more time gaming, while 42% said they’d be less likely to watch NFL games that weekend. I ndian River County students have Thursday off , giving young GTA VI fans an unexpected chance to spend part of release day in Vice City. The district closed schools because of forecast conditions and flooding concerns, while St. Lucie schools reopened and Palm Beach County schools remained open, except for West Boca High School, which is closed because of heavy flooding in the parking lot.

entry.title: Flood victims demand answers as FEMA delays disaster decision amid millions in damage
entry.summary: Dumpsters line driveways, bulldozers tear through debris and homes sit gutted along Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach, where families are still picking up the pieces after historic flooding devastated parts of Martin County. For some residents, the water is still receding. For others, the cleanup has only just begun. Now, as another round of rain threatens the Treasure Coast, families already facing thousands of dollars in repairs are asking a question they can't afford to leave unanswered: How will they pay to rebuild? WATCH REPORT BELOW: Flood victims demand answers as FEMA delays disaster decision 'It's like an apocalypse here' For Linda Weisbecker, the destruction is difficult to put into words. 'It's like an apocalypse here,' she said, standing amid the devastation in her neighborhood. For nine days, Weisbecker and her neighbors navigated waist-deep floodwaters, unable to begin assessing the full extent of the damage. 'Once we got through that and the water came out, we just all started pitching in, going in to see what we can salvage from each home,' said Weisbecker. Neighbors worked together, sorting through waterlogged belongings and salvaging whatever they could. Now, the home she once knew is little more than an empty shell. 'We are fully gutted. Our house is empty,' she said. 'We lost everything, from pictures of our children and their lives, our friends, our grandkids, now we have great-grandkids. Everything [my husband] had since he was 13 on is gone.' Demolition is supposed to be the first step toward rebuilding. But for Weisbecker, it's also a painful reminder of how much work and money lies ahead. 'You do think about that process and you sit there and you say to yourself, how am I gonna do this?' Weisbecker said. Weisbecker was approved for a $25,000 grant through Florida's State Housing Initiatives Partnership, or SHIP, program, which provides housing assistance to eligible residents. While the grant offers some relief, the cost of rebuilding a flood-damaged home can quickly exceed that amount. And not every family will qualify for the same assistance. 'This is very urgent for people to get back into their daily lives,' Weisbecker said. 'This is total devastation. For everyone.' Millions in damage but no federal disaster declaration New estimates released by Martin County reveal the staggering financial toll of the flooding. According to county officials, the storm caused: $14 million in beach damage Nearly $1 million in damaged roads that now
entry.article_text: For everyone."New estimates released by Martin County reveal the staggering financial toll of the flooding.According to county officials, the storm caused:$14 million in beach damageNearly $1 million in damaged roads that now need to be repaved$3 million in residential losses affecting families still struggling to recoverAdditional costs in county staff overtime associated with the emergency responseThose figures put the known damage at approximately $18 million, not including additional expenses.A federal major disaster declaration could open the door to FEMA assistance for the public infrastructure repairs and potentially provide additional relief to affected residents.But so far, no such declaration has been approved.Without federal reimbursement, County Spokesperson Martha Ann Kniess said Martin County could be left responsible for covering millions of dollars in public recovery costs itself, forcing officials to find funding elsewhere in the county budget or identify other sources of assistance.And that uncertainty comes as residents are already struggling to afford repairs to their own homes.During an emotional Martin County Commission meeting Tuesday, flood victims pleaded with local leaders to do more to secure financial assistance."Please. Fight for us!" one resident urged commissioners.Others questioned why help was taking so long, particularly as more rain threatened their already damaged properties."And the answer from this dais is wait 13 more days?!?" another resident asked.Commissioner Eileen Vargas of District 1 told residents she is doing everything she can to try to expedite the process, but 'doesn't have all the answers.'"I did, through contacts, reach out to FEMA to try and get this going," Vargas said.According to Vargas, a new FEMA director is expected to take office Nov. 30, which she hopes will turn the tide. "He is going to personally petition President Trump to declare our area a disaster," Vargas said.However, a federal declaration is not guaranteed, and even if approved, not all damages or recovery expenses would necessarily qualify for reimbursement.WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey contacted FEMA, questioning the length of the response and when residents could expect answers.In its response, FEMA confirmed it had received the major disaster declaration request and that the request remains under review.The agency referred additional questions about the response and recovery timeline to the Florida Division of Emergency Management.WPTV also contacted the state agency but had not received a response as of Wednesday.In the meantime, Martin County is working to distribute emergency housing assistance through Florida's SHIP program.The county currently has approximately $1 million in SHIP funding available, with eligible residents able to apply for grants of up to $25,000.Additional assistance may be available through loans of up to $75,000, though those loans are subject to repayment requirements and liens.County officials acknowledged that the existing funding could run out quickly, particularly given the scale of the destruction.Michelle Miller, Martin County's human services director, told commissioners the state has promised additional disaster relief funding, but doesn't know when that funding could come in. "They haven't confirmed the amount yet but has assured us we will be getting some disaster relief funds," Miller said.But there are limitations.Some programs require homeowners to pay for repairs upfront before seeking reimbursement.

entry.title: Woman dies after Port St. Lucie hit-and-run; police say driver was playing 'ding dong ditch' beforehand - WFLX
entry.summary: Woman dies after Port St. Lucie hit-and-run; police say driver was playing 'ding dong ditch' beforehand    WFLX
entry.article_text: A 24-year-old woman has died from injuries she suffered after she was struck while riding an electric scooter in a hit-and-run crash in Port St. Lucie , police said Wednesday. The woman died at approximately 9:23 p.m. Tuesday, according to the Port St. The crash happened around 5:10 a.m. Monday near the intersection of Southwest Gatlin Boulevard and Southwest Feather Terrace. Police said the woman was riding an electric scooter when a vehicle struck her. Investigators allege the driver left the scene without stopping to help her or notify law enforcement. The department’s Traffic Homicide Investigations Unit later identified the vehicle as a gray Chevrolet Tahoe and located it at a Port St. Lucie home, according to police. Investigators identified the alleged driver as 18-year-old Tristan Sanchez-Chasmer. Police said investigators learned Sanchez-Chasmer had been playing “ding dong ditch” with friends shortly before the crash. According to the department, the group was leaving a home where they had been participating in the prank when the vehicle struck the woman. Sanchez-Chasmer was arrested and charged with leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury, a second-degree felony, police said. Following the woman’s death, police said they anticipate the State Attorney’s Office will pursue enhanced or additional charges as appropriate based on the circumstances and the outcome of the investigation. Police did not identify the woman in Wednesday’s news release.

entry.title: 18-year-old charged in Port St. Lucie hit-and-run that critically injured woman riding e-scooter - WPTV
entry.summary: 18-year-old charged in Port St. Lucie hit-and-run that critically injured woman riding e-scooter    WPTV
entry.article_text: An 18-year-old driver has been arrested after Port St. Lucie Police Department investigators say he struck a 24-year-old woman riding an electric scooter to work and left the scene, leaving her critically injured. Police say the driver had been playing a "ding-dong-ditch" prank with friends shortly before Monday morning's crash.WATCH: E-Scooter Hit-and-Run in Port St. LuciePolice identified the driver as Tristan Sanchez-Chasmer. He was arrested on a felony charge of leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury, according to the department.The crash happened near Southwest Gatlin Boulevard and Southwest Feather Terrace. Investigators said the woman was traveling west on the sidewalk toward Southwest Rosser Boulevard and had entered a crosswalk when she was hit by a gray Chevrolet Tahoe making a left turn onto Southwest Feather Terrace.Port St. Lucie Police Chief Leo Niemczyk said Tuesday the woman remained unconscious and in critical condition."We're deeply concerned for her recovery, and our thoughts are with her loved ones," Niemczyk said.Police said a witness stopped to help the woman, called 911 and was able to get the SUV's license plate information. Investigators used that information to identify the vehicle and the driver. Investigators said Sanchez-Chasmer had two friends with him and had been playing "ding-dong-ditch" shortly before the crash. "They were specifically playing, I'll call it ring and run, ding-dong-ditch, at a house that belonged to a friend of theirs, and apparently the mother came to the door and they fled the scene," Niemczyk told WPTV.Niemczyk said investigators believe the people inside the SUV realized a collision had occurred."They're aware that they hit something. I'll say that," he said.According to Niemczyk, Sanchez-Chasmer and the two passengers did not call 911.Niemczyk said the decision to leave the scene was key to the criminal investigation."Had they remained on scene, provided aid, it would have been a very different criminal outcome," Niemczyk said. "There probably wouldn't have been criminal charges at that point."Sanchez-Chasmer was charged with leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury. According to published reports citing law enforcement records, he was being held on a $5,000 bond. Police have not announced charges against the two passengers. WPTV returned to the intersection after the crash and spoke with 15-year-old John Rogalewski, who said he rides an e-scooter to school and is sometimes on the road early in the morning."I'm looking at my surroundings almost the whole time," Rogalewski said. "I'm making sure every time I have to cross the street that there's not a car coming up, and that it is my sign to go, no matter how long I have to wait to cross."Police said the 24-year-old woman was wearing a helmet when she was struck.The investigation remains active, according to police, and toxicology results are still pending.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: Treasure Coast counties prepare for flooding as heavy rain and gusty winds move in - WPEC
entry.summary: Treasure Coast counties prepare for flooding as heavy rain and gusty winds move in    WPEC
entry.article_text: The Treasure Coast is bracing for a soggy stretch as counties prepare for possible flooding from heavy rain. Indian River County The Indian River County Emergency Operations Center remains at Level 2, or partial activation, because of ongoing flooding and the potential for more heavy rain. Emergency services, human services and infrastructure partners are coordinating response and recovery efforts. The county urges residents to avoid flooded roads and floodwaters, watch for rising water in low-lying areas and monitor weather conditions and official updates. Residents with flood-related questions or information can call the Emergency Information Center at 772-226-4000 during operating hours. Due to the heavy rain and gusty winds, solid waste services may be disrupted. Waste Management curbside collections may be delayed, and residents should not put carts in the street if it is flooded. See also: Florida deputies rescue 2-year-old girl found in pond near apartment complex Waste Management collects recycling in blue carts countywide. It collects garbage, yard waste and bulk waste in unincorporated Indian River County, Fellsmere, Sebastian and Indian River Shores. Residents in other cities and towns should check with their local governments for service updates. The county recommends putting carts out by 6 a.m. on collection day, closing lids, bagging garbage, and avoiding overfilled carts. Cardboard should be flattened and placed inside recycling carts, and yard waste should stay inside yard waste carts. Residents should bring carts back in as soon as possible after collection. The landfill and all five Customer Convenience Centers may close early or remain closed if conditions become unsafe. The east-central Florida coast faces a Slight Risk, or Level 2 out of 4, for excessive rainfall. Localized flooding is possible, especially along the coast, and some areas could receive 4 inches or more of rain. Martin County Martin County officials expect 3 to 6 inches of rain, with localized amounts of 8 to 12 inches, beginning Tuesday afternoon and continuing through Nov. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office says it is working with the county’s emergency operations center to monitor rainfall and identify roads that could become difficult to pass. The sheriff’s office plans to deploy high-water rescue vehicles in flood-prone areas. Having the vehicles nearby could help deputies reach residents who need assistance and motorists who become stranded, the office said. The sheriff’s office advises residents to turn around if water covers the road. Standing water may be deeper than it appears and can hide damage. If a regular route is flooded, drivers should take another route or wait somewhere safe. Residents should never drive around barricades or enter flooded areas to see how high the water is. Martin County Fire Rescue also advises residents to be prepared to evacuate if flooding threatens their homes or neighborhoods and to have an emergency kit ready for household members and pets. The Community Information Center will be open to provide flood-related information. Okeechobee County Okeechobee County is also preparing for severe flooding. The Okeechobee County Sheriff’s Office says its emergency operations center will remain active as staff coordinate response and recovery efforts from past flooding. Sandbags are available at Okeechobee County Public Works, 804 Northwest Second St. Lucie County Public Safety Department is monitoring the forecast and reminding residents to secure loose items that could be damaged by wind. Gusty northeast winds of 25 to 30 mph are forecast Tuesday and Wednesday, with gusts of 35 to 40 mph along the coast. Residents should secure tarps, patio furniture and other unsecured items. A rip current advisory remains in effect for St. Strong onshore winds can create dangerous rip currents and rough surf. Lucie County Fire District says its firefighters, paramedics and telecommunicators are prepared to respond as the area faces more heavy rain and recovers from recent flooding. The district has high-water vehicles and a rescue boat available to assist during flood-related emergencies. Free sand is available while supplies last at two self-service locations: County Fairgrounds: 5601 W. Midway Road, Fort Pierce, in the west parking lot Lawnwood Stadium: 2000 Virginia Ave., Fort Pierce Residents should bring their own bags, shovel and other supplies. Residents can use Community Connect to share household information that could help firefighters prepare for an emergency. The county has extended the deadline to Nov. 30 for residents to report flood damage through an online survey. The information will help document flooding across the community and inform recovery efforts. The survey is open to property owners and tenants throughout St. Lucie County, including Fort Pierce, Port St. Lucie Village and unincorporated areas. It asks where flooding occurred, how buildings were affected and what impacts residents and businesses experienced. Residents can complete the flood damage survey by Nov. Officials urge residents across the region to avoid flooded roads and keep roadways clear for emergency responders. If you encounter flooding, turn around and find a safe alternate route.

entry.summary: A massive indoor pickleball facility is opening its doors in Boca Raton. Boca Paddle by City Pickle is officially welcoming players to 25 brand-new courts. It's the city's first fully climate-controlled indoor pickleball and padel club. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Massive pickleball facility opens in Boca Raton Day passes cost $40, with Boca Raton residents getting $5 off. The center also features a restaurant and bar, a shop, and fitness and recovery spaces like a sauna and cold plunge. One of its co-founders says Boca Paddle is unlike anything else in the city. Boca Raton's mayor says the city is the right fit for this type of facility. The area that we're in right now, here in North Park, is in need of revitalization. And this facility, by itself, takes a huge step in that direction to help revitalize this part of the city,' Boca Raton Mayor Andy Thomson said. The facility will also be the home of a new professional team. 'I'm excited that we're a home for the Palm Beach Royals , which is major league pickleball's newest franchise. They paid $16 million last year. They're going to be based here,' Boca Paddle Co-Founder Brian Levine said. By the numbers, the facility spans 100,000 square feet and cost around $20 million to build. It has 14 indoor pickleball courts and nine outdoor courts, with six padel courts. entry.title: Flood risk lingers across the Treasure Coast and Palm Beaches before a drier weekend - WPEC
entry.summary: Flood risk lingers across the Treasure Coast and Palm Beaches before a drier weekend    WPEC
entry.article_text: Flooding remains a concern across the Treasure Coast and Palm Beaches today, with another round of heavy rain possible Friday before conditions begin to dry out this weekend. While rain rates and coverage may ease compared with recent days, additional downpours could worsen existing flooding, especially in low-lying areas and places where water has not drained. Flood concerns continue today Bands of showers and storms are expected to move onshore from the Atlantic. A persistent easterly breeze is steering those rain bands toward the coast, while disturbances higher in the atmosphere help keep showers going. Some locations could see another 1 to 2 inches, with isolated totals of 3 to 5 inches possible. Even lower amounts could cause problems in areas already saturated or dealing with standing water. A Flood Watch remains in effect through this evening for Palm Beach County. For the Treasure Coast and Okeechobee County, the Flood Watch continues through Friday evening. Check local alerts for updates, since conditions and alert timing can vary by county. Rain may linger Friday The flood risk should gradually become less widespread Friday, but another day of rain is possible. A developing area of low pressure near the Bahamas could influence how much moisture and onshore flow remain in place. The broader setup is beginning to shift: the upper-level disturbance that helped support the heavy rain will begin moving away, and some drier air starts working into the region. However, that change will take time, so don’t assume a few quieter hours mean the flooding threat is over. Drier weather returns this weekend As the developing low moves north along the coast, its influence on South Florida should fade. Rain chances are expected to drop this weekend, bringing a welcome stretch of drier weather and time for water to drain. Coastal hazards will take longer to improve. Rough seas and dangerous rip currents are expected to continue along the Atlantic beaches, and boating conditions may remain hazardous into the weekend.

entry.title: Indian River County schools closed Thursday as heavy rain raises flooding concerns - WFLX
entry.summary: Indian River County schools closed Thursday as heavy rain raises flooding concerns    WFLX
entry.article_text: All School District of Indian River County public schools and district offices will be closed Thursday, Nov. 19, because of expected heavy rain and potential flooding, district officials announced Wednesday. Officials cited already saturated ground and concerns about whether students and employees could safely travel to and from schools. The storm system is expected to affect Indian River, Brevard and Volusia counties between 3 a.m. Thursday, according to the district. Indian River County remains under a flood watch as another round of rain moves through the Treasure Coast. The National Weather Service forecast calls for a 95% chance of precipitation Thursday, with about 1.74 inches of rain possible. The district said saturated conditions were a key factor in its decision to cancel classes and close offices. "With ground conditions already saturated, we cannot be confident that students and staff will be able to travel safely to and from school," the district said. "Weather conditions may also affect staff members' ability to report to work." The closure comes about two weeks after prolonged rainfall caused significant flooding in Indian River County. A flood watch for Indian River County remains in effect through Friday evening. The National Weather Service is also reporting a high surf advisory and rip current statement for the area. Indian River County officials have warned residents that roads not officially listed as closed could still have standing water or other hazards. Drivers should obey barricades and never attempt to drive through floodwater. The school district said student, family and employee safety remains its highest priority. Officials will continue monitoring conditions and said any additional information will be released through official district communication channels. entry.title: Jensen Beach Festival of Giving brings together more than 50 local nonprofits
entry.summary: More than 50 local nonprofits are coming together for the third annual Festival of Giving at the Children's Museum of the Treasure Coast, filling the Jensen Beach museum with holiday displays while allowing community organizations to share the work they do throughout the region. Christina McIntosh, community outreach and events coordinator for the Children's Museum of the Treasure Coast, said participating nonprofits come from communities stretching from Palm Beach County north through the Treasure Coast. 'Those are the five counties that our education department here at the museum works with and works with the schools,' McIntosh said. More than Christmas decorations The Festival of Giving uses decorated Christmas trees and holiday displays to introduce visitors to nonprofit organizations serving South Florida and the Treasure Coast. For the organizations involved, the gathering also provides a chance to learn more about one another. Treasure Coast Community Singers is among the nonprofits participating. 'The really great thing about this event is that we get to know other nonprofits,' Sharon Savageaux of Treasure Coast Community Singers said. We get to understand what they do. And we can help spread their word.' The singers also performed at the museum during a festival breakfast event. A Grinch-themed tree with a community mission The GFWC Hobe Sound Womans Club is also participating, decorating its display with a Grinch theme. Sandy Vucik, who represented the organization at the festival, said the money it raises supports several community organizations, including Family Promise, CareBag and Real Life Childrens Ranch in Okeechobee. Vucik said the club is currently helping 19 children at the ranch. 'We're really hoping to give them a nice Christmas,' Vucik said. The holiday setting gives visitors a chance to discover organizations they may not otherwise encounter while allowing nonprofits themselves to make new community connections. Family Night brings Santa, cookies and hot chocolate to Jensen Beach. The festival includes several special events beyond its nonprofit displays. entry.summary: Martin County Sheriff's Office prepares for potential flooding with high-water vehicles    WPBF
entry.article_text: Martin County officials continue to prepare for expected heavy rainfall across the Treasure Coast. That includes the sheriff’s office getting its high-water rescue vehicles ready for potential flooding. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 Sheriff John Budensiek calls them their worst-case-scenario vehicles, the ones they use in natural disaster responses like hurricanes and flash flooding. They are called MTVs – light medium weight tactical vehicles. They’re retired military vehicles that sit up high and are heavy enough to drive through hurricane-force winds and high water. Budensiek said he has his team on standby for any urgent calls from the emergency operations center. “Hopefully we don't need them. But we're in a position where if we get the rains that are expected and if we get the flooding that we've had here in the last couple of weeks, again, we're prepared to try to help our citizens as best we can,” Budensiek said. In addition to the two high-water vehicles at the sheriff’s office in Stuart, there’s also another stationed in Indiantown should that area get flooded. Tradition Parkway east of Hazel Drive: Crews were pumping water off the road after the outside lanes flooded in both directions. Police urged drivers to take another route if they encounter standing water and to stay clear of barricades. Conditions can change quickly. The Lawnwood Stadium site has run out. The fairgrounds site is self-service. Bring a shovel and plan to fill your own bags. The county has a limited supply of bags and encourages residents to bring their own. Residents in unincorporated St. Lucie County can report flooding that threatens homes, businesses or personal safety to flooding@stlucieco.gov. entry.title: Movie theater set to return to CityPlace in downtown West Palm Beach
entry.summary: A movie theater is coming back to CityPlace in downtown West Palm Beach, according to Related Ross. The developer confirmed it has submitted redesign plans for the previously approved 515 Fern building to include a 35,000-square-foot movie theater with 800 seats. The building, originally approved in 2023, has also been reduced in height by 36 feet to 24 stories. The design updates weve submitted for the approved 515 Fern building reflect what we've heard from the community, said Jordan Rathlev, executive vice president of Related Ross. Residents have told us they miss going to the movies at CityPlace and want a movie theater back in the downtown. These changes will create a reimagined movie-going experience in the heart of West Palm Beach. The announcement comes three years after the former movie theater at The Square closed and was demolished in 2023 to make way for new development. An opening date for the new theater has not been announced.

entry.title: PSL police have a GTA VI release-day warning: Port St. Lucie is not Vice City - WPEC
entry.summary: PSL police have a GTA VI release-day warning: Port St. Lucie is not Vice City    WPEC
entry.article_text: The wanted level in Port St. Lucie should stay at zero, police say. As Grand Theft Auto VI arrives Thursday, the Port St. Lucie Police Department posted a playful safety briefing reminding fans that real life doesn’t come with a respawn button and that U.S. 1 and Crosstown are not racetracks. Five stars might be impressive in GTA , but trust us, you don’t want that kind of attention in Port St. Lucie, the department wrote. Its other reminders: patrol vehicles aren’t available for test drives, red lights aren’t suggestions, sidewalks aren’t shortcuts and the SWAT team isn’t a feature anyone wants to unlock. What happens in Vice City stays in Vice City, the post said. Lucie might come with a police report. The game officially launches Nov. 19 for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S. Rockstar’s fictional state of Leonida draws on Florida , with Vice City serving as its Miami-inspired centerpiece. The game follows Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos, whose criminal plans pull them into a conspiracy spanning the state. CBS12 has been following the Sunshine State’s transformation into a real-life part of the game’s promotion. In September, a giant pink Welcome to Vice City sign went up on Miami’s Kaseya Center as part of a deal between Miami-Dade County and Rockstar Games. County officials said the arrangement was expected to bring in nearly $1 million in revenue and create marketing opportunities. Miami has also leaned into the Vice City connection with release-week events. The Miami Heat held a Night in Vice City celebration Wednesday, the night before launch. A release-day party is planned Thursday at the Clevelander South Beach, and Rockstar’s GTA VI : The Festival is scheduled for Saturday, Nov. See also: Who’s responsible for improving drainage after St. Lucie County’s historic flooding? Police in other cities have also used the GTA VI release to remind players to keep the game’s crime on screen. The Atlanta Police Department posted that GTA is not a real place, but Atlanta is! and warned that reckless driving, drunk driving, auto theft and violence have real consequences. Keep it in the game, the department wrote . In South Florida, law enforcement leaders raised a different concern before release day. The Miami-Dade Association of Chiefs of Police opposed plans to promote the county as Vice City, saying the game depicts violence against women and law enforcement. Miami-Dade Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz also questioned whether public agencies should promote a game built around crimes her department works to prevent. For drivers tempted to bring a little of the game’s chaos onto local roads, PSLPD’s advice is simpler: drive safe, play smart and leave the wanted level in the game. Could 'sick days' coincide with release? The release could affect more than gamers’ free time. A GameSquare survey of 1,000 U.S. employees found that 10% of full-time employees surveyed who identify as gamers planned to skip work on launch day, while another 30% were considering taking time off. Of those considering time off, 36% said they would call in sick. The survey also found that 42% expected the game to make them less productive at work. Surveyed gamers expected to spend about $400 on the game and related purchases, and anticipated playing a median of 15 hours during the opening weekend. The survey found 70% might skip watching sports to spend more time gaming, while 42% said they’d be less likely to watch NFL games that weekend. I ndian River County students have Thursday off , giving young GTA VI fans an unexpected chance to spend part of release day in Vice City. The district closed schools because of forecast conditions and flooding concerns, while St. Lucie schools reopened and Palm Beach County schools remained open, except for West Boca High School, which is closed because of heavy flooding in the parking lot.

The National Weather Service forecast calls for a 95% chance of precipitation Thursday, with about 1.74 inches of rain possible. The district said saturated conditions were a key factor in its decision to cancel classes and close offices. “With ground conditions already saturated, we cannot be confident that students and staff will be able to travel safely to and from school,” the district said. “Weather conditions may also affect staff members’ ability to report to work.” The closure comes about two weeks after prolonged rainfall caused significant flooding in Indian River County. A flood watch for Indian River County remains in effect through Friday evening. The National Weather Service is also reporting a high surf advisory and rip current statement for the area. Indian River County officials have warned residents that roads not officially listed as closed could still have standing water or other hazards. Drivers should obey barricades and never attempt to drive through floodwater. The school district said student, family and employee safety remains its highest priority. Officials will continue monitoring conditions and said any additional information will be released through official district communication channels. Because of the large number of customers affected, officials said the advisory could remain in place beyond the initial 48-hour timeframe. For the Rowe family, that has meant relying on bottled water and boiling water for daily needs. "Boiling water, doing what they told us to do," Rowe said. "It's something small, I'm not really sweating it. We're going as far as turning on the water in the fridge so the ice doesn't get accumulated with that tainted water." Residents are advised to continue boiling water used for drinking, cooking, making ice, brushing teeth and washing dishes until the city announces the notice has been lifted. For updates, residents can visit the City of Port St.

entry.summary: St. Lucie schools closed Wednesday as more flooding threatens Treasure Coast    WPEC
entry.article_text: Just two weeks after historic flooding forced schools to close for three straight days, St. Lucie County students are getting another day off as more heavy rain threatens the area. Lucie Public Schools announced Tuesday that all schools and district offices will be closed Wednesday due to the threat of significant rainfall and localized flooding. The announcement comes after the district dismissed students two hours early Tuesday as worsening weather conditions raised concerns about flooding. It's the latest disruption for the district, which was forced to close schools for three consecutive days Nov. 4, 5 and 6 after historic flooding left roads underwater and communities struggling to recover. Lucie County clears drains, prepares for more rain after historic flooding Now, with the ground already saturated, district leaders say they aren't taking any chances. According to the district, forecasts from the National Weather Service indicate the potential for significant rainfall, although uncertainty remains about exactly when and where the heaviest rain will fall. "Given the already saturated conditions in our community, the District believes taking a cautious approach is in the best interest of our students, families, and employees," district officials said in a statement. John Carroll High School also announced it will be closed Wednesday, Nov. 18, due to the threat of heavy rainfall and flooding across the region. The decision follows an early dismissal Tuesday and a review of weather forecasts and local flooding conditions. School officials said all Wednesday activities, including athletics, practices, extracurricular programs and other events, have been canceled. John Carroll anticipates reopening Thursday, pending weather and road conditions. Administrators will continue monitoring forecasts and coordinating with local authorities before making further decisions. Updates will be shared through the school's official communication channels. All after-school activities, aftercare programs, and athletic events scheduled for Wednesday have also been canceled. District officials said they will continue monitoring rainfall, flooding, road closures, and access to schools, bus stops, and transportation routes throughout Wednesday. A decision on whether schools will reopen Thursday is expected Wednesday evening. Families are encouraged to monitor the district's official website and social media channels for updates.

entry.title: Amendment 3 task force tries to get the message to Florida residents
entry.summary: Indian River Countys Tax Collector and Property Appraiser have formed Task Force 3, to get the word out for residents to qualify the new Homestead Exemption coming with Amendment 3. What people really need to understand is, there's less than five weeks to get a driver's license to become a resident of the state of Florida, said Property Appraiser Wesley Davis. WATCH: Amendment 3 task force tries to get the message to Florida residents Indian River Co Launches Amendment 3 Task Force Florida residency is a key component to being able to qualify for the exemption, which is rising to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, after voters approved the referendum on election day. New homeowners coming into the state after January 1, 2027 will have to wait five years for the new full exemptions. Current renters in Florida can still qualify for the new exemption on any future home they buy. The sense of urgency right now is that you don't need to have a homestead by the end of the year, Davis says. What you need to do to qualify for the homestead exemption is you must be a resident of the state of Florida by the end of the year.' That also includes current residents who have failed to get a Florida ID and still hold a driver's license from their previous state, says Tax Collector Carole Jean Jordan. They can establish residency in an apartment, and then when they buy a home, they can file for homestead. The local officials also pointed out county offices will be closed around the upcoming holidays. The impact of Amendment 3 will be felt in future county budgets, and both department heads acknowledge there are already discussions about budgeting next year. Estimates are that the county could lose about 20-30 million dollars over the first couple of years under the amendment. This will not end property taxes, Davis says. About half of everybody's tax bill goes to education, and education is not affected by this at all.

entry.title: Lone Pine Estates residents brace for more rain while still recovering from flooding
entry.summary: Weeks after floodwaters devastated Lone Pine Estates, residents are still cleaning up and recovering. Now, another round of storms is bringing back fears of what could happen next. WPTV reporter Christy Waite has been listening to neighbors' concerns for weeks. WATCH: Lone Pine Estates residents brace for more rain while still recovering from flooding Lone Pine preps for more rain She drove through the Lone Pine Estates community and saw drier conditions, but neighbors were using sandbags to protect their homes. For residents like Lacey Stone, the possibility of more flooding is frightening. Stone said she was able to get more sandbags at Home Depot as she prepared her home for additional rain. But the previous flooding has already taken a toll on her family and finances. Ive missed two weeks of work, and I am a single widowed mother. Its just been really hard financially, Stone said. Residents are not only worried about getting through the next storm. Some are questioning what can be done to prevent their neighborhood from flooding again. Stephanie Gabriel said drainage remains a major concern. Neighbors told Waite they feel the city failed them and want to see solutions that could better protect the community from future flooding. Many of the residents in Lone Pine Estates do not have flood insurance because the area is not considered a flood zone. As more rain remains a concern, families in Lone Pine Estates are balancing two challenges at once: preparing for what could come next while still trying to recover from what happened weeks ago.

entry.summary: St. Lucie, Martin County schools to release students early Tuesday ahead of heavy rain    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie Public Schools will dismiss students two hours early Tuesday as rain moves into the area, with heavier rainfall possible in the evening. The district said it made the decision as a precaution based on information from the National Weather Service . Parents and guardians are encouraged to consider conditions in their neighborhoods. Absences caused by weather will be excused, the district said. Heavier rain is possible Wednesday through Friday and could lead to school closures. The district is monitoring conditions with the St. Lucie County Emergency Operations Center and the National Weather Service. The district said it will announce any changes to Tuesday’s after-school activities and athletics based on weather conditions. Families should check the district’s official channels for updates. Neighboring Indian River County schools will also operate on a modified schedule Tuesday, Nov. 17, with students dismissed early, according to the School District of Indian River County. The district announced the following dismissal times: High schools: 12:20 p.m. Middle schools and K-8: 1 p.m. Elementary schools: 1:50 p.m. Wabasso School: 12:30 p.m. Morning arrival times will remain unchanged, and transportation will operate as normal during early dismissal. Extended Day will be available Tuesday morning but closed in the afternoon. All extracurricular activities must conclude by 2:30 p.m. The district said additional updates will be shared as information becomes available. RELATED: Heavy rain returns this week, bringing major threat of flooding across south Florida Palm Beach County schools are still scheduled to open Tuesday, Nov. The district will continue monitoring the weather and share updates if anything changes. Okeechobee County schools will also be open. Martin County schools will also remain open Tuesday; however, all after-school activities will be cancelled. The ground is already soaked from the rain we experienced the first weekend of the month, so it won't take much to create flooding concerns. Right now, up to 4-5 inches of rain is possible, but higher isolated amounts can't be ruled out.

entry.title: Flooded roads reported in Vero Lake Estates as Indian River County schools close - cw34.com
entry.summary: Flooded roads reported in Vero Lake Estates as Indian River County schools close    cw34.com
entry.article_text: The Indian River County Sheriff’s Office is reporting more flooded roads in the Vero Lake Estates area as heavy rain moves through the county Thursday. The sheriff’s office urged drivers to stay off flooded roads, warning that water can be deeper than it appears and can stall vehicles. High-water vehicles are in the area, and anyone who becomes stranded should call 911. Ryan Lloyd, Indian River County’s emergency management chief, told CBS12 News the county has received about 5 to 7 inches of rain so far. He said the north end of the county, including Sebastian, Fellsmere and Vero Lake Estates, has gotten more than the rest. Another 3 to 5 inches is expected by midnight Friday, Lloyd said, and the area is still at risk for pockets of 10 to 12 inches or more falling in a short time. Lloyd said the county’s water management systems are full and the ground is essentially saturated, so new rain is running off onto roads. The county’s emergency operations center is at a Level 2 partial activation, and National Guard members are there with high-water vehicles. Lloyd said there had been no requests for high-water rescues as of Thursday afternoon. He urged residents to avoid nonessential travel, turn around at flooded roads and never drive around barricades. Please do not drive to neighborhoods that are flooded because that can actually push floodwaters into homes and create a bigger problem than what some of those residents may already be facing, Lloyd said. The weather prompted the School District of Indian River County to close all public schools and district offices Thursday. The district said saturated ground and expected rain could make travel unsafe for students and staff. Lloyd said schools will also be closed Friday. A Vero Beach football game scheduled for Friday night has been moved to Saturday at 7 p.m., he said. CHIME IN: Send in your weather photos and videos The National Weather Service issued a flood advisory Thursday morning for eastern Indian River and northeastern St. Lucie counties, reporting that 2 to 4 inches of rain had fallen in parts of the area. The advisory warned of minor flooding in low-lying and poorly drained areas. A flood watch remains in effect for Indian River County through Friday evening, with more showers and thunderstorms possible. See also: Flood risk lingers across the Treasure Coast and Palm Beaches before a drier weekend The county’s road closure map , viewed at 2:47 p.m. Thursday, listed 13 road closures and six lane closures. Among the roads marked closed were 100th Court, 103rd Avenue, 104th Avenue, 83rd Street and 87th Street. The map also showed a long-term closure on 13th Street Southwest, scheduled to remain in place until Jan. Lane-closure listings included 101st Avenue, West 98th Avenue and two locations near Barber Street and U.S. The county also warned that heavy rain and gusty winds could disrupt trash collection. Residents whose streets are flooded were asked not to put carts in the water; the landfill and customer convenience centers could close early if conditions become unsafe. The City of Fellsmere also urged drivers to use extreme caution, identifying two potential trouble spots: New York Avenue near Hickory Street and North Broadway. The city said those roads could close if rain continues. City Hall remains open and operating normally. Lloyd said there are no known water main breaks or significant power outages in the county. The county’s Emergency Information Center, at 772-226-4000, will be open overnight Thursday for questions and flooding reports, and the county will decide Friday whether to keep it running. Residents can report flood damage to homes and businesses through the county’s emergency management website .

entry.title: Port St. Lucie restores water service, but boil water notice remains
entry.summary: Water service has been fully restored to the Tradition and western Port St. Lucie areas following a major water main break Tuesday, but a precautionary boil water notice remains in effect. The break happened near Glades Cut Off Road when a contractor working on a construction project unrelated to the city damaged a 36-inch water main, according to city officials. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Tradition water service restored after water main break Crews completed repairs Tuesday evening and began flushing the water main shortly afterward. The city initially recommended a 48-hour precautionary boil water notice Tuesday at noon for the Tradition area, including Western Grove, Riverland, Wilson Grove and Southern Grove, west of Interstate 95 to Becker Road. The notice also covers communities along Glades Cut Off Road, including Copper Creek, Wylder and Verano. City officials said water quality testing began Wednesday. Because of the number of customers affected, a significant number of samples must be collected and tested before the notice can be lifted. Residents should continue boiling water until the city confirms it is safe to use without boiling. Restored water service does not mean the boil water notice has ended. The city is investigating the incident and expects to pursue appropriate action to recover costs from those responsible. Updates will be posted at CityofPSL.com .

entry.title: 'Today we are homeless': Jensen Beach family displaced by historic flooding pleads for help rebuilding home - WPTV
entry.summary: 'Today we are homeless': Jensen Beach family displaced by historic flooding pleads for help rebuilding home    WPTV
entry.article_text: A Jensen Beach family displaced by historic flooding is searching for more permanent housing and money to rebuild after water destroyed much of the inside of their home. Lisa and Jeremy French, who have two young boys, told WPTV's Michael Hoffman they ultimately have one goal: to get their family back home.WATCH REPORT BELOW:WPTV first met the French family shortly after historic rainfall hit South Florida and the Treasure Coast. Floodwater had surrounded their neighborhood, forcing residents to use kayaks to get around and check on neighbors.Days later, much of the water has receded. The damage has not."My floorboards are outside," Lisa French said.Hoffman returned to the French family's Jensen Beach home for an update, but the family said it was not safe to go inside.French said the flooding wiped out much of what her family had accumulated over the years."Our appliances are gone, our cabinets are gone, every piece of furniture," French said.The family is now trying to determine how to pay for repairs while securing a more permanent place to live.WPTV met French again at the Hoke Library in Jensen Beach, where a Multi-Agency Resource Center has been helping people looking for assistance following the flooding.French told Hoffman that her home flooded days after the rain had stopped.Martin County told WPTV that the family's home is near the Savannah Preserves, an area where excess water naturally flows from other flooded areas.French, however, questions whether other actions involving water entering the preserve contributed to what happened at her home."They're saying it's from natural rain, but they dumped Monday and Tuesday, nonstop into the savannas," French said.The impact of the flooding extends beyond the physical damage.Through tears, Lisa and Jeremy French pleaded for help before the Martin County Commission as they described what their family is facing."Today we are homeless," Lisa French told commissioners. "We have nowhere to host Thanksgiving. We have nowhere for our boys to have Christmas. We don't have beds to come home to."The couple has two young boys. French said she wants them to continue growing up in the Jensen Beach home the family worked hard to maintain.For now, however, the family says it needs more permanent housing while trying to determine where the money to repair the home will come from.French said the uncertainty surrounding assistance has left her worried there could still be a significant financial gap, even if additional aid becomes available."Who's going to fill in the gaps?" French said. "And, you know, maybe I feel like somebody should take accountability."Despite the uncertainty and extensive damage, the family says it has not given up hope of returning."We just want to go home," French said. "Like, that's at the end, that we just want to be home with our family."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

entry.article_text: The victim of a hit and run crash in Port St. Lucie has passed away, which could lead to more serious charges against the driver who police say hit her. The victim, Alexis Cuellar, 24, of Port St. Lucie was critically injured when she was hit while riding her e-scooter on her way to her job at a nearby Wendy's at about 5:10 in the morning on Monday, November 16. Police say Tristian Ray Sanchez-Chasmer, 18, of Port St. Lucie had been playing ding-dong-ditch with friends before the crash and the Chevy Tahoe he was driving hit Cuellar in a crosswalk at SW Feather Terrace and SW Gatlin Boulevard and he did not stop to check on her or render aid. He was charged with leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury. A former prosecutor says it's likely Sanchez-Chasmer will now face a more serious charge of leaving the scene of a crash involving death, and he could also be charged with vehicular homicide. See also: Flooded roads reported in Vero Lake Estates as Indian River County schools close "A lot of these cases take time because you've got to go through an exhaustive review to make sure you get it right, you know, to find out, was he speeding excessively? Was he blowing through stop signs? Was he driving erratically? They'll look at the black box inside the car, that's the event data recorder. They're gonna check to see braking. They'll check to see the marks on the road. They'll look to see the throttle position before impact," said Dave Aronberg, former Palm Beach County State Attorney. Aronberg says if those two charges are filed they would each carry a maximum penalty of 30 years in prison, which means Sanchez-Chasmer could potentially face up to 60 years in prison if convicted.

Lucie said water service has been fully restored after crews completed repairs Tuesday evening and began flushing the system. A precautionary boil water notice for about 21,000 customers in western Port St. Lucie has been extended 24 hours while the city completes water-quality testing. The advisory affects customers in Tradition, Riverland, Western Grove, Wilson Grove, Southern Grove, Copper Creek, Wylder and Verano, as well as properties along Glades Cut Off Road. For Marcus Rowe, the first sign of trouble was a sudden drop in water pressure. "I went to turn on the faucet, and the water pressure was low. I was like, 'what's going on'?" See also: 'We can all do something': Couple urges action for children in foster care City officials said water quality sampling is underway, but the boil water notice will remain in effect until laboratory testing confirms the water is safe to drink. Because of the large number of customers affected, officials said the advisory could remain in place beyond the initial 48-hour timeframe. For the Rowe family, that has meant relying on bottled water and boiling water for daily needs. "Boiling water, doing what they told us to do," Rowe said. "It's something small, I'm not really sweating it. We're going as far as turning on the water in the fridge so the ice doesn't get accumulated with that tainted water." Residents are advised to continue boiling water used for drinking, cooking, making ice, brushing teeth and washing dishes until the city announces the notice has been lifted. For updates, residents can visit the City of Port St.

entry.title: Treasure Coast counties prepare for flooding as heavy rain and gusty winds move in - WPEC
entry.summary: Treasure Coast counties prepare for flooding as heavy rain and gusty winds move in    WPEC
entry.article_text: The Treasure Coast is bracing for a soggy stretch as counties prepare for possible flooding from heavy rain. Indian River County The Indian River County Emergency Operations Center remains at Level 2, or partial activation, because of ongoing flooding and the potential for more heavy rain. Emergency services, human services and infrastructure partners are coordinating response and recovery efforts. The county urges residents to avoid flooded roads and floodwaters, watch for rising water in low-lying areas and monitor weather conditions and official updates. Residents with flood-related questions or information can call the Emergency Information Center at 772-226-4000 during operating hours. Due to the heavy rain and gusty winds, solid waste services may be disrupted. Waste Management curbside collections may be delayed, and residents should not put carts in the street if it is flooded. See also: Florida deputies rescue 2-year-old girl found in pond near apartment complex Waste Management collects recycling in blue carts countywide. It collects garbage, yard waste and bulk waste in unincorporated Indian River County, Fellsmere, Sebastian and Indian River Shores. Residents in other cities and towns should check with their local governments for service updates. The county recommends putting carts out by 6 a.m. on collection day, closing lids, bagging garbage, and avoiding overfilled carts. Cardboard should be flattened and placed inside recycling carts, and yard waste should stay inside yard waste carts. Residents should bring carts back in as soon as possible after collection. The landfill and all five Customer Convenience Centers may close early or remain closed if conditions become unsafe. The east-central Florida coast faces a Slight Risk, or Level 2 out of 4, for excessive rainfall. Localized flooding is possible, especially along the coast, and some areas could receive 4 inches or more of rain. Martin County Martin County officials expect 3 to 6 inches of rain, with localized amounts of 8 to 12 inches, beginning Tuesday afternoon and continuing through Nov. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office says it is working with the county’s emergency operations center to monitor rainfall and identify roads that could become difficult to pass. The sheriff’s office plans to deploy high-water rescue vehicles in flood-prone areas. Having the vehicles nearby could help deputies reach residents who need assistance and motorists who become stranded, the office said. It asks where flooding occurred, how buildings were affected and what impacts residents and businesses experienced. Residents can complete the flood damage survey by Nov. entry.title: St. Lucie County prepares for more rain after historic flooding; schools closed Wednesday - WPEC
entry.summary: St. Lucie County prepares for more rain after historic flooding; schools closed Wednesday    WPEC
entry.article_text: Crews are clearing drainage systems and checking waterways in St. Lucie County as another round of rain threatens areas still recovering from historic flooding. Lucie Public Schools is releasing students two hours early Tuesday. The district announced Tuesday afternoon that schools and offices will be closed Wednesday as a precaution. All after-school activities, aftercare programs, and athletic events scheduled for Wednesday are also canceled. District officials will continue monitoring rainfall, flooding, road closures, and the accessibility of schools, bus stops, and transportation routes throughout Wednesday. A decision regarding school operations for Thursday, November 19, will be announced Wednesday evening. Lucie officials say Public Works crews are inspecting drainage systems, clearing blockages and lowering water levels where possible. The ground remains saturated, increasing the risk of flooding even if rainfall is lighter than it was during the early November storms. See also: Heavy rain returns this week, bringing major threat of flooding across South Florida The National Weather Service has issued a flood watch for St. Lucie County from Tuesday afternoon through Friday evening. Forecasters expect 3 to 6 inches of rain across the area, with higher amounts possible in some locations. Two weeks ago, floodwaters stranded cars, trapped families and forced some residents to wade through deep water. Videos from that flooding showed high school freshman Noah Julian swimming from his school bus toward his home in a flooded Port St. Another video showed 7-year-old Ella Ghodooshim walking through chest-deep water with her mother near Oak Hammock K-8. That mother, Thassia Rodrigues, told CBS12 her only concern was getting her daughter safely across the flooded intersection. "As long as I can get her across and get her to safety, that was my main concern," Rodrigues said. She described how quickly the flooding overwhelmed the neighborhood, leaving parents struggling to reach their children. "It was pretty scary and in a matter of minutes we had everything just flood," she said. Lucie Public Schools told CBS12 News that decisions about closures and early dismissal are based on forecasts and information from the National Weather Service and Emergency Operations Center. The district said the information available before the previous flooding did not indicate schools needed to close or dismiss students earlier. This time, officials said the forecast supported releasing students two hours early to get them home before the heaviest rain. The district said it was awaiting additional updates from the National Weather Service at 2 p.m. and Emergency Operations Center at 4 p.m. Tuesday before making any further decisions about school schedules. Parents picking up their children near Oak Hammock K-8 Tuesday told CBS12 News they welcomed the earlier dismissal. "It's kind of nice that they're doing it early so we have time to get them and not have to rush," said Nathan Leach, whose child attends the school. Rhett Linton, another parent, recalled kayaking through the flooded intersection during the previous storm. "I'm super happy that they are stepping up and taking precautions," Linton said. Rodrigues, who was captured on video helping her daughter through the floodwaters, also praised the district's decision. Lucie County, we appreciate you guys," she said. Officials are urging residents to plan ahead, monitor forecasts and local alerts, and limit unnecessary travel. Drivers should never enter standing or moving water. Floodwater can stall a vehicle and cause costly engine damage. If you cannot tell how deep the water is, turn around and find another route. entry.title: Martin County School Board rescinds termination of teacher Matthew Theobald for his comments on Charlie Kirk - WPBF
entry.summary: Martin County School Board rescinds termination of teacher Matthew Theobald for his comments on Charlie Kirk    WPBF
entry.article_text: The Martin County School Board voted this week to reinstate Matthew Theobald, a teacher at Spectrum Academy, after a judge ruled his social media posts about conservative activist Charlie Kirk’s death did not justify suspension or termination. Theobald was initially targeted by the Martin County School District for several online comments following Kirk’s murder in Utah in September 2025. The school board voted to suspend Theobald without pay and recommended his termination. Both parties agreed to an administrative hearing to address the matter. In June, the judge ruled that the school board failed to prove Theobald engaged in immorality or willful neglect of duty, which would have been grounds for dismissal. The judge also stated that Theobald’s Facebook comments did not disrupt his students, the learning environment, or reduce any teacher’s ability to teach. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 Martin County School District leadership responded to the ruling by saying it would review the judge’s recommendation. This week, the school board officially voted to adopt the judge’s recommendation, rescinding Theobald’s suspension and termination. He will also be awarded back pay and benefits through June 30. School board member Marsha Powers said she voted in favor of the decision but explained her reasoning. “I have serious concerns about the process that brought this matter before a judge who does not live or work in the community,” Powers said. Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app. Board member Tony Anderson responded to Powers’ comments, saying he understood her concerns but noted the board had already placed the issue in the judge’s hands. “It’s a decision we have to live with,” Anderson said. WPBF 25 reached out to Matthew Theobald for comment but has not yet received a response.
