entry.title: Florida emergency management director responds to FEMA delays as Jensen Beach flood victims wait for help - WFLX
entry.summary: Florida emergency management director responds to FEMA delays as Jensen Beach flood victims wait for help    WFLX
entry.article_text: Nearly three weeks after historic flooding forced families from their homes and caused millions of dollars in damage across Martin County, residents are still waiting for a federal disaster declaration that could unlock critical financial assistance. Now, after a WPTV report on the delays and growing frustration among flood victims, Florida's top emergency management official is responding to questions about the state's recovery efforts—and what help families can expect if FEMA funding never arrives. Watch more from Kate Hussey: In an exclusive interview with WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey, Jared Perdue, director of the Florida Division of Emergency Management, confirmed the state submitted an expedited federal disaster declaration request Nov. 9, one week after the initial flooding. But nearly two weeks after that request, a decision remains pending. "We've been very engaged with FEMA, and we did actually submit an expedited disaster declaration request to FEMA on November the ninth," Perdue said. "FEMA has been very closely coordinating with us in reviewing that, and I'm sure they're going to make quick work of it." The uncertainty comes as Martin County estimates approximately $18 million in residential and public infrastructure damage, with families still struggling to afford repairs and another round of historic rainfall complicating recovery efforts. Along Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach, the devastation is still visible. Dumpsters line driveways, waterlogged belongings have been discarded and homes have been stripped down to their frames. For Linda Weisbecker, whose home was among those severely damaged, the destruction has been overwhelming. "It's like an apocalypse here," Weisbecker told WPTV in an earlier interview. For nine days, Weisbecker and her neighbors navigated waist-deep floodwaters before they could begin salvaging what remained of their homes. "Once we got through that and the water came out, we just all started pitching in, going in to see what we can salvage from each home," she said. But much of what Weisbecker lost cannot be replaced. Our house is empty," she said. "We lost everything, from pictures of our children and their lives, our friends, our grandkids, now we have great-grandkids. Everything [my husband] had since he was 13 on is gone." Weisbecker has been approved for a $25,000 grant through Florida's State Housing Initiatives Partnership, or SHIP, program. But for families facing tens of thousands of dollars in repairs, that assistance may cover only a fraction of the cost. And not everyone will qualify. "You do think about that process and you sit there and you say to yourself, how am I gonna do this?" Weisbecker said. That question is at the center of WPTV's ongoing investigation. Martin County estimates the flooding caused: A federal major disaster declaration could make certain public infrastructure repairs eligible for FEMA reimbursement and potentially open the door to individual assistance for qualifying residents. But approval is not guaranteed. When WPTV initially contacted FEMA, the agency confirmed it had received the disaster declaration request and that it remained under review. FEMA referred additional questions about the response and recovery timeline to the Florida Division of Emergency Management. Hussey subsequently pressed Perdue on what would happen if the federal government denied the request. "If FEMA ultimately denies federal assistance, does Florida have a Plan B, or are these families simply on their own?" Hussey asked. Perdue did not identify a specific alternative state funding program, instead emphasizing Florida's experience responding to natural disasters and its ongoing coordination with federal and local officials. "This is something that we're very used to doing. I mean, in Florida, we deal with natural disasters all the time," Perdue said. "We have a great relationship with FEMA, and usually those things go very well." He added that the state remains focused on immediate response efforts, including search and rescue operations and meeting residents' emergency needs. In the meantime, Martin County is working to distribute approximately $1 million in available SHIP funding to qualifying residents. Eligible homeowners may receive grants of up to $25,000, with additional assistance potentially available through loans of up to $75,000. However, those loans come with repayment requirements and liens. Income eligibility restrictions could also leave some families without assistance, even if they cannot afford to rebuild on their own. "There's going to be a lot of heart-wrenching cases where somebody barely missed the limit," Commissioner Blake Capps said during a recent Martin County Commission meeting. Capps proposed establishing a separate county-funded emergency assistance program for residents who fall through the cracks. But when WPTV asked where that money would come from, Capps acknowledged a funding source had not yet been identified. we'd have to talk to staff," he said. County Human Services Director Michelle Miller previously told commissioners the state had promised additional disaster relief funding, although neither the amount nor the timeline had been confirmed. "They haven't confirmed the amount yet but has assured us we will be getting some disaster relief funds," Miller told Hussey. Hussey raised those concerns directly with Perdue, asking whether the state had other programs available for families who earn too much to qualify for existing assistance but not enough to pay for repairs. Perdue pointed to the state's partnerships with nonprofit organizations and its deployment of emergency personnel to assist with cleanup. "We've actually activated the National Guard, and are also partnering with nonprofits to do what they call the muck and gut of homes that have been flooded," Perdue said. That work includes removing damaged drywall and other waterlogged materials to help prevent mold growth. "We're providing the assistance that we can and partnering with those nonprofit organizations as well," he said. However, Perdue did not identify a specific funding program to cover rebuilding costs for homeowners who do not qualify for existing assistance. The financial uncertainty extends beyond individual homeowners. Martin County faces approximately $15 million in combined beach and road damage, with additional emergency response expenses still being assessed. County spokesperson Martha Ann Kniess previously told WPTV that without federal reimbursement, Martin County could be left responsible for covering those costs, potentially forcing officials to redirect money from elsewhere in the budget or identify other funding sources. Hussey asked Perdue whether the state would help cover those expenses if FEMA denied federal assistance — or whether the financial burden could ultimately fall on local taxpayers. Perdue did not commit to providing state funding for those repairs. "We are and have been doing damage assessments ever since we submitted the first disaster declaration request," he said. "As those damage assessments come in, we'll continue to coordinate with FEMA and make sure all that information is submitted." The state's response follows an emotional Martin County Commission meeting Tuesday, where residents pleaded with elected officials to do more to secure recovery funding. Fight for us!" one resident urged commissioners. Others questioned why families were being asked to wait even longer for answers. "And the answer from this dais is wait 13 more days?!?" another resident asked. Commissioner Eileen Vargas said she had reached out to FEMA through personal contacts in an effort to expedite the process. "I did, through contacts, reach out to FEMA to try and get this going," Vargas said. Vargas also told residents she expected a new FEMA director to take office Nov. 30 and hoped that development could help move the disaster declaration forward. But even if a declaration is approved, not all losses or recovery expenses would necessarily qualify for federal assistance. As Martin County continues to recover from the Nov. 2 flooding, Perdue said the state is also responding to another significant rainfall event affecting communities across Florida. Ron DeSantis expanded the state's emergency executive order to include 21 counties. The state has mobilized resources from the National Guard, State Guard, Florida Highway Patrol and Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, among other agencies. "We're actively still responding to the previous flooding event on November 2, and now we're actively dealing with a current, another historic rain event that's brought record amount of flooding in many counties throughout the state," Perdue said. The overlapping disasters have added urgency to recovery efforts, particularly for residents whose homes remain exposed after being gutted. Perdue said state resources remain available for immediate needs, including food, water, shelter and emergency medical assistance. We're fully mobilized," he said. We're going to be with you till the very end, and we're going to make sure we help everybody get back on their feet." Despite those assurances, several critical questions remain unresolved. FEMA has not announced a decision on Florida's expedited disaster declaration request. The state has not identified a specific alternative rebuilding assistance program for homeowners who do not qualify for existing aid, nor has it committed to covering Martin County's public infrastructure losses if federal funding is denied. For residents like Weisbecker, the uncertainty is more than a question of government funding. It's a question of whether they can afford to return to the homes they've spent years building their lives in. "This is very urgent for people to get back into their daily lives," Weisbecker said. "This is total devastation.

entry.summary: St. Lucie County closes stretch of Glades Cut Off Road between LTC Ranch and Wylder    WPEC
entry.article_text: A portion of Glades Cut Off Road in Port St. Lucie will be closed for the foreseeable future, the City of Port St. The county announced the closure. The city announced on Thursday that a portion of Glades Cut Off Road between LTC Ranch Parkway and Wylder Parkway (Commerce Centre Drive) will be closed starting Friday, Nov. 20 and continuing until further notice. See also: Weather-related closures, impacts across South Florida and the Treasure Coast According to the city, a culvert failure beneath the roadway near 8880 NW Glades Cut Off Road has caused erosion beneath a travel lane, prompting the closure. In the meantime, drivers are encouraged to use alternate routes while the area remains closed. Motorists can detour by using LTC Ranch Parkway or Wylder Parkway to Midway Road, then going south to reach Glades Cut Off Road. For more information, contact the St. Lucie County Public Works Engineering Division at 772-462-1707.

entry.title: Monument to honor two fallen deputies will be unveiled in Indian River County - WPBF
entry.summary: Monument to honor two fallen deputies will be unveiled in Indian River County    WPBF
entry.article_text: A monument honoring two Indian River County sheriff’s deputies killed in the line of duty will be unveiled tomorrow at the sheriff’s office, happening on the first anniversary of Sgt. Terri Sweeting-Mashkow’s death. The monument will commemorate the lives of Sgt. Terri Jean Sweeting-Mashkow and Cpl. “It’s going to be really beautiful and special for them, for the future of our agency going forward,” Sheriff Eric Flowers told WPBF last month. The ceremony’s timing marks one year since Sweeting-Mashkow was killed while serving an eviction notice at a home along Governor’s Way. Investigators said Michael Halberstam opened fire, fatally shooting Sweeting-Mashkow. The memorial will also honor Cpl. Richard Raczkoski, who was killed in September 1986 after being shot at a convenience store near Vero Beach. Last month, the man convicted of killing Raczkoski, William Reaves, was executed after receiving the death penalty. “The public will have a place on our campus to come and see those two that have lost their lives, and it will be there forever for them to always be memorialized there in front of our new building,” Flowers said. The ceremony begins at 10 a.m. Saturday at the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office. entry.title: How much rain did we get? See the highest totals across Treasure Coast and Palm Beaches - WPEC
entry.summary: How much rain did we get? See the highest totals across Treasure Coast and Palm Beaches    WPEC
entry.article_text: Indian River and Palm Beach counties saw the highest totals The highest report among the five counties came from The Acreage in Palm Beach County, where 12.92 inches were reported since Tuesday morning. Other notable Palm Beach County reports included 7.91 inches in Royal Palm Beach, 7.30 inches in Haverhill and 7.20 inches in Sandalfoot Cove. Indian River County also saw several high totals. Sebastian Inlet reported 10.29 inches, while Vero Lake Estates had reports of 8.49 and 7.51 inches. Other reports included 7.23 inches in Fellsmere and 6.90 inches in Roseland. Totals varied across the Treasure Coast In St. Lucie County, the highest report was 6.24 inches at the county fairgrounds. Indrio reported 4.92 inches, while Tradition and Paradise Park received 4.70 and 4.68 inches, respectively. Martin County’s highest report was 5.11 inches at Philo Farms. Other reports included 3.79 inches in Indiantown, 3.72 inches in Caloosa and 3.28 inches in Palm City. Okeechobee County had lower totals Rainfall reports in Okeechobee County were lower overall. The highest listed total was 2.81 inches in Kissimmee Prairie, followed by 2.32 inches in Country Hills. Okeechobee reported 1.58 inches. Heavy rain was concentrated in pockets These reports show how unevenly the rain fell. Most locations across the five counties saw totals of only a few inches, while certain communities caught repeated or heavier downpours that pushed their totals much higher. The highest localized amounts were concentrated in Indian River and Palm Beach counties.

entry.title: Florida emergency management director responds to FEMA delays as Jensen Beach flood victims wait for help - WFLX
entry.summary: Florida emergency management director responds to FEMA delays as Jensen Beach flood victims wait for help    WFLX
entry.article_text: Nearly three weeks after historic flooding forced families from their homes and caused millions of dollars in damage across Martin County, residents are still waiting for a federal disaster declaration that could unlock critical financial assistance. Now, after a WPTV report on the delays and growing frustration among flood victims, Florida's top emergency management official is responding to questions about the state's recovery efforts—and what help families can expect if FEMA funding never arrives. Watch more from Kate Hussey: In an exclusive interview with WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey, Jared Perdue, director of the Florida Division of Emergency Management, confirmed the state submitted an expedited federal disaster declaration request Nov. 9, one week after the initial flooding. But nearly two weeks after that request, a decision remains pending. "We've been very engaged with FEMA, and we did actually submit an expedited disaster declaration request to FEMA on November the ninth," Perdue said. "FEMA has been very closely coordinating with us in reviewing that, and I'm sure they're going to make quick work of it." The uncertainty comes as Martin County estimates approximately $18 million in residential and public infrastructure damage, with families still struggling to afford repairs and another round of historic rainfall complicating recovery efforts. Along Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach, the devastation is still visible. Dumpsters line driveways, waterlogged belongings have been discarded and homes have been stripped down to their frames. For Linda Weisbecker, whose home was among those severely damaged, the destruction has been overwhelming. "It's like an apocalypse here," Weisbecker told WPTV in an earlier interview. For nine days, Weisbecker and her neighbors navigated waist-deep floodwaters before they could begin salvaging what remained of their homes. "Once we got through that and the water came out, we just all started pitching in, going in to see what we can salvage from each home," she said. But much of what Weisbecker lost cannot be replaced. Our house is empty," she said. "We lost everything, from pictures of our children and their lives, our friends, our grandkids, now we have great-grandkids. Everything [my husband] had since he was 13 on is gone." Weisbecker has been approved for a $25,000 grant through Florida's State Housing Initiatives Partnership, or SHIP, program. But for families facing tens of thousands of dollars in repairs, that assistance may cover only a fraction of the cost. And not everyone will qualify. "You do think about that process and you sit there and you say to yourself, how am I gonna do this?" Weisbecker said. That question is at the center of WPTV's ongoing investigation. Martin County estimates the flooding caused: A federal major disaster declaration could make certain public infrastructure repairs eligible for FEMA reimbursement and potentially open the door to individual assistance for qualifying residents. But approval is not guaranteed. When WPTV initially contacted FEMA, the agency confirmed it had received the disaster declaration request and that it remained under review. FEMA referred additional questions about the response and recovery timeline to the Florida Division of Emergency Management. Hussey subsequently pressed Perdue on what would happen if the federal government denied the request. "If FEMA ultimately denies federal assistance, does Florida have a Plan B, or are these families simply on their own?" Hussey asked. Perdue did not identify a specific alternative state funding program, instead emphasizing Florida's experience responding to natural disasters and its ongoing coordination with federal and local officials. "This is something that we're very used to doing. I mean, in Florida, we deal with natural disasters all the time," Perdue said. "We have a great relationship with FEMA, and usually those things go very well." He added that the state remains focused on immediate response efforts, including search and rescue operations and meeting residents' emergency needs. In the meantime, Martin County is working to distribute approximately $1 million in available SHIP funding to qualifying residents. Eligible homeowners may receive grants of up to $25,000, with additional assistance potentially available through loans of up to $75,000. However, those loans come with repayment requirements and liens. Income eligibility restrictions could also leave some families without assistance, even if they cannot afford to rebuild on their own. "There's going to be a lot of heart-wrenching cases where somebody barely missed the limit," Commissioner Blake Capps said during a recent Martin County Commission meeting. Capps proposed establishing a separate county-funded emergency assistance program for residents who fall through the cracks. But when WPTV asked where that money would come from, Capps acknowledged a funding source had not yet been identified. we'd have to talk to staff," he said. County Human Services Director Michelle Miller previously told commissioners the state had promised additional disaster relief funding, although neither the amount nor the timeline had been confirmed. "They haven't confirmed the amount yet but has assured us we will be getting some disaster relief funds," Miller told Hussey. Hussey raised those concerns directly with Perdue, asking whether the state had other programs available for families who earn too much to qualify for existing assistance but not enough to pay for repairs. Perdue pointed to the state's partnerships with nonprofit organizations and its deployment of emergency personnel to assist with cleanup. "We've actually activated the National Guard, and are also partnering with nonprofits to do what they call the muck and gut of homes that have been flooded," Perdue said. That work includes removing damaged drywall and other waterlogged materials to help prevent mold growth. "We're providing the assistance that we can and partnering with those nonprofit organizations as well," he said. However, Perdue did not identify a specific funding program to cover rebuilding costs for homeowners who do not qualify for existing assistance. The financial uncertainty extends beyond individual homeowners. Martin County faces approximately $15 million in combined beach and road damage, with additional emergency response expenses still being assessed. County spokesperson Martha Ann Kniess previously told WPTV that without federal reimbursement, Martin County could be left responsible for covering those costs, potentially forcing officials to redirect money from elsewhere in the budget or identify other funding sources. Hussey asked Perdue whether the state would help cover those expenses if FEMA denied federal assistance — or whether the financial burden could ultimately fall on local taxpayers. Perdue did not commit to providing state funding for those repairs. "We are and have been doing damage assessments ever since we submitted the first disaster declaration request," he said. "As those damage assessments come in, we'll continue to coordinate with FEMA and make sure all that information is submitted." The state's response follows an emotional Martin County Commission meeting Tuesday, where residents pleaded with elected officials to do more to secure recovery funding. Fight for us!" one resident urged commissioners. Others questioned why families were being asked to wait even longer for answers. "And the answer from this dais is wait 13 more days?!?" another resident asked. Commissioner Eileen Vargas said she had reached out to FEMA through personal contacts in an effort to expedite the process. "I did, through contacts, reach out to FEMA to try and get this going," Vargas said. Vargas also told residents she expected a new FEMA director to take office Nov. 30 and hoped that development could help move the disaster declaration forward. But even if a declaration is approved, not all losses or recovery expenses would necessarily qualify for federal assistance. As Martin County continues to recover from the Nov. 2 flooding, Perdue said the state is also responding to another significant rainfall event affecting communities across Florida. Ron DeSantis expanded the state's emergency executive order to include 21 counties. The state has mobilized resources from the National Guard, State Guard, Florida Highway Patrol and Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, among other agencies. "We're actively still responding to the previous flooding event on November 2, and now we're actively dealing with a current, another historic rain event that's brought record amount of flooding in many counties throughout the state," Perdue said. The overlapping disasters have added urgency to recovery efforts, particularly for residents whose homes remain exposed after being gutted. Perdue said state resources remain available for immediate needs, including food, water, shelter and emergency medical assistance. We're fully mobilized," he said. We're going to be with you till the very end, and we're going to make sure we help everybody get back on their feet." Despite those assurances, several critical questions remain unresolved. FEMA has not announced a decision on Florida's expedited disaster declaration request. The state has not identified a specific alternative rebuilding assistance program for homeowners who do not qualify for existing aid, nor has it committed to covering Martin County's public infrastructure losses if federal funding is denied. For residents like Weisbecker, the uncertainty is more than a question of government funding. It's a question of whether they can afford to return to the homes they've spent years building their lives in. "This is very urgent for people to get back into their daily lives," Weisbecker said. "This is total devastation.

entry.article_text: Indian River and Palm Beach counties saw the highest totals The highest report among the five counties came from The Acreage in Palm Beach County, where 12.92 inches were reported since Tuesday morning. Other notable Palm Beach County reports included 7.91 inches in Royal Palm Beach, 7.30 inches in Haverhill and 7.20 inches in Sandalfoot Cove. Indian River County also saw several high totals. Sebastian Inlet reported 10.29 inches, while Vero Lake Estates had reports of 8.49 and 7.51 inches. Other reports included 7.23 inches in Fellsmere and 6.90 inches in Roseland. Totals varied across the Treasure Coast In St. Lucie County, the highest report was 6.24 inches at the county fairgrounds. Indrio reported 4.92 inches, while Tradition and Paradise Park received 4.70 and 4.68 inches, respectively. Martin County’s highest report was 5.11 inches at Philo Farms. Other reports included 3.79 inches in Indiantown, 3.72 inches in Caloosa and 3.28 inches in Palm City. Okeechobee County had lower totals Rainfall reports in Okeechobee County were lower overall. The highest listed total was 2.81 inches in Kissimmee Prairie, followed by 2.32 inches in Country Hills. Okeechobee reported 1.58 inches. Heavy rain was concentrated in pockets These reports show how unevenly the rain fell. Most locations across the five counties saw totals of only a few inches, while certain communities caught repeated or heavier downpours that pushed their totals much higher. The highest localized amounts were concentrated in Indian River and Palm Beach counties.

entry.title: Flooding leads to partial road collapse in Port St. Lucie - WPBF
entry.summary: Flooding leads to partial road collapse in Port St. Lucie    WPBF
entry.article_text: A road and nearby property in Port St. Lucie have partially collapsed following historic flooding, leaving residents concerned about the growing damage and the safety of surrounding homes. “All this was flooded,” said Yoshi Duran, a neighbor who showed the damaged area near her home. From aerial views, the extent of the collapse is clear, with sections of the road and property having fallen into the hole. “It’s not anything to laugh about. It is a dangerous situation because they’re not knowing when it can cave in,” Duran said. The collapse occurred during the flooding, as water poured in and the land buckled until it finally gave way. Duran said the hole has been expanding daily since then. Because what’s going to happen, you know? What’s going to happen to the houses that are around this area?” Duran said. City officials are aware of the issue and are working to address it. “We want to repair these as quickly as we possibly can. Unfortunately, it takes some time,” said Scott Samples, public information officer for Port St. Samples explained the damage was caused by excess water both on the road and in a culvert below it. He said the city is currently determining the best way to fix the problem. “You want to make sure you’re doing it as well and as correctly as you possibly can. So that may require some studies to take place before you actually start the work,” Samples said. For Duran, that work can’t come soon enough. We understand everybody is short-staffed. But we need answers,” Duran said. City officials said there is no timeline for the repairs since they're still trying to figure out the best way to fix the problem. entry.title: West Palm Beach and Vero Beach set new rainfall records after heavy South Florida rain - WPBF
entry.summary: West Palm Beach and Vero Beach set new rainfall records after heavy South Florida rain    WPBF
entry.article_text: Heavy rain that moved across South Florida on Thursday helped break daily rainfall records in both West Palm Beach and Vero Beach. Both cities recorded more rain on Nov. Stay up to date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 West Palm Beach received 3.08 inches of rain, breaking the previous record of 2.99 inches set in 2021. Vero Beach recorded 2.25 inches of rainfall, topping the previous record of 1.73 inches set in 1987. The record-setting totals came after rounds of rain moved through parts of South Florida and the Treasure Coast. While the wet weather has eased, residents could still see a few lingering showers heading into the weekend. For Friday, temperatures are expected to remain near normal for this time of year, with highs in the upper 70s and low 80s. Conditions will be cloudy, and some areas could wake up to fog during the morning hours. A stray shower cannot be ruled out, although rain chances remain low. On Saturday, a mix of sun and clouds is expected with highs in the low 80s. Isolated afternoon showers will be possible, with rain chances around 30%. Looking ahead, drier weather is forecast beginning Sunday. Most of next week is expected to stay dry, though a cold front approaching Wednesday could bring a few showers. The front is also expected to cool temperatures into the mid-70s by Thanksgiving. Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app.

entry.summary: CBS12 News Athlete of the Week: Vero Beach's Latravious Woods Chases State Championship    WPEC
entry.article_text: From cheering in the stands to making big plays under the Friday night lights, Latravious Woods is living out his childhood dream. The Vero Beach High School wide receiver now plays for the same Fighting Indians team he grew up watching. But the junior has an even bigger goal: bringing a state championship home. See Also: Tennis Star Coco Gauff Returns Home for Billie Jean King Cup Since joining the team as a freshman, Woods has grown into a key playmaker and leader his coaches and teammates can count on, both on and off the field. "He's a guy that you hope to get the ball in his hands, however it needs to happen," Fighting Indians Head Coach Lenny Jankowski said. "And he's got some position versatility." Woods has also embraced his leadership role. "I know a lot about the program and how things and how coaches want things done," Woods said. "I just make sure everybody's just up-notch and like we all on the same level. Nobody heads down." Last week, Woods delivered another big performance, racking up more than 100 total yards and two touchdowns in Vero Beach's playoff win over Fort Pierce Central. But his impact goes beyond the stat sheet. Even when the ball isn't coming his way, Woods makes sure he's giving everything he has. "Even though I don't have the ball in my hands, I just got to go 100% every play because, you know, if I was to have the ball in my hand, I would want somebody to go 100% for me," Woods said. "So I'm going to give 100% for my teammates and my coaches because I want the same when I have the ball." After making the playoffs in all three of his high school seasons and reaching the state championship in 2025, Woods has unfinished business. He's determined to help Vero Beach take that final step, but he's keeping his focus on one game at a time. "Being back there this year and just finishing it all the way this time, it would feel so great," Woods said. "And I know the whole Vero community would love it." entry.title: Flooding leads to partial road collapse in Port St. Lucie - WPBF
entry.summary: Flooding leads to partial road collapse in Port St. Lucie    WPBF
entry.article_text: A road and nearby property in Port St. Lucie have partially collapsed following historic flooding, leaving residents concerned about the growing damage and the safety of surrounding homes. “All this was flooded,” said Yoshi Duran, a neighbor who showed the damaged area near her home. From aerial views, the extent of the collapse is clear, with sections of the road and property having fallen into the hole. “It’s not anything to laugh about. It is a dangerous situation because they’re not knowing when it can cave in,” Duran said. The collapse occurred during the flooding, as water poured in and the land buckled until it finally gave way. Duran said the hole has been expanding daily since then. Because what’s going to happen, you know? What’s going to happen to the houses that are around this area?” Duran said. City officials are aware of the issue and are working to address it. “We want to repair these as quickly as we possibly can. Unfortunately, it takes some time,” said Scott Samples, public information officer for Port St. Samples explained the damage was caused by excess water both on the road and in a culvert below it. He said the city is currently determining the best way to fix the problem. “You want to make sure you’re doing it as well and as correctly as you possibly can. So that may require some studies to take place before you actually start the work,” Samples said. For Duran, that work can’t come soon enough. We understand everybody is short-staffed. But we need answers,” Duran said. City officials said there is no timeline for the repairs since they're still trying to figure out the best way to fix the problem. entry.title: More than 1,000 runners lace up for the Florida Panthers Stash Dash 5K to fight men's cancer
entry.summary: More than 1,000 people laced up for the Florida Panthers Stash Dash 5K on Saturday. Organizers said this was the largest race in the event's seven-year history. WATCH: Over 1,000 run in Florida Panthers Stash Dash 5K to fight cancer Over 1,000 run in Florida Panthers Stash Dash 5K to fight cancer Runners, joggers and fast walkers grabbed their sneakers and met up outside Amerant Bank Arena. Each runner brought their own personal story of how cancer has changed their lives or the lives of their loved ones. But now they run as one to stick it to cancer. The 5K raises awareness for men's cancer research and prevention, which gives the race its unique name the Stash Dash. As athletes took to the course, others came to a chalkboard to share who they fight for, including Ruth Anngauvreau. 'I'm a cancer survivor. I've had breast cancer 10 years ago,' Anngauvreau said. Anngauvreau says during her treatment, her husband was her rock, and now she will run beside him in the race. 'It's cool to see that there are so many people that are out here fighting for somebody,' Anngauvreau said. She says she came to honor her brother-in-law, who passed away from lymphoma. 'Here for him too,' Anngauvreau said. 'I hate cancer. dealt with it. My dad passed away from cancer. My brother-in-law. It's affected so many people I know,' Anngauvreau said. She wants to remind others it's important to stick together. 'Whatever your belief system is, to just stay strong through it and know that you're not alone,' Anngauvreau said. As runners took the last difficult steps of the race, family and friends were there to cheer them on across the finish line, conquering the 5K and sticking it to cancer. Participants went home with a shiny medal.

entry.title: More than 140 fall ill aboard cruise ship that departed Fort Lauderdale
entry.summary: More than 140 passengers and crew on board a cruise ship that departed from South Florida last week have reported becoming sick with a mystery gastrointestinal illness, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says. According to information provided by the CDC, the Princess Cruises ship Caribbean Princess departed Port Everglades in Fort Lauderdale on Nov. 11 on a 12-night journey. The outbreak was then reported days later on Nov. 15. RELATED STORY | Nearly 200 passengers rescued after tanker hits river boat in New Orleans: 'Miracle on the Mississippi' At least 134 of 2,936 passengers and 14 of the 1,132 crew members have reported symptoms such as vomiting and diarrhea, according to the CDC. In response to the outbreak, Princess Cruises and the crew on board the ship said there have been increased cleaning and disinfection efforts according to their outbreak and response plan. In addition, passengers and crew who are sick have been isolated. 'Norovirus is often the cause of gastrointestinal illness outbreaks on cruise ships, but we don't always know the cause of the outbreak when we begin an investigation,' the CDC said on its website. 'Finding the agent that caused an outbreak (causative agent) can take time.' So far, the cause of the illness is unknown. 'Princess Cruises can confirm that a limited number of guests aboard Caribbean Princess have reported mild gastrointestinal illness,' the cruise line said in a statement to CBS News Miami. 'Our crew responded promptly by implementing enhanced sanitation protocols across the ship, including comprehensive cleaning and disinfection measures.' RELATED STORY | CDC sidelines itself as hantavirus cruise ship outbreak grabs global attention The statement says that while most guests remain unaffected by the illness, it is continuing to monitor the situation. According to the CDC, cases of illnesses that have been reported are totals for the entire voyage. 'It does not mean all people are sick at the same time, such as when they arrive or leave a port or ship,' the CDC continued. The Caribbean Princess departed Fort Lauderdale on a round-trip, 12-day Panama Canal trip that is expected to return on Nov. 23.

entry.title: One year after sergeant's killing, Indian River County unveils tribute to fallen deputies - WPEC
entry.summary: One year after sergeant's killing, Indian River County unveils tribute to fallen deputies    WPEC
entry.article_text: Separated by nearly 40 years in death, two fallen Indian River County deputies are now united in remembrance. Family, friends, colleagues and community leaders gathered Saturday at the Indian River County Sheriff's Office to unveil a monument honoring Sgt. Terri Sweeting-Mashkow and Deputy Sheriff Richard Raczkoski. The unveiling marked exactly one year since Sweeting-Mashkow, a 25-year veteran, was shot and killed while responding to an eviction call near Vero Beach on November 21, 2025. Deputies were serving an eviction notice at a home in the gated Bermuda Club community when investigators say Michael Halberstam opened fire . Sweeting-Mashkow was killed, Deputy Tino Arizpe was wounded, and locksmith David Long was shot and later died at the hospital. Deputies returned fire, killing Halberstam, who died the following day. "Terri was an amazing deputy. She had a beautiful heart, and she will be missed," Sheriff Eric Flowers said following her death. See also: Florida revokes licenses for 'illegal aliens' tied to alleged Broward DMV scheme, CFO says The monument also honors Deputy Richard Raczkoski, who was fatally shot on September 23, 1986, while responding to a call at a Vero Beach convenience store. His killer, William Reaves, 77, was executed one month before Saturday's unveiling, on October 20, 2026, nearly 40 years after the murder, according to previous reports . Investigators said Reaves shot Raczkoski four times as the deputy tried to flee following a struggle over a gun. Now, nearly four decades after the first tragedy, both deputies' names stand together in a permanent tribute. The sheriff's office said the monument represents the strength of its law enforcement family and serves as a reminder that those who gave their lives protecting the community will never be forgotten.

entry.title: New memorial honors two Indian River County deputies killed in line of duty
entry.summary: The sound of bagpipes and taps filled the air Saturday as the Indian River County Sheriffs Office unveiled a new memorial honoring two deputies killed in the line of duty. The memorial, located outside the sheriffs offices new administration building, honors Sgt. Terri Sweeting-Mashkow and Cpl. Richard Raczkoski. Their deaths happened 40 years apart. Now, their names have a permanent place together. WATCH: New memorial honors two Indian River County deputies killed in line of duty New memorial honors fallen deputies The unveiling came exactly one year after Sweeting-Mashkow was killed while serving an eviction notice at a home in the Bermuda Club community. 47-year-old Sweeting-Mashkow was one of three deputies serving the eviction notice on Nov. 21, 2025, when authorities said 37-year-old Michael Halberstam retrieved a weapon and opened fire. Sweeting-Mashkow was killed, and Deputy Florentino Arizpe was shot in the shoulder. A locksmith who was there for the eviction, David Long, was also critically wounded and later died from his injuries. Sweeting-Mashkow had served with the Indian River County Sheriffs Office for more than 25 years. Her death marked the second line-of-duty death in the 100-year history of the Indian River County Sheriff's Office. For those who gathered Saturday, the passage of a year has not made that loss feel distant. Its an honor to be out here but also very sad, community member Joanne Knott said. To think that it happened a year ago is strange because it feels like it was yesterday. The memorial also reaches back four decades, honoring Cpl. Richard Raczkoski, who was killed in the line of duty 40 years ago. The two heroes that are on this memorial are two people that our community will remember forever, Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers said. Hundreds of family members, friends, law enforcement officers and community members gathered for Saturdays unveiling, paying their respects. I am so glad that they did this for Terri and Raczkoski, one community member said. For those at the ceremony, the memorial is also a reminder of the risks law enforcement officers face each time they go to work. All of these officers that step out into the community, they never know what their day is going to bring, says Knott. Flowers hopes the two names on the memorial will be the only ones it ever bears: I hope we never have to add names to this memorial again.'

entry.article_text: Indian River and Palm Beach counties saw the highest totals The highest report among the five counties came from The Acreage in Palm Beach County, where 12.92 inches were reported since Tuesday morning. Other notable Palm Beach County reports included 7.91 inches in Royal Palm Beach, 7.30 inches in Haverhill and 7.20 inches in Sandalfoot Cove. Indian River County also saw several high totals. Sebastian Inlet reported 10.29 inches, while Vero Lake Estates had reports of 8.49 and 7.51 inches. Other reports included 7.23 inches in Fellsmere and 6.90 inches in Roseland. Totals varied across the Treasure Coast In St. Lucie County, the highest report was 6.24 inches at the county fairgrounds. Indrio reported 4.92 inches, while Tradition and Paradise Park received 4.70 and 4.68 inches, respectively. Martin County’s highest report was 5.11 inches at Philo Farms. Other reports included 3.79 inches in Indiantown, 3.72 inches in Caloosa and 3.28 inches in Palm City. Okeechobee County had lower totals Rainfall reports in Okeechobee County were lower overall. The highest listed total was 2.81 inches in Kissimmee Prairie, followed by 2.32 inches in Country Hills. Okeechobee reported 1.58 inches. Heavy rain was concentrated in pockets These reports show how unevenly the rain fell. Most locations across the five counties saw totals of only a few inches, while certain communities caught repeated or heavier downpours that pushed their totals much higher. entry.article_text: Families across the Treasure Coast are watching the forecast closely after historic flooding overwhelmed parts of Port St. Just as many neighborhoods are drying out, forecasters are warning another 4 to 6 inches of rain could fall over the next few days, raising concerns about renewed flooding in areas still recovering from the record rainfall. The flooding two weeks ago left cars stranded, some families trapped in their homes and others wading through deep water. "It was horrible," said Port St. Lucie resident Crisostomo Santiago Perez. "Water was on top of the cars almost, covering hoods." Among those caught off guard was freshman Noah Julian. 2, Noah stepped off his school bus to find his neighborhood along Coleman Avenue flooded. A video recorded by neighbor Martina Elieson quickly spread on social media, showing the teenager swimming through floodwaters just to reach his driveway. "When I see the video, I'm like, what?" said Noah's father, Romeo Julian. We got alligators here, snakes, sharp objects could have cut him up. A thousand things could've happened to him." With another round of heavy rain in the forecast, residents say they aren't taking any chances." "Today I'm going to get stuff before flood comes," Perez said. See also: From banks to flights, outages leave south Floridians frustrated St. Lucie Public Schools is also preparing ahead of the storm. The district announced a two-hour early release Tuesday in an effort to avoid a repeat of the flooding issues that affected students taking the bus home earlier this month. "But why it always takes one thing to make them wake up." Meanwhile, county crews have been inspecting and clearing canals and drainage systems ahead of the expected rainfall. Officials warn that because the ground is still saturated from recent storms, it will take far less rain than usual to cause flooding in neighborhoods, streets and other low-lying areas. Residents are encouraged to monitor local forecasts and be prepared for changing conditions as the rain moves into the area.

entry.title: Florida emergency management director responds to FEMA delays as Jensen Beach flood victims wait for help - WFLX
entry.summary: Florida emergency management director responds to FEMA delays as Jensen Beach flood victims wait for help    WFLX
entry.article_text: Nearly three weeks after historic flooding forced families from their homes and caused millions of dollars in damage across Martin County, residents are still waiting for a federal disaster declaration that could unlock critical financial assistance. Now, after a WPTV report on the delays and growing frustration among flood victims, Florida's top emergency management official is responding to questions about the state's recovery efforts—and what help families can expect if FEMA funding never arrives. Watch more from Kate Hussey: In an exclusive interview with WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey, Jared Perdue, director of the Florida Division of Emergency Management, confirmed the state submitted an expedited federal disaster declaration request Nov. 9, one week after the initial flooding. But nearly two weeks after that request, a decision remains pending. "We've been very engaged with FEMA, and we did actually submit an expedited disaster declaration request to FEMA on November the ninth," Perdue said. "FEMA has been very closely coordinating with us in reviewing that, and I'm sure they're going to make quick work of it." The uncertainty comes as Martin County estimates approximately $18 million in residential and public infrastructure damage, with families still struggling to afford repairs and another round of historic rainfall complicating recovery efforts. Along Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach, the devastation is still visible. Dumpsters line driveways, waterlogged belongings have been discarded and homes have been stripped down to their frames. For Linda Weisbecker, whose home was among those severely damaged, the destruction has been overwhelming. "It's like an apocalypse here," Weisbecker told WPTV in an earlier interview. For nine days, Weisbecker and her neighbors navigated waist-deep floodwaters before they could begin salvaging what remained of their homes. "Once we got through that and the water came out, we just all started pitching in, going in to see what we can salvage from each home," she said. But much of what Weisbecker lost cannot be replaced. Our house is empty," she said. "We lost everything, from pictures of our children and their lives, our friends, our grandkids, now we have great-grandkids. Everything [my husband] had since he was 13 on is gone." Weisbecker has been approved for a $25,000 grant through Florida's State Housing Initiatives Partnership, or SHIP, program. But for families facing tens of thousands of dollars in repairs, that assistance may cover only a fraction of the cost. And not everyone will qualify. "You do think about that process and you sit there and you say to yourself, how am I gonna do this?" Weisbecker said. That question is at the center of WPTV's ongoing investigation. Martin County estimates the flooding caused: A federal major disaster declaration could make certain public infrastructure repairs eligible for FEMA reimbursement and potentially open the door to individual assistance for qualifying residents. But approval is not guaranteed. When WPTV initially contacted FEMA, the agency confirmed it had received the disaster declaration request and that it remained under review. FEMA referred additional questions about the response and recovery timeline to the Florida Division of Emergency Management. Hussey subsequently pressed Perdue on what would happen if the federal government denied the request. "If FEMA ultimately denies federal assistance, does Florida have a Plan B, or are these families simply on their own?" Hussey asked. Perdue did not identify a specific alternative state funding program, instead emphasizing Florida's experience responding to natural disasters and its ongoing coordination with federal and local officials. "This is something that we're very used to doing. I mean, in Florida, we deal with natural disasters all the time," Perdue said. "We have a great relationship with FEMA, and usually those things go very well." He added that the state remains focused on immediate response efforts, including search and rescue operations and meeting residents' emergency needs. In the meantime, Martin County is working to distribute approximately $1 million in available SHIP funding to qualifying residents. Eligible homeowners may receive grants of up to $25,000, with additional assistance potentially available through loans of up to $75,000. However, those loans come with repayment requirements and liens. Income eligibility restrictions could also leave some families without assistance, even if they cannot afford to rebuild on their own. "There's going to be a lot of heart-wrenching cases where somebody barely missed the limit," Commissioner Blake Capps said during a recent Martin County Commission meeting. Capps proposed establishing a separate county-funded emergency assistance program for residents who fall through the cracks. But when WPTV asked where that money would come from, Capps acknowledged a funding source had not yet been identified. we'd have to talk to staff," he said. County Human Services Director Michelle Miller previously told commissioners the state had promised additional disaster relief funding, although neither the amount nor the timeline had been confirmed. "They haven't confirmed the amount yet but has assured us we will be getting some disaster relief funds," Miller told Hussey. Hussey raised those concerns directly with Perdue, asking whether the state had other programs available for families who earn too much to qualify for existing assistance but not enough to pay for repairs. Perdue pointed to the state's partnerships with nonprofit organizations and its deployment of emergency personnel to assist with cleanup. "We've actually activated the National Guard, and are also partnering with nonprofits to do what they call the muck and gut of homes that have been flooded," Perdue said. That work includes removing damaged drywall and other waterlogged materials to help prevent mold growth. "We're providing the assistance that we can and partnering with those nonprofit organizations as well," he said. However, Perdue did not identify a specific funding program to cover rebuilding costs for homeowners who do not qualify for existing assistance. The financial uncertainty extends beyond individual homeowners. Martin County faces approximately $15 million in combined beach and road damage, with additional emergency response expenses still being assessed. County spokesperson Martha Ann Kniess previously told WPTV that without federal reimbursement, Martin County could be left responsible for covering those costs, potentially forcing officials to redirect money from elsewhere in the budget or identify other funding sources. Hussey asked Perdue whether the state would help cover those expenses if FEMA denied federal assistance — or whether the financial burden could ultimately fall on local taxpayers. Perdue did not commit to providing state funding for those repairs. "We are and have been doing damage assessments ever since we submitted the first disaster declaration request," he said. "As those damage assessments come in, we'll continue to coordinate with FEMA and make sure all that information is submitted." The state's response follows an emotional Martin County Commission meeting Tuesday, where residents pleaded with elected officials to do more to secure recovery funding. Fight for us!" one resident urged commissioners. Others questioned why families were being asked to wait even longer for answers. "And the answer from this dais is wait 13 more days?!?" another resident asked. Commissioner Eileen Vargas said she had reached out to FEMA through personal contacts in an effort to expedite the process. "I did, through contacts, reach out to FEMA to try and get this going," Vargas said. Vargas also told residents she expected a new FEMA director to take office Nov. 30 and hoped that development could help move the disaster declaration forward. But even if a declaration is approved, not all losses or recovery expenses would necessarily qualify for federal assistance. As Martin County continues to recover from the Nov. 2 flooding, Perdue said the state is also responding to another significant rainfall event affecting communities across Florida. Ron DeSantis expanded the state's emergency executive order to include 21 counties. The state has mobilized resources from the National Guard, State Guard, Florida Highway Patrol and Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, among other agencies. "We're actively still responding to the previous flooding event on November 2, and now we're actively dealing with a current, another historic rain event that's brought record amount of flooding in many counties throughout the state," Perdue said. The overlapping disasters have added urgency to recovery efforts, particularly for residents whose homes remain exposed after being gutted. Perdue said state resources remain available for immediate needs, including food, water, shelter and emergency medical assistance. We're fully mobilized," he said. We're going to be with you till the very end, and we're going to make sure we help everybody get back on their feet." Despite those assurances, several critical questions remain unresolved. FEMA has not announced a decision on Florida's expedited disaster declaration request. The state has not identified a specific alternative rebuilding assistance program for homeowners who do not qualify for existing aid, nor has it committed to covering Martin County's public infrastructure losses if federal funding is denied. For residents like Weisbecker, the uncertainty is more than a question of government funding. It's a question of whether they can afford to return to the homes they've spent years building their lives in. "This is very urgent for people to get back into their daily lives," Weisbecker said. "This is total devastation.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie family waits years for swale liner as standing water brings mosquitoes - WFLX
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie family waits years for swale liner as standing water brings mosquitoes    WFLX
entry.article_text: Lucie family says it has spent nearly four years trying to get a swale liner installed to keep stagnant water from lingering in its yard, a problem the family says leaves water sitting for days and turns the property into what they jokingly call a "mosquito hotel." Oprah Fasulo and her mother, Divika Todd, brought the problem to WPTV's Michael Hoffman after meeting him at WPTV's Let's Hear It community meetup in Jensen Beach. Their frustration centers on a yearslong wait and changing rules over who is responsible for installing the swale liner. Now, the city says the family is not alone and that it recently received approval to add a contractor to help speed up installations. Fasulo and Todd told Hoffman their problem dates back to when their Port St. At the time, the city was changing its rules surrounding responsibility for installing swale liners, which are designed to help keep water moving rather than allowing it to remain on properties. According to the family, installation had been the city's responsibility before shifting to builders. It has since shifted back to the city. Their house, they said, was built between those changes and never received one. The family eventually contacted Port St. "They said that they have to install it. The homeowners are not allowed to install it," Fasulo said. Fasulo said she understood that requirement. What frustrated her was how long her family was told it would take. "I understand that totally, but they told us that it was three years; it would be done," she said. Now, Fasulo said the family has been told it could take another two years. That's when they turned to WPTV. "We've seen you guys get results," Fasulo told Hoffman. The family provided WPTV with pictures showing water collecting around the property even after lighter rainfall. They also walked Hoffman around their property to show him the problem firsthand. The standing water wasn't the only issue they encountered. Mosquitoes quickly made their presence known. "Mosquito hotel," she said. For the family, however, the nickname highlights a problem they've been trying to resolve for years: Water takes days to clear from their property, and they say they cannot install the needed liner themselves. Hoffman brought the family's concerns to the city and sat down with Scott Samples to ask why the process has taken so long and what is being done about it. Samples said the family is not the only one waiting. "We were recently approved to add a contractor to help us to expedite getting some of these put in," Samples said. The city is also evaluating how to use its available resources to address the outstanding installations more quickly, Samples told WPTV. "We're looking at, again, how can we maximize the resources that we have available to help the residents as quickly as we can, knowing that we're limited," Samples said. "You know, so we try to put this, there's plans, and then you have to adjust those plans as you go as well. So we're sort of in that process right now." For Fasulo and Todd, that still does not provide a date for when their swale liner will finally be installed. But after nearly four years of waiting, they now have WPTV asking those questions alongside them. "You guys have helped in the past with this issue," Fasulo said. "So we decided to ask you guys to help us and whoever else is in need and not getting answers from the city." WPTV will continue following the family's case and pressing Port St. Lucie for updates on when the work will be completed. entry.title: 'We need answers': Martin County officials address outrage over proposed data center - WFLX
entry.summary: 'We need answers': Martin County officials address outrage over proposed data center    WFLX
entry.article_text: A controversial proposal to build a more than 1.6 million-square-foot data center just half a mile from an elementary school is drawing growing opposition in Martin County, where residents are raising concerns about everything from environmental impacts to whether they'll have a say in the project's approval. WATCH: 'We need answers': Martin Co. officials address outrage over proposed data center On Friday morning, a small but vocal group of residents gathered outside the Martin County Administrative Center, demanding answers about the massive development proposed for a parcel of land off Kanner Highway, west of Interstate 95. They had planned to attend a meeting with the county's Growth Management Department. But less than 17 hours before it was scheduled to begin, the county canceled it, citing overwhelming public interest. Residents showed up anyway. "We need answers, and we need them quick," said Chris McIntyre, whose son graduated from nearby Crystal Lake Elementary School. "This story cannot die, or else this is the death of Crystal Lake School." McIntyre, who goes by Coach Mack, became emotional discussing what the proposed development could mean for the school and surrounding neighborhoods. "Now that's the death of an A-rated elementary school that I love," he said, his voice breaking. Residents have raised concerns about potential noise pollution, water consumption, increased electricity demand, higher utility bills, wildlife displacement, declining property values and possible health impacts on children attending Crystal Lake Elementary. Michael Panella, another resident opposing the project, became emotional while explaining why the fight is so personal. These little ones are innocent," Panella said, referring also to students of Crystal Lake. Dan Wilson, president of the Locks Landing homeowners association, represents a community less than two miles from the proposed site. “They’re probably dropping now because, oh, the data center going there. We don’t want to move there,” Wilson said of property values. "We have residences right here, tons of residents. We're all going to have to deal with this." Residents acknowledge they don't yet know for sure what the long-term consequences of the project might be. They don't know whether electricity bills will increase, how much noise the facility could generate or what wildlife habitat might be lost. But they do know that once something of this magnitude is built, there's no easy way to undo it. The controversy intensified Thursday evening when Martin County announced the cancellation of an informal Growth Management meeting scheduled for 9:30 a.m. 19, the Martin County Board of County Commissioners posted the following message online: "This meeting has been canceled. Due to the level of public interest, a more formal meeting will be scheduled and publicly noticed in advance to accommodate any and all residents who wish to attend, learn more, and share their thoughts. Stay tuned to our website and social media as meeting details are finalized." For residents who had planned to attend, the cancellation only added to their frustration. "The thing that frustrates me the most about this is the fact that they were willing to do this meeting in private," said resident Alisha Gibbs. Gibbs described herself as "disgusted" and "absolutely appalled" by the situation. But Martin County Deputy Growth Management Director Pete Walden told WPTV Investigative Reporter Kate Hussey that the meeting was never intended to be a formal public hearing or a decision-making session. Instead, Walden said, it was an informal meeting requested by members of the public who wanted to ask county staff questions about the development — something his department routinely accommodates for other projects. He said information about the meeting circulated online, creating the impression that county officials were privately considering a decision on the data center. When interest grew beyond what the county could accommodate, officials decided to cancel. "We could not accommodate that. We didn't have any rooms or anything available for that size," Walden explained. "So we had to cancel, and we'll do some workshops in the future. I believe the applicant is also going to reach out for some public presentations on the subject." When asked why residents weren't being given more opportunities to weigh in, Walden maintained the county has been transparent. "We are transparent through the process, and everything can be made available to anyone that is interested," he said. Walden said additional public meetings and workshops will be scheduled to allow residents to ask questions and learn more about the project. But the canceled meeting is only one of several controversies surrounding the development. Another major point of contention is the timing of the developer's application. 27, Martin County commissioners approved a one-year moratorium on data centers, temporarily restricting new applications while the county reviews its development regulations. But records show the application for this project was submitted the day before the moratorium was proposed on October 13. That timing means the project is not subject to the temporary restriction, according to county officials. Walden acknowledged the timing but said the county cannot control when developers submit applications. "They obviously saw like everybody else that a moratorium was coming, and they got their application in ahead of time," Walden said. "We don't direct applicants ... and we certainly can't pick and choose when these things happen." WPTV reached out to the project applicant and the law firm representing it, requesting comment on the timing of the application and residents' environmental, energy and health concerns. Neither responded by publication time. Perhaps the most significant concern for opponents is whether residents will have any formal say in the project's approval. Under a county ordinance adopted in 2010, during the Great Recession, Martin County established an administrative approval process for certain targeted industries to encourage economic development. Data centers fall within the county's targeted industry classifications. According to Walden, the proposed development is also covered by an existing planned unit development, or PUD, agreement that allows qualifying targeted industries on platted industrial lots to receive administrative approval. That means the project could potentially move forward without a public hearing or recorded vote by county commissioners. For residents demanding a voice in the decision, that distinction is critical. Hussey asked Walden whether there was anything the county could do to give residents more of a say in whether the development is approved. "With the moratorium, we'll be looking at our code to make revisions so everything is appropriately reviewed as it comes in," Walden said. "To give the public more of a say in future projects?" Hussey asked. "Correct," Walden responded. Residents are also demanding answers about how a development of this size could affect surrounding neighborhoods, wildlife and students at Crystal Lake Elementary School. The proposal initially called for just under 1 million square feet of development. An updated application brings the total to approximately 1.6 million square feet, including an existing warehouse. Among the concerns raised by residents are the potential effects of noise from cooling equipment, increased water and electricity consumption, wildlife habitat loss and possible impacts on nearby property values. Those concerns remain questions, not established consequences of the proposed development. Walden said the county will review the project's potential impacts before making any approval decision. He also emphasized that despite speculation circulating in the community, the data center has not been approved. "There is a misconception that this project was already approved — that's very far from the truth," Walden said. "This is our first data center to be reviewed. We're going to take our time ... and make sure everything is properly vetted." The county says a staff report examining the project is expected to be released in December. Following that report, officials plan to schedule a public forum, likely including a presentation from the applicant, where residents can ask questions and learn more about the development. No date for that meeting has been announced. For opponents, the controversy goes beyond whether a data center belongs on acres of industrial land. It's about who gets to decide what their community becomes — and whether the people who will live with the consequences have a meaningful opportunity to influence that decision. The residents who gathered outside the county building Friday made clear that canceling a meeting would not end their opposition. "If they want to actually please the public, they would deny this proposal," Gibbs said.

entry.summary: CBS12 News Athlete of the Week: Vero Beach's Latravious Woods Chases State Championship    WPEC
entry.article_text: From cheering in the stands to making big plays under the Friday night lights, Latravious Woods is living out his childhood dream. The Vero Beach High School wide receiver now plays for the same Fighting Indians team he grew up watching. But the junior has an even bigger goal: bringing a state championship home. See Also: Tennis Star Coco Gauff Returns Home for Billie Jean King Cup Since joining the team as a freshman, Woods has grown into a key playmaker and leader his coaches and teammates can count on, both on and off the field. "He's a guy that you hope to get the ball in his hands, however it needs to happen," Fighting Indians Head Coach Lenny Jankowski said. "And he's got some position versatility." Woods has also embraced his leadership role. "I know a lot about the program and how things and how coaches want things done," Woods said. "I just make sure everybody's just up-notch and like we all on the same level. Nobody heads down." Last week, Woods delivered another big performance, racking up more than 100 total yards and two touchdowns in Vero Beach's playoff win over Fort Pierce Central. But his impact goes beyond the stat sheet. Even when the ball isn't coming his way, Woods makes sure he's giving everything he has. "Even though I don't have the ball in my hands, I just got to go 100% every play because, you know, if I was to have the ball in my hand, I would want somebody to go 100% for me," Woods said. "So I'm going to give 100% for my teammates and my coaches because I want the same when I have the ball." After making the playoffs in all three of his high school seasons and reaching the state championship in 2025, Woods has unfinished business. He's determined to help Vero Beach take that final step, but he's keeping his focus on one game at a time. "Being back there this year and just finishing it all the way this time, it would feel so great," Woods said. "And I know the whole Vero community would love it." entry.title: One year after sergeant's killing, Indian River County unveils tribute to fallen deputies - WPEC
entry.summary: One year after sergeant's killing, Indian River County unveils tribute to fallen deputies    WPEC
entry.article_text: Separated by nearly 40 years in death, two fallen Indian River County deputies are now united in remembrance. Family, friends, colleagues and community leaders gathered Saturday at the Indian River County Sheriff's Office to unveil a monument honoring Sgt. Terri Sweeting-Mashkow and Deputy Sheriff Richard Raczkoski. The unveiling marked exactly one year since Sweeting-Mashkow, a 25-year veteran, was shot and killed while responding to an eviction call near Vero Beach on November 21, 2025. Deputies were serving an eviction notice at a home in the gated Bermuda Club community when investigators say Michael Halberstam opened fire . Sweeting-Mashkow was killed, Deputy Tino Arizpe was wounded, and locksmith David Long was shot and later died at the hospital. Deputies returned fire, killing Halberstam, who died the following day. "Terri was an amazing deputy. She had a beautiful heart, and she will be missed," Sheriff Eric Flowers said following her death. See also: Florida revokes licenses for 'illegal aliens' tied to alleged Broward DMV scheme, CFO says The monument also honors Deputy Richard Raczkoski, who was fatally shot on September 23, 1986, while responding to a call at a Vero Beach convenience store. His killer, William Reaves, 77, was executed one month before Saturday's unveiling, on October 20, 2026, nearly 40 years after the murder, according to previous reports . Investigators said Reaves shot Raczkoski four times as the deputy tried to flee following a struggle over a gun. Now, nearly four decades after the first tragedy, both deputies' names stand together in a permanent tribute. The sheriff's office said the monument represents the strength of its law enforcement family and serves as a reminder that those who gave their lives protecting the community will never be forgotten.

entry.title: Martin County flood victims fear more devastation as county braces for another foot of rain - WPTV
entry.summary: Martin County flood victims fear more devastation as county braces for another foot of rain    WPTV
entry.article_text: Just weeks after historic flooding destroyed homes and displaced families in Jensen Beach, Martin County residents are bracing for another round of heavy rain — with up to 12 inches forecast over the next three days.For families still struggling to recover, the threat of more flooding comes as county commissioners work to determine what caused the initial disaster and how to help those who lost nearly everything.On Tuesday, flood victims packed a Martin County Commission meeting, pleading for financial assistance and answers.WATCH REPORT BELOW: Along Cheri Drive in Jensen Beach, the signs of destruction remain. Dumpsters line driveways, damaged belongings sit outside and families are still trying to salvage what's left of their homes.Lisa French, her husband, Jeremy, and their two young sons are among those displaced after floodwaters rose as high as 3 feet inside some homes two weeks ago."It's like we're kind of stuck," French told WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey. French said her home had about 3 to 6 inches of flooding that sat inside for more than a week, causing mold to grow 3 to 4 feet up the walls. "So they, yeah, they tore the walls down in the house," said French. "They just chipped up the last bit of the tile, and it's empty." Now, with more rain approaching, French fears her family could face another disaster before recovering from the first."Of course, we're afraid because we all flooded in our houses," she said.New figures released by Martin County show at least 36 homes sustained damage, with an estimated $3 million in residential losses. Commissioners estimated another $14 million in damage to beaches, and at least $1 million in damage to roadways that now need repairs. For some residents, the destruction represents a lifetime of memories washed away."We've lost everything," one elderly Jensen Beach resident told commissioners. "We have 60 years of our life — kids, grandkids, everything. It's all gone."As residents demand answers about what went wrong, commissioners approved shifting $200,000 from the county's stormwater budget to investigate whether development and changes to local drainage systems contributed to the flooding.Commissioner Blake Capps called the investigation "a good starting point.""It may be that we need to augment the study beyond the $200,000 that we approve today," said Capps. Meanwhile, county crews are working around the clock to prepare for the next storm, lowering retention pond levels, deploying additional pumps and draining flooded properties."We have people 24 hours a day pumping that material down," Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton said.Commissioners also approved financial assistance for eligible flood victims through the state's State Housing Initiatives Partnership (SHIP) program.The assistance includes grants of up to $25,000 for income-eligible homeowners and loans of up to $75,000 secured by liens on their properties.But there's a catch: The grants are reimbursement-based, meaning homeowners must first pay for eligible repairs before receiving the money.For families who lost everything, that presents another obstacle."We don't have $25,000," French said. "A lot of people don't have $25,000, so it's great, and we're appreciative, but I mean, our house is empty, and $25,000 is not going to do much for us." The other problem: the county currently has just $1 million in SHIP funding available, and commissioners warned the money could run out quickly, even with additional state funding promised."They haven't given us the amount yet, but they have assured us that we will be getting some disaster relief funds," said Human Services Director Michelle Miller Strict income limits could also disqualify some flood victims who cannot afford to rebuild on their own. The income cap for a family of one is $86,040. The cap for a family of two is $98,400. For a family of four, it's $122,880. When reporter Kate Hussey asked Capps what would happen to those families, he acknowledged the county needs to explore other options."There are going to be a lot of heart-wrenching cases where someone barely missed the limit, and we're going to need to take a look at what we can do for those folks," Capps said.For residents like French, the need is immediate."We just need somebody to step up," she said. "We need funding." With another round of heavy rain approaching, Martin County is distributing sandbags at Halpatiokee Regional Park to help residents protect their properties, with a limit of 25 per person. The County's Emergency Operations Center is scheduled to be staffed beginning Tuesday at 2 p.m., and the county is coordinating with the National Weather Service and Florida Division of Emergency Management (FDEM).Fire Rescue is also standing by with multiple high-water rescue trucks.Commissioners also said a Federal Emergency Management Agency representative is expected to visit Nov. 30 to assess the damage — a potential step toward securing federal disaster assistance.But for families still displaced and facing the possibility of more flooding, the uncertainty remains.
